# Command and Conquer: Generals: Zero Hour: Reforged

EA opened the source of Generals and Zero Hour, the game that is still on sale and still runs on
Steam. This build is that source with the bugs the game shipped with fixed and everything below added.

**130 changes. ~580 engine source files ported. 14 automated test suites. Around 60 original bugs
found and fixed, EA's own, not port damage.**

---

## Art of Defense on random maps, a first playable version

Pick Art of Defense in the Random tab's list of map types, or start `-randommap <seed> [players] aod`, and you get a new tower defence map every seed, built for the people in the room: it is a humans-only mode, and a computer seat in the room opens again. Every player gets a lane of his own, and the map is a mirror, so every lane and every patch of ground beside it is the same as everyone else's. Alone, your lane runs from one edge of the map to the other. With two to six players the map is a round plateau ringed by mountains, and each lane comes in from the mountains and winds through its own slice of the plateau to a pit in the middle, where every lane ends. A lane is a trench with cliff walls: the waves cannot climb out of it and you cannot drive down into it, so you build on the high ground beside it and shoot down into the lane, and every narrow turn is a place to hold.

No two seeds play the same lane. The seed picks one of ten shapes: square switchbacks, a zigzag, a wide S, a tight wiggle, long hairpins, terraces that climb and fall in steps, a comb with dead-end bays to build over, a fork round an island where the waves take one branch, a sawtooth or a run of loops. Every shape fits every room from one to six players, bar the fork, which needs more ground than a six-way slice has and hands over to the next shape. The seed also picks the ground, temperate, desert, winter or steppe, and the hour from morning to night.

Twenty waves, each one the same for every lane: Technicals first, which reach the end in about seventy seconds, then Rebels, Red Guards and Rangers, Humvees, rocket soldiers and tanks, Comanches from wave 12 so a wall of anti-tank guns is not enough, and ranks from wave 8 on. Every fifth wave an Overlord with three times its health leads the column. The waves shoot back at whatever shoots them from the rim and then walk on; they never turn off the lane for your base. A unit that reaches the end goes in a flare and takes a life from the lives you share, the Overlord five; lose twenty and you lose together, see off all twenty waves and you win together. Each kill pays the player whose lane it died in, and every wave pays everyone as it starts. No more than 80 attackers walk at once, every lane its share, so a late wave cannot pile up enough tanks to bring the game down the way the old Art of Defense maps did.

This is the prototype: no wave counter on screen yet. Saves from before this change still load; the new mode needs this build on every machine.

## Key Grid: the command bar laid out like your keyboard

Layout under Options > Interface has a fourth choice, Key Grid. The commands stand in three staggered rows of six at full size, Q W E R T Y over A S D F G H over Z X C V B N, the way your left hand lies on the keys, and with Grid Keys ticked every button wears its letter and that letter presses it. You read the key off the bar instead of learning one per unit.

A button keeps its spot from bar to bar. A Dozer, Worker or Istihkam lays its buildings out in the order they open up: power and supply on Q and W, then the factories in the order their requirements allow, defences along A, and the Z row opens with the tech building, the structure the most others list as a requirement. The Command Center takes the last free key of its row, since you rebuild it rather than open with it. The orders never move: S stop, D attack move, X guard, Z unload, B rally point, N sell, and on a unit that fights A, C and V stay free for force attack, hold position and move. Passengers fill in from N leftward. A GLA Worker's fake buildings sit on their real buildings' keys, so H never moves a building.

The minimap's box takes each map's own shape at today's size. Tournament Desert, a tall map that left half of the old 322 by 232 glass black, gets a 239 by 313 glass with nothing wasted. The money sits on a column beside the map with the power standing in it as a meter, the signal keys, Options, beacon, idle worker and chat ride on a shelf over the map, and a factory's queue climbs above the shelf. The select army and idle unit buttons and the build tabs are gone from this layout; their keys still work. Select all, matching units, the command center and the idle worker move to J, U, M and I, deploy to K, follow to L and the held key for a line of walls to O, and Key Grid keeps its keys in a file of its own, so what you set for Classic and Red Alert Style stays as it is.

Pick a squad by its number and a switch appears on the column. Press it or Ctrl+Tab and the key rows show the squad's build tray in place of the commands, each unit on a letter that builds it into the squad; leave the squad and the commands come back.

Options > Interface also has a Grid Keys box for the other layouts, after Age of Empires IV's grid hotkeys. Ticked, a command button is pressed by where it stands on the bar, Q W E R T Y U over A S D F G H J, whatever its own letter. Picking Key Grid ticks it, picking another layout clears it, and you can change it after.

## Computer players give up, fire, rebuild and drive like players

- A beaten computer kept playing on with a handful of units. Above Hard the rules for giving up stretched with the level, so an Insane seat waited nearly 20 game minutes and held on until it was worth 3% of the strongest enemy: six eight-player Insane matches on Twilight Flame at double speed saw 27 seats knocked out and 3 GGs. Every level above Hard now gives up as Hard does, and Hard gives up at 12% of the strongest enemy side held for 40 seconds (it was 8% for a minute). The same six matches: 34 seats out, 17 of them by GG. A seat that says GG leaves the match two seconds later, its units to a living ally or destroyed.
- The computer let its superweapon and its troop drops sit ready for the map scripts to fire them: a Scud Storm waited 49 seconds on average, a nuclear missile 22, an infantry drop 84. They now go off within two seconds of being ready, at the same target, and a drop still keeps off the defences the computer knows. In the six matches the Scud Storms fired 71 times by minute 29 where they fired 47.
- A computer that lost several power plants built them back one at a time, and the plant went up at the far end of an outward walk, over a thousand from its base. Now it builds as many as it is short at once, and in the dark puts them inside its base first. Time spent without power over the six matches fell from 5,635 to 3,905 seconds, the longest outage from 800 to 310.
- A computer's supply trucks drove to piles under defences they knew and were shot there: against a walled-in player on the turtle bench 158 of its trucks and workers died to his guns in four matches. A truck now leaves a pile a known defence covers for another; 4 were lost, and the computer earned 9% more.
- Siege guns moving with an attack rolled forward in jerks: the computer sent each one a new order every two seconds, and every order makes a unit stop for a new path. Units waiting at the edge of a known defence were sent to the same spot again every second. A unit already on its way now keeps its order. In the six matches the siege guns got half the orders by minute 27 (6,915 where they got 13,646), and the units at a defence's edge a sixth of the repeats.
- Two allied computers played two games side by side: the team board that tells an ally whom you attack and where you are hit was read only by the personalities, never by a computer on Normal. In eight 2v2 Hard matches not one call was answered. A Normal computer now joins its ally's attack and sends its idle units into an ally's base when it is hit, the ally a computer or a person. Computer against computer it wins no more on its own (14 of 30 2v2 games against a team without it); it is there for two players against two computers. The two also attacked one after the other, each on its own clock. Now when one sends its wave, the other sends what it has gathered along with it, once that is worth half a wave: 25 joint attacks in 32 2v2 games.
- A computer whose planned factory spot turned unsafe looked for another one only inside its base, and a crowded base often had none, so that factory never went up: an Elo 1800 China walled in beside a turtling player built no War Factory in 30 minutes. It now also looks on the ground behind its base, away from the enemy. Against a player behind 48 defences on two maps, three armies each at Elo 1800 and 2800, the computer won 10 of 12 matches where it won 5, killed 14 defences a match where it killed 10, and lost half as much to them for each one killed.
- An Overlord, a Paladin or a Tomahawk without a rank fought on until it died; only veterans were pulled out to be repaired. Now any unit that cost 1,000 or more goes back to be mended once it is down to 30% health on Hard (25% on Medium, up to 40% above Hard). Dozers and supply trucks keep their jobs.
- On some seeds the random map put both starts of a duel almost on top of each other, 3 to 19 cells apart where every other placement keeps 32, and the match was over in a few minutes. The starts now keep that distance on every seed. Those maps change, so random maps carry a new version.
- A USA computer left its Strategy Center on Hold the Line for the whole match. It now switches to Bombardment when an attack sets out against known defences and to Search and Destroy when it sets out against open ground, and back to Hold the Line when it is outmatched at home. It never switches while its base is under fire, since every change stuns the army for five seconds. This is the first of the generals' own styles; in 80 USA mirror matches at Elo 1800 the side with it won 31 to 30, so it costs the computer nothing.
- The other three American generals now play in styles of their own. The Laser General puts a laser turret beside each power plant that has none, the one nearest you first, since his lasers go dark without power, and leaves a turret behind each attack as it moves out, so a beaten-back attack falls back onto its own guns. The Superweapon General aims the Particle Cannon at your biggest army it can see, where it used to burn the dearest corner of your base, builds EMP Patriots past the usual count out of its spare money, and on most matches gathers bigger attacks and sends them less often. The Air Force General buys aircraft first, less eagerly the more anti-air it has seen, drops the Carpet Bomb on your army, sends a hurt Comanche home at half health, and on most matches sends its jets, the idle ones and those going out with an attack, at the anti-air building nearest the attack's road before the attack gets there. None of them builds anything extra in the first two and a half minutes.
- The four GLA generals now play in styles of their own. The GLA general calls his army home through the tunnels when his base is hit, keeps a fighter standing over each hole a lost building left until it is back up, and sends the Scud Launchers idling at home to shell your supply and power from beyond the guns he knows about. The Toxin General drives his Toxin Tractors into knots of infantry, drops the Anthrax Bomb on your army or on the road between your supply pile and your supply center, and sends a tractor to poison that road. The Demolitions General lays demo traps in front of his chokepoints whatever his personality, dresses a Bomb Truck as one of your own vehicles and drives it at your most valuable building, and once he has the suicide upgrade a cheap unit near death walks up to something of yours worth the trade and blows itself up beside it. The Stealth General spends his first science point on the GPS Scrambler once he has the rank for it, raises it over each attack as it sets out, sends the attack down whichever road none of your detectors he knows about watches, and raids your supply center with his invisible units down a side road none of your detectors watches. Each move is drawn by chance when the match starts, so a match does not show all of them every time.
- The four Chinese generals have styles of their own too. China asks for its Internet Center early and puts a Propaganda Tower out past the front of its base, on ground none of your guns it knows covers, where its attacks gather and its wounded come back. The Tank General sends an expensive tank or a veteran one back for repair at 45% health, holds his Tank Drop for up to two minutes until his own army stands among your buildings out of your guns' reach and drops the tanks right there, and after a heavy first attack keeps half-size ones rolling out behind it for a minute and a half instead of waiting to gather again. The Infantry General sends loaded Assault Troop Crawlers at your supply trucks and supply center in the first ten minutes and lets the men out on top of them, holds his attacks until the horde is bigger, and leaves his garrison, capture and supply raiding teams to their jobs where they used to be held back for the next attack. The Nuke General aims his missile where it takes out the most of your factories and power plants instead of the richest spot, and walks any of his units standing about in a radiation field out of it. Of 160 China mirror matches at Elo 1800, one side playing its style and one without, 121 were decided and the side with it won 60.
- The Türkiye computer now plays to its guns, which shoot far and see little. Its Spotters walk ahead and stand just outside the reach of the defences it knows about, so the Firtinas and Sakaryas behind them have something to shell, and with an attack on the road they walk a little in front of it. A Firtina or Sakarya whose attack has lost every tank and soldier in front of it drives home instead of rolling on blind into your base. The recon flight looks at the front of your base, where the defences stand, and then at its middle, rather than at the spot the computer already knew best, and the Kargu swarm and the drone munitions go where your defences stand thickest once there are four of them together or its attacks are held back by your guns. It also waits for somewhat bigger attacks and puts up a defence a little sooner. Most of these moves are drawn by chance when the match starts. In 80 Türkiye mirror matches at Elo 1800 the side with them won 34 to 37, inside the noise of that many games.
- A hurt dear unit pulled out to be mended had only repair docks to go to, so a GLA vehicle drove home and stood there. It now also goes to stand in a Propaganda Tower's aura, or into a GLA tunnel, which mends it whole in five seconds, and comes out by the same mouth. A mended unit without a rank was never taken back into the army; it is now.
- A computer on a small map often had no room for its barracks or War Factory, and lost without ever building one. EA's spacing check counted the computer's three-cell margin twice on one side of every neighbouring building, so nine in ten of the spots its dozer turned down had nothing on them. It now counts that margin once, and a player's own placement is checked exactly as before. On the seed that showed it, the USA barracks goes up at 40 seconds of play where it took three minutes or never came. Over 40 matches at Elo 1800 the computer with the fix won 18 to 10.
- A dear unit at low health was pulled out of a fight its side was winning by nineteen to one, then drove a thousand paces home alone and died on the road. It now stays in a fight that is going its way.
- A hurt unit sent back for repair took the repair bay's own road, straight across whatever stood between, and Overlords died on the way home. When the computer knows guns or an army on that road, the unit now walks round them first and drives into the bay once it is there.
- A computer's Humvee full of missile men kept its distance by its own machine gun's reach, so it drove in close enough for the tanks to answer. It now keeps to the reach of the men firing out of it, and the soldiers with rockets and missiles get the seats first.
- A computer ally only answered a person's attack when he marked it with a beacon or a chat command. It now sees it on its own: once your army away from home is fighting an enemy and is worth half of one of its own attacks, it turns on that enemy and sends what it has gathered to join you.
- The computer's scouts walked between the start positions and nowhere else, so an expansion or an army out in the open stayed unknown until it arrived. Once every base is found, a scout goes to look where your army was last seen and at the supply piles it cannot see. A strike that came off cooldown fell on whatever was in sight, a lone power plant as readily as an army; it now waits up to a minute and a half for a target worth the shot, and takes the knot of your units its own attack is fighting when nothing of its own stands under it. CIA Intelligence and the spy satellite go up once the computer has seen nothing of you for a minute.
- A garrisoned building was never a target the computer chose on purpose: its attacks walked past a Bunker full of missile men, or pounded the walls while the men inside kept shooting. Now the units it has that clear buildings, flashbang Rangers, Dragon Tanks, Toxin Tractors, Microwave Tanks and whatever else carries such a weapon, go at a garrison they know of near them, up to three to a building.
- The computer looked after every one of its units in every fight at once, a hundred hands where a person has two. Each level now has a budget of how many units it can attend to a second: an Easy computer's units in a big fight mostly keep doing what they were last told, while Hard and the levels above it keep their full attention.
- On a map whose three attack roads all run under your guns, the computer picked the least defended of them and still walked into the guns. From Hard up it now looks for its own way across the map round the defences it knows and the ground where it has lost units before, and takes it when that way meets less than half the guns and is not much longer. It still attacks the same place.
- The levels above Hard bought more money and faster attacks, and nothing in how they fight: against a walled-in player the Elo 2800 computer killed fewer of his defences than Hard did. Above Hard the computer's long-range guns that go out with an attack now walk further ahead to shell the defences it knows, a little further at Brutal and up to the full length of a siege at Insane.
- A computer set to a Random personality drew any of thirteen alike, so a Demolitions General sat behind walls as often as a Nuke General rushed. Random now picks one of three plans, a rush, an economy or a fortress, leaning by the general: the Demolitions General rushes more than half the time, the Nuke and Superweapon Generals fortify half the time.
- The personality list had thirteen to pick from, and in 40 games each against a Normal computer on Hard most of them played like Normal with another unit mix, or lost to it: Air Force 12 wins to 22, Raider 13 to 20, Armor 13 to 19, Tech 13 to 18. The list now keeps Normal, Random and the five that play their own way without losing: Rusher, first attack at 3 minutes where Normal's comes at 7.7 (19 wins to 14); Turtle, ten defences to Normal's three or four (13 to 12); Economist, more supply centers and the spare money for an ally (18 to 10); Infantry, three fifths of its army on foot and nine attacks every ten minutes to Normal's six (22 to 12); and Sneaky, half again as many stealth units, in by the flanks (20 to 10). Random now draws from all five, still leaning by the general: the Infantry General plays Infantry two games in five, the Stealth General plays Sneaky three in ten, the Demolitions General rushes two in five, and the Nuke General and Türkiye dig in two in five, where the Tank General almost never fields an infantry army. A replay recorded with a Random computer before this change plays out differently. A replay or save with one of the dropped personalities plays as it did, and its load screen still names it.
- A GLA computer with the Raider personality now digs a tunnel beside the road your supply trucks drive between your supply center and its pile, off to one side and out of reach of the guns it knows about. Its raiders wait inside the tunnel network where you cannot see them, and come up when one of your trucks or workers passes by and the army it last saw near there is weaker than they are.
- A computer whose supply piles ran dry asked for a new supply center, then spent the money on rebuilding its War Factory and its defences, and sat on 44 in the bank for the rest of the match with seven supply Chinooks and nowhere to take their loads. Once it earns almost nothing, the new supply center and power come before anything else it would build.
- A mission's computer player that owns another side's dozers next to its own built nothing all match. On 12kill's Sneak Attack, the Zero Hour GLA finale remade so you play the USA, the GLA player takes over China's bulldozers and its own workers with one base plan for both, and every bulldozer and worker stood in the base. Each pass the first building on the plan went to a dozer that could not build it, and that failure held the one building start the game allows a frame, so everything after it on the plan waited for good. Such a building is now skipped the way the original game skipped it. In the first five minutes on Normal the GLA player now builds 67 buildings and 68 units and attacks your base, where it built none before.
- Replays with a computer player recorded before this change will not play back.

## Huge battles run lighter

- Late-game fights with thousands of units cost the computer players less to think about: picking a target and deciding when a unit pulls back skip the checks for enemies that are out of reach. At about 3000 units a frame takes roughly 14% less time. Replays recorded on an earlier build can drift apart in very dense battles. Another 3 to 4% comes off that frame because the game no longer looks up every unit's armour again on every tick to get ready for those target searches. That part plays out exactly as before: the same 3000-unit battle ends on the same checksum.
- The cursor over the ground costs less: the game keeps the last spot it found under the mouse until the camera moves, the ground changes or a tick passes, where it used to cast the ray again. A frame with no heat haze on screen skips the haze pass, and freeing memory takes a shorter path. None of it changes what you see or how a match plays.
- A rare out-of-sync between players and observers in the same match, set off by fogged enemy buildings, is fixed: whether a unit reuses its last target search no longer depends on what a particular machine has drawn.
- Big standing armies cost less to run, and nothing plays any differently. A China tank in a horde used to tell the screen thirty times a second how large to draw its horde badge, because a change of damage look shrank the badge back to the default; EA's own note in the code calls it a weak solution and asks whoever comes next to fix the drawing instead. The drawing now keeps the size, and the tank only wakes when it rechecks its horde, as it always did. The end-of-match advice stopped walking every unit each player owns on every tick, and whether one team counts another as an enemy, asked over and over in a fight, is worked out once a tick and remembered. In a 7656-unit test battle the game's own work per tick fell from 21.9 to 19.4 ms, and from 8.7 to 7.1 with the armies standing still. That battle ends on the same checksum as before, and replays recorded on the last build still play back.
- The same battle got cheaper again, and this time it plays a little differently, so replays recorded on earlier builds no longer play back. A tank stuck in a crowd asks the units around it to step aside, and each of them used to search as far as it took to find a free spot, often clear across the crowd; now a unit steps aside near at hand or not at all, and in that battle the tanks spent half as long blocked. Parked units that touch no longer tell each other every tick that neither of them is moving, and an idle dozer or worker rests until it next has something to look for, waking at once for any order or new job. The game's work per tick fell from 19.4 to 15.1 ms, and from 7.1 to 5.9 with the armies standing still.

## Fixes from the bug reports of November 24 and 28

- The grown minimap's frame showed a dark line down its right edge every few inches, and at 125 and 150 percent its top edge met the corner with a seam. The frame is one clean piece at every size now.
- Minimap Size jumped to a big radar on tall maps and then did nothing along the rest of the slider. The radar now grows a little with every step.
- Some random maps built from a shipped map drew the same road twice, one on top of the other. Each road is drawn once.
- Saving over an existing save showed no Overwrite? question, and its buttons did not answer the mouse. The question is back and its buttons take clicks, and answering it no longer leaves the menus ignoring the mouse.
- Play vs AI turned down clean 4.4.0 installs. It accepts them now, and its warning shows as a full sentence.
- A Construction Dozer clears a whole cluster of revealed Demo Traps without blowing up the rest under itself. It stopped after the first trap it found on its own and stood idle beside the next one, which went off, and a trap it had just made safe could still go off in the moment it was taken away. It now goes on from barrel to barrel through the cluster. Replays in which a dozer clears mines on its own may not play back.
- The camera scrolls far enough to bring the map's last rows up above the interface. It used to stop at the same distance from every edge, so the command bar hid a strip along the bottom of the map and the Red Alert style sidebar one along the right, and only hiding the interface showed them. Each edge now goes as far as the open part of the screen needs, and never less far than before; turning the camera, dropping the bar low or hiding it changes the limit with it.
- In the console's `freecam` the mouse wheel narrows and widens the lens, from 10 to 120 degrees across, for a long shot of one tank or a wide one of a whole base up close. Landing puts the normal lens back, and `freecam x y z heading tilt fov` repeats a shot with its lens; leaving the freecam prints the lens with the rest of the pose.
- Under Ragdoll Deaths a soldier who had fallen lies where he fell after a save is loaded, instead of getting up into his death animation and dying again. Saves made by this version need it to load.
- Under Ragdoll Deaths a hunched body, the homeless civilian's most of all, keeps the shape of its back when it lands instead of being pressed flat into the ground with its spine pulled out of joint, and the Missile Defender's brown hip bag stays on his hip instead of turning with his leg and sticking out through the body.
- Under Ragdoll Deaths a Ranger dropped by parachute, or one sliding down a Chinook's rope, went limp while still alive and lay on the ground as a body once he landed: all five of one paradrop on Twilight Flame, nobody shooting. He now lands on his feet; only a soldier who dies goes limp.
- Roads darken with the night. With Day and Night ticked, a road the camera had in view when the light turned kept the daylight it was drawn with and glowed against the dark ground beside it under Classic graphics and Direct3D 9; it now takes each change of light with the ground under it, the Apocalypse's red nights and a mission's change of hour too.
- With Ground Foliage on, the grass, stones and dead trees no longer stop in a straight line where the map's ground ends and the land past the edge carries on bare: they thin out over the last hundred and twenty units instead.
- The superweapon countdowns in the top right say which superweapon each one is, its name across the top of the picture, and the seconds left are written large under it in the owner's colour on a soft shadow, where they were a small white number in the corner. The Classic HUD keeps EA's list of lines.
- Units on guard go back to the spot you posted them on once the fight is over. A guard whose circle you had sized with the mouse wheel, even by one notch while aiming, stayed wherever its last kill left it: four of six Crusaders posted that way sat up to 163 from their spot after clearing a few Workers. Now they drive back, as a guard without a sized circle always did, and still turn straight onto the next enemy in the circle before they do. Replays with a wheeled guard in them may not play back.
## The game room in the new menu look

- The room you set up every skirmish, LAN game and online custom game in is the next screen in the new menu look: the thin lit frame with its ruler ticks, one lit key (Play Game, Start or Accept), and every drop-down and check box drawn in the same lines instead of EA's 2003 art.
- Seats sit under a head for their team, the smallest team first, so a 4 v 4 reads as two blocks of four and a 1 v 31 last stand shows the one player on top. Players with no team come first, open and closed seats last. Change a seat's team and the row moves to its new group once the list closes, and lights up for a second so you can see where it went.
- Every row is the same size at 32 seats as at 8: the list scrolls past what fits, with "12 SEATS ABOVE" and "13 SEATS BELOW" at its edges, and the wheel, those strips and the track move it a seat or a page at a time. Each seat is one line now, seated or open: a taken seat was 90 pixels tall and an open one 52, so the list jumped every time a seat filled, and a computer's level stood in bigger type over a cramped personality box. Every row is 56 tall with its boxes on one line in one size of type, a portrait for every seat (an empty dashed frame for an open one), a computer's level and personality side by side, and in a network room HOST, READY or NOT READY and the online rating at the end of the player's name box. The arrow on every drop-down is a narrow strip instead of a square, so TEAM and HANDICAP show their value in full.
- In a LAN or online room the chat is a tab beside the rules instead of a band under the seats, so all eight seats stay on screen, and a closed chat counts the lines you have not read. SEND beside the line sends what Enter sends; in a LAN room that button used to send an emote.
- The map keeps its own shape: a wide map like Iron Dragon fills the column 542 by 278 with its name under it, a squarer one stands at the left with its name beside it. A joiner reads "The host picks the map" where Select Map would be.
- The mode question behind the Mods buttons is a box in the same look: a card a mode with its picture, a line on what it plays and how many seats it takes, the default lit, Esc to cancel and Enter for the lit card.

## The Apocalypse room in the new menu look

- The Apocalypse room was the Classic room cut to four rows, and it lied: Team, Unit Limit, Peace Time, Tech Respawn, Pile Limit, Pro Rules and Day/Night all looked like live boxes, and changing one made it jump straight back, because the mode sets them itself. They now stand read only under SET BY THE MODE, with Teams: All allied and Difficulty: Adapts beside them, and RULES holds only what the host really picks: speed, starting cash, superweapons and shared income.
- The four seats stand under a SURVIVORS head that says what each one costs: the waves sized for the seats taken and boss health at x1.5 for two survivors, x2.5 for four. An open seat says how much every wave grows if someone takes it.
- Apocalypse is for players only now. Solo Play's room is your seat alone, with no computer allies to fill in beside you, and a LAN or online room holds up to four players in co-op with every seat Open or Closed until someone joins. No seat list in an Apocalypse room offers a computer, and a computer seat left in a saved room opens for a player instead.
- Under the seats, THE NIGHTS draws one day to scale with the first wave's tick on it, then nights 1 to 9 and the twelfth on: when each falls at the room's speed (night 1 at 3:10 at 1.5x, 4:45 at 1.0x), how many new kinds of the dead it brings, and the Blood Moon boss on nights 3, 6 and 9. The skirmish room, with no chat to fit, names every kind. Every figure is read from the mode itself, so the room cannot drift from the match.
- The map column says what you get, a basin made new every match with a start for each seat, with a key for its marks and the deadly fog's red round the preview. In a LAN or online room the chat stays open under the nights, and the skirmish foot says how you are scored in place of a win and loss record the mode never counts.
- In every room the mouse wheel scrolls the seats with the pointer over a drop-down as well. The boxes cover most of a seat row and swallowed the wheel without doing anything with it, so the list only scrolled with the pointer over a portrait or a gap.
- The track beside a long seat list takes its thumb in hand now: press it and drag, and the seats follow a seat at a time. A click on the track above or below it still pages. A drop-down left open while the room moved its row (a seat set to Open regroups the seats) is closed first instead of staying a list's height taller than its box, an unseen window over the seats that took their clicks.
- In the Apocalypse room the generated basin's preview stands square again (it was stretched to twice its width), the rules the mode sets read clearly under SET BY THE MODE, and the room is titled APOCALYPSE with its version beside the tagline.
- A drop-down you had just picked from snapped shut the next time you opened it, so every second open took two clicks, in every menu. It opens on the first click now.

## The Direct Strike lobby in the new menu look

- The Direct Strike room was a steel console 804 pixels tall in the middle of a 1080 screen, bare backdrop above and below it and every plate and key a picture. It now fills the same lit frame as the other rooms: the two teams in wings at the sides, the army pictures 226 pixels square where they were 128, and one START key 640 wide under the island. The title, the room's facts and BACK sit along the top as on the end screen.
- The island is the map you will play. The room shows the generated island's own picture with the lane, both fortresses and every plot drawn over it, each plot in its player's colour and yours ringed in gold, and a key under it names the marks.
- An open seat adds a computer in one click: ADD COMPUTER and four keys, Easy, Medium, Hard and Brutal, where the seat list took two. A player who is not the host gets one TAKE SEAT key on it. The seat swap, the move by the other team's name and the Mixed armies box work as before.
- Readiness reads from across the room. Each team's head says READY 2/3, a lane along the foot fills a segment a seat from each team's fortress toward the middle, and in a LAN or online room the line over it says WAITING FOR 2 PLAYERS until it says ALL READY. In a network room every picture wears a HOST, READY or WAITING tag, and a player's ping sits in his name's line.
- The lists never cover START: the army picker opens inside its own team's wing, the team size and speed lists open upward over the island, and the current choice in every list is a blue row with a tick. Gold means you and nothing else; hover is cyan, as in the other rooms.

## Select Map and the army screen in the new menu look

- Select Map was a list of names, and you picked a map you could only see after clicking it. It is now a grid of the maps themselves, eight across and four rows on a 1080p screen, each picture at its map's own shape with its name under it, the player count on the picture and in skirmish your best win on its foot (EASY, MEDIUM, HARD, or HARD x7 for Hard in every other seat). The pick is lit, the map under the pointer says its players, supplies and tech and what to beat next, and a double click accepts. The same in skirmish, LAN and online.
- Each tab says how many maps it holds, and the end of a list leads on: the last row's empty places become UNOFFICIAL MAPS with its count and RANDOM MAP, never to an empty tab and never to Random while an online room records stats, where the Random tab says why it is off. A short list grows its pictures to fill the row, and an empty Unofficial tab says where your own maps go.
- The picked map's name, its players, supplies and tech, and in skirmish its medal and the next one, stand beside the preview where the room shows its own map. Cancel and Accept moved to the foot, Accept on the very spot Play Game holds, so the key under your pointer does not jump when the picker closes. A map clicked again while it is the pick still answers; the old list took the second click for a deselect.
- The Random tab draws its map types as the same grid under a row of five size keys, and its preview says STYLE: the type's own map shows how the new one will look, not where its start spots go, since those are placed when the map is built.
- The army screen is one row a side: a tick box, the side's name, how many of its armies are in the draw, and a RANDOM USA, RANDOM CHINA or RANDOM GLA key where a click on the side's name used to do that without saying so. Every army is named under its picture. The right side is THE DRAW, the count, every army a Random can land on with the ones in it lit and the game's own words for each, or, with one general picked, his portrait, his strategy, his features and the other generals of his side to weigh him against. BACK and CONFIRM sit in the foot, CONFIRM on Play Game's spot.

## The main menu in the new menu look

- EA's main menu was a stack of drop-downs laid out for an 800x600 screen and stretched: Multiplayer opened a list of Online and Network, a campaign took three lists in a row (Generals or Zero Hour, then the mission, then the difficulty), and the side emblems and EA's logo filled what was left. It is now one rail on the right in the new menu look, the game's name and version at its head and the shell map clear and undimmed beside it. Multiplayer opens the LAN lobby in one click, and Direct Connect is still in there. A side opens one panel beside the rail: the original and the Zero Hour campaign as two tabs, the missions as numbered tiles, and Easy, Medium and Hard as keys that start the mission you picked. Mods shows Direct Strike and Apocalypse as two cards. Every button says in one line what it opens, Enter presses the lit key and Esc goes back up one.
- Online play starts from the launcher's Online key: the game opens on the login over the main menu, or straight on the hub when it remembers you, and Back from the online screens lands on that menu, whose rail keeps an Online key to go back in. A game started any other way no longer shows an Online button that could only tell you to use the launcher.
- Exit Game asks "Close Zero Hour Reforged and go back to the desktop?" in its own box, where it used to borrow the in-match "Are you sure you want to exit?", and it asks in a window too: a windowed game used to close on the first click. The credits roll in a column of glass over the live shell map, with this edition's people first.
- The glass under every menu panel and box is frosted now: the shell map or the match behind it shows blurred, so the battle still moves under the words without fighting them for your eye. Under Direct3D 9 the glass stays plain darkened as before.

## The loading screens in the new menu look

- Every match loads on one board in the new look: the map's own picture behind see-through glass, the thin lit frame round it, the two sides facing each other across the map. A 1 v 1 shows each general as a poster as tall as the screen allows, a 4 v 4 four cards a team with the general's name and strategy under the army, and past four a side or at 32 seats each player is one line, sixteen to a side, every name still at 18 px on a 1080p screen and none under 9 at 720. Team heads say READY 3/4, the word turning green once the whole team has loaded, and when your own load is done the bar names whoever the match is waiting for: "WAITING FOR KARA MURAT · 23%".
- Your own row carries the gold light, and gold means you and nothing else: every other name is white, with the player's colour as a stripe down his row, along his portrait's foot and on his start spot. A computer seat shows its level and its personality; a Normal one only its level.
- Direct Strike and Apocalypse load under their own names. Direct Strike lists its wave clock, income and wave lifetime under RULES and its tips teach the mode, and its two wings are the lane's two sides with every army named, a computer that drew Random included, since your enemies' plots show them from the first wave anyway; Apocalypse shows its nights as a band of day, dusk, night and dawn with each clock at the match's speed, the first wave and the Blood Moon under it. A random or generated map shows a question mark and "Random map" in place of the picture.
- A campaign mission keeps its picture and gains its place in the campaign, MISSION 3 OF 7 with a pip for each, counted along the campaign's own order. A saved campaign game now loads on the same frame, the mission's picture, its briefing and the date of the save, where it used to show EA's bare title picture. The map transfer before a LAN game lists every player on the board's rows, as many as the room seats, where EA's screen stopped at eight. The Generals' Challenge load keeps EA's screen, with the new loading bar.

## The end screens in the new menu look

- The score screen after a match now fills the same lit frame as the rooms, with the result as its title (VICTORY, DEFEAT, TEAM 2 WINS) and the map, format and length after it. The two teams stand in wings facing each other, and a line under the header shows how the match's score split between them. One to four a team are cards with the army's picture, the army's value drawn over the whole match and every figure under it; past four a team they are lines, several teams each get a band with their place and totals, and a free for all lists all 32 places, two columns of sixteen, with your own place large in the header.
- Gold now means you and nothing else: your row's light, your name, your ring on the map, your line on the charts, your frames on the build order. A winner reads VICTORY in green, and a column's best figure is cyan with a cyan bar under it, which the foot names. Two seats with the same name are numbered, Hard AI (2).
- The foot holds the map with every start on it (numbered rings up to eight players, a dot a player past that) and four highlights: most destroyed, top earner, biggest army, first superweapon, each with what it measured. After a LAN or online match the chat sits there instead, and a CHAT key swaps between the two. After Quick Match or Play vs AI the rating card takes the same place.
- Build order no longer stretches the first five minutes and squeezes the rest. The time axis now folds away every quiet stretch where nobody built and runs everything it keeps at one even scale, so a 20 minute match with a four minute lull no longer leaves a fifth of the page empty. Each picture sits at its true moment and is never pushed later to make room; units are framed in the player's colour, structures in grey.
- Graphs draws the local player's line white-gold inside a gold edge, so a yellow player's line no longer reads as yours, and past sixteen players its legend splits into two columns.
- Direct Strike's results screen moved into the same frame: a wing a team with its fortress's end health large in the head, a row a seat with the army, the top unit and the seven figures led by damage, and the timeline of the middle and both fortresses under them, with its tower marks and a tick every wave. Rematch (Lobby after a network match), Watch replay and Menu sit on the key row. The finale's slow motion and the dealt result card stay as they were. Apocalypse keeps "Survived m:ss" as its title and beside every seat.

## The options screen in the new menu look

- Options was nine tabs across the top of an 800x600 panel. The Water tab was hidden on every Windows machine, and seven world looks sat on the Display tab only because Graphics and Effects had run out of room. It is now eight tabs down a rail on the left, System, Graphics, World, Effects, Audio, Controls, Interface and Hotkeys, each with its count and the groups it holds written under it (SCREEN · FRAME RATE · NETWORK), so you read where Sun Shafts lives before you open anything. Light, sky, ground and water are World's; smoke, fire and wreckage are Effects'; the network rows are System's last group.
- Look, Classic or Reforged, and the Quality track with its Low, Medium, High and Ultra notches stand under the tabs on every tab, because they are the two choices that rewrite rows on three of them. In a match Quality says LOCKED IN A MATCH.
- Each tab shows every one of its settings at once, what people change first at the top of each group. There is no MORE bar to open any more: a tab longer than the screen (Controls, at 862 pixels of rows in an 822 pixel column) scrolls under the mouse wheel with a thin track at its right edge, and the explanation on the right stays where it is while you scroll.
- The right half explains the setting under your pointer: what it changes in two sentences, what it needs with a light for each need met, the settings that wait on it, a list's choices, and the whole tab as it stands. It talks about the picture, not your frame rate: the milliseconds on an RTX 2060 that used to stand beside every row, and the tab totals under Graphics and Effects, are gone, since they said nothing about your own card.
- The settings that move the interface show where it goes instead of describing it. Layout draws the screen three times, Reforged, Red Alert Style and Classic, with the bars, the radar, the sidebar's tabs and cameo wells where the game puts them, and the one you use framed green. Interface Width draws a 32:9 screen at Full, 21:9 and 16:9 in the layout you picked, Minimap Size draws the radar at 100%, where your slider stands and 200%, and Health Bars, Health Bar Colors and Player Colors draw a handful of units, yours, an ally's and two enemies', with the bars and colours each choice gives them. Fullscreen Fit draws a 4:3 picture stretched over a widescreen monitor next to the same picture kept in shape between black bars.
- The look settings get side-by-side pictures of each choice, Shadow Quality at Low, Medium, High and Ray Traced, Volumetric Smoke off and on, and so on for forty-odd settings, as the shots are taken; until a setting's shots arrive its pane reads as before.
- A setting you cannot change says why in place of its box: Reforged look only, Direct3D 11 only, Needs Cast Shadows, Classic water only, Off while Legacy Sound is on, Fullscreen only. A RESTART or NEXT MAP tag beside a name tells you when it takes hold, with a legend at the foot.
- Texture Filtering and Anisotropic Samples are one list, Bilinear to Anisotropic 16x; the two Heat Haze boxes, the fork's and EA's, are one; the volumes are five faders side by side. Every Options.ini line you already have is read as before.
- On Hotkeys the picked command stands under the bar's keys with its key large and every other command bound to that key under it, so a clash shows before you play it.
- The Hotkeys page showed None beside the ally signals and the command bar's tabs, so you could not see what to press. It shows the real keys now: Alt+Z, Alt+X and Alt+C for the signals, Ctrl+Q, Ctrl+W, Ctrl+E and Ctrl+R for the tabs.
- A button whose key the launcher had set for its place on the bar ignored the in-game Hotkeys page: you gave it a new letter, Accept saved it, and the match kept the old one. The page now changes the key for that place, the button and its tooltip wear the new letter, a button you moved is gold, and Reset gives it back the game's own letter there without touching the same button on other bars.

## Single player screens in the new menu look

- Generals' Challenge was twelve medallions on EA's world map, and nothing on it said who you would fight or in what order. It is now nine cards under USA, China and GLA, each the general's portrait with his army under it. Point at one and the lower half becomes his dossier: rank, tactics, where he is stationed, his portrait down to the foot of the screen, and his challenge as a row of tiles from battle 1 to Leang's final, every opponent ringed on a map at his own base. PLAY GAME stays dimmed until you pick, and the difficulty you chose on the main menu reads beside BACK.
- The replay list shows what is inside each file: the date and time it was recorded (newest first, where it used to be alphabetical), the map, how many played, how long it ran and which version made it. A replay from another version is greyed with OLDER after it. The one you pick opens a column of its own with the map's picture and every start in its player's colour, the game speed, whether it was played out, left early or fell out of sync, and each player with his army, his team and whether he dropped. Deleting a replay asks with No lit, so Enter never deletes one.
- Load Game names the campaign and mission of every save and marks the saves a mission makes as it opens. A save this build cannot read is greyed with LOAD GAME dimmed, where it used to look like any other until it failed on Load. The picked save shows the campaign's missions as tiles with its own lit, the mission's map, the difficulty and how long it had been played.
- Save Replay on the end screen and Save / Load in a match are boxes in the same look, the new save first, and every question they ask comes up in the common question box. A replay name with a character Windows cannot take, a slash or a colon, is turned down in plain words before anything is written, where the box used to show Windows' own "The filename, directory name, or volume label syntax is incorrect". Turkish letters are saved as their plain ones, "Maç" as "Mac"; a dotless ı used to reach the disk as the digit 1.

## Message boxes in the new menu look

- Every question the game asks outside a match, from Exit to a failed join, used to come up in EA's fixed box of 2003: drawn for an 800x600 screen and stretched, 300 by 328 of that screen whatever it held. It is now the first piece of the new menu look: a thin lit blue edge with a ruler's ticks round see-through glass, the title in capitals over a lit rule, the question at 18 px on a 1080p screen and 12 at 720, and the box as tall as its text, 28 px a line. The key Enter presses is lit and sits at the right; Escape answers No or Cancel, and the foot says which key does what. A key acts only when the box saw it pressed, so the Enter that sent a chat line or a join no longer answers the box that opened from it.
- The rest of the game's boxes followed. Escape in a match now opens a box standing clear of your command bar, with the battle still readable round it: Return to Game lit on top, Restart or Surrender and Exit set a little apart below. Surrender and Restart ask with No lit, so a stray Enter keeps you in the match.
- The waiting-for-players screen had seven fixed rows, one for every other player whether he had stopped answering or not, and the engine seats 32. It now lists only the players who went quiet or are rejoining, each with the seconds before he is dropped draining away and his votes against the number that drops him ("2 / 5", every other player still connected), and everyone still talking on a line of names under them. Past eight it puts two to a line. Its only key is Quit Game and Enter never presses it.
- Victory, Defeat and Game Over are a band over the match with the map and the match clock under the word, where EA showed a picture. The connection screen of an online start lists every seat with a lamp for how far it got, and the friends list and its right-click menus have the new layout; what a friend's row shows comes with the friends feature.

## Online login, hub and Quick Match in the new menu look

- Signing in online is one box in the middle of the screen over the shell map, where it used to be a full panel that stopped halfway down. The server, its ping and three big figures (players on, open games, players in Quick Match) stand on the left, the email and password on the right with one lit Sign In key, and a lit line runs under it while it connects. Every online page now carries your rank picture, name, tier, ELO and Bot ELO along its title row and the server with its ping beside the tabs, and a maintenance notice sits in that title row instead of hanging over the page.
- The hub's Play vs AI and Quick Match cards show your last five results as W and L chips. The recent matches table mixes both modes newest first, and each rating change carries a bar as long as the change. The Custom games card lists the first three open games with their map and free seats. A player with no matches yet gets the ladder's top five where his empty table would be.
- Quick Match puts your picks in one box beside the army cards and the colour boxes: the general's portrait, your ladder figure, place, record and how many are queued. While it searches, three big figures say how long it has searched, how many others search on your server and which win chances it takes now, over a 0 to 100 track that marks the next widening and where widening stops; your last five Quick Matches sit under it. When an opponent is found both seats face each other with your win chance between them and the match's mode, server and speed beneath.

## Game lists in the new menu look

- The online Custom games page and the LAN lobby are one screen in the new look. The games fill a list with a column each for the game, its mode, its map, the seats taken out of how many with a bar, the host's ping online, and whether it is Open, Full, Playing or from another build; the first game is picked for you, and the picked one shows its map, host and every seat (army, colour and record where the game knows them) in the right column over the players. Click GAME or PING to sort by it.
- Host Game and Create Game ask which of the three modes the room is for, Classic, Direct Strike or Apocalypse, so the separate Mods key is gone. Join is the lit key while a game you can take is picked, Host Game otherwise, and Enter on an empty chat line joins the picked game.
- Host Game, the password box and Direct Connect are boxes over the lobby in the same look, with Enter for the lit key and Esc to cancel. Join Game now has a JOIN key; EA's only joined on Enter.
- Direct Connect's Join with no address, or one mistyped, used to send you after whatever number happened to be in memory and say nothing for five seconds; it now tells you at once to type their address. Host pressed while such a join still waited did nothing at all, and now hosts. In the LAN lobby with no game picked, the player list took no clicks: an invisible piece of EA's old screen lay over it.

## Ladder, skins and the player card in the new menu look

- The ladder is a table of twenty on a faint zebra where grid lines used to be: place, nick, the rank's portrait and name, the ELO at row size with a thin bar of how close it comes to the page's best, then wins, losses and win rate. ELO is the green head with a caret, because that is the order the server pages by. Your own row is gold, on the page or pinned under it past a dotted gap, and the row under the pointer lights up. Click any row and that player's card opens over the ladder.
- Your place sits beside the table in big figures with your rank portrait, your ELO and rank, the next rank and how many points it still wants over a track, and your wins, losses and win rate. An unranked player reads 3 of 5 games, PLACEMENT and how many games are left. The Ranks box lists all eight bands with their ELO ranges, yours on the gold edge.
- The ranks sit where Generals Online players know them: Sergeant from 1000 ELO, then one rank every 200 up to General at 2000. General used to start at 1500 and Lieutenant at 1075. Everyone keeps their ELO; only the name beside it moves.
- Skins sizes the cards to the unit: the Chinook's seven looks come in rows of three, two and two, the Worker's two stand one above the other, and no slot is ever left empty. A green tick is what you wear, a cyan one a pick you have not saved and a grey one the look you still wear while another is picked. The Worker's Special Thanks is framed in cyan with a white star now, since gold on these screens means you. SAVE is the lit key while there is something to save, the platform's key the rest of the time, and the status line under the cards says Saved or what went wrong in one short sentence.
- The player card is one box in the same frame: the nick large, where he is, both ELOs with their rank portraits, the open tab's figures across the card, the two army boxes with GAMES and WIN RATE over their columns, and the last five with WIN in green and the ELO change at row size. While the history is still coming the card shrinks to the figures. Enter or Esc closes it, and the screen under it takes no clicks until you do.
- Not there yet: a card opened from someone else's ladder row has his ratings and record but no match history, because the ladder does not send account numbers.

## Password rooms online

- The password box in Host Game did nothing online: the room opened to everyone. On a server with friends the password now locks the room, the game list marks it, a wrong password is refused as one, and a friend you invite walks in without it. Against an older server the game behaves exactly as before.

## Team vs AI online

- Play vs AI was you against one computer. With friends in your party, Play takes the party of two, three or four against as many computers, on a four, six or eight player map, every human on one team. Each of you plays the army picked on the Quick Match page, and the match runs over the relay like a Quick Match. A friend in the party has to be on the online home screen when Play is pressed; if not, the card says so and nothing starts.
- Making the party is two clicks: outside a room, right-click a friend in the friends list and pick Invite, and he takes it with JOIN on the box that pops up on his screen. The Play vs AI card then lists the party with a LEAVE key beside it, and its Team key steps 1V1, 2V2, 3V3 and 4V4. Pick a team bigger than your party, or any team on your own, and PLAY becomes FIND TEAM: the card counts the wait ("Finding a team · 3V3 · 0:42") and the key reads CANCEL until the server fills the seats and the match starts.
- The party needs no friendship: any signed-in player's card, from the ladder or a lobby, has INVITE TO PARTY. A party searches as one block, so two of you at 3V3 or 4V4 get the empty seats filled from the queue around you. While you are in a party the Team key never offers 1V1, and Quick Match is greyed, its key and tab on the home page and its Search, with "You are in a party. Quick Match is solo." beside them.
- The mode has its own Team Bot ELO, apart from the ladder and from Play vs AI's. The computers play at your team's average plus the same random step the 1v1 draws, and each of you moves by your own amount against them, so a new account climbs faster than an old one on the same win. A team whose strongest and weakest player sit more than 400 apart cannot start. Leaving before the end is a loss; a match that went out of sync counts for nobody. Without a party a player can queue alone, and the server puts players within 400 of each other together.
- Two copies plus two computer seats played 14,400 frames over the relay at 40 ms of fake latency without one checksum mismatch; three plus three did the same, four plus four 18,000 frames, and four, six and eight human seats with no computers 9,000 each. Two copies signed in to a local server made a party, started from Play, played 3,600 frames together against two computers and both left: each was rated the same loss, 800 to 710 against computers drawn at 947.

## Friends online

- EA's buddy list ran on GameSpy and has had nobody on it since 2014. On a server with friends it is your friends list again: every online page has a FRIENDS key beside the server line with how many of them are on, and the list shows a green dot for each one signed in and where he is, "In a room · Iron Dragon", in a match or in the lobby. Type a name next to ADD FRIEND, or pick Add friend on a player's card or on his name in the lobby's player list. A request to you carries a REQUEST chip; right-click it to accept or deny.
- Sitting in a room, right-click a friend who is signed in and pick Invite. He gets a box under the head of whatever online page he is on: who asks, the room and its mode, JOIN and DECLINE, and a bar running down his two minutes. JOIN takes him to the custom games page and into the room, past its password; from Quick Match, the ladder or the end screen it walks him there first, and from a room of his own it asks before he leaves it. An invite that came during a match waits for the end screen.
- Ignore on a player now blocks him on the server as well, so his requests, invites and messages stop on every PC you sign in from. Against a server without friends nothing here shows and the buddy list is EA's.
- Not there yet: no line in the match tells you an invite came in, and adding a friend from a room's seats or the end screen's rows needs its own right-click.

## Computer guards, medics and paratroopers stop wasting time

- A computer's base guards kept grabbing a target their teammate had picked, a Comanche overhead or a tank across the map, dropped it the same instant because they could not reach it, and grabbed it again a few seconds later. One four-player Hard match logged 52,257 of those turns, a single Microwave Tank 7,616 of them. A guard now takes the team's target only when it stands inside its own circle and it can hit it, and it no longer picks an aircraft out of its weapons' reach. Over the same twelve four-player matches the turns fell from 60,149 to 18,793.
- Paratroopers and soldiers the computer leaves behind your lines stood where they landed, or walked home past your buildings. A Ranger, Rebel or Red Guard out on the map now walks into the nearest building worth taking, yours or a tech building, before it looks for a fight. It stops trying a building once the walk in has failed, where ten Rangers used to stand 470 from an Arms Dealer being sent again every two seconds.
- The computer dropped its paratroopers wherever your base was worth the most, which was usually among your Gattling Cannons. In 16 Hard Air Force matches against China 214 paratroopers died to defences, 147 of them still standing where they landed. A Medium or Hard computer now drops paratroopers, and springs a Rebel ambush, only where no defence it knows of reaches, and keeps the power while every spot is covered. Over 32 Hard Air Force matches against China and GLA the paratroopers lost to defences fell from 160 to 32.
- An America computer earned barely half what a GLA one did. Its Chinooks all queued at the nearest supply pile, which loads one Chinook at a time for ten seconds, while other piles in reach stood idle: a load left its home pile every 196 to 252 frames, exactly the time one load takes, all match long. And 98 of the 120 Chinooks a Hard America lost in its first six minutes against Medium GLA were shot unloading at a supply center that a Stinger Site or Quad Cannon could reach, while that center bought a fresh one for 1,200 each time. A computer's Chinook now weighs the line at a pile against the flight to another, stays away from a supply center under anti-air guns it knows of, and no Chinook is bought for such a center. Hard America against Medium GLA on the same 20 maps in both seat orders: money earned in the first six minutes rose from 25,250 to 31,800 (GLA's 44,972 to 47,182), Chinooks lost in that time fell from 113 to 78, and the record went from 13 wins and 19 losses to 16 and 13.
- Hurt soldiers the computer called to its Ambulance could reach the door and stand there for over a minute without getting in. They are now called in again from the door. In six America mirror matches the soldiers stuck at the door fell from 9 to 1, and the average wait from the call to getting in from 61 to 52 seconds.
- Replays with a computer player recorded before this change will not play back.

## The levels above Hard stand and fight

- Brutal, Vicious, Savage and Insane grew more careful with every step past Hard. A unit hit by a gun wanted ever better odds before it would go for it (4.4 times the worth of what covers the gun at Insane, twice at Hard), and every unit near it walked away with it, so the extra army the higher levels build spent its fights leaving: one Insane China logged 259 soldiers backing out of fire in a single match. Above Hard a unit under fire now answers it as Hard does. Against Hard, 40 games each at double speed on the same maps: Brutal wins 23 to 11 (17 to 13 before), Vicious 21 to 12 (20 to 12) and Insane 21 to 14 (23 to 12), and Insane now kills 137 units a game to Hard's 108 where both killed 114. Insane against Vicious is 20 to 14. Only Brutal's step clears the noise of 40 games; Vicious is not yet a step above Brutal.
- Insane earns well over Hard's income and used to sit on most of it: a median of 19,960 in the bank in the middle of a match against Hard's 6,142, with one War Factory working flat out and no ground left for a second one inside its base. On a small map it failed to place a War Factory 2,854 times in 40 games. A computer whose bank piles past three times what it means to keep now builds the extra factory behind its base, out as far as a superweapon may go, and one whose bank passes twice that keeps more units queued at each factory, two on Hard and one more for every 500 of rating above it. Against Hard, 40 games at double speed on the same maps: Insane's bank falls to 16,674, it builds 213 units a game where it built 186, and it wins 23 to 12 (21 to 14 before); Savage banks 11,214 where it held 15,644 and wins 21 to 12 (20 to 14). Most of what Insane still banked belonged to the matches where an enemy unit stood in its base: it spent nothing extra while its home was under attack, and those seats held a median of 36,000.
- One enemy soldier in the computer's base used to keep its whole army home. An Insane GLA kept every attack at home for a whole match over intruders worth 300 to 3,600 and finished on 312,429 in the bank; another kept one War Factory all game with 43,535 banked because a single Ranger stood in its base. Now an attack still leaves when the army staying behind outweighs the intruders by the odds it answers them with, and a computer whose bank has piled up keeps building factories and units while it is hit. A real push still outweighs what stays and meets the whole home force. Insane against Hard, 40 games at double speed on the same maps: matches where Insane kept its attacks home more than 50 times fell from 11 to 4, its bank from 18,223 to 16,048, and it wins 25 to 11 (23 to 11 before). Against the walled-in player who pushes at minute 15 and 25 he still wins 1 game of 9 at Hard, Vicious and Insane and none at Medium, as before.
- When your helicopter flew over the computer's base, every idle unit it had went after it. A China computer on a small map sent 248 units at one scout Helix, met the 154-tank push behind it out in the open, away from its own guns, and lost its base two minutes later. Now only units that can hit the intruder go, nearest first, and against an aircraft only enough to beat what it sees: 36 went in that match and the base held to the end. A ground push is still met by everything that can shoot it.
- Against the walled-in player who masses and attacks at minute 15 and 25, nine games a level: he now wins 1 of 9 against Medium, 1 against Hard, 1 against Vicious and none against Insane (0, 1, 2 and 1 before), and the computer wins 5, 5, 6 and 6 (5 at every level before).
- Replays with a computer player recorded before this change will not play back.

## The computer builds its base and stays to hold it

- A building you put up near the computer's base used to freeze its own base plan for the whole match. EA's AI treats any enemy building near a spot as danger and skips the spot, every time, and never tries another. On a small map a turtle's power plants stood 350 to 400 from the computer's base: a Medium China never built its first power plant and so built nothing at all, and an Insane China got one barracks, no War Factory and 13 of the 44 guns it wanted, and met a 154-tank push at minute 15 with an army of infantry and 100,000 in the bank. A building that cannot shoot no longer counts as danger inside the computer's own base, and a planned building whose spot is really under the guns moves to the nearest safe spot in the base instead of waiting all match.
- An Insane computer's soldiers at home walked off the edge of the map because a Gattling Cannon a thousand away had hit one of them on the way back from a fight. Told of the gun, every one near ran for "quiet ground" outside the map, and 126 of its 164 units stood in that walk when your tanks came. A unit already out of a gun's reach now stays where it is.
- On a small map the computer put its guns and factories one and a half base widths out from its command center, wherever that fell, and with the starts 500 apart that was inside the other player's base. An Air Force General built a Patriot 155 from the other America's command center and a China a Gattling Cannon 270 from it; every Chinook the America sent to its supplies died under them, and it earned 1,800 in a 27 minute match where neither side ever attacked. Nothing of a computer's base now goes up on the enemy's side of the map or close to his start, and a spy satellite's marker no longer counts as an enemy standing on the building spots under it. Over 160 games at double speed on the same 20 maps, matches that ran to the time limit fell from 28 to 14, games the higher level lost before the first attack was due fell from 19 to 11, and Insane against Vicious went from 15 to 19 to 21 to 16 (22 to 12 on 20 more maps, 18 to 14 before).
- Against a walled-in player who masses his army and attacks the computer's base at minute 15 and again at 25, nine games a level at double speed: the player now wins 1 of 9 against Medium (6 before), 1 against Hard (3), 1 against Vicious (4) and none against Insane (4), and the computer wins 5, 5, 6 and 6 of 9 where it won 0, 4, 2 and 2.
- Medium fired a ready general's power half a minute late since the last change; only Easy waits now, a minute as before.
- Replays with a computer player recorded before this change will not play back.

## The computer goes after your superweapon

- A Scud Storm, Particle Cannon or nuclear silo the computer had seen was worth a tenth of its price to its own strikes, by a note EA left in the code ("Superweapons cannot be killed by any superweapon"), so its strikes went to your power plants and your army and never to the silo. Now a superweapon it has seen counts at half its price on Easy, its full price on Medium, twice on Hard, and more on every level above.
- The computer's jets and helicopters fly at a superweapon of yours it has seen: a third of its armed aircraft on Easy, two thirds on Medium, all of them on Hard and above, sent again every minute on Easy, every 30 seconds on Medium, every 15 on Hard and sooner above. Such a strike is no longer called off for the anti-air guns on the way. It only goes for a superweapon it has actually seen; the game's warning that one was built says nothing about where it stands, and the computer gets no more than that.
- Easy now uses its general's powers too, a minute after each one is ready. It fired none in 40 games; it fires about one a game now, against nearly seven for Medium.
- On the turtle bench, a walled-in player firing a superweapon on its cooldown from minute six, nine games a level at double speed: Medium killed the superweapon in 7 games of 9 (1 before), Hard 8 (7), Vicious 8 (6) and Insane 7 (6), and it now dies at a mean of 12 to 14 game minutes where it lasted 15.5 to 17.7.
- Replays with a computer player recorded before this change will not play back.

## The computer stops sitting on its army

- Every level kept a large part of its army standing at home. The guard teams the base scripts fill are only called out once you are nearly beaten, and an Insane computer held a twelve-thousand attack at your defences for minutes while 56,000 more of its army stood in the base behind it. Now whatever stands idle at home past a share of the whole army goes out: Easy keeps three fifths at home and looks every minute and a half, Hard keeps under a third and looks every 40 seconds, and each level above keeps less and looks sooner. The spare units join the next attack and count towards the odds it weighs against your guns, or go out on their own. They still stay while their base is under attack, and a small group still will not walk into defences it cannot beat.
- An attack your defences hold back now waits at most two minutes forty on Hard instead of three, and less the higher the level. The computer counts its own losses on the road as part of what holds it back, so one that lost an attack used to sit out the full three minutes.
- On a small map a computer could send the same attack 4,000 times in one match without it ever leaving. Its road to you ended inside its own base area, so every attack walked a few steps, stood idle at home and was sent again on the next look, and an Insane computer that had taken its enemy's command centre next to its own base ran a match out with 267,000 of army that never fought. An attack whose road ends at home now hunts down the nearest enemy it can find instead, and stays put when it finds none. That match sends none of those attacks now, and with the seats swapped the Insane computer wins it about a minute of game time sooner. One thing is still missing there: what the enemy keeps alive at the end is something the computer cannot find, so the match still runs to its time limit.
- Above Hard the smallest attack a computer will send stays at Hard's. Insane sent nothing under 11,700 of army, two and a half times Hard's figure, and so attacked later and less often than Hard did.
- On 40 games a pair at double speed, Hard now sends 8.1 attacks a match against Medium where it sent 6.0, Medium's first attack leaves at 5.5 game minutes instead of 5.9 and Easy's at 7.0 instead of 8.4, and Hard loses fewer units to your defences for every kill (0.075 against 0.087). The levels above Hard still do not beat Hard by as much as their names promise; that is the next piece of work.
- Replays with a computer player recorded before this change will not play back.

## Ground markers in machined steel

- Every targeting marker on the ground is new, and every ground-aimed power of every side and general has one of its own, forty in all, each shaped for what the power does and moving its own way while you aim and on the click. The paradrop is a parachute canopy that breathes and snaps open, and the troopers' own canopies come down where they really land. The A-10 rings the circle its missiles land in, with strafe tracks streaming along its run inside it and six missiles closing in pairs. The Fuel Air Bomb ripples overpressure rings out of its detonator until one shock rolls past the rim. The radar van gets a sweeping scope, the spy drone a camera iris that opens, the repair a gear that ratchets round and lights green, the anthrax a lumpy gas cloud that churns, the EMP a zigzag lightning ring that knots up and fires one pulse, the nuke a trefoil that slams upright inside twelve arcs, the Particle Cannon a spinning gyroscope whose scorch follows the real beam, Turkiye's Kargu swarm drones that circle and dive, and the UAV the racetrack it flies inside the circle it watches. A marker is the shape of what the power hits: a power that lands on a circle draws circles and arcs only, so the spy satellite, the artillery barrage, the minefield, the tank drop, the crate drop and the Helix's nuke lost the squares and hexagons they first wore, and only strips like the carpet bombs and the napalm run stay straight. They are drawn the way the mouse cursors are: thin flat strokes in one colour with a dark line round every mark, and the cursors' four small triangles closing on the target from the four sides of every frame, so a marker and the cursor aiming it read as one set. The guard's shield is the guard cursor's, as a thin outline. Each side shows in its fittings, America's octagon studs, China's gold rivets, the GLA's crooked bolts and Turkiye's turquoise light line. The colour still says the family at a glance: gold for drops, orange for air strikes, amber for barrages, red for superweapons. The guard keeps its ring and swinging brackets. A missile out of your own silo, the nuke, the SCUD Storm and the cruise missile, no longer draws a lane in from a map edge it never flies from; the cruise missile's route starts at its launcher. The Comanche's rocket pods, a dozer's mine sweep and the Maroon Beret's drones play their marker on the click too.
- The Particle Cannon, the Laser General's cannon and the supply crate drop never had a targeting circle at all; now they have one, the cannon's as wide as its beam sweeps.
- Air powers now show where the planes come from. A lane slides in from the map's edge nearest your building, as wide as the formation flies, with chevrons marching towards the target and an arrow at the rim. Paradrops and bombers mark every drop on the lane before you click, and a carpet bomb whose last bombs fall past the target shows the turn they fall on as a bracket, since the plane's exact turn depends on how fast it is flying. A plane that turns over the target, the crate drop and China's carpet bombers, also shows the rest of its flight: where its first and last drops leave it, the straight line it takes off the map from the last one, and a ghost plane flying the whole path while you aim.
- A marker is for aiming, and it leaves with the click. Once you fire it plays a short release over the target and is gone. The first version kept a lane trailing every plane and missile and a countdown ring round the target until the strike landed, which buried the very spot you were watching under lines. The strokes are finer as well, as thin as the cursors' own.
- The Spectre shows its orbit and the line it flies in on, and the whole orbit turns counter-clockwise, the way the gunship really circles; its dashes used to run the other way. Turkiye's Kargu swarm and swarm munition draw their lane from the base they launch from, not from the map's edge.
- Markers lie on the water's surface where they cross the sea, not on the seabed under it.
- Move and attack clicks close in on the point as the cursor's own mark, four arrowheads for a move and four triangles for an attack, and leave the cursor's yellow dot for a second and a half.
