- The order lines from your selected units to where they are heading are easier to pick out on busy ground, and each starts at the edge of its unit's ring instead of over the hull. The mark a move click leaves and the rings at every queued point are twice their old size.
- The unit or building you order an attack on blinks in your own colour now. It used to blink a strong red whatever colour you played.
- The rally point is new as well. EA's blue laser and the flag that only showed with one building selected are gone: every selected factory runs a dashed line in your colour from its door to its point, the dashes creeping towards it, and there a hairline pole stands in a fine ring on the ground with a slim pennant on top, cut a different way for each side: swallow-tailed for America, stepped for China, torn for the GLA, slanted for Turkiye. A new point snaps down with a faint ping, the pole drops in, the pennant unfurls and the line grows out of the door to it; aiming one shows a ghost ring and line under the pointer first; factories sharing a point share one ring, their lines meeting there; a building you are placing shows where its units will gather. It stays readable in the shroud, keeps one size and shape on the ground at every zoom, shrinking on the screen with the ground as you pull back, and is drawn in the mouse cursors' own hand, every stroke one pixel of dark line round your colour, which holds its width all the way round the ring instead of thinning at the top and bottom. The first version, a steel frame round a full flag with block arrows marching on a double rail, read as far too heavy.
- Classic graphics keep the original markers. Only you see your own markers after you fire, as before; there is still no warning marker for enemies.

## Watching a match at a glance

- Watching a match looks like playing one now. The watcher's HUD is one more command bar in the same three-tier steel as the sides' bars, built from three of them: America's radar box in the bottom left, China's centre panel for the player you follow, and Turkiye's box in the bottom right for the players. Going from your own bar to watching after you lose moves nothing under your eye.
- The radar's glass is the map's square, and beside it stand five keys: the standings, the vision, chat, options and the menu. Hover one and a card on the radar's ledge says in one line what it does and which key does it.
- The box on the right is as tall as its list and no taller: one column to 16 seats, two past that, a head for each team with its army's worth, and a row a seat with its seat number, its army's picture, its colour in a light keyline so purple and charcoal hold on the dark glass, and its army in one format, "$18.9k". The best army carries a white rule and the list's foot says what the rule means. Over the list sit the clock, the teams' shares of every army poured into one power bar with a mark at its middle so a close game reads at a glance, and two dropdowns for the camera (free, follow, director) and the stat.
- The standings key turns the box into one list of every seat ranked by the stat you pick, with seven columns: money, income, army, kills, power, builds and the superweapon's clock, the picked one wider and lit. Click a column's word to rank by it. Two seats with one name carry their seat number, "Hard AI 14" and "Hard AI 29". Gold means the player you follow, in every list, and nothing else.
- Click a row and that player's panel opens where your own command grid would stand: his money in the tab, his power poured into the rail, his general's picture with a star a rank, his income a minute, kills and losses, power used of made, fourteen kinds of unit with their counts, the next three things he builds with their clocks, and his two soonest powers counting down. A base under attack still pulses red on its row.
- Tab lists every seat, all 32, a column a team, with money, kills and a mute key beside every other human, and its foot carries the map, the match's length, its speed and how many are watching.
- Alt+S opens the standings and Alt+V steps the vision; Alt with F, G and D, A, T and P, and 1, 2 and 3 pick the camera, the vision and hide the radar, the right box or the panel, Alt+0 clears the screen for a clean shot, Alt with the arrows steps through the seats and the stats, and the wheel over the box steps the stat. Every one of those keys has its own line in the Hotkeys menu, under Observer; they only answer while you watch, so they never steal a key from your own game. No word on the HUD is smaller than 14 pixels at 1080.
- EA's observer bar, the column of eight player buttons beside the radar and the readout box are gone. The column stopped at eight players; the box holds all 32. The upgrades a player owns, which the first version of this HUD listed on his card, have no place on the new panel yet.
- Watching a match, the Esc menu, Options and message boxes opened underneath the observer panels. The panels step aside while one is open and come back when it closes.
- With the fog of a player turned on, the radar is his: units only their own player sees on his radar, which every watcher saw on the map, now show for that player alone.

## Night falls on the battlefield

- A new box under the match rules, Day and Night, for the host of a skirmish, a LAN game or a custom online room. Ten game minutes of day, a minute and a half of dusk, four minutes of night, a minute of dawn, and round again. At night every unit and building clears the fog of war a fifth less far: the dusk takes it down in two steps and the dawn gives it back the same way, so a scout that sees a base at noon has to walk closer to see it at midnight. Guns still reach as far as they always did, so a tank can fire at a spot its own eyes no longer show, as long as someone else is looking. Pausing stops the clock with the game.
- It is off unless the host ticks it, and it stays off in Quick Match, Play vs AI, the Apocalypse and Direct Strike. Replays and saves from before this change play exactly as they did; a replay of a match with the box ticked brings its nights with it.
- Now you see it fall. With the box ticked every match opens at noon, whatever hour the map was made for, with the sun at its highest, and the first dusk comes five game minutes in. The sun crosses the sky through the day and the shadows turn with it, long and warm after dawn and before dusk, short at noon. At dusk its shadows fade as it sets, the moon comes up with shadows of its own, and the light sinks to a cold blue moonlight. The sun's light fades with its shadows, so the turn to the moon happens in the dark and nothing jumps. Over the same few seconds the cloud shadows thin out and the water darkens to its night sky. Dust and smoke darken with the light instead of glowing tan on a black field, and infantry take the map's own night lighting. Faces turned away from the moon keep about three fifths of their daylight, so a tank in the dark is still a tank and not a black cut-out. Dawn brings the day back the same way. With the modern graphics on Direct3D 11 it all moves smoothly with no hitch; Classic graphics and Direct3D 9 move the sun in five degree steps and relight the ground over a few frames. A map built dark keeps more of its own light, and one whose daytime light was left black falls back to its own hour instead of blinding you.
- And the lights come on. Forty-five seconds into the dusk the first windows light up, and over the next twenty the rest of the town follows, each building in its own time; street lamps and posts follow within six seconds and vehicles switch their headlights on within four. Thirty seconds into the dawn they go out the same way. A building or tank made in the night has its lights on from the moment it appears, and a map made for night opens at noon with its windows dark and lights them at dusk like everywhere else. Replays of matches with the box ticked from before this change go out of step once the first lights come on, a little under six game minutes in.
- Night has a moon now. Players told us that at night they could hardly see anything, and they were right: the night maps lit a tank at about a third of an afternoon, some had no moon at all, just a dim light straight down, and the Reforged lighting took a little more off on top. With the Reforged lighting a night map now gets a deep blue moon about 40 degrees up, so every hull and wall has a lit side and a dark side, and a blue sky light keeps the shade readable; a map whose own moon was brighter keeps it. The Day and Night box's moon is two thirds brighter and bluer too, and smoke and dust lighten with it. It still reads as night, blue ground under black shadows with the windows and headlamps glowing. On Dark Night's village square the picture's average brightness went from 49 to 66 on the map's own night and from 21 to 32 at midnight with Day and Night ticked. The Classic lighting keeps a night map exactly as EA lit it.
- Dusk and dawn swapped the sky in a single frame, day clouds cutting to night stars. The clouds now fade into the stars over the turn of the light, and the moon fades in with them.
- And now the lights light something. A lit window used to be paint on the wall and nothing more. With the modern graphics on Direct3D 11, a building whose windows are lit throws a warm pool across the street around it and onto the tanks and soldiers standing there, street lamps and stadium floodlights pool light on the road under them and glow at the head, and a searchlight leaves a white patch where its beam comes down. It works on maps made for night and in the Day and Night box's nights alike, and a lamp knocked over goes dark. The ten nearest lights in view take part, after the fires of the Firelight option, so a burning base keeps its glow. Buildings themselves never glow. Over Tournament City's downtown at night, ten lights lit, the average frame went from 1.68 to 1.93 ms on our test machine. Classic graphics and Direct3D 9 look as they did, and nothing here touches the game itself, so replays and online games are unaffected.

## Apocalypse v1.0, a survival mode

- Solo Play has a Mods button under Skirmish, and it asks Direct Strike or Apocalypse. Apocalypse opens the skirmish room on a fresh Apocalypse map with you and one computer ally; seat up to three computers beside you or close them all and hold out alone. Every Start builds a new map for the seats you filled.
- LAN and online custom games can be Apocalypse games too. Create Game and Host make a classic room straight away again, without asking every time you host; the Mods button beside them asks Direct Strike or Apocalypse and makes that room. An Apocalypse room seats up to four, everyone in the room builds the same map from its name, and the game list and the room's title say which mode it is. Each player stands on the start that matches his seat, so the first day's waves come at the first seat's walls.
- A new random map kind for any number of players: everyone starts together in a basin walled in by cliffs, supply right behind every base and a pile outside each pass for whoever dares a sortie. The dead walk in from the edges of the map without end and go for whatever of yours is nearest. You lose together when the last of your buildings and units falls; they never run out. They come as red-skinned Zombies, fast Runners that come at night, and hulking Brutes. Day gives you room to build, dusk thickens the waves, and night brings runners and brutes in waves twice the size, under a red sky with every building's night lights on. Each dawn hands the next day back, and each new day the dead come one rank tougher. In a two-player test the first six and a half minutes sent 1,085 of them and the bases killed 1,060.
- A thin red fog now rings the map along every edge. No scout, radar or power ever sees into it, the dead rise anywhere inside it and walk out at you, and any of your units still standing in it after four seconds dies there. Smoke, dust and the fog take the red of the sky, faint by day and deep at night. Apocalypse replays and saves made before this change will not play back.
- The dead no longer trickle in one by one. Each wave masses at one or two passes, which glow a deeper red twenty seconds ahead, and at night they hit several passes or all of them at once. A wave grows with every one before it and grows faster when you hold the last one far out. Runners and brutes cost the horde more than walkers. Any soldier the dead kill gets up three seconds later as one of them.
- Apocalypse is a co-op map for two to four players now, always on the biggest map the generator makes. The ruled ring of cliffs is gone: each player gets a lobe of his own in a ragged basin, no two the same shape, facing the pass that comes in where the land outside lies lowest, and every lobe opens onto a shared heart with a supply dock and tech derricks. Past the escarpment lies a stretch of wilderness, hills, a dry riverbed and woods in clumps, about a minute's march for the dead before the fog, and the fog's edge follows the land instead of a ruler, reaching in down the valleys and holding back off the ridges. There is always one pass more than players, sometimes two, so at least one sits on the seam between two of you and needs you both. The waves take the fronts in turn so nobody sits out the night, and every third one goes for a seam on purpose. A fallen ally leaves the waves as big as they were.
- The fog glows red where the dead gather in it, brighter the thicker they stand, so you see a horde massing before a pass long before it comes through. It shows how many, never who.
- In Apocalypse a small steel tray at the top of the screen keeps the match's time, and a bar along its foot shows the day and night with the sun or the moon riding it, the time left until the light turns and how many nights you have lived through.
- You can no longer click or drag-select the dead, so a box over your own army around a horde picks up only your army. Attacking them, force-fire and attack-move work as before.
- Allies no longer send each other money in an Apocalypse match; the Tab screen's money column is gone there, as in Direct Strike.
- Killing the dead now promotes your general. The dead belong to the civilians, and the game has never scored a civilian's losses, so a whole night of kills left you at rank 1 with nothing on the score screen. Every zombie you kill now counts as a kill and earns your general's points, 10 for a walker, 8 for a runner and 40 for a brute. It pays no bounty and gives the unit that fired no rank. In a five minute test the two seats came out with 226 and 780 points; rank 2 takes 800.
- The Supply Drop Zone pays in Apocalypse. Its cargo plane comes in over the map's edge, through the red fog, and the fog killed it four seconds in with the crates still aboard: the logs of earlier test matches hold 202 of those deaths. A plane that one of your general's powers flies in from off the map, a supply drop, a paradrop or a bomber, now crosses the fog unharmed. Aircraft you order into the fog still die there. In the same test the drop zone went from paying nothing to 1500 a drop.
- Apocalypse nights run lighter. Every time a computer player weighed sending a unit to plant a charge or hack a building, it looked up the button set of each of its 150 to 210 units by name against every button set in the game, and on a four-seat night that lookup alone ate a twentieth of the game's time. It now remembers the answer per unit kind. On the same four-seat map and seed the average game tick fell from 16.0 to 14.2 ms, and the computer players make exactly the decisions they made before: 18,000 frames in, the match carries the same checksum. Classic skirmish and Direct Strike computers ran the same lookup and get the same saving on a smaller scale.
- The dead no longer queue for directions. Every zombie used to ask the route finder for its own way to the middle, up to ten a frame at night, and stood in the fog until its turn came: on a four-seat night the longest wait was 473 frames, nearly sixteen seconds. The map now keeps one shared chart of the way in from every spot to the nearest of your buildings, redrawn piece by piece as walls go up and come down, and a zombie reads its route off it the moment it rises. On the same map and seed, played side by side, the route queue's share of a night fell from 8.3% of the game's time to 4.4%, the deepest it got from 304 to 195, the longest wait from 473 frames to 279, and the average game tick from 24.0 to 22.1 ms. They walk for your nearest building on the way in instead of for the middle, so the first thing they hit is whatever of yours stands nearest their pass. A zombie now counts as having reached your bases when it gets to one of your buildings, and a wave counts as having broken through when ten of them did since the last, so the waves still grow and shrink about as before: the test match ended on a 210% share against 190%, with 167 of the dead at your buildings where 46 had walked in to the middle. A save made mid-night carries the chart exactly as it stood.
- The dead answer the sky and the wall now. Spitters lob acid 150 out and hit a helicopter on the move, Bloaters walk into your nearest building and burst, a wall section going with them, and flocks of six Carrion Bats bite aircraft and ground alike. From the second night Screechers hunt your aircraft and paratroopers first. A Bloater shot early bursts where it falls and takes the dead round it along. Flyers count as aircraft, so every anti-air gun aims at them.
- The tank front walks in. Juggernauts in bone plate shrug off rifle fire and need your tanks, Spine Lancers throw bone spears that go through armour, Shield-bearers spit your rockets and missiles out of the air before they land, Bone Mortars shell your base from 320 out, and from the fourth night one Siege Ram for each of you a wave comes for your walls and rolls over your tanks. The Brute has his own body at last, broad and bald with fists like clubs. A Shield-bearer's dart is an ivory streak with a puff of bone chips off his spur and a burst of splinters where it strikes the missile, where it borrowed the Paladin's magenta laser; a Spitter's acid gob flies as a green glob trailing a dark fume, and a Bone Mortar's cluster draws a dark marrow-red trail along its arc; a Burner's shoulders burn with a man's flame instead of a burning building's; and under Classic Graphics the acid gobs and the Bone Mortar's shells now show in flight, where they flew unseen.
- A Shield-bearer's dart brings a Tomahawk's missile down in one hit. It used to leave the missile flying on a fifth of its health, so a Tomahawk salvo landed on him anyway. Apocalypse replays recorded before this change will not play back.
- The first day is walkers only. Runners and Brutes wait for the first dusk, and each new kind of the dead has a night it first walks, at dusk and night from then and by day from the day after. Flyers take at most 15 percent of a wave until the fourth night, 25 after it.
- Your general ranks up faster on the dead: a zombie kill pays 20 points for every point of threat it carries, 20 for a walker, 40 for a runner, 120 for a brute, twice what a walker paid before.
- The dead hunt the gaps now. Crawlers drag themselves over the wall beside the pass you hold, Bile Lobbers retch over your garrisons from 200 out and every lob that lands kills two men inside, Burners set your infantry alight and leave a fire where they fall, Gasbags burst into a toxin cloud that stays, and from the third night Gas Divers drop onto aircraft parked in a clump. From the second night packs of four Hounds come at whichever of you has built the least defence at home.
- The dead learn to hide and to help each other. From the third night Stalkers walk unseen and are only found when their knife fingers are already in your gunners, unless a detector sees them first; from the fourth, Burrowers come hidden under the soil and tear up through your wall, leaving a hole that spits the dead for 30 seconds, and the Rotmother heals every one of them near her by 5 percent a second. Howlers drive the dead round them to strike harder from the second night. From the fifth, a Shocker's touch or death shuts your tanks, aircraft and defences down for five seconds, and Leeches crawl into any vehicle left alone and drive it at you with the next wave. A vehicle they take pays your general like any kill.
- The hosts come with the fifth night. The Abomination, a rolling wheel of fused bodies that bullets barely dent, leaks radiation where you hit it and bursts into eight walkers where it dies. The Broodmother drags six crawlers about her and grows a new one fifteen seconds after you kill one; kill her and the brood drops with her. Spore Drifters float over your walls and burst into poison after ninety seconds if nothing shoots them down first. From the fourth night a Bloat Sack rolls in with ten walkers inside; kill it far out or they pour out at your gate. From the sixth night the Brood Carrier flies in with eight bats about it and drops six crawlers where it falls. The Runner has its own lean, bare body and sprint at last.
- Every third night is a Blood Moon, and its peak wave brings a boss. The Colossus walks in on night 3, three storeys of fused bodies that heads for your most expensive building, crushes every tank in its way and throws your army aside with each stomp. The Wyrm flies over your walls on night 6 and breathes bile on aircraft and ground alike. The Plague King comes on night 9: the dead that fall near him get back up, and when you kill him he falls, lies four seconds and stands again. From night 12 two of the three come together. A Blood Moon wave is half as big again, brings twice the elites, and the fog goes the colour of blood, the night's light a deeper red than on the other nights. A boss has half its health again for every player past the first.
- The dead no longer come out of the fog in neat rows. Each wave spills out in clumps, with stragglers lagging behind and empty ground between, and packs of hounds and flocks of bats come loose instead of in formation.
- Waves now have a rhythm. A night opens with a probing wave, builds, and two thirds in throws its peak at every gate at once, then gives you a breath before dawn. Each wave leans on one kind of threat: a shambling horde, fast hunters, wall breakers, spitters and burners, or a sky full of flyers.
- Nobody wins an Apocalypse match, you only last, so the game no longer tells you that you were defeated. When a player falls, everyone reads how long he held out; the match ends on Game Over instead of Defeat, the defeat voice and the failure music stay quiet, and the score screen's headline is how long you survived, with the time beside every team. Spectators see the time held on a fallen player's banner too, and an Apocalypse match no longer counts as a loss in your skirmish record.
- Apocalypse replays and saves recorded before this change will not play back.
- The toxin cloud a Gasbag, a Gas Diver or a Spore Drifter leaves where it dies poisoned the dead as well, so the walkers behind a Gasbag died in its cloud and cleared the way for you. It now hurts only the living. Apocalypse replays recorded before this change will not play back.
- The Juggernaut and the Siege Ram shrug off rifles and Gattlings for real: their bone plates take a tenth of small-arms fire, down from 15%, after twenty Rangers were seen gunning a Juggernaut down on their own. Bring tanks, rockets or artillery.
- A Broodmother's and a Brood Carrier's young now count toward how many of the dead can walk at once. Deep into a four-player night they had stood 252 over the 700 the director allows, which is where the late nights got heavy.
- The Plague King raises his staff while the fallen around him get up again, and a Broodmother heaves as she lays each new crawler.
- With every player on one team in the lobby, an Apocalypse match now ends when the last of you falls, with the Game Over screen and the score screen after it.

## Computer allies stay in their own corner

- A computer ally whose base filled up kept walking its new buildings outward and took the first open ground it met, and the flattest open ground near it was usually your start. One player found a Hard America ally's airfields, factories and Tomahawks packed into his corner, and the next game a China ally put every war factory and barracks there. A computer now treats ground nearer an ally's start than its own base as his and builds elsewhere; an ally who has lost everything gives his corner back.
- A computer that falls behind earns more, and it judged that by its team's worth a player at a time. Beside a weak partner in a two against one it read itself as losing to the lone enemy it outnumbered and banked up to two and a half times what its trucks brought in, and in one 27 minute match a Hard ally built 1,731 units. It now sets its whole team against the whole enemy team, so in a two against one the lone computer is the one that gets the catch-up money.
- Replays with a computer player recorded before this change will not play back.

## The computer builds superweapons like a turtle does

- A Hard computer waited for its twelfth finished defence before its first superweapon and then stopped at two, while a player behind his walls put up five and wiped it in one push; the levels above Hard asked for even more guns per superweapon, so they built fewer still. Every level now pays four defences for each one, and once the first stands the computer adds another whenever the bank holds its price. In twelve four-player Hard matches on Twilight Flame all 48 computers put one up, the first at a median of 3.8 minutes, and held a median of three by the end, ten at most. Easy and Medium still build the one their scripts ask for.
- A computer walled into a small corner of the map had nowhere to put one: on the turtle bench a GLA computer asked for its SCUD Storm up to 300 times a match, sat on 108,000, and was told there was no room every time. When nothing fits inside the base, a superweapon may now go up to half again as far out, behind the base and never on the side facing you. The same GLA computer on Hard now has its SCUD Storm up two and a half minutes in, in two of its three bench matches; at the levels above Hard its walled-in base still finds no room.
- A computer threw away a building whose planned spot was only too close to its own supply pile, or lay off the edge of the map, as if an enemy stood there, and never looked for another spot. A China computer on a small map lost its only supply centre this way twice a match, earned nothing and never built a War Factory; an America one lost its power plant and War Factory. It now moves the building to the nearest spot that fits. On the turtle bench that China computer builds its supply centres and its War Factory and wins all six of its matches, where it won two; the GLA computer above Hard now gets its SCUD Storm up in two of three.
- Brutal, Vicious, Savage and Insane built their superweapons exactly like Hard: four defences for each, and a spare only once the bank held its whole price, so on Twilight Flame all four held a median of four or five. Now the higher the level, the hungrier it is. Brutal and Vicious put one up on every three defences, Savage and Insane on every two, and a spare goes on order once the bank holds 83, 71, 56 or 45 percent of its price, the rest saved as it comes in. In four-player matches on Twilight Flame the first one now stands at a median of 6.7 game minutes on Hard, 5.8 on Brutal, 5.4 on Savage and 5.0 on Insane, and the most standing at once is a median of 4, 5, 10.5 and 9. Hard and the levels below it play exactly as before.
- Replays with a computer player recorded before this change will not play back.

## Computer allies give up as a team

- A computer weighed only itself before typing GG, so allied Easy seats facing one strong player each saw a lost match and gave up unfought; seven Easy seats against one player given 180 tanks were all gone before a shot was fired. A computer now sets its whole team's worth against the strongest enemy team. In ten matches of two allied Easy seats against one computer at a rating of 4200, three seats gave up, each with its team under a fifth of the enemy's worth.
- Replays with a computer player recorded before this change will not play back.

## Soldiers fall where they are hit

- Ragdoll Deaths, under Options, Display, is a new setting, off by default. A soldier who dies goes limp and drops the way the bullet or the blast pushed him: shot from the left he folds to the right, a rocket at his feet lifts him and throws him clear, and on a hillside he comes to rest along the slope he fell on. Every side's infantry falls this way, and so do the heroes, the generals' own soldiers, pilots and civilians: on a test field of 17 kinds of soldier, from Rangers and Red Guards to Colonel Burton, a Toxin Rebel and a burning civilian, every one of them went down limp. Past the 24th body falling at once, a death plays the old animation. Switch it in the middle of a match and the next death follows the new choice while those already falling finish their fall. Looks only: where the body lies, how long it stays and when it goes are what they always were, so your opponent's setting is his own and replays play the same either way. Off under Classic Graphics.

## Wrecks slide off walls, shells clear the hill

- The slope the game reads off the ground, which tanks and cars tilt to as they drive and wrecks bounce off, was worked out wrong on every hillside. EA's formula took one corner's slope from the wrong pair of heights, leaving the right one unused, and then blended the four corners of each patch crosswise, so each corner's slope pulled hardest at the opposite corner. The slope now comes from each patch's own four corners, blended the way the heights already were. The heights themselves have not moved.
- A soldier beside a building or a tank was checked for contact as a square of his own width, turned the way he faced. Turned 45 degrees, that square reached 41% further than he does, so he touched corners he was clear of, or stopped touching them, by turning on the spot. He is a circle now. A thin box laid across a wider one with no corner of either inside the other, a wall across a hull, did not count as touching at all, and now does. Along two sides of every building a strip up to half a map cell wide was never checked against what stood in it; every cell a building covers is checked now.
- A unit that only ever moved a little at a time, a tank turning slowly on the spot or one edged along by the crowd, drifted away from where the game had it filed, and anything that looked for it nearby looked at the old spot. Small moves add up now until it is filed at its new place.
- Two idle units that ended up on top of each other could shuffle forever. Both were told to step aside, from both sides, every step, and when the nearest free spot was where one of them already stood it was sent there again and again. Now one of them steps aside, once.
- The game's test for whether something is in the air was set for the original game's step and read 2.25 times too high at today's speed, so a unit thrown up by a blast counted as standing on the ground while still well above it. It reads the original height again.
- A burnt hull or a piece of debris that has come to rest stays at rest. When a bounce ended, EA's game put back a setting nothing had ever filled in; once that was fixed, hulls and plates bounced again every time something nudged them and snapped level at each landing. A body now stops bouncing when it lands, until another blast throws it.
- A carpet bomb no longer spins a wreck up like a top. Every hit added to the spin with nothing to stop it, so a dozen bombs in a second turned a hull faster and faster. The spin hits give tops out at two hits' worth.
- Wrecks and debris that hit a wall fall down it. EA's game stopped a body dead every frame it touched a building, its fall included, so a hull thrown against a wall hung there and crawled down it, and one coming down on a roof was held in the air over it. Only the speed going into the wall is taken away now: the body keeps falling and sliding along it, and leaves at a share of the speed it hit with.
- Debris from a dying vehicle leaves with its throw and nothing more. Each piece starts inside the hull that threw it, and the push that parts overlapping bodies shot it out at up to 150 units a second on top of the throw. The pieces ignore their own hull now, and that push has a ceiling. A crashing jet's wings and plates took the jet's whole speed with them, because their weight was set only after the speed was handed out; they leave with their share now. Two bodies meeting dead centre pushed each other weaker the closer they got and never parted, and a hull marked as never moving was shoved around like anything of its weight. Both are fixed.
- A wreck sliding into parked tanks or a squad of soldiers stops against them instead of going through them.
- A unit thrown by a fuel-air bomb or a nuke bounces off the buildings it hits instead of ending up inside them, and one that comes down on a roof keeps its life; it used to be wiped out on the spot. A tank thrown onto a bridge no longer dies for the river under the span. One knocked down on an aircraft carrier's deck gets up again: the game took the deck for the air and kept it down for good.
- Debris and bodies that fall on a roof slide off it. They used to vanish the moment they touched it.
- A soldier killed by a rocket or a blast is thrown away from it, up to 45 degrees either side. EA threw him any way at all, so he flew into the blast as often as out of it.
- A car killed by a fuel-air bomb or a nuke goes as high and as far as the blast throws it. It used to get the toss a driving car takes from a shot on top of that, and went about twice as high and as far.
- However hard the hit, a thrown car now tips at most 80 degrees in the air. A heavy supply truck hit hard went nearly end over end, and a car thrown down a slope or off a ledge stayed up long enough to tip past upright, after which it unrolled on landing in a fast barrel roll.
- A car thrown onto a roof lands on it and blows up there. The game only knew terrain and bridges as ground, so up on a roof it counted as still in the air until its landing time ran out.
- A helicopter or a jet shot down over a building crashes on the roof, with its fireball, its burnt hull and the crash damage to the building. The game used to delete it the moment it touched the roof: no blast, no hull, gone. A falling helicopter that drifts into a wall stops drifting and drops beside it instead of passing through, and one that crashes on a roof does not plough on through the building.
- A toppling building crushes what lies under its whole width. EA's game halved that width twice, so only the middle half of the falling building hurt anything. The strip under its tip took a hit every game step, so the damage there went with the step rate, and once the building lay flat it went on crushing past its tip. The tip now crushes once, when it lands.
- A burning tree burns the soldiers touching it as often as in the original game. At today's game speed it fired a third less often.
- Artillery fired over a ridge clears it. A shell's arc was set by its height over the straight line to the target, so an Inferno Cannon shell fired over a hill went into the hillside. The arc now rises as high as the ground in between asks for, up to a launch about 72 degrees up. A shell following a moving target near a crest no longer jinks up in mid-air, and shells stopped coming down a step short of their aim, further short downhill: the game's gravity kept pulling on a shell whose path already allowed for it. A shell in the air when you save flies the same path after you load.
- A Turkiye shot aimed where none of your radars reach misses some of the time, but a weapon that hits at once, with no shell in flight, never missed. Those land on the ground beside the target now, like the rest.
- A Dragon Tank's flame whose target is gone falls to the ground like any other shot instead of bursting in mid-air. A missile turned toward a flare that burnt out at that very moment could crash the game; it keeps its own target now.
- Replays recorded on an earlier version will not play back on this one. A game saved on an earlier version still loads and plays on by these rules from there; a save made on this version does not load in an earlier one.

## Ray traced sun shadows

- Shadow Quality under Options, Effects has a fourth choice above High: Ray Traced. High's shadow is a picture of the battlefield seen from the sun, and every shadow is read off it, so its edge can never be finer than that picture's dots. Ray Traced follows a line from each pixel on your screen to the sun and checks it against the real triangles of every tank and building in the way, so their shadows are as sharp as your screen at any zoom. Leaves, fences and rotors still take their shadow from High's picture, which keeps their gaps.
- Ray Traced shadows soften the way the sun's do: hard where a tank's tracks meet the ground, wider toward the far end of a tower's or a tree's shadow, by how far that spot is from what casts it. The softening is measured on the ground, so zooming in shows the same soft edge larger instead of a sharper one. On Twilight Flame the soft edge reaches about half a unit of ground either side on average, at the usual zoom and at half the distance alike, and three units at its widest.
- At Low, Medium and High, a building's shadow no longer ends in stairs when you zoom out. The further out the camera, the larger the area each dot of the sun's picture covers, and the edge used to be read off a single dot, so on Twilight Flame at the wheel's limit on Low a shadow's edge stepped in blocks about six units of ground across. Every dot the edge touches now counts by how much of it lies under the edge, so the edge fades over two dots at any zoom and no step shows.
- With Ambient Occlusion on as well, Ray Traced also works out the soft dark round a building's foot and under a tank by sending short lines from every spot on the ground to see what closes it off from the sky, where the old occlusion could only guess from what the screen shows: the back of a building and the far side of a tank count now. Around a base on Twilight Flame a sixth of those lines hit something and the ground there keeps about 82% of its ambient light, open ground all of it. It costs about 1.2 ms more of the graphics card's frame than the old occlusion at 1280x720.
- At Ray Traced, the flash of an explosion, a tank's muzzle flash and the glow of a fire (Firelight's too) now cast shadows. Until now their light went straight through walls, so a shell bursting behind a building lit the street in front of it. Now every lit spot on the screen checks for a building or a tank between itself and the flash, and keeps the light only if nothing is in the way, so the near side of a building glows and the far side and the ground behind it stay dark. The colours, reach and fade of every light are the game's own. A nuke's flash still lights the whole village square on Dark Night, and only the stone tower and the trees throw shadows across it. In a busy night fight on Dark Night about a third of the lit ground is shaded this way; it costs about 0.6 ms of the graphics card's frame at 1280x720. A light can still slip through a gap in a crowd of tanks.
- Leaves, fences, shrubs and the ground foliage now count for Ray Traced's ambient occlusion and for the shadows of explosions and fires, leaf by leaf: a line that passes through a gap in the leaves goes on, one that meets a leaf stops, the same cut the sun's shadow already makes. When a nuke lands beside Dark Night's square, a third of the ground its flash reaches is shaded, where a ninth was before, and every tree throws a long dark streak away from the blast. On Alpine Assault's mound thirteen times as many of the occlusion's short lines hit something (11 829 against 889), so the ground under the trees and the trees' own crowns darken where they used to stay flat. Grass under an explosion's flash is lit by it now: it went down after the flash's light and stayed dark, at 63% of the brightness of the ground round it under a nuke, 71% now. With Ambient Occlusion, Firelight and Ground Foliage on at 1280x720 the graphics card's frame went from 4.35 to 4.18 ms on Alpine Assault, the occlusion getting cheaper in the same change, and from 4.85 to 5.47 ms on Heartland Shield.
- Pine trees at Ray Traced are as bright as at High again. The ray traced sun darkens what is already on screen, and the pines were drawn before it, so each took the shade of its own needles and came out 21 to 30% darker than the same pine at High; they go down after the sun's shade now. With MSAA on, the thin bright or dark line along a tank's or a building's edge wherever it crossed a shadow is gone: each smoothing sample on the edge takes the shade of its own surface, for about 0.1 ms.
- Ray Traced's ambient occlusion no longer looks grainy. Each spot sent two lines a frame and the result was smudged over its neighbours, which left cloudy dark blotches on open ground, roofs and tree crowns and a grain that crawled when you scrolled. Now every frame sends its two lines in new directions and adds them to what the frames before found at the same spot of ground, up to sixteen frames, so a base's yard comes out smooth and the dark stays where buildings and tanks really close off the sky. A tank that drives off takes most of its shade with it at once and the last of it within about half a second. On Twilight Flame at 1920x1080 with the camera still, the share of the picture that flickers from one frame to the next fell from 1.5% to 1.0%, for about 0.07 ms more of the graphics card's frame.
- It is new and still experimental, and it costs: on Twilight Flame at 1280x720 the graphics card's frame went from 1.18 ms to 2.35 ms, on Heartland Shield from 1.36 ms to 2.94 ms. Water, smoke and anything see-through keep High's shadows.
- It needs Direct3D 11 on Windows. Under Direct3D 9 and in the Mac and Linux builds the choice is not in the list, and a saved Ray Traced draws High there. The Performance / Quality slider never picks it. Looks only: replays and network games play the same with it on or off.

## Supporter and Bug Hunter skins

- Backing the project now shows on your supply line. A supporter's Chinook and China Supply Truck wear a gunmetal hull with metal lines that climb with what you gave in total: Iron, Bronze, Silver, Gold, Emerald with green inlay, and at the top Reforged, gold on platinum with navy pinstripes. Every general's Chinook takes it, the Air Force General's Combat Chinook included, and so does the truck, its burnt hull and the pieces it throws when it dies. Your team colour stays on the trim, the crates keep their own paint, and a unit wears one grade at a time.
- Players whose bug reports got something fixed get the Bug Hunter dozer: worn work steel, a safety yellow blade in black hazard bands, and on the China dozer's cab roof a struck-through bug. It comes for the USA and the China dozer alike, and you can wear both at once.
- The first skin for a soldier, and the rarest one there is: Special Thanks, for the GLA Worker. Nobody earns it by playing or paying; it is handed out by hand on zerohour.gg to the people this project owes. Your team colour still shows on his cap and trousers, the crate he hauls is repainted too, and he keeps it on a Combat Bike. On the Skins tab it is the one look framed in gold, its name in gold under a gold star, locked or not.
- Both are picked where Splinter Camo is, on the Skins tab once you are signed in online, and both have a set painted for Classic Graphics. In a match everyone sees them, the replay too; they change nothing about how the units work.
- The Skins tab shows the skins themselves now, where it used to show their names on blank cards. Your units sit on the left by side, USA, China and GLA, each with its cameo and how many of its looks you own. Pick one and its looks fill the middle, three to a row with the normal paint first, each card the real unit in that paint and nothing but its name under it: a tick marks the one you wear, a padlock the ones you lack, with a bar of how many you have and a filter for all of them, the ones you own or the ones you still lack. The look you click turns slowly on a steel plate across the whole right panel, with its name and one button: Wear, Worn, or for a look you lack what earns it (Gold Supporter, Redeem a Code, Bug Hunter Badge), which opens zerohour.gg. A look you do not own is shown in shadow rather than hidden, so you can see what the Reforged Chinook looks like before you back the project.

## Sunlight between the buildings

- Options > Display > Picture has Sun Shafts, Off, Low or High. A low sun now lights the dust in the air as well as the ground: in a town or a forest the air in front of a wall the sun is behind stays dark, and the sunlit ground in a narrow gap between two shadows takes soft warm streaks running the way the shadows do. Open ground in full sun stays as it was, and nothing standing in shadow is ever brightened. The air also glows a little toward the sun along the top of the screen, and turning the camera round moves the glow to the other side. It is meant to be quiet, strongest on morning and evening maps and gone at night; with Day and Night ticked it fades out at nightfall, comes back at dawn and runs warmer through the dusk. Air over the black shroud never lights up, so it gives nothing away.
- It follows the sun's own shadows, so a unit hidden from you casts no band. It needs Direct3D 11 and the shadows on, and stays off under Classic Graphics.
- Ground Relief, under Options > World and off by default, lets the stones, cracks and ridges of the ground catch the map's sun, so a rocky slope shows its relief where it used to lie as a flat painted sheet. It needs Direct3D 11.

## Buildings stay whole at full zoom-out, bridges lie flat

- The rebuilt units and buildings swap to lighter copies as they shrink on the screen, and the lightest copy of some of them had lost its walls. China's Propaganda Center turned into its red roof floating over bare ground at full zoom-out, and the damaged Propaganda Center, the damaged Black Market and a few hundred neutral buildings lost their bodies the same way. A lighter copy that has lost more than half of the model is never drawn now: the building stays on the next one up. 1,271 of the 6,135 rebuilt models skip such a copy.
- Options > Display > Models has Full Detail at Distance, for anyone who would rather see every unit and building at full detail however far out the camera is. It applies the moment you press Accept.
- The big road bridges over the canyons of Killing Fields, and every other Tampico bridge, drew as a wall of grey streaks hanging into the gorge. The game measured the rebuilt bridge's pieces wrong, took the whole bridge to be one unit long and stretched it over the gap. The pieces are measured right now and the bridge lies flat across the canyon in its sections again, deck, railings and piers.
- A bridge whose two ends stand at different heights, which random maps built from an official map can give, leaned its piers and side walls sideways unless it ran from west to east: EA's code tilted every bridge as if it did. Each bridge now tilts along its own length; a level bridge draws exactly as before.

## Land past the edge of the map

- Pull the camera out over a corner of the map and the ground now carries on where the black void used to start. It rolls into low hills with no repeating pattern in them, wears the edge's own grass and rock in patches that fade into one another along ragged borders rather than in stripes running straight out, with the rock inside a patch turned a different way every seven steps or so instead of laying the same ridges in rows a few steps apart, and about 1600 units out it has faded into the colour of the horizon, which is also what fills the screen past it. A flat camera used to look out over a black band that read as a black sky. Where the map's edge runs into the sea, the sea goes on too, out over sea floor that stays under the water instead of climbing out into a beach; on Tournament Island the water used to stop dead in a straight line along the edge. That sea now keeps the depth of the water beside it, so Tournament Island's shallows run on past the corner instead of ending in a lighter square with a dark line round it where the sea floor past the edge dropped away. With Atmosphere on, the haze used to start in a hard line exactly on the playable edge and hide everything past it; now it thickens gradually from the edge of the terrain outward, so the land shows beside the map and is all haze by the time it ends. It is only a picture: nothing can go there, and the game itself does not know it exists. Both terrain detail settings draw it; the low one builds a small texture of the edge's own ground for it rather than the full terrain texture it does without.
- That land past the edge is no longer bare. Woods stand on it in clumps with open ground between, brush along their margins, scattered rocks, and further out crags blown up from the same rocks, thinning as the land fades into the horizon. What grows there is what the map grows itself, weighted toward what it puts near its own edges: pines and autumn oaks past Alpine Assault, palm groves and willows past Golden Oasis. A map that places none of a kind gets what its edge's ground calls for, firs in snow, palms and cactus in desert, pines and oaks elsewhere. The trees sway in the map's breeze, catch its light and throw shadows with the rest, and nothing stands on the sea, so Tournament Island stays an island. Pulled all the way out over a corner it costs about 0.3 ms a frame: 4.71 to 4.96 ms on Golden Oasis, 3.39 to 3.77 on Alpine Assault, uncapped at 1080p. Like the land under it, it is a picture only; nothing can reach it and the game does not know it is there.
- The out-of-bounds strip round the playable map is no longer solid black when a match starts. It sits a shade darker than ground in the fog, so you can see the terrain under it and still tell where the map ends. The light used to drop to that shade inside one fog cell at the playable edge, a straight line along the map like a ruler laid across the sea; it now falls off over four cells, about 160 units, round the corners too. On maps whose playable area stops short of the terrain, Twilight Flame among them, a band past the top edge and a strip past the right one stayed pitch black, wide enough that an observer saw the top of the map drawn dark; that ground now takes the same shade as the rest of the strip. A mission script that shrouds the border makes it black as before, and one that clears it clears it.

## Direct Strike plots twice the size, jets on the plot

- Your plot holds twice what it did, 192 slots, and it stands upright now: 16 slots across its front and 12 deep, where the first version of the bigger plot was 12 across and 16 deep. The grid reads the way your army marches, and a full wave walks out a third wider than before.
- Every income level you buy raises an oil derrick behind your plot, up to four in a row, and everyone in the match can count them, watchers and replays included. They are scenery: they pay nothing extra, cannot be shot, taken or clicked, and stand clear of the grid.
- The upright plot changes the island under it, and every random map gets a new name with it, so a replay recorded on any random map before this version no longer plays back. That is every Direct Strike and Apocalypse replay too.
- The two air rows behind the plot are gone. A jet goes on the plot like any other unit, in any slot it fits. It still never marches: its copy waits off the map with your squadron and strikes when the fronts are about to meet. Jets you place in the same row fly in line, and one placed further back takes off further back. Computer seats put their jets at the back of the plot.
- The fortress drops to 4000 health and the watch tower to 1500 to go with it. A full plot sends a wave of up to 80 units, and at 6000 two such waves ground each other down in the middle for good: five of twelve computer 3v3s on Hard and Brutal had no fortress down after 40 minutes. At 4000 nine of the same twelve end on a fortress kill, eight of them between the 22nd and the 27th minute, at a median of 25.6.
- Direct Strike replays and saves recorded before this change will not play back.

## Direct Strike keeps to its own rules

- Nobody sends money to anyone in Direct Strike or the Apocalypse any more. The money column on the Tab screen is gone in those matches, and a gift sent from an older copy of the game is turned away.
- The hero portrait in the bottom left corner is gone from Direct Strike. Your hero keeps his own card on the Direct Strike bar.
- The rank, upgrade and passenger chips over a plot unit were flat grey boxes, the last plain fills left on the Direct Strike bar. They now wear your side's steel like the cards in your hand, the picture sunk in one glass well and the price in another.
- Dragging a box over the field selects nothing in Direct Strike. Clicks and the plot work as before.
- Marching waves no longer wear the "F" formation letter. They still march together at their slowest unit's pace.
- The watch tower and the fortress see stealthed units now, the tower out to 250 and the fortress out to 325, a little past their own guns.
- Units no longer earn rank in the field. The only rank a unit has is the one you bought for it, and your general's points still come from kills as before.
- A Troop Crawler's Red Guards and the pilot a ranked American vehicle throws out when it dies were never part of the wave. You could click them and give them orders, and they never died of old age. They join their wave now: nobody can select them, they march with it, and they die when the unit they came out of would have.
- A jet on your plot sent a fresh copy with every wave while the last one was still flying, so one Aurora in a 1v1 became three by the third wave. A plot jet now has one copy alive at a time. When a wave finds it still up, that copy takes the upgrades and the rank you bought since, and the next copy goes out once its 130 seconds are over.
- The fortress shoots at aircraft. It had no gun that could reach them, so helicopters hovered over it untouched while the Watch Tower in front of it shot them down. It now carries the tower's own anti-air gun on the same turret: two Comanches parked over it, which used to sit there at full health, are both down eight seconds after they arrive. It is still one turret, and it finishes whatever it is shooting before it turns. Helicopters that arrive first cost a tank wave about two seconds of the fortress's fire; tanks that arrive first keep it until they are dead.
- Direct Strike rooms open at 1.0x, and the speed chip beside the team size picks 1.0x, 1.25x, 1.5x or 2.0x: the host's pick in a LAN or online room, your own in skirmish, and Rematch keeps it. The waves, the lifespans and the countdowns now run on game time, so a match at 1.0x is the same match as at 1.5x played slower: a wave every 67.5 seconds instead of 45, and every unit lives 195 seconds instead of 130, which is enough for the back row of a full plot to reach the front. Before, a LAN room hid its speed box and played whatever its host last picked, and at 1.0x that back row died of old age on the way. At 1.5x nothing changes.
- The Watch Tower patches itself up between pushes: once it has gone ten seconds without a hit it regains 5 health a second, so a tower that survived one wave is close to full for the next. Under fire it never heals.
- The Watch Tower's cannon hits a fifth harder, 12 a round instead of 10, up to 144 damage a second once it has spun up. China's Gattling Cannon in the normal game is unchanged.
- Bringing down an enemy Watch Tower pays 500 to every player on your team, once per tower.
- No tech tier has a single unit any more. The GLA's Toxin Truck moves up to tier 2, and the Bomb Truck and the Battle Bus to tier 3 beside the Scud Launcher; China's Helix moves to tier 3. The GLA reads 8, 5 and 3 units, China and the USA 6, 5 and 3. The Stealth General, who had nothing in tier 3, now has the Bomb Truck and the Battle Bus there.
- The Nuke Cannon, the Scud Launcher and the Tomahawk do 60 percent of their damage to units in Direct Strike, so one shell no longer flattens a whole block of a packed wave; against towers and the fortress they hit as hard as ever. The Aurora's bomb does 75 percent to towers and the fortress, and the Pathfinder takes two shots for a Red Guard or a Rebel instead of one. The normal game is unchanged.
- The Microwave Tank has a job in Direct Strike: its beam stuns enemy vehicles with the ECM Tank's numbers, while its field keeps cooking infantry. Towers and the fortress cannot be stunned.
- Black Lotus carries a light gun in Direct Strike, 20 a shot every half second at short reach, so she does more than hack. Jarmen Kell already shot infantry. A hero uses a button at most once every 30 seconds of game time.
- A Dragon Tank lays its wall of fire, and a Toxin Truck its slime, at most once every 20 seconds of game time per unit.
- A Dragon Tank no longer burns down its own fortress. Its wall of fire hurts everything standing in it, your own buildings too, and a fresh Dragon meets the enemy right at its own walls, so it laid the wall through them: in a staged siege its walls took 1,516 health off its own fortress in eight minutes. A wave unit now holds back any button that can hurt its own side, the wall, rocket pods, neutron shells, while it stands within 250 of its own fortress or Watch Tower, and fires it freely out in the lane.
- Colonel Burton no longer stands idle in a wave. When the man he went for with his knife died before the blow landed, he stayed locked on the knife, never fired his rifle again and never walked on, for the rest of his life. He now drops the knife and marches.
- Your waves walk straight through your own fortress and Watch Tower instead of squeezing round them. The enemy's still block his units, so nobody stands inside an enemy building to fight it.
- A Spy Satellite scan on the Direct Strike bar: 200 a scan, click anywhere on the map and 300 around the spot is uncovered for ten seconds, then shrinks away over five, and hidden units in it can be shot. One scan every 45 seconds. Until now only the Watch Tower and the fortress could find a camouflaged Rebel or a Stealth Fighter in the lane.
- A Hacker can hack the internet in Direct Strike. Switch it on in the abilities panel and his wave copies stay behind and earn cash for their whole life instead of walking up to the enemy's buildings; it starts off. The Terrorist's car bomb stays off the list: only civilian cars can be turned into one, and a Direct Strike map has none.
- Direct Strike replays and saves recorded before this change will not play back.
- A Hacker starts his building hack from 250 in Direct Strike, just outside the Watch Tower's guns. From 150 he stood under them and died while he set up his laptop, so a lone Hacker never switched a tower off. Direct Strike replays with a Hacker in them recorded before this change no longer play back.
- Holding the middle pays more the longer a match runs. The first four waves pay as before; from then on the team past the centre line earns 150 more on every wave than on the last, up to 4500 on top. Between evenly matched teams the waves used to cancel in the middle for 45 minutes and more; six computer 3v3 matches at 1.0x now all end, at a median of 24 minutes, the longest at 40. The income figure on your bar includes it. Older Direct Strike replays no longer play back.
- Direct Strike matches land on 20 to 25 minutes at 1.0x. Every unit a wave sends out, its passengers and the jets included, goes out with twice its health, a suggestion from the players: fights in the middle last long enough for the winner of one to reach the tower instead of both waves melting together. Damage your units do to an enemy tower or fortress pays you half of it, so a push that hurts pays for the next one; bringing a Watch Tower down pays its attackers 750 among them on top of the 500 bounty. On 24 computer 3v3 matches at 1.0x all 24 now end, at a median of 21.5 minutes, where the same seeds ran a median of 28.3 with the longest still going at 40.7.
- The last two income levels cost more: 1000, 1000, 1500 and 2000, so the fourth is a choice and not a matter of course.
- The computer players fight smarter. They counter the enemy waves already on the lane and the plot whose wave is due next, not just every plot on the other side; two of every five units they buy are solid all-round picks under the counters, so four infantry plots no longer answer each other with infantry for an hour; their opening leans on front tanks with the hero soon after; a team's computers open tier 3 one at a time; they buy one rank or upgrade every two waves at most, and park carriers, detectors and jammers right behind the front instead of in front of it.
- Direct Strike replays and saves recorded before the doubled health will not play back.
- On the end screen of a LAN or online match the first key is called Lobby, since that is where it takes you; in skirmish it is still Rematch.
- Once a Direct Strike match is decided, a player whose connection goes quiet no longer keeps everyone else on the disconnect screen: no four-minute wait for a reconnect, and a seat silent for 12 seconds is let go so the results stay in front of you.
- Leaving a Direct Strike room with the back arrow no longer flashes the ordinary skirmish room's lists and buttons through the fade.
- Tech tiers take time. Tier 2 or 3 is paid when you click it and opens 45 seconds later at 1.5x (67.5 at 1.0x, the same share of the match at every speed); the tier key fills up from the bottom with the time left beside it, and you cannot start the next tier until it is in. Income levels still pay from the next wave. The computer players wait it out and keep buying units meanwhile.
- Mixed armies. The host can tick Mixed armies in a Direct Strike room, skirmish, LAN or online, and every seat gets its own hand drawn from the USA, China and GLA together: 6 tier 1 units of 21, 5 tier 2 of 15, 4 tier 3 of 10 and one of the three heroes. The draw comes from the match's own seed, so everyone in the room and the replay see the same hands, and the computer players buy from theirs. Each player keeps a hand of his own. The upgrade deck follows the hand: a China seat that drew a Crusader can buy the American upgrade that Crusader uses, from whichever side sells it, up to twelve upgrades.
- Direct Strike replays and saves recorded before the tech wait will not play back.
- Direct Strike replays and saves recorded before this change will not play back.
- Every Direct Strike replay recorded before this change no longer plays back, with stealthed units in it or not, and neither does an Apocalypse replay with a money gift in it.

## The Direct Strike lobby, one console for everyone

- The Direct Strike lobby and the end screen now wear one steel frame for every player in the room, whatever army they picked, so the host and his guests look at the same screen. The seats point at the lane, team against team, a strip of lights on every seat turns your team's colour when the player is ready, and a bar along the foot fills from each end as the teams get ready.
- Change seats in the lobby. Click an open seat to sit there, or a computer's seat to trade places with it, the computer taking the seat you left with its army and colour; clicking the other team's name moves you to its first open seat, or to its first computer's when none is open. You keep your army and colour, and everyone's Ready is cleared, as when anything else in the room changes. In a LAN or online room the host makes the move for you, and refuses a seat that was closed or taken by a player meanwhile.
- The chat fills the middle of the lobby, eleven lines, and the map sits on one line above it.
- Watchers wear that frame too. The observer's bar, radar frame, player panel and spectator drawers were blue-grey steel with America's emblem in the corner, America's rank bar and America's superweapon tray; they are now the lobby's brushed, scratched grey steel with bronze trim and the emblem in grey, and someone watching a Direct Strike match or its replay sees the top of the HUD in it instead of America's.
- Replays and saves from before this change play as they did: nothing in the match changed. Everyone in a room needs this version, as always.

## Direct Strike waves leave from behind the fortress

- A wave now appears behind its own fortress, with the fortress between it and the lane, and marches out past the fortress and the watch tower. It used to appear in front of the tower. An enemy that wants to sit on your spawn has to get past both first. The walk to the enemy fortress is 90 cells longer.
- Direct Strike replays and saves recorded before this change will not play back.

## Direct Strike matches end around the 25 minute mark

- The fortress has 6000 health instead of 4000 and the watch tower 2000 instead of 1200, behind the same armour. At the old numbers the waves took a fortress in a few ticks. We tried 12000 and 4000 and matches dragged past half an hour with both fortresses standing. At 6000 eighteen computer 3v3s on Hard and Brutal, over six islands, ended on a fortress kill at a median of 26 minutes: three before 20, seven between 20 and 30, seven between 30 and 38, and one still undecided at 40. There is no clock that ends a match. A long one runs long.
- Computers save up for tanks again. A computer seat that wanted something dearer than it could pay waited only while the gap was under 300, a figure from the days of 30 second waves. With 45 second waves it spent down every tick, never held enough for a 900 tank again, and filled its plot with infantry the watch tower's gun mows down forever: in one Hard match the seats bought up to 48 infantry each after their opening tank and nobody touched a fortress in 90 minutes. Now it waits whenever the next tick's pay would cover the gap, and that match ends on a fortress kill at 25 minutes.
- The time since the match began sits under your wave's chip at the top of the screen.
- Direct Strike replays recorded before this change will not play back.

## Direct Strike waves every 45 seconds

- Waves now go out every 45 seconds instead of every 30, a team's seats still taking turns, and the first leaves a minute and a half into the match instead of half a minute, so there is time to fill the plot before anything marches. Income comes on the same ticks and adds up to the same 533 a minute as before: 400 a tick, and 100 more a tick for each income level, which still earns back its 1000 in seven and a half minutes.
- Direct Strike replays recorded before this change will not play back.

## A loaded game plays on the way it was saved

A save taken after Jarmen Kell sniped a crew out of a vehicle loaded into a different game: a Lane War match saved at the 7:46 mark split from the straight run within half a second, and a plain skirmish did the same. Three things were missing from the save. Where every unit stood and was heading on the movement grid was rebuilt from positions on load, so units held in place came back blocking cells they had left. A hijacker sitting in a captured vehicle was put back on the map as if he were standing beside it, and when the car died he never looked around again. And whether a hit on your unit calls its neighbours in was forgotten until the first second of play turned it back on. All three are in the save now. The same Lane War save ends on the same checksum as the run that never stopped, 21000 frames in, and the skirmish one matches at 3000. Older saves still load and behave as before.

The second round went after the rest. Saved from your own seat while your Technicals were hitting back, a game loaded with them asking for a new route on the first frame, because their counter-attack was started over instead of read back from the save. A route search left half done at the end of a frame was thrown away, so that unit searched again and the queue answered everyone behind it late. Units leaning on each other at the save stood still after the load, since nothing checked them for collisions again. A team's members came back in reverse order, so a script's "team stop" moved them the other way round. The movement filters, the speed caps after a bump and the width of the road measured beside each route were all started fresh. All of it is in the save now. A two-player skirmish saved at 3000 ends on the same checksum as the run that never stopped at 6000, and rewinding a Twilight Flame replay to the 1:30 checkpoint plays on to the end without going out of sync.

Then the load itself. Every unit is first made fresh and only then handed what the save holds, and a few did real work in that moment. An Infantry General's bunker laid its minefield round the bottom corner of the map, a Laser General's Avenger built a second turret, and a mob or a garrison would have filled itself a second time. Nobody had saved those extra pieces, and since they kept the numbers the load had given them, every unit built afterwards got a different number from the one it got in the game that never stopped, and with it different frames to take its turns on. An eight-player Twilight Flame match rewound to any checkpoint from 1:30 on went out of sync at the very first check, 100 frames later. Teams came back in the reverse order too, so two one-man teams starting their scripts on the same frame swapped their orders. A unit saved on its way back to the post it guards forgot where it was going and set off for the corner of the map, and a GLA rebuild hole left by a building that fell turned into a wall after the load, though in the game itself units walked straight across it. Now the same match saved at 1:30 ends on the same checksum as the straight run at 2:13, and saved at 0:30 it still matches at 5:16.

Late in a match four more turned up. A tank saved while crossing a bridge came back measuring its height from the riverbed under it, so for its first step it took itself for airborne and slid without the grip of its tracks. And every patch of ground keeps its units in the order they last stepped onto it, which is the order bumps and searches meet them in; the load listed them in the order it put them back instead, so a soldier pushed by two of his own on the same frame took the two shoves the other way round. A computer's attack wave given its next order while still carrying out the last one forgot the queued order: EA's save kept each team's current script and dropped everything lined up behind it, so in one eight-player match 13 of 38 teams under orders came back from a load with nothing to do once they reached their staging point. And a player already beaten when the game was saved was beaten again on the first frame after the load: his defeat announced a second time and the whole map revealed to him twice over, which the game counts. All four come back as they were saved.

By then an eight-player Twilight Flame match saved at 21:30 played on to 25:33 and ended on the same checksum as the match that never stopped. The last small differences go too. Every team formed after a load got a number one higher than in the saved game. Putting each unit back on the map counted as the neutral side walking into a trigger zone, and the scripts saw it on the first frame. The script conditions that count units in an area keep their last answer until something is built, destroyed or crosses a zone, so a tank that had died but not yet burned out still counted; the load threw those answers away and counted again. The Infantry General's minefield woke up once on every load, and a building that releases units from fixed points on its model worked those points out again from the loaded model. All of it is in the save now. Older saves still load and behave as before.

One more surfaced once every general played his own style. A computer waiting on a general's power whose building is down or switched off looks again every ten seconds, and the load forgot when the next look was due and looked at once. A Rebel Ambush whose Command Center had just gone back up fired one frame earlier after the load than in the game that was saved, and the two matches parted from there. The next look is saved now. So is the computer's own copy of the rule that says when each of its teams may be built: the load made a fresh one, which checked at once instead of waiting out its delay, so a team due a few seconds later came straight away. The same went for the copies of the scripts every team of a kind runs, and for the script that waits for a transport to empty, which forgot how full each transport had been. Older saves still load and behave as before.

The Nuke and Air Force Generals still split a loaded game from the saved one. A unit's first chase after a target is the only one that lets its turret swing onto whatever passes by, and once a unit had chased and turned to another target, that first chase was over for good. The save forgot it, so after a load a unit that had long since used its first chase looked round for passers-by again, and that look moved every random draw the game made after it. An eight-player Nuke General match saved twenty thousand frames in parted from the straight run eleven seconds later. The flag is in the save now, and so is where each unit's last route led, which an attack move that loses its way measures its next try from. The Air Force match split for another reason: a weapon that fills its clip after a few idle seconds, as a Comanche's rockets do, forgot when that was due, so a Comanche saved with one rocket left flew on with one for the rest of the game while the saved game reloaded it. That moment is in the save too. Older saves still load and behave as before.

The next split in that Air Force match was a paratrooper. Rangers ride in their parachutes inside the drop plane, and the game hides a soldier from the world only through the parachute, which hides nothing itself; the plane hides the parachute and everyone in it. On a load the plane came back before its parachutes were filled, found them empty and hid no one, so every Ranger still aboard sat in the open, and every enemy in reach of the plane could pick a target the saved game never saw. The men stay hidden aboard after a load now. The Air Force match saved at 20000 frames matches the straight run on the next frame, and an eight-player match loaded at 39601 frames holds too. The Air Force match still parts from the straight run further on, for a reason still being chased.

## Direct Strike ends on its own cards

- A Direct Strike match no longer ends on the frame the fortress dies. The fortress gets five game seconds to come down while the camera slides over and in on it, still from the side, the fall runs in slow motion in a skirmish and the edges of the screen darken. Only then is the match decided, and the result waits until the last piece of the ruin has settled, so you see the whole fall.
- The stock Victory and Defeat windows and the score screen are gone from Direct Strike. The result is dealt as one card over two card backs, your general with Victory or Defeat and the match's length, and a moment later the results screen lays out a tall card for every player in his own side's colours: his general, the unit that killed most for him, and seven numbers (waves sent, units placed, money earned and spent, kills, damage to towers and fortress, time held past the middle). Under them a timeline shows who held the middle and both fortresses' health through the match, with the moment each tower fell.
- If the second fortress falls while the first is still coming down, both teams are out and the match is a draw. Before, the team whose fortress fell second won anyway.
- A team whose players have all left a network game, by Exit, Surrender, a dropped connection or a kick vote, loses on the spot and the other team gets its result card at once, with "Team 2 left the game" under the match's length. A player who leaves takes his plot and his waves with him, and if a teammate plays on, the fortress and towers pass to that teammate, so the team fights on. Computer seats never leave, so a team with a computer in it plays on to the end.
- Rematch starts the same seats, armies and colours again on a new island in a skirmish. In a LAN or online game the room closed when the match began, so there Rematch leaves for the lobby as Back to Menu does, and the host opens a new room. Watch Replay plays the match you just finished from its first frame. Back to Menu leaves for the screen the match was started from.
- A player pressed Rematch after his opponent had left an online 1v1 and got an empty framed box instead of the room. The game's disconnect window, the likeliest box, now closes whenever the match it belongs to closes, and its buttons do nothing harmful if they outlive it. We could not make the box appear on a LAN, with the other side leaving cleanly or going silent, so this is a guard and not yet a proven fix. On a LAN, Rematch pressed while that window is up waits until its reconnect timer runs out, about 20 seconds, and then lands in the LAN lobby.
- Older Direct Strike replays and saves no longer play back: the match record is part of every check the game makes.

## Direct Strike with every general

- All twelve armies play Direct Strike, the nine Zero Hour generals beside USA, China and GLA, and Random draws from all of them. Each general's buy panel is what his own factories build in a skirmish, in his own versions with his own look and upgrades: the Laser General's Laser Tank, the Tank General's Emperor, the Infantry General's Mini-Gunners, the Nuke General's Overlord and Helix, Toxin, Stealth and Demolition units with their general's weapons. What a general lacks is gone from his panel. The Laser and Superweapon generals were sold a Paladin and the Toxin and Demolition generals a Hijacker, none of which their armies have; now they are not.
- Older Direct Strike replays and saves no longer play back.

## Direct Strike jets hunt aircraft, Hackers reach the fortress

- A jet bought onto the air rows used to fly its strike to the point where the fronts meet and turn back there. Each strike now flies down the whole lane to the enemy's end as an attack-move, so a jet bombs what it meets on the way, infantry included. A jet that can hit aircraft goes for the enemy's aircraft first: their jets on a pass, and helicopters marching with a wave. In a test a MiG chased an Aurora six times over one strike and later shot down a Comanche on the lane, while an Aurora, which cannot hit air, bombed a Red Guard wave. Jets still park off the map, rearm and fly again.
- Upgrades bought for a jet on the plot now go up with every copy it flies, as they do for ground units.
- Colonel Burton's knife and the Dragon tank's wall of fire were never used in a lane fight. Both reach less than half as far as the unit's gun, and an enemy rarely gets that close before the guns decide it. Now the unit picks the nearest enemy on the ground inside its gun's reach and closes on him to use them.
