- A Hacker can switch off a watch tower or a fortress, which used to refuse him outright. Capturing them is still impossible. In a test three Heroic Chinese Hackers walked up to the American fortress and kept it switched off for the last 26 seconds of the run.
- The car bomb and the internet hack are off the list of abilities your waves use. A car bomb turns one of your own wave vehicles into a bomb, and the lane pays its own income.
- Older Direct Strike replays and saves no longer play back.

## Direct Strike computers build their own plots

- A computer seat in Direct Strike now plays its plot the way you do. Between its own waves it buys units and sets them down over the whole plot, tanks in the front third, infantry and helicopters in the middle, artillery and anti-air in the back third, each band filled from the middle outwards and in depth before it widens. Its general's hero goes down once. When money is left over it sends jets into the air rows, and later it ranks up and upgrades its best units. A harder computer reads what the other team has on its plots and buys against it, more anti-air against jets and more anti-armour against tanks.
- From Medium up it also tidies and trades. A unit that had to stand outside its own band is moved back into it once room opens there, and late in the match a unit that trades badly against what the other team fields is sold, half back after its first wave, for one that trades clearly better. Easy never does either, Medium starts moving from the sixth wave and selling from the sixteenth, Brutal from the first and the sixth.
- How well it plays follows the AI rating, not four fixed levels. Easy takes six seconds over each choice and keeps 600 in the bank. Brutal decides every second, opens the tech tiers sooner and spends everything it has. No level buys income, which takes ten waves to earn back its price. A tier or the hero waits until the plot is worth twice its price, and a dearer unit is only waited for when one more wave's pay would buy it. Every rating between them plays its own point on that curve, and a rating past Brutal carries it on.
- Two computers with the same army and the same rating no longer favour one team. Each used to decide on its own beat, seven frames apart, so the second always saw the other's last purchase before the wave went and the first never saw his. Over 48 matches of China against China the team that looked last won 36; GLA against GLA it won 12. Now every computer decides on the same frame against the plots as they stood before anyone bought: 72 mirror matches split 33 to 39 between the teams, and every plot won between 41 and 58 percent of its matches. The island itself never mattered: the same match played on four different islands ended the same way every time.
- A computer seat started Direct Strike richer than you: 4200 as America, 3600 as China and 2200 as GLA, against the 2000 every seat is meant to have. The skirmish computer's own scripts were still running in the lane and paid it on the first frame, a grant EA wrote to cover a bug in the normal game. Those scripts no longer run in Direct Strike, and every seat starts on 2000 whatever its army.
- A computer seat no longer says GG and surrenders in Direct Strike when the other team's army is worth far more than its own. A team there loses only when its fortress falls, and a test match had ended on a surrender seven and a half minutes in with both fortresses at full health. A Direct Strike replay recorded before this change in which a computer gave up no longer plays back.
- Direct Strike replays with a computer seat recorded before this change will not play back.

## Direct Strike gets its own door

- Solo Play has a Direct Strike button under Skirmish. It opens a room drawn in the match's own steel, nothing of the old lobby left in it: team 1's three seat cards down the left and team 2's down the right, facing each other, each with the general's face in its well, or for plain USA, China or GLA the picture off the side's Command Center build button, enlarged ahead of time to fill the well so it stays sharp, the seat in your side's build. A computer seat asks only how hard it plays, Easy, Medium, Hard or Brutal; no persona, no handicap. The army chip opens a picker of all twelve armies with their generals' faces, plus Random. The room is one compact block in the middle of the screen: an empty or closed seat is a thin row instead of a blank card, and beside Start a 1 v 1, 2 v 2 or 3 v 3 box opens or closes the seats on both teams at once. LAN and online rooms send it like any seat change, so everyone in the room sees the new size.
- There is no map to pick. Every match is played on a new island built from a fresh seed the moment you press Start, and the seed rides in the map's name, so the replay builds the same island again. The rules a lane game has no use for (starting cash, superweapons, unit cap, income sharing, the tech and supply rules, game speed) are gone from the room, and the island never turns up in the Skirmish, LAN or online map lists.
- Create Game on the LAN screen asks Classic or Direct Strike first. A Direct Strike room plays by the same rules, the host's machine picks the seed when the room opens and every machine builds the island from it, and the game list marks the room "Direct Strike" for anyone deciding where to join. Each card's ping bars come from a real round trip to that machine, measured every second; a LAN room used to measure nothing at all. A long chat line wraps inside the panel instead of running off its edge, and the mouse wheel over the chat scrolls back through it. A LAN chat packet holds 100 characters while the chat box takes 128, so everyone else saw a long line cut off at the hundredth; it now goes out in pieces cut at a space and arrives whole, on older builds too.
- Online works the same way. Host a custom game and it asks Classic or Direct Strike; the room is the same screen as the LAN one, chat between the teams, a ready lamp and ping bars on every card, kick through the seat's own list, and the island is built from the seed the host's room carries. Direct Strike games online are never rated, so a lane match can't move your place on the ladder.
- Hosting a game now opens a mode picker in the Direct Strike lobby's steel: three cards side by side, Classic, Direct Strike and Apocalypse, each with a small picture of the mode, its name and version and one line on who plays it, and Cancel under them. Escape closes it.
- Direct Strike now says which version of the mode you are playing: "Direct Strike v1.0" on the main menu button, in the room's title and in the LAN and online game lists.
- In 4.3.0 pressing Back in any Direct Strike room, skirmish or online, crashed the game to the desktop. It was more than half of that version's crash reports. Back now takes you out of the room. The same fault waited behind Start, Send and every pick in the room's lists, and it is gone there too.

## Direct Strike towers and fortresses break where they are hit

- The Watch Tower and the fortress come apart piece by piece. Each shell knocks out the chunks where it lands, as wide as its blast, and never a chunk whose loss would leave the rest hanging in the air. At zero health a tower stands half a second while the death blast clears, then falls away from whoever killed it, and the ruin stays where it landed, a piece left over a hole dropping onto the ground under it. A fall nobody was watching still lands and throws its dust on time, the mouse picks the structure by what is left of it, and a save keeps every hole and every ruin lying the way it fell.
- With the old hard-edged shadows (Direct3D 9 or Classic graphics, with Shadows For Props on) the pieces cast their own shadows as well. A holed tower used to lay the shadow of the whole tower, holes and all, and the moment it fell its shadow was simply gone; now the holes show in the shadow, the falling pieces carry theirs down with them and the heap lies in its own. Under Twilight Flame's low sun the holed tower's lattice shadow runs as long as the whole tower's did.
- The GLA Command Center no longer blinks out when it dies. Shells punch holes in its walls and dome as it takes damage and the holes close again as it is repaired. The killing blow, a nuke's included, brings it down for real: only knee-high stumps of its walls stay, and everything above tips over and lands flat in a low heap of mud brick inside its own footprint, where it lies a while before it sinks away. The canvas awnings fall with it and no longer turn into black slabs on the way down. The Direct Strike fortress and Watch Tower mend the same way, so a tower that patches itself up between pushes closes its holes as its health comes back.

## The computer stops paying for guns it has already seen

- The Air Force General's supply Chinooks flew to the middle docks on Tournament Desert under China's Gattling Cannons, trip after trip, and in 16 Hard matches against China 564 of them were shot down by buildings, 465 by Gattlings. A Medium or Hard computer's Chinook now passes over a pile whose flight crosses an anti-air gun it knows about and gathers from another. Over the same 16 matches it lost 190, and the Air Force won 7 where it had won 5.
- A computer jet flying home to rearm took the straight line back from wherever its strike left it, across any Gattling Cannon in the way, and that is how 94 of the 124 jets the Air Force lost to Gattlings in those matches died. On Medium and Hard it now flies home round the guns it knows about. The Air Force lost 88 jets to Gattlings, 70 of them on the way home.
- A hurt veteran used to be walked out of the fight to be repaired at once, wherever it stood. It turned its back on the enemy and died a few steps on: in the same 16 matches, 984 of the Air Force's veterans and 1,276 of China's died within 15 seconds of being sent off, nearly all inside 3 seconds and 30 metres of where they started, without firing. On Medium and Hard a veteran under enemy guns now fights on where it stands and leaves once it is clear: 167 and 66 died that way. Against GLA the GLA lost 20 where it lost 523. Easy plays as before.
- Turtle behind forty defences, mass an army, and the computer used to hand it to you a piece at a time. A tank left idle at the end of its road went hunting on its own, straight at the nearest thing it could shoot, which was usually the forty guns. On Medium and Hard a unit away from home now hunts only when the units round it outweigh the guns it knows cover its target; short of that it walks home and leaves with the next wave.
- The computer now remembers where its units die. Every unit lost away from home marks the ground it fell on, the mark fades by half in about four minutes. Hard picks its attack road and the spot where its wave gathers by it, and Medium and Hard both weigh it before a wave or a hunt goes. A road it lost a wave on last time is the road it avoids, even when the guns that did it have gone back into the fog.
- A Medium or Hard wave now counts the defences it knows on its road and round the middle of your base, and the ground it has been losing units on, before it leaves. Short of them (Medium wants to match them, Hard to beat them by half) it waits at its gathering point and grows. It never waits more than three minutes: a turtle still gets attacked, by everything that could be gathered in that time.
- Your defences now count when the computer judges who is winning. A base of forty guns and no army used to read as an enemy already beaten, and every computer sent each team the moment it was built. Medium counts about a third of their worth and Hard half, beside your army.
- Every general of America, China and GLA now has a list of guns that fire past their own sight, and the computer adds one of them to a share of its attack teams on every difficulty.
- A Medium or Hard computer fires its general's strike powers (the A-10s, the Spectre, the fuel air and MOAB bombs, the carpet bomb, the artillery barrage, the EMP and the anthrax bomb) the moment they are ready, at the target its scripts would have picked. Easy fires what its scripts name, as Easy always did, and that now includes Turkiye, whose Easy used to fire its own powers on cooldown.
- A turtle whose outer ring stood near the computer's base used to freeze it for the whole match. On a small map one Patriot two base widths away counted as an attack on the base, and every unit the computer sent at it kept the alarm going: a Hard GLA bought nothing and sent no wave from minute three to minute thirty, sat on 243,000 in the bank and walked 5,213 idle units at that Patriot in small groups. The computer now reads your guns and the army you park at home as your base. On the 12 match turtle bench, everything the computer lost fell from 85,000 a match to 26,000 on Hard and from 96,000 to 44,000 at a rating of 2800, and what it killed rose from 34,000 to 51,000 and from 17,000 to 46,000.
- A rich computer stopped forming attack teams. Its factories stayed queued with its favourite units, a team waited for a factory with nothing in it, and a Hard GLA built one team in thirty minutes and kept 485 units at home. Past its savings target a team now takes its turn in a busy factory and picks up the idle units first. The computer at a rating of 2800 sent no wave in any bench match before and sends about 80 a match now.
- The long guns get used. The SCUD Launchers the computer's teams were given never left the factory queue (43 ordered in one match, none built), and a gun waiting at home sat out of reach of every defence. Now they are built, and a gun waiting at home walks out to shell a defence it knows and outranges from a spot no other known gun covers. Units lost near your guns count toward the ground the computer avoids even when those guns stand close to its own base.
- On the turtle bench these last changes win as many matches as before or more (3 of 6 on Hard against 2, 2 of 6 at a rating of 2800) but lose more units to your defences (12 to 18 a match on Hard, 25 to 38 at 2800): the waves still go before the computer knows most of your guns. The two wins it lost were China's infantry stumbling into your parked army as if defending its own base.
- Replays with a computer player recorded before this change will not play back.

## The computer plays its general's own units

- Every computer side now works out which units are its general's own. Each unit its buildings offer is weighed against the same unit at the other generals of its faction, on price, health, time to kill and the veterancy its factory gives it, and the ones that come out ahead are its signature units. Its attack teams lean to them, it buys them and the factories that make them first, and a hoard past its savings target goes on them. A unit its enemy's army counters, or one that keeps dying without a trade, is dropped for a while. A general can name its own set by hand in the player template instead.
- A computer's jets and helicopters keep out of anti-aircraft fire it already knows about. Before an armed aircraft commits to a target, the flight there is checked against every enemy gun it has seen that can shoot the air, by what each gun is allowed to hit and how far it reaches. A strike that would cross one is called off for the nearest known target with a clear way in, or the aircraft goes home. An anti-aircraft gun itself is a fair target only when nothing else covers it and the strike kills it. A signature aircraft needs a better matchup before it goes in, and loses favour altogether once the anti-air it knows of is strong.
- A replay or saved game with a computer player in it, made before this change, will not play back.

## The match film stops missing strikes

- A filmed match (the Bot Cup's camera) missed 21 of the 52 general's powers in one cup match. A carpet bomb or an A-10 strike flies in from the edge of the map and its bombs fall twenty seconds or more after it is called, and the camera gave up on a power that had hit nothing after twelve. It now waits up to thirty seconds, knows from the first run of the match when each strike comes down, and is on the target four seconds before the bombs.
- A scan never takes the camera, whatever is going on where it looks. A spy satellite over the middle of a battle used to cut away to it as if it were a strike; a radar scan, a spy drone, a cash hack, a leaflet drop, a paradrop or an ambush now only drops its flag under its player's card. The paratroopers' fight takes the camera on its own once it starts.
- The film no longer splits the screen, not between players and not between two powers. One camera has the whole picture, and a second power landing off it, or a second fight, plays in a small framed window in the lower right corner with the name and army of whoever called it. Before, the second power had to land most of a screen's width further away than that to get any picture at all, so an artillery barrage called on the same frame as a superweapon across the same base was shown nowhere. A superweapon takes the window from a smaller power at once.
- A superweapon or strike that neither the camera nor the window caught comes back as an instant replay: the match is played through a third time and the two seconds before the hit and six after it are filmed on their own, with a list of where each one fits into the match film at the next quiet moment.

## Crashes from the 4.0 reports

- The commonest crash of 4.0 was fixed in 4.1; this round closes what the reports left behind.
- A modded unit with a very detailed model no longer crashes skirmish and online games when it casts a shadow. It casts its shadow normally.
- A mod that renames or replaces units no longer stops 4.1 at startup with an error about TalentsReforged.ini. The general's talents skip the units the mod doesn't have.
- A mod whose Generals' Challenge file misspells a general's name (Project Raptor's does) no longer stops the game at startup.
- A mod whose art has no sky box no longer crashes the moment a match starts on a map that turns the sky on.
- A modded point-defence laser whose weapon the game cannot find stands idle instead of crashing the match.
- A skirmish where a saved setting had turned a computer opponent into the Civilians no longer crashes as the match loads. The lobby throws the broken setting away and opens fresh.
- Pressing an arrow key in an empty list, such as the skirmish map list, no longer crashes the game.
- A cargo plane, Chinook or gunship checking whether it had flown off the map could crash the game if the terrain's graphics were being rebuilt at that moment. It can't any more.
- A rare crash right after a busy moment in a match, when two parts of the game looked up the same unit model at once, is gone.
- On Linux and Steam Deck (Wine/Proton) with no working sound output the game used to crash at startup. It now starts and plays without sound.
- Coming back to a match after a long time away, or after the graphics driver restarted, no longer crashes the game when you open the quit menu.
- A custom map whose train or ferry had no track laid out for it crashed the game the moment that transport was sent on its way, a bug as old as EA's release. It now stays where it is and opens its doors.
- Some Intel and AMD graphics drivers handed the EA logo a picture far smaller than the movie, and copying the frame into it overwrote the game's memory with black pixels: a crash at startup, or a strange one at the first map. The game now refuses such a picture and skips the movie.
- When the game runs out of memory or meets a bad value deep inside, its crash report now says where.
- Skirmish, LAN and online matches against a computer above Hard (Brutal and up) crashed a minute or two in, on every machine in the match at the same moment: about 35 reports from some 25 installs. The raiding party grew past the room kept for eight raiders and wrote over the computer's own notes. Such a computer now keeps at most eight raiders.
- A unit still riding in a transport, tunnel or garrison that had already been deleted could crash the game later: when loading a save in the middle of a match, when leaving for the menu after the score screen, when a map script changed the playable area, and in a tunnel network fight. Gone.
- A transport, garrison or Angry Mob nexus whose starting passengers name a unit the game's data doesn't have now comes out empty instead of stopping the game. Mods ran into this.
- Taking down a beacon while something neutral was selected crashed a long network match, both seats at once.
- Tank tracks in very large battles could run past the room set aside for them and crash Direct3D 11. Track drawing stays inside it now. A tank killed before it ever moved also no longer holds a track slot for the rest of the map, which is how later tanks ended up with no tracks once the slots ran out.
- The save and load window crashed when Delete or Overwrite was pressed with nothing selected.
- Starting a second match in the same session could crash on its first frame, a model reading a unit that no longer existed. It doesn't now.
- A control bar layout that fails to load says so and closes cleanly, where it used to crash at startup. A missing score screen layout no longer crashes the end of a match either.
- Opening the map list in a LAN room crashed the game when the screen it loaded had no Random tab, which ours has had since v3.6.0 at least, so an older or modded copy of it was being read. The list now opens with Official and Unofficial maps only.
- One player's Radeon RX 9070 XT at 4K refused the game its graphics five starts in a row, each one ending on the "make sure DirectX is installed" message. The driver answers "device lost" when another program or the driver itself is holding the screen for a moment, and the game gave up on that first answer. It now keeps asking for a few seconds before it does.
- The launcher shows the state of your install even when a folder inside the Generals folder can't be read. A downloaded file that antivirus removed before it was installed is reported as that, and fetched again on the next Install. A connection that drops during the launcher's own update counts as your network failing, not as a launcher fault.
- A game that would not start and showed the "make sure DirectX 8.1 is installed" box now tries again before it shows anything. It waits while the screen is held by something else, then starts on Direct3D 9 alone, then tries the other display outputs. If every try fails, the box says what to do: update the graphics driver, close overlays and fullscreen programs, do not start the game over remote desktop or on a locked screen, restart the PC, or start with -win. 13 reports came in for this box, eight of them from one player who retried for 12 minutes.
- On a big map with a huge army the minimap could ask for more than 65535 indices in a single picture and crash the match, several times in a row (9 reports on 4.2.0). It now draws in as many pieces as it needs.
- Closing the map picker and opening it again within one frame crashed the game. Fixed in skirmish, LAN and online.
- Pressing Continue on the score screen after you had left a LAN match could crash. You now land in the LAN lobby.
- "Ran out of pathfind zones" on player-made maps of 2000 by 2000 cells: the ids are handed back block by block now, and maps that already worked path exactly as before. The two maps from the reports were not on hand, so this is untested on them.
- Researching an upgrade in an online or LAN game could desync a few seconds later. The buyer's game took the money and the other game never saw the purchase: 11 of the 17 mismatch reports, and in three of those matches the buyer's money differed by exactly the upgrade's price between the two machines. A general's promotion or talent bought in the same way had the same fault. Orders now carry a number that every machine derives the same way.
- The picture wrote its own copy of a unit's speed, facing, armour and weapon readiness into the game while the simulation ran beside it, so selecting a reloading unit changed its weapon state on your machine only. The picture now only reads.
- A crash report now names the window that was being drawn.
- A match no longer crashes when a tank shell is handed an impossible flight path. It hit about frame 200 and was seen on a GeForce GT 730 thirteen times on v4.3.2.

## Long matches keep a short log

- A player sent us a 58 MB log from one match against four Hard computers, and 613,000 of its 955,000 lines were the same one: the game noting, on every pass, that its window was minimized. That line is gone. The one that says the window went away or came back stays. A network game held up by a silent player wrote another line on every pass for every seat, 87,000 of them in one of our tests; only a developer's build writes that one now.
- A computer playing the Infantry General read its Helixes' buttons over and over. It keeps one answer for each kind of unit, and a Helix with the bomb and one without carry different buttons, so every Helix it looked at threw the other's answer away and worked it out again, with a line in the log each time: 291,000 times in a 75 minute match, two thirds of that match's log. It now remembers both. The same match with the same seed wrote a 15 MB log instead of 39 MB and ended on the same checksum.
- An Avenger that died wrote "Object 'AmericaTankAvengerLaserTurret' already registered with partition manager" to the log, 96 times in that player's match. The mistake is as old as EA's release: the dying tank put its turret back into a world the turret had never left. It did no harm and it no longer happens.
- We looked for memory that grows over a long match and found none to fix. Four Hard computers with two Laser Generals among them, 75 minutes of game time without a picture: 1.0 GB a few seconds in, 1.09 GB at the end, 9 MB of that in the last quarter. The same match drawn at 1280x720 for an hour climbed from 5.1 GB four minutes in to 5.9 GB, more than half of that by minute 17 as units and effects were loaded the first time they appeared, and 18 MB in the last quarter of an hour.

## Jets turn for home after the strike

- A jet turns back the moment its last round is gone. Since 4.0 it first broke away a quarter turn from the target and only then came round for home, a wide 90 drawn over the enemy's anti-air, and a jet's turn at cruise speed was twice as wide as EA's. Now the empty jet heads straight for home and pulls its hardest turn to get there: it bleeds speed into the bank and comes round on the tightest circle it has, still banking like a jet, never pivoting on the spot. Three jets sent from their airfield at tanks 1300 out: the Raptor is pointed home 1.0 s after its fourth missile where it took 1.8 s, flies on 95 past the firing point where it flew 159, and its turn is 85 wide where it was 217. The Stealth Fighter turns 57 wide where it turned 135. The Aurora, coming off its bomb run at supersonic speed, used to coast on 970 past its drop before it came round; now 370, and it is pointed home in 1.5 s instead of 3.6. Every jet still clears its target by as much as before or more, and a jet sent home by you or idle too long turns back the same way. A replay recorded before this change, with jets attacking the ground, will not play back the same.
- Units picking their own targets, a jet on attack-move above all, no longer chase wreckage. A dead Overlord's flung gun barrel has one point of health and belongs to the side that lost it, and the target pick, which favours what it kills fastest, rated it above every tank on the field: an Aurora flew round the map at supersonic speed after one and spent its bomb on it. Debris and hulks are never picked by themselves any more; you can still order a shot at one.
- A jet empties its racks in one run. When a tank swerved out of its sights or got under its nose between two missiles, the jet used to swing round its whole wide turn and fly a second pass, through the same anti-air, for the missiles it had left. Now it fires them there and then and the missiles find their own way. In 14 staged strikes by a Raptor, a MiG and a Stealth Fighter on parked and driving tanks, 3 of 36 racks were split over two passes before; now none of 38 is. A Raptor that used to come back 3 seconds later for its fourth missile puts all four in on the first pass. A Stealth Fighter that only ever got one missile off at a Scorpion now fires both. This is a buff against moving targets: the same damage arrives sooner, with fewer trips through enemy fire, though a missile let go at a bad angle can miss.
- An order you queue with Alt behind a jet strike now follows the strike. Send a MiG at a tank, Alt-click a point to the side, and once its racks are empty it flies off that way and then home. It used to ignore the point, go home, reload and fly the same strike again, and only reached the point once the target was dead. A strike with nothing queued behind it is still flown again after the reload, and a second strike queued behind the first waits for the reload as before.
- A jet coming home straight down the runway's line from beyond its far end, as an Aurora does after a strike out there, could weave from side to side without ever turning round and fly on off the map. Pointed away from the runway, it chose which way to turn round afresh every moment by the side of the line it was on, so each swing across the line turned it back the other way: one Aurora crossed the line three times and flew out to 677 past the runway before it came round. It now chooses its side once and turns round that way. Two Auroras sent home from strikes in line with the runway, the cases that weaved, turn round on one side and are down on the runway within six seconds of starting the landing; 26 other approaches by Raptors and Auroras from either end, on the line and beside it, fly exactly as before.

## Computers, aircraft and modes, 23 November

- Easy computer players never asked for an airfield, so an Easy USA or China opponent had no air force all match. All seven sides build one now: in a Twilight Flame match with four Easy seats, all four had begun theirs before frame 4700.
- The Medium Superweapon General waited for a barracks before building its first one, a typo in EA's build order, and fielded no infantry until then. The Medium Air Force General had the same typo on its Strategy Center. Both build now: the barracks stands at frame 957, the Strategy Center at frame 8787.
- The Air Force General's Combat Chinook flew off to gather supplies the moment it left the Supply Center. It goes to the rally point and waits there like a gunship now. Sent to a supply dock it still gathers, and the plain Chinook is unchanged.
- A jet queued from the group panel ignored an order given while it was taking off. Your order wins.
- At the native 1.5x speed, rotor dust, a strafing run's ground trail and a crashing vehicle's sparks came out a third thinner than at retail speed. They have retail's density at every speed.
- A unit that killed the Angry Mob member it was told to attack used to chase the rest of the mob across the map. It carries on only to members within its reach.
- Apocalypse played alone from the second start sent the day waves at the empty side. Every front now faces a start somebody holds.
- Direct Strike: holding a unit card over your plot lights the ground green where the unit fits and red where it does not.
- A Direct Strike LAN room resent its settings to everyone on every frame. It sits still now.
- Ticking Day and Night on an Apocalypse or Direct Strike map left the map's own buildings on their daytime look. The cycle is off on those maps before anything is placed.
- Random massif maps and maps built in a shipped map's image no longer roll a night, and template rivers lay their bridges evenly.
- In a network match nobody can send orders, or a "player left", under another player's seat.
- A banned account got a bare "banned" at sign-in. The login screen says until when, and why when the site gives a reason.
- Installs of EA's censored German edition, German2, have their language files recognised like those of every other retail language.
- At the farthest zoom with the camera tilted flat, a big map's far corner could lose its shadows.
- After alt-tabbing out of fullscreen a map could come back without its trees and bushes until the camera moved.
- On night maps, searchlights placed as map props wear their night model again.
- Leaving a match could crash when the next screen had falling snow: the snow read the last map's fog of war after it had been freed.
- Idle units and idle turrets stood and watched an enemy drive into their reach for two or three seconds. They open fire within about a second. Old replays no longer play back.
- A game saved while the computer's dozer was looking for room to build carries on where it left off after the load.
- A Bomb Truck disguised as an Avenger gave itself away after Composite Armor, because it had no plates. The disguise now wears what the copied player's units wear.
- New option Damage Numbers (Interface), off by default: the damage a hit does rises over the unit in red. When several attackers hit one target at once, the figure is the sum.
- Tank dust on night maps glowed tan over moonlit ground. It takes the night's tint.
- Ground foliage popped in over a second or two after a minimap jump. It fills in within a few frames.
- With Smooth Motion off and vsync on, a battle state could hang for an extra refresh and the next arrive late. Each one shows on time now, and scrolling stays smooth when a tick runs longer than a refresh.
- Box-selecting a whole line of defences stuttered once per defence while their reach was drawn. The fields fill in over a few frames.
- Apocalypse rooms on LAN and online no longer leave an empty gap under the fourth seat, chat fills it, and the skirmish, LAN and online rooms preview the generated map instead of "?".
- In an online Direct Strike room your own seat card shows your ping light.
- Every room on a generated map, Apocalypse included, left preview pictures in your Documents folder, a new set each time a seat changed, and nothing ever cleared them: one test PC had 618 of them, 29 MB. The game now clears the old ones the first time it draws a map preview and makes this session's again as they are needed. A LAN start on a generated map also no longer waits on a map transfer it never needed, which could hold the game on the transfer screen for two minutes when someone started early.

## Screen and controls

- The command bar and menus no longer go dark now and then, as if a shadow fell over them. The sun's shadows and smoke land only on the battlefield.
- Zoomed all the way out and looking toward the edge of a map, the sun's shadows stopped short of the top of the screen, because the area they cover was stretched over the black past the map. It now covers only ground that is drawn, and reaches a little further at its widest, so the far rows of trees and buildings keep their shadows.
- A new match no longer opens on a black screen with only a corner of the map showing. The camera starts over your base every time.
- Camo Netting no longer hides your base from you. A desert base used to vanish into the sand; your own and your allies' camouflaged buildings now keep a little over half their paint, faded and shimmering over the bent ground behind them, so you can read every one at a glance and still tell it is hidden. Camouflaged units keep their fainter ghost, and the enemy still sees nothing until a detector finds it.
- Zoomed all the way in, the camera now stops 150 above the ground, where it stopped at 90, so the closest look keeps more of the fight around a unit in the picture. From there the wheel takes about twelve notches to the whole map. Mission cutscenes and replays still fly their camera as low as they were made to.
- Layout under Options, Interface now reads Reforged, Red Alert Style and Classic. Reforged is the bar you know, every addition in place. Classic is that bar as the original game had it: no build tabs and no socket for them, no signal keys over the minimap (their hotkeys still work), no production list over the radar, no hero button, no squad list or its build tray, the original game's superweapon countdowns, a name and a time in the owner's colour that blink once charged, instead of icons, and the general's powers in the new tray steel as one column that grows up from the bottom, the map clickable between the buttons. Both keep the original game's keys.
- Own two Particle Uplinks or three Scud Storms and the power's button says in gold how many are charged once two or more are, as the original game did, on every layout. This version had wiped that number every frame. The Red Alert style sidebar's General button only shows while you have points or a talent pick to spend, its star flashing; powers fire from the Upgrades and powers tab and their keys, and the wing of power buttons beside the sidebar is gone, and Ctrl+G opens the General's Powers window at any time. The sidebar also leaves out the numbered squads' list with its build tray, and the idle unit keys and the beacon key along the bottom strip; the squad keys and the idle unit and beacon hotkeys work as before.
- The Classic layout's idle worker key is the original game's again. It sits under the options key where it always was, with the last alert key below it, and a click or its hotkey selects the next idle worker and brings the camera to him, or to the tunnel or transport he waits in. The column of select army and idle infantry, vehicle and aircraft keys beside the command grid is gone from Classic; their hotkeys still work. The Classic bar is narrower for it: the steel now closes right after the command grid on every side, so no empty socket stands where the column was, and the battlefield beside it takes your clicks. Reforged and Red Alert Style now do the same; untick Jump to Idle Worker under Options > Interface and they keep the camera where you left it, as before.
- A command button's tooltip names the key that really presses it, as "Barracks (Q)", the same letter the button wears in its corner: the one you set on the Hotkeys page, the fixed letter of attack move, stop and the other orders, or the grid's letter with the command grid on. A button you took the key off, or one that lost its letter to another, shows no key. The card only knew the letter marked in the button's name, so it went on pointing at B for Barracks whatever key you had given it.
- Change the Layout, HUD Width or resolution in the middle of a match and the minimap still moves the camera. After the first change it kept drawing the map but read every click through the minimap that was thrown away, so a click did nothing or sent the camera somewhere you had not pointed, until the next match. Switched Classic, Red Alert Style, Classic, Reforged, Red Alert Style, Reforged and back to Classic in one match, the minimap now takes the camera where you click in all seven.
- Options, Interface has a Selection Outlines box. Untick it and the glowing rings under your selected units and the line around a selected building are gone; order lines and click markers stay.
- Units you put on guard go straight from one kill to the next enemy in their circle. They used to take a step back toward the middle of the post, then turn round for the man standing beside them; a Crusader with three Rebels in reach sat for about seven seconds between kills, and now fires again the moment one drops. A guard circle you widened with the mouse wheel is ground to hold: after a fight a unit still inside it stays where it is, where the whole group used to drive back to the one middle spot after every kill. A guard without a widened circle still walks back to its post, and planes and helicopters on guard fly back to theirs and circle it, widened or not, as they did in EA's game. A replay recorded before this change will not play back the same.
- The group build tray shows how many units are still in production for that group, takes a little less of the screen, and its fold tab is wider, so a quick click in a fight lands.
- Men in an Overlord's or an Emperor's Battle Bunker get out again. Evacuate and the seat buttons did nothing to them since 1.0: the order named the tank, the men sat in the bunker on top of it, and the check that a man is really inside what he is told to leave only looked at the tank. It asks the bunker too now. The Helix's bunker was never affected. A replay in which someone tried to empty such a bunker will not play back the same.
- Frame Rate Limit now applies in the menus as well as in a match. Pick 144 or 240 and the main menu runs at that rate instead of being stuck at 60; Off still holds the menus at 60, so an idle menu doesn't run your graphics card hot.
- Reskinned units no longer load. A bright green Helix or glowing red GLA infantry put in as loose files, in your Documents folder or in an extra archive beside the game is ignored, so every player sees the units the game ships. The few textures this version adds of its own are checked when you join a game, and a changed copy is turned away like changed rules.
- Signing in online now checks every game file the game reads, the archives and the loose art, data and screen files alike. An edited or swapped file stops the sign-in with its name and a word to reinstall from the launcher or delete it and restart, so a reskin never reaches an online match. The first start reads the whole install in the background, and a sign-in pressed meanwhile waits on "Checking game files..."; after that, updates included, only a file that changed is read again.
- The group panel's build tray fills from the left again, in the order the buttons are laid out, and the count digits, the "+N in production" text and the fold chevrons read at a glance; with the tray folded, every chevron on its ledge points the way it will slide out. Its tooltip opens beside the button you point at, and a control group you have just made opens the tray at once instead of after you select it again.
- Skirmish difficulty names (Easy to Insane AI) are translated: Turkish, German, French, Russian and Ukrainian lobbies no longer show them in English. The new Output options and the Turkiye tooltips are translated too.
- The menus and the Options screens no longer fall back to English in German, French, Russian or Ukrainian. About 900 lines were missing in German and 670 to 680 in each of the others: settings, their tooltips, the lobbies, the online screens and Reforged's own modes. All of them are in now.
- No button, check box or option name runs out of its box in any language. Every translated label is 15 characters or less now, so the German "Vertikale Synchronisation" is "V-Sync", and a check run on every build turns away a longer one before it reaches you.
- A building's garrison pips under its health bar are bigger, so you can see at far zoom whether a house is manned.
- Order lines stay solid when the camera is fully zoomed out instead of breaking into dashes, and the ring an order draws is on the ground, under the unit it marks. The attack circle and the attack line also work on a contact you only see on the radar.
- A seat set to a Custom Selection pool shows "Custom Selection" in the lobby's army box, so the other players can tell a pool was set.
- Buildings have their contact shadow from the moment they appear, and Ambient Occlusion keeps its full strength at the edge of the screen. Weather's sand no longer lifts the black shroud.
- Foliage is cleared under a building a mission script or a power creates, the way it is under one you place.
- Fires near the middle of the view get the light when there are more fires than lights, so the ones you look at are the ones that glow.
- Text no longer comes back blank after you return from the lock screen or the graphics driver restarts.
- A save from a game running at another logic rate now says which rate it was made at. A LAN join that is refused says whether the build or the data files differ.
- The repeat button on a unit that cannot be built right now is greyed.
- A radar ring no longer hangs on for one frame under a unit that has just walked into sight.
- Options, Interface has a Hit Flash box, off by default. Tick it and a unit flashes briefly when it is hit.
- A script timer and a save keep the script's input lock, so a save made in the middle of a cinematic no longer loads with your units free to retaliate.
- The online Quick Match server no longer crashes when a map pool is empty.
- Watching a replay no longer reports "out of sync" when nothing is wrong.
- The computer's fights add up the same way after a load as in the match that was saved. Replays of games with a computer player recorded before this change may not play back.
- On Mac and Linux the vertical sync box now does what it says. The picture was held to the monitor's refresh whether it was ticked or not; off, as it is by default, it now runs free as it does on Windows, and on it waits for the monitor. Thanks to SimonWaldherr.
- On Linux, Modern water's swells can follow the map: tick Map-Aware Waves under Options, Water and they bend toward the shore, run along channels and die down behind islands, each sea taking its waves from its own open side. Off by default, and off draws the waves exactly as before. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- On Linux, Underwater Clarity under Options, Water lets Modern water show the shallows: a sunken ruin or a reef standing up out of deeper water shows through the sea that hid it. A broad flat seabed far from shore and anything deeper than about five units keep the murk the map's maker gave them, so a campaign sea under full-size ships stays a sea. Off by default. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- On Linux, a Modern water rule, the kind a modder writes to turn a map's green pools into toxic sludge, can now make that water look like more than a recolour: cloudy so the bottom fades out, rough and dull instead of glassy, its ripples flattened, its waves held down as if the wind could not move it. Each goes from 0 to 1 and the rules the game ships set none of them, so every map looks as it did. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- A damaged or deliberately broken map or game file packed with one of EA's compression schemes could make the game write past the end of the memory set aside for it, the lengths in its header taken on trust. That held for the two oldest schemes and for RefPack, the one most maps are packed with. The game now checks them and refuses the file. A map's scripts got the same trust: a script line claiming more than the twelve settings it has room for wrote past them, and a cinematic caption whose font was written in an unexpected shape was read past its end. Such a map is now refused, and such a caption shows in the normal font. None of the 367 maps checked comes near the limit. Thanks to SimonWaldherr.
- Typing `yardım` or `saldır` in chat, with the Turkish dotless i, now asks your computer allies for help or an attack on Windows. The Windows build had read those two words in the wrong alphabet and never matched them; only the plain `yardim` and `saldir` worked. Thanks to SimonWaldherr.
- A Linux or Mac game can join a Windows player's network game. The Mac and Linux builds left out this version's own unit models and the Turkiye voices, so they counted 8894 models where Windows counts 9199, and every Windows host refused them as running different rules. Both now ship with the game. Thanks to polyfloyd.
- A mission whose script asked whether a radio line had finished before playing it could cut to its next scene as the line began, the old answer still standing. Playing a line now starts its wait afresh, and the other lines keep theirs. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- A mission countdown keeps its pace while a cinematic freezes the world. At 1.25x and up the timer took its share of the frame the world stopped on, again every frame the cutscene ran, so it ran at 1x or 2x until the scene ended, whichever the frozen frame happened to hold. It now counts on at the game's speed, and a save keeps where it was between two ticks. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- A mission's countdown clock no longer skips a second or ticks backwards, also right after loading a save.
- A mission cutscene's camera turns, zooms and tilts smoothly on a fast monitor. It moved 30 times a second and held still in between, so filmed at a high refresh rate the camera stood still on about 70% of the pictures while it was meant to be moving; it now moves on every picture, and stands on 16 to 24% of them. Pause still holds it, a cut is still a cut and your own camera keys take over at once. Skirmish, online games and replays keep the old camera. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- Scripted camera pans in missions now end exactly when the scene's timer cuts instead of a hair early, and at 2.0x game speed on a slow machine they no longer fall behind the action.
- In a mission on a fast monitor the aircraft and every other animated model keep moving on a picture that repeats the last game moment, where they used to stop dead for it while the camera went on, so a plane flying with the camera twitched backwards on the screen. Pause and a scripted freeze still hold them, and skirmish, online games, replays and recordings keep the old clock. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- A laser fired just before a pause or a cinematic freeze now starts at the gun's muzzle instead of the middle of the vehicle.
- The original Generals campaigns speak their briefings again. EA's load screen played the narrator at a set point of the mission movie, and the code that did it had been cut, so the voice never came. It starts at that point once more, or as the load screen opens when the movie is missing or turned off for a slow machine, plays once per mission and stays quiet with voices muted. Zero Hour's training mission names a briefing voice too and now plays it. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- The startup check for reskinned units that lost a piece of their original no longer flags a piece the reskin's own data takes out on purpose with a line naming it. A piece lost without such a line, or added to the original later and missing from the reskin, is still reported. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- On a Mac the game finds Zero Hour in Steam's own Mac library, and in any other library Steam lists there, an external drive's included, and a GOG copy inside a CrossOver or Whisky bottle. It used to look only where Steam keeps games on Linux and asked for the folder. Thanks to SimonWaldherr.
- A Mac crash inside the system's own window drawing is gone. Apple's graphics code could hand the game memory it had taken from the system and the game freed it as its own; on a Mac the game now takes and frees ordinary memory the system's way, as Linux already did. Thanks to SimonWaldherr.
- On Mac and Linux the Modern picture gets the Windows glow: fire, muzzle flashes and team colour stripes past white bloom and fold back through the same tone curve, Internal HDR included, and the Reforged lighting style's grade and local contrast land before the health bars and the interface are drawn, so they keep their colours. Classic graphics looks as it always did. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- On Mac and Linux the Ambient Occlusion option works too: the ground darkens at the foot of buildings, walls and cliffs and under the tanks parked against them, put on before the water, the smoke and the fire so none of those take a corner's shade. It works with the post chain off, as it does on Windows. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- On Mac and Linux smoke and dust no longer slice into the ground and the buildings they drift through in a hard line; they thin out where they meet them, as on Windows. Fire and explosions take the Windows look as well, the flame curling and burning away as it ages instead of a flat sprite fading out. Classic graphics keeps the old sprites. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- On Mac and Linux the GPU Particles setting now does what it does on Windows: particles past the cap go to the graphics card instead of the oldest ones being deleted to make room. The card moves them by the same formulas the Windows build uses, and a system it cannot take stays on the processor as before. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- On Mac and Linux a unit hit by an EMP crackles with its arcs again, a building without power takes the Windows outage look, a cloaked unit bends the picture behind it like glass and a detected stealth unit wears the heat shimmer. Classic graphics draws them as before. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- On Mac and Linux the Team Glow option is no longer greyed out: team colour on the models glows through the picture's bright range as it does on Windows, from the next map on. It stays off until you tick it, and Classic graphics keeps the plain paint. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- On Mac and Linux a defence's range on the ground is the smooth Windows ring in its owner's colour, laid over the terrain itself, in place of the blocky tiles that stepped across the cells. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- On Mac and Linux the Water Foam option draws on the Classic water: foam breaks along the shores of ponds and rivers and the banks soften into the ground, as on Windows. Classic graphics keeps EA's water. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- On Linux the Atmosphere option paints the sky and fades the far end of the map into the horizon, and Warm Light lays its low haze in the valleys, both under the fog of war as on Windows and with the post chain off too. Classic graphics has neither, and the Mac build does not have them yet. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- On Linux the Weather option works: rain, blowing sand and snow fall, the trees sway and smoke drifts with the wind, and a weather haze takes over from Warm Light while it lasts. A map with its own snow keeps it, Classic graphics stays clear, and the Mac build waits for its own. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- On Mac and Linux a big blast throws its ring through the picture as it does on Windows, bending the battlefield and leaving the health bars and the interface straight, and Heat Haze (its box is still greyed there, `-heathaze` turns it on) makes the air shimmer behind flames, exhausts and beams. Both want a post effect such as Glow on, and Classic graphics has neither. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- On Mac and Linux three boxes that sat there doing nothing now work. Battle Marks leaves craters, scorch and tread marks on the ground, Water Splashes throws spray, foam and rings where a shell lands in Classic water, and Collapse sinks a destroyed building into the ground, a big one jolting the camera as it goes. Classic graphics keeps all three off, as on Windows. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- On Mac and Linux headlights throw their cones on the ground at night, a blast lights the walls and tanks round it for the moment it burns, and the Firelight box works: fires light what stands near them, pixel by pixel as on Windows. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- On Mac and Linux Sky And Ground Light works: a model's tops take more of the sky's light and its undersides less, as on Windows. Off, or under Classic graphics, the light is what it was. Thanks to Shin-Aska.
- Custom maps that carry their own name file now show their real name in the map list instead of MISSING.

## A dropped player's army stays, and he can come back to it

- When a player's game crashes or his connection drops, the others sit on the disconnect screen for the usual 30 seconds and then play on without him, but his base and army no longer blow up: they stay where they stood, idle, and can still be attacked. A vote from everyone else still throws a player out the old way, base and all.
- A player who starts his game again can take his seat back. Everyone stops for a moment while his game plays the match up to where they are, the disconnect screen reading "Waiting for Tank to reconnect", and then the match goes on with him in command of his army again. In testing a player killed 30 seconds in came back a minute later, caught up 2000 frames in about four seconds and played on to the end of a 2-minute match with every check agreeing. Online, the hub shows a Rejoin card for the match you dropped out of; press it and your game fetches the match from another player in the room and catches up the same way. While it catches up you see the match's loading screen with its bar filling ("Rejoining match 42%"), not your army fast-forwarding, and with the world left undrawn the catch-up runs faster. The chat says "Tank lost connection" when a player drops, "Tank is back" when he returns, and "has left the game" only for a quit, a vote-out or a forfeit; the disconnect screen counts down to the moment a silent player leaves the lockstep.
- A player who never comes back no longer holds the match hostage. Once every enemy of yours has been gone for five minutes of game time, the match is yours, in a LAN game too, and a ranked match is scored that way. The screen counts it down ("Tank is away. The match is yours in 5:00 unless they come back"), and a rejoin before the count runs out cancels it.

## Play vs AI online

- The online hub has a PLAY VS AI button under Options. One press starts a 1v1 against a computer player as strong as your AI rating, on a map and seed the server picks. The AI rating is a second rating zerohour.gg keeps beside the ladder's, an Elo in whole numbers, and the hub shows it left of the button.
- You play the army saved in your skirmish setup, or a random one when none is saved; the computer's army is random. Cheats and the developer switches that change a match are off in it.
- Your units wear the skins you wear online in Play vs AI too, where they used to go out in stock paint, and the replay on your own machine shows them the same way.
- Win or lose, the match ends back on the hub, where the line beside the button reads "1.0x speed, AI rating 1213 -> 1270", or says why the match was not rated, with your games against the AI and the share you won under it ("35 games · 60% won"). Quitting is a loss, and so is a match left unfinished by a crash or a lost connection. A game whose files differ from the release cannot start one and says so.
- You pick the speed now. Play vs AI has a 1.0x to 2.0x box on its card and plays the match at what you chose. Quick Match has the same box: two players who picked the same speed get it, and when one wants it faster the slower player is asked "IronVizier wants to play at 1.5x. Accept?" with 15 seconds to answer. Yes plays the faster speed; No, or no answer, keeps the slower one, and the faster player watches the answer come in before the countdown starts. Nobody is matched or skipped over speed.
- A computer playing one of the nine generals on Scorched Earth, the one map in the Play vs AI pool that comes from the original Generals, stood idle: a power plant, a few guns and not a single credit earned, so you walked in and won. It was handed plain China's (or America's, or the GLA's) build orders, which ask for buildings a general cannot build. It now plays its own general's, on that map and on every other map made before Zero Hour. In 18 test matches on Scorched Earth, every general earned money where all 18 had earned none before. Replays of such a match recorded before this change will not play back.

## Every online screen in the game's own look

- The online screens used to be EA's 2003 windows with our labels bolted on. Sign-in, the hub, Quick Match, the custom lobby, the ladder, skins and the player card now stand on the same panel and ruler as the options screen and the rooms, with the same buttons, tabs and seat cards. Five tabs run along the top of every page (Home, Quick Match, Custom games, Ladder, Skins), your line sits at the right end of them with your nick, tier and both ratings, and each page's subtitle names the server you are on, its city and your ping to it, with a ping light.
- The sign-in screen has a server panel beside the form: players online, open games and players searching for a Quick Match, as they stand now.
- When the online service goes down for maintenance or has something to say, a plate hangs from the top of the screen in the menus and in your match, in Turkish or English with your game, with the local time it should be back. The sign-in screen says so before you try, and a game, Quick Match or Play vs AI the server turns away says maintenance instead of a bare failure.
- The hub opens with Play vs AI. Its card shows your AI rating with the rank portrait of its tier, your games and win rate against the computer, and the speed you play at. Quick Match has its own card: your ladder rating, your place, your record, how many are in the queue, and a countdown when an abandoned match has locked you out. Custom games lists the open games and the players in them. Under the cards sit your last six matches of both kinds with the opponent, the map, the rating change and how long ago. Sign out is on the button row.
- Quick Match shows armies as cards by general, with the colours in boxes beside them and your ladder rating next to them. Each card carries its general's portrait from the Generals' Challenge, and a side without a general shows its headquarters, the same pictures the army screen in the rooms and skirmish now uses. Searching shows a clock and the window of opponents it will accept now as a track, with the next widening counted down. When an opponent is found you see both armies, both ratings and your chance of winning before the three seconds run out. The map stays hidden until the load screen, since ranked maps are generated.
- The lobby lists games with their ping lights and an Open, Full or Playing chip, puts the chat rooms on tabs with their head counts, and sorts the players by rating. In a game room each human's ladder rating follows his nick.
- The ladder is a table with a win percentage column, your own row pinned under it when you are off the page, your place beside your rank portrait, a track to the next tier, the ranks with their ranges, and Jump to my page. Skins is one card per unit that says Worn, Owned or Not owned and counts the changes you have not saved yet.
- The player card has a tab for Quick Match and one for Play vs AI. Each gives the rating, the win rate by the army the player picked and by the army he met, and his last five matches.
- After a Quick Match or a Play vs AI game the score screen shows a rating card: the old rating, the new one, the tier, how far the next tier is, and whether the result is on its way, confirmed, left unrated or unanswered.
- The ranked screens speak ELO now, the same number the zerohour.gg ladder and your profile show. Your line at the top of the online pages, the Quick Match card and screen, the lobby list and its order, the seats in a room, the player card with its match rows, the ladder with its ranks and the track to your next one, and the score screen after a match all read a whole ELO like 1213 where they used to show the old 0 to 30 rating with two decimals. The line after a rated game reads "ELO +12 -> 1213". The rank bands on the ladder follow the site's: Sergeant from 1000, Lieutenant 1075, Captain 1150, Major 1250, Colonel 1350, General 1500. The AI rating is called Bot ELO, as on the site. A server that has not sent an ELO yet still gets the old rating shown.
- The online screens stopped explaining themselves. Sign-in lost its four help lines, the hub's cards their paragraphs, Quick Match its hints, the score screen after Play vs AI its "how the AI rating moves" box, the lobby its chat prompt, and the long hover texts are one line each. What is left is titles, numbers, buttons and the lines that tell you something went wrong; the cards and panels closed up over the space, and the hub's recent matches show six rows instead of five.
- Fixed on the way: a label that looked for an optional shorter form, and the load screen's count of its tips, each logged a missing-text line for text that was meant to be absent.
- A winner who left a finished online match through the quit menu's Exit used to land on a score screen that said Defeat. The match now stays won.
- On 4:3 screens the Quick Match army cards no longer have lettering a third too big for them.
- Needs the updated game server and site: the player counts, the server name, the ping lights and the match histories come from them.

## Every computer plays to one rating

- A computer player's strength now follows one number, an Elo: Easy plays at 800, Medium at 1300 and Hard at 1800, and every habit moves along with it: the higher the number, the sooner it decides and the bigger the wave it waits for. Money too: Easy earns what you earn and at most a quarter more when it falls behind, Hard half again and up to two and a half times, where every difficulty used to earn half again and up to triple. Easy also waits half as long again between buildings and between teams, which every difficulty used to share, and the number of supply trucks it runs follows the same line. Medium sits halfway along the line now and plays harder than it did. Replays recorded before this change will not play back.
- Hard is no longer the top of the list. Every seat's drop-down in the skirmish, LAN and online lobbies offers four more past it: Brutal AI at 2200, Vicious AI at 2600, Savage AI at 3400 and Insane AI at 4200. Each is the same computer carried further along that line, quicker to decide than Hard and with bigger waves. No balance pass has measured them yet. The name follows the seat to the load screen, the score screen and the broadcast plates, your skirmish setup remembers it, and a LAN host's guests see it on their seats.
- The scale used to be the online ladder's, Easy 0, Medium 15 and Hard 30, with the four levels above Hard at 45, 60, 90 and 120. Moving it onto Elo left Easy, Medium and Hard playing exactly as they did. Brutal and the three above it sit a little lower on the line than before (Brutal at 2200 plays what 42 did, Insane at 4200 what 102 did); in Direct Strike every level plays the plan it played. A saved game keeps each computer at its level, Brutal as Brutal and Insane as Insane, and a computer saved at a rating of its own at the strength it had. Play vs AI's computer plays at the Bot ELO the server drew for the match, and your AI rating on the hub, the player card and the score screen is that Elo too, a whole number.

## Ranked Quick Match plays blind

- Every ranked Quick Match is played on a map generated for that match from its seed, sized for the seats in it, so nobody has learned it in advance. The map list on the Quick Match screen is gone, since there is nothing left to veto.
- The map starts black, as in a skirmish with the shroud on, where every other online game starts with the whole map revealed under the fog. The load screen shows a question mark where the map would be and no start spot for anyone, your own included. Start spots stay random.
- Lobby games, LAN and skirmish start on the map they always did, revealed under the fog. A ranked replay starts black too; a replay recorded before this change still plays back.
- The black start belongs to ranked Quick Match alone. Hidden Map, the box that let a skirmish, LAN or custom online host start the match blind, is gone from all three rooms, Direct Strike and Apocalypse included, and Day/Night moves up into its place. A room never starts black on an old remembered choice or a skirmish setup saved with the box ticked. A replay recorded with Hidden Map on still plays back black.
- A LAN game plays at 1.0x unless its host picks another speed, and a ranked Quick Match at 1.0x unless both players agree on a faster one: the pace of the 2003 game, where every network game used to run at 1.5x. A build order learned against the original clock holds again, and a fight gives you half again as long to react as it did. Custom online rooms stay at 1.5x. A ranked or LAN replay records its speed and plays back at 1.0x.
- The host of a LAN or custom online room picks the speed: Game Speed sits at the top of the match rules with the skirmish room's four choices, 1.0x, 1.25x, 1.5x and 2.0x. A LAN room still opens at 1.0x and an online room at 1.5x, everyone else sees the box greyed and following the host, a change unticks Ready like any other rule, and each lobby remembers the host's last pick. A recorded stats room stays at 1.5x. The replay plays back at the speed the match had. The map preview in both rooms gave up a row to make room for the box.
- A custom game played after a Quick Match, without signing out in between, counted as ranked: its score screen showed the ladder card and your stats filed it under Quick Match. It now counts as the custom game it was.
- Any match on a random map keeps its question mark on the load screen as well, in skirmish, on LAN and in online rooms: the board used to draw the generated map with your start spot and your allies' on it, so a spot the game picked for you at random was out before the first frame. The lobby still shows the spots players picked themselves, and a replay or an observer still sees the real map.
- When your game cannot build a ranked match's map, the match is now called off at once for both players with no penalty.

## Explosions after ZH Enhanced

- A building's blast throws a ring of dust out from its foot that settles in about three seconds, with clods of earth, the bigger buildings a bigger ring. Turn on Collapsing Buildings and the dust goes up round a building as it sinks. A civilian building that comes down floor by floor kicks up dust at every stage.
- A tank dies one of three ways: its turret flies off (about one in five), it blows up where it stands (three in five), or it catches fire and blows up some six seconds later (one in five). The Crusader, Paladin, Battlemaster, Overlord, Emperor, Scorpion and Marauder all do, and so do the Challenge generals' Paladin, Overlord and Toxin Scorpion. The Demolition General's tanks still blow themselves up as often as before. Every wreck burns for about fifteen seconds, then smokes for fifteen more; the hulk stays as long as it always did.
- Shell and missile hits light the ground for longer and shake the view by how big they are, tank shells scorch the ground, and a howitzer or artillery shell landing on dry ground throws up dust and dirt that a shell landing in water does not. The small tank gun kicks up a ring of dust. The Nuke Cannon's shot shakes the view hard.
- The nuke goes off in the order a real one would: flash and dust at once, the fireball, then the rings, the cap and the stem, under a white light that rises and takes three seconds to fade. The MOAB goes off in three stages with a skirt of smoke, and the Particle Cannon, dying, gathers a charge for two seconds before it lets go. The EMP Pulse no longer turns the whole battlefield blue-white: its ground flash grew to some 6000 across, fifteen times the width of the pulse, and now stops at the edge of what the pulse switches off. Its flash, its flares and the light it throws on the ground are the pulse's blue, where the grey flares added up to a white core and the ground light was an explosion's orange.
- Every blast keeps the colours the game always had: fireballs and smoke are drawn in EA's own keys again, and a dying tank or turret no longer leaves a black ball of soot hanging over it. The fireballs now move as they burn, swelling and breaking into lumps. Every fireball card picks one of four shapes as it is born and about half are drawn the other way round, so one blast holds them all mixed and no two deaths repeat; smoke and flames flip the same way. Each puff of smoke and each flame starts at its own point of a churning loop, so two fires side by side never burn in step. Two looks come back from the 2002 beta, laid over the ones you know: a GLA Technical or buggy that dies now throws a ring of grey-brown dust across the ground under its orange glow ring, with a dirty ball of smoke in the middle, and a tank that blows up swells into a fireball about twice as wide, spraying dark chips of dirt and yellow sparks that cool to red as they drift down. Every shell that lands on a tank throws a smaller shower of the same sparks, where it used to flash three white specks for a sixth of a second. Both are gone in about three seconds.
- A badly hurt Raptor, Aurora or other American jet sputters fire from its engine, each black puff born round a short orange tongue, where before it only smoked until it was already going down. A Helix landing or lifting off blows a ring of dust out across the ground instead of pulsing a pale ring under itself. The B-52, the A-10, the Spectre, the cargo planes and China's carpet bomber draw contrails you can see from the default camera, about five wide and gone in two and a half seconds, where theirs were a faint thread. The Raptor's, the Aurora's and the Stealth Fighter's afterburners burn a short orange plume from a blue glow at the nozzle on takeoff and on an attack run, where each engine flashed a white blob as wide as the tail.
- Jets fly like jets. The wingtips draw thin white vortices only while a jet turns hard, where every Raptor, Aurora, Stealth Fighter and MiG used to trail two lines in level flight, and a harder break or a pull-out puts vapour over the wing. The Aurora punches a cone of vapour round its airframe as it goes supersonic on its attack run, and a low pass at that speed raises a ripple of dust along its track, in the colour of the sand, grass, dirt or snow under it, or spray off water. Any jet skimming water throws a line of spray behind it, and the Aurora draws its own contrail up high. On the runway the wheels smoke at touchdown and the takeoff roll blows dust back off the tarmac. A hurt jet trails a thin grey line before the black smoke of a badly hurt one, and a shot-down jet winds a spiral of smoke behind it as it rolls, sheds pieces on the way down and scorches a furrow where it hits.
- Every helicopter flying low blows the ground under it outward, dust in the ground's own colour or spray off water, the lower the thicker, and a Comanche at its usual height still raises a ring of dust you can see on sand; over water the rotor tips wear a ring of condensation of their own above the spray. A decoy flare lights the ground under it as it falls, a falling bomb draws a thin grey line behind it, and with Heat Haze on the air shimmers behind an afterburner and round a Comanche's or a Spectre's gun after a long burst.
- Fire halos glow orange instead of washing out cream at every Glow level, and the Reforged lighting adds local contrast that lifts tanks, craters and cliffs off the ground, for under a tenth of a millisecond.
- Smoke shades itself softly. A thick column, a China power plant's chimney or a burning wreck's, used to come out lit on the sun's side and near black on the other, split down its length by a hard line. The shade now deepens gradually across the back half of the plume, and the far side keeps about half its light, where it kept a fifth.
- Rocket and missile trails are one smooth line. Every puff a rocket left was a corner, so the fire line and the white smoke behind a Tank Hunter's, a Rocket Buggy's or a Stinger's rocket zigzagged from one puff to the next. Now the trail bends through its puffs as a curve, is never wider than the smoke itself, and fades out at its tail instead of ending in a square cut. Under the white line, the 2002 beta's soft grey smoke comes back: it swells and drifts off the line for about a second, thinner than the beta's so a Patriot volley still shows its rockets.
- These effects show under the Reforged look; Classic Graphics keeps EA's, apart from the tanks' three ways, which are part of the game and the same for everyone. A replay or saved game from before this change will not play back.

## The computer builds a second army from what it takes

- A Hard computer player that gets its hands on another side's Dozer or Worker now builds that side's base with it. A GLA Hijacker goes for a lone USA Dozer before any tank, Jarmen Kell shoots the driver out of one and a Rebel climbs in, and the stolen Dozer drives home and puts up a USA Command Center beside the GLA one, then a Power Plant, a Supply Center, a Barracks and a War Factory, which train Humvees and Missile Defenders into the GLA army. The computer saves for that Command Center ahead of its own base and army, its own building carries on around it, and the stolen Dozer only lays each foundation: one of the computer's own builders puts the building up while the Dozer waits at home for the next one, so killing the Dozer no longer stops what it already placed. The foreign Barracks and War Factory train as its own factories do, out of the same money as the rest of its army.
- A captured Command Center is no longer sold on the spot. Black Lotus took a USA Command Center, it trained a USA Dozer at once and was sold the moment the Dozer was out, and the Dozer drove home and built the USA base there. A captured Barracks or War Factory of another side is kept to train that side's units.
- Its capturing infantry go after your buildings as well as the oil derricks, when the building is worth at least twice the soldier and neither it nor the walk to it sits under your guns. A Ranger took an unguarded China Command Center, and the China Dozer it trained put a China Command Center up in the USA base.
- Medium works a stolen Dozer or a captured Command Center the same way but does not go looking for them; Easy does neither. A replay or saved game from before this change will not play back.

## The computer presses its units' buttons

- A Hard computer player used to leave every unit button alone: Comanches never fired their rocket pods, Missile Defenders never lased a tank, Jarmen Kell never shot a crew out. Now its units weigh each button against what their guns would do and press it when it pays. Four Comanches cut a pack of eight Battlemasters down to two in the time their guns alone took to kill four; four Missile Defenders lasing two Overlords killed one and left the other at 820 of 1100, where without the laser both drove on at 1520 of 2200 between them. Kell snipes the crew out of the nearest tank, Rangers throw flashbangs into a crowd of Rebels (all ten down in under a third of the time the rifles took), Maroon Berets send Kargu drones onto the tightest pack, Sungur lase like Missile Defenders, Nuke Cannons switch to neutron shells on a garrisoned house (twelve Rebels dead in one volley, where the plain shells took four times as long to bring the house down on them), and Demolition Rebels blow themselves up among tanks worth half again what they cost. A charge, TNT or a Beret's Designate Target is walked up only when the target dies sooner with it, walk and fuse counted, than under the guns already on it, so Colonel Burton keeps shooting a tank his rifle kills faster than a twenty second fuse would. Medium uses the buttons that need no walk, only on the target it already shoots; Easy uses none. Heroes go to work on their own now, where the computer used to send them off as scouts for the whole match. Colonel Burton slips into the enemy base under his camouflage, plants a remote charge where it hurts most, superweapons, the Command Center and the factories before defences, power and supply, and a building one charge fells before one it only scratches, then steps clear, sets it off and moves on to the next; an enemy soldier at arm's length gets the knife. The knife used to stay in its sheath, because the rifle's three-round burst always looked quicker on paper; in a test, three Red Guards who walked up to him now went down to the blade, one stroke each.
