A building his charge leaves above half, which is a Command Center with a dozer patching it, is left alone for a minute while he works through the rest. Against a test base he blew up a War Factory, a Barracks and a Bunker inside a minute and a half, where without his buttons he stood still. Caught in a fight, a hero fights what its gun can beat and steps back out of sight of what it cannot before going back to work. The Demolition General's Jarmen Kell plants his charges the same way. Black Lotus switches off every tank around her in turn, mid-fight, then captures the enemy's buildings, or empties a Supply Center of a thousand when a capture there would sit under a Fire Base: she had three Crusaders dead in the water and the Command Center in her hands inside half a minute. What the computer builds counts these weapons only when it will press them. A replay or saved game from before this change will not play back.

## The computer knows which guns hurt what it sends

- The computer's map of enemy guns weighed every gun by its price, so a Gatling Cannon counted the same against a tank column as against a squad of Rangers, and an Avenger, which shoots only aircraft, did not count at all. Each gun now carries three figures worked out from what it actually does to vehicles, to infantry and to aircraft in this match's armies, and the computer reads the one that matters for what it is moving: a tank column picks the road the anti-tank guns do not cover, infantry keeps off the machine guns.
- On Hard, the Chinooks and helicopters now plan their flights round the guns that shoot aircraft. They used to fly round tanks, which cannot touch them, and straight over anti-aircraft guns that only shoot the sky.
- A computer unit pulled out of a fight takes the way out with the least fire along the whole drive, where it used to take the way that left the guns' reach soonest. A hurt Battlemaster with a Crusader behind it and a Paladin between it and home drove straight over the Paladin; now it pulls out to the side. A drive home whose straight line crosses enemy guns goes round them. And a unit sent home hurt that mends on the way, from a heal aura or a heroic rank's repair, turns back to its team once it is at 65% and out of every gun's reach. It used to drive the whole way home first, mended or not.
- A replay recorded before this change will not play back, and a game saved before it loads with the old map until the next round of looking replaces it.
- The map remembers. A column that drove into the fog used to vanish from it the moment it left sight, and the computer walked into it a second later; now its guns stay on the map where it was last seen and fade out over fifteen seconds. A column on the move is drawn a second ahead of where it stands. In the test three Gattling tanks drove off into the fog on a hurt Crusader's only quiet side; it used to pull out 180 straight at them and was down to 72 of 480, and now it drives round where they went and is still at 161.
- A gun's reach has a shape now. A Nuke Cannon cannot fire at anything closer than 150, so the ground at its feet reads as safe. In the test a Crusader at a third of its health parked 90 from one: it used to pull out through the cannon's real reach and leave it at half health; now it stays and kills the cannon without a scratch. An anti-aircraft gun's last quarter of reach counts half, so a flight's turn point swings round the gun's middle. Ground reach counts in full to its edge: at half, a hurt Crusader 140 from a Battlemaster read itself half covered, stayed, and died where the old map would have pulled it out.
- Defences and garrisoned buildings are drawn apart from the armies. A drive round a known Gatling Cannon or a manned Bunker counts it twice, since it will still be there when the column arrives and a tank may not: a hurt Crusader with a Gattling Cannon on its road home reads 710 of fire down that road where it used to read 355. A building that is unpowered, being built or being sold no longer counts as a gun at all. The computer's raids pick, of two targets as well covered, the one with more of your money and production round it and fewer fixed guns over it.
- Radiation, toxin and fire fields and the mines it has spotted are on the map, and a drive or a step back goes round them. An aircraft does not care, and the map knows that. In the test a hurt Crusader with a Poison Field on its road home used to back straight into the field; now it backs out past its edge, and ends on the same 157 of 480. A field counts for half a Battlemaster's fire: at eight Battlemasters' worth, as first built, the Crusader fled sideways into a real Battlemaster's reach to dodge a little poison and ended at 103. A hurt unit whose own gun reads exactly even with what covers it pulls out too: by class a hurt Crusader equals a Battlemaster to the bit, and a third of a tank in an even fight is a dead one.
- A Hard computer's jets and Comanches no longer give up a strike because an anti-aircraft gun sits on the straight line: they fly a turn point round it, summing the air defence along the whole flight, come in from there, and fly home round the same gun once they are empty. In the test a Raptor sent at an Overlord with a Gattling Cannon halfway used to turn for home untouched; now it swings 1100 wide, puts 400 damage into the Overlord and lands back at 131 of 160. On the first try it was told to fly round and flew straight through the Gattling anyway, both ways, and was shot down: the computer's move order to a jet already attacking only lay on top of the attack for twenty seconds, and the attack won. It is a proper flight path now. A jet that does give a strike up picks its next target by what is worth hitting: sent at a Gattling Cannon it could not kill, the Raptor turned on a Supply Center 1050 away and took 510 off it, where the old pick went for a Battlemaster half as far.
- Our guns are weighed against the army the computer remembers you having, so a field of tank guns no longer counts as cover against helicopters, and a wave gathers on the last stretch of its road our side still holds rather than going home whenever a known gun covers the old gathering spot. Over 9000 frames of two Hard computers on the same generated map, the waves gathered 26 times where they used to gather 20. A team that lost a fight with no quiet ground short of home was also meant to regroup at the front line; it never did in five long games, and was taken out.
- A replay with a computer player in it, recorded before this change, will not play back, and a game saved before it loads with the old map until the next round of looking replaces it.

## The score screen is the lobby's twin

- The score screen used to be one flat table sorted by score, so a 4v4 read as eight strangers and you had to remember who stood with whom. It is laid out like the lobby you started from now. The left column holds the standings in teams, each under a band with the lobby's team colour square and its name, a team of two or more with a gold Winner or a "Defeated 12:40" chip and its totals. The players are the lobby's seat cards: the faction icon, the name in the player's colour, the general under it, or beside it where eight players leave one line a card. A free-for-all is a plain ranked list. Winners come first, then every other team by how long it held out, then by score; a match left before anyone won keeps the teams still standing above the beaten ones and shows no chips.
- Every card has the score, units built, lost and killed, buildings built, lost and destroyed, and money earned and spent, thousands separated. With three players or more the best of each column is gold, money spent never. Eight players in four teams fit at 1280x720 with the chat open: the cards press closer, and the chat list gives up some height, before anything runs off the panel.
- The right column is the lobby's map column. On top, VICTORY or DEFEAT in the Generals' lettering, or "TEAM 2 WINS" when you watched or played a replay; a match you left before anyone won reads DEFEAT, as your record counts it. Under it the map at its own shape with every taken start spot in its player's colour, the winners ringed in gold and the beaten dimmed. Then the highlights: who destroyed the most, who earned the most, who had the biggest army and who put up the first superweapon, with the side added where eight "Hard AI" share a name. At the foot, where the lobby keeps its rules, the match's length, game speed and starting money. The header says what was played: "4v4 · 23:41", "2v2v2v2 · 31:05", "Free for all (8) · 18:20".
- After a LAN or online match the chat sits under the standings, where the lobby keeps it, and your rating line still lands there. After a skirmish or a replay that space shows each player's share of all the armies on the field over the match, up to the moment it was decided.
- Graphs is one chart with nine series to pick: army value, income per minute, money earned, cash, units, buildings, power, value destroyed and units lost. Draw it as one line per player, or as each player's share of the whole, see-through bands stacked by team with an ink line between teams, which reads the same in a 1v1 and an eight-way free-for-all. A beaten player's line stops with a cross where he fell instead of running on at zero, and dark house colours are lifted so a dark red line still shows on the black. Superweapons, powers and promotions sit in two lanes over the chart, one seat's moments sharing a marker with a "×3" count, never two seats in one. The legend is the same team cards with each player's last value and peak; point at one to pick its line out, click it to hide it, and point at the chart for everyone's value at that minute with each team's total.
- Build order keeps its timeline with the stretched first five minutes, grouped by team, so eight players fit with their names beside them, and two buildings made in the same second no longer sit on top of each other.
- No word on the score screen or the observer's panels runs into the next one any more. A label too long for its room is shortened the way its own language does it: Turkish, German, French, Russian and Ukrainian cut a word after a consonant with a period ("Kazanılan" to "Kaz.", "Gebäude" to "Geb."), English drops vowels first ("Destroyed" to "Dstryd"), and the column heads and the camera lever carry hand-written short forms ("Harc.", "Oync."). Player names are never shortened, only cut with "…" when even that does not fit.
- Watching a replay, the bar's buttons are as wide as their words, so "Duraklat" no longer runs into "0.5x", and the observer panel shows the watched player's money on one line, "$ 10,000", inside its box instead of across its frame.
- The match records army value, value destroyed and value lost alongside what it already kept, and when each player was beaten. It changes nothing in the match; replays and network games play the same.

## Soldiers close ranks, and orders reach the spot

- Soldiers you order together with no vehicle among them now settle about a cell apart round the click. Each one used to keep a square of ground twice the size of his body, so a squad stood spread out with the nearest mate 19 away; now it is under 10. In a test column the last Missile Defender came in three seconds sooner. Put tanks or trucks in the group and the vehicles take the same places they always did; the soldiers then close up round them, never on a spot a vehicle is heading for and never across the path of one already parked. In a test of 20 Rangers with 6 Crusaders the nearest mate went from 21 to 13, and the tanks arrived no later.
- An attack move, or an order that pulls a group in tight on a point, keeps trying while each try brings the unit closer. It used to give up after a few tries as much as three tank lengths short of where you pointed. The computer's orders keep the old rule.
- A soldier wedged between parked vehicles could swing his nose left and right on the spot for the rest of the match, and the game counted the swinging as getting somewhere. It no longer does, so he is freed like any other stuck unit.
- A unit that has to reach its target to hit it no longer loses its way there when the game is busy finding routes for many units at once.
- A unit shoved aside by a friendly one could drive on along a route that had already been thrown away. That is fixed, after the same fix in TheSuperHackers' version of this source.
- After a saved game is loaded, the computer's attack moves behave as the computer's again, and a unit halfway through being freed from a jam carries on where it was.
- A transport whose passengers shoot out of it now brings them into an attack move's fights. The Infantry General's Troop Crawler, sent on an attack move past an enemy Power Plant, used to drive up to it and stop there for good while its eight soldiers never fired: the order went to the Crawler alone, whose own gun is a stand-in that does next to nothing, and soldiers riding inside pick only units for themselves. Now everyone aboard who can hit the target gets it, and the Power Plant goes down. Any transport with firing seats hands its target over the same way, to the passengers within reach of it. If nobody aboard can hurt the target, the transport drives on and leaves it be.
- A replay recorded before this change will not play back.

## Water maps run like dry ones

- On Tournament Island, Bombardment Beach and every other map with a lot of sea, a fast PC fell from about 240 frames a second to 70 or 80. Two things this build added to water were paying for it on every frame. The reflection of the units and buildings in the water was drawn again each time the picture was, 240 times a second on a fast card, for a soft darkening that moves no faster than the game does. It is now drawn at most 30 times a second, and between those it stays fixed to the water, so it does not swim while you scroll and a jump across the map draws it fresh at once. And on any map with water the sun's shadows were being drawn for every tank and building in a wide box round the view, seen or not, because the water's reflection might show one. Now only the ones that can throw a shadow into the view or into its reflection are drawn. The water looks the way it did. Modern water keeps drawing its reflection every frame.

## Grass that moves with the wind

- Grassland used to be a flat painted texture under the tanks. With Ground Foliage on, tufts of grass, dry straw and a few wild flowers stand on the grass ground of a map and bend with the same breeze that sways the trees, a gust rolling across the field rather than every blade nodding at once. Round leafy bushes and dry scrub grow among them, thickest where a field gives way to dirt or rock, and fallen twigs lie in the grass and on the dirt beside it. Where trees stand together the ground under them grows into a thicket: bushes and big ferns, young saplings where the wood thins out, the odd fallen log and stump, the tall grass giving way under the canopy, and a layer of fallen leaves under broadleaf trees or needles under pines that reads as the same ground in shade. A lone tree gets a fern or two. The trees themselves stop looking stamped out of one mould: each stands up to a third taller or a quarter shorter than the next, some slimmer, some broader, and a shade lighter, darker, warmer or cooler, and the ones standing on snow carry snow on their upper branches. Where no unit can go, on cliffs and in the strip past the edge of the map, the desert grows bleached dead trees with bare gnarled branches, alone or in twos and threes, and snowfields grow clumps of snow-laden firs. Bare ground gets its own: gravel and pebbles on dirt, rock and desert, a few small stones scattered over them, and stones and boulders gathered at the foot of every cliff, where rock that fell would lie. They are sandstone in the desert, granite in the hills and dark basalt on burnt ground, take the colour of the ground they lie on and have a shadowed side. They keep off roads, water and the ground under buildings, a base built in a match clears its own patch, and they grow in from the edge of the view instead of popping up. Everything that stands up casts its shadow in the sun, each tuft its own blades swaying with it, the trees and boulders theirs; only what lies flat on the ground throws none. It needs the full terrain detail: the lower terrain detail setting shows none. The art is the fork's own, painted from scratch. It is off by default; tick Ground Foliage under Options, Display, and it grows on the map you are playing the moment you press Accept. The Performance / Quality slider turns it on only at Ultra. The box is greyed under Direct3D 9. It draws on Direct3D 11 and in the Mac and Linux builds; Direct3D 9 (`-d3d9`) and Classic Graphics show no grass. Looks only; units walk through it, and replays and network games play the same with it on or off.

## Smoother light on hills and cliffs

- On Direct3D 11 with the HD textures, the sun now lights the ground pixel by pixel from a smoothed copy of the map's heights. Before, the light ran in straight lines across each tile and you could see the grid of triangles on every slope. Hills and cliffs now shade in one soft sweep, and roads on them take the same light. Bridges, the lower terrain detail, Direct3D 9 and Classic Graphics keep the old light. Looks only; nothing in the match changes.
- Pulled back, the ground stops looking like wallpaper. A field of grass or sand is one small texture laid down again and again, and from far the same dark tuft and the same bare patch stood in rows across the whole map. Broad stretches of ground are now a shade lighter or darker, a touch warmer or cooler, in soft shapes that never line up with the texture's repeat, so the rows break up. The shading is fixed to the map, so nothing swims when you scroll, the map's overall colour stays where it was, and at the closest zoom the ground looks exactly as before. Same rule as the light above: Direct3D 11 without Classic Graphics, full terrain detail.
- The cloud shadows drifting over the map came from one small picture repeated every 315 units, and from the highest camera you could count the rows of the same grey blot. The clouds are now laid out from that same picture over a stretch eight times as wide, in pieces shifted and mirrored at random, and gathered into banks 600 to 1200 units across with thinner cover between them, so the grid is gone and the map reads as passing weather. Up close they keep EA's shapes, a bank a little darker than the old cloud and the open stretches lighter, the map as dark on average as before, drifting at the same speed in the same direction. The cost on the graphics card is unchanged. Both renderers get it, Direct3D 9 too; Classic Graphics keeps EA's repeat.

## Ally Aid: fly your teammate an army

- Turkiye has a new rank 3 general's power, Ally Aid, in the promotion window beside Gokbey Landing, on the Headquarters and on the powers tray. Aim it at the ground and a card in your side's own command bar steel opens where you clicked, every unit it carries on a build button like the ones on the bar, its price on the corner and its name underneath. Click a unit, or roll the wheel up over it, to add one; right click or roll down to take one off; hold Shift for five at a time. The count sits on the button the way a build queue does, a unit you cannot build yet tells you why when you point at it, and the card adds up the planes and the bill as you go before you press OK. Cargo planes take off together from your edge of the map and drop the lot under parachutes, Altay tanks included.
- You pay the units' own price and 500 a plane, and the money goes when you press OK. A plane carries eight soldiers or two vehicles, one order flies four planes at most, and a unit you could not build right now, for want of its factory or a prerequisite, is greyed out, so the power skips nothing in your tech tree.
- Aim at or near an ally's units or buildings and everything lands as his, in his colour and under his orders. Anywhere else, or in a game with no ally, it lands for you. Four minutes pass between drops, which keeps a player from pouring his whole economy into a teammate.
- The planes can be shot down, and a plane lost on the way takes its whole load with it, with nothing paid back. In a test with eight Avengers under the route, both vehicle planes of a four-plane order went down with their two Altays and two Kirpis, and only the sixteen soldiers landed.
- Every plane makes one pass. A drop close to your own edge of the map used to send a full plane over the marker with four soldiers still aboard, round in a 12 second loop and back, and the yellow circle stayed on the ground the whole time. The planes now start further out and may finish dropping just past the marker, and the circle goes the moment a plane is empty. The same fix reaches every paradrop and cargo drop in the game: a plane that pushed its last man out just short of the marker and crossed it before the next one was due used to count that as a missed run and go round again with nothing in the hold. It heads home now.
- The load spreads over the drop zone instead of piling on one spot. Every chute of a plane used to steer for that plane's single point, so its two tanks came down within 2 of each other, one on the other's roof. Now each unit gets a landing place of its own before the planes take off, the tanks first and well apart, the soldiers in the gaps, and the zone grows with the order. Every place is clear ground inside the map: no cliff, no water, no building, nothing already standing there. In a test, four Altays and eight soldiers sent to an ally's base came down with at least 58 between any two tanks, each tank within 11 of its place, and no two soldiers closer than 24; with two Kirpis in place of two Altays the closest pair was 46 apart. A soldier pushed out far from his place can still come down short of it.

## Splinter camo for 1K

- The game can draw skins your zerohour.gg account owns. The first three are Splinter Camo: the Crusader, the Battlemaster and the Scorpion, every general's version but the Laser General's Crusader, damaged or not. You pick one skin per unit inside the game: sign in online and press Skins in the online menu, where each unit shows Default and every skin it has, the ones your account does not own greyed out, and Save puts your pick on your account. In an online room everyone in the match sees your tanks in their camo, the replay too, with your team colour still on the trim. Classic Graphics has a set of its own, painted on the classic tanks, so the skins show whichever look you play. Looks only: the tanks fight exactly as before, and a player whose game lacks the skin sheets just sees the normal tank. Quick Match carries both players' skins too. A saved pick counts from your very next room or Quick Match, with no sign-in between, and a code you redeem on zerohour.gg while the game is open shows up the next time you open Skins. LAN and skirmish games never show a skin.
- The camo is cut in hard-edged shards of three tones, each tank in its own side's paint: urban greys on the Crusader, China's olive taken dark on the Battlemaster, sand and rust on the Scorpion. A shard runs on unbroken from hull to turret and over the edge from roof to side, the way sprayed paint does, and the cut still reads at the game's camera. The tones are kept muted so your team colour stays the one bright thing on the tank. Damaged tanks and wrecks wear the same camo under their soot.

## Turkiye gets a game plan

- Turkiye used to sit idle for the first minutes: its artillery hit nothing until a spotter, the guns, a screen and a radar all stood together, and keeping the eye alive took all your attention. Now there is one obvious road. Open with Mehmetcik Riflemen, a Spotter Team and a Cobra raid; in the middle game dig a Siper in front of a spotted Firtina line; late, put a Bayraktar over the target and bring the Akinci and the Kargu base.
- The Mehmetcik's rifle does 8 a round instead of 5, so the first squad out of your Barracks wins its fight with the other side's first squad. The Barracks' new MPT-76 Rifles take it to 11 and the reach from 120 to 150.
- The Spotter Team costs 300 instead of 700 and trains in 6 seconds instead of 10. Losing one is a setback now, not the end of your artillery.
- The Siper is your forward radar post: rockets and shells keep their lock 400 around it, and the rank 3 Forward Radar card (it opened the Mobile Radar before) stretches that to 600. The Mobile Radar is gone from the Factory.
- The Bayraktar is a full eye on its own. It carries a radar circle of 450 wherever it flies, so a Bayraktar over the target is all a Firtina line needs.
- Three radars doing one job became three jobs. The Radar Tower is the base's long radar and the home of Target Classification, and costs 600 instead of 800 with a power draw of 2 instead of 3. The Koral lost its radar and is the electronic warfare truck, blinding drones and spotters and breaking missile locks, for 1400 instead of 1600. The Grand Bazaar is the economy building and sells Export Contracts: every Supply Center then pays 30 every 2 seconds instead of 20, every Grand Bazaar 35.
- Turkiye's upgrades went from 16 to 21, and from five borrowed from other sides to two. New: MPT-76 Rifles and the CBRN Kit (Turkiye's own chemical suits) at the Barracks, a Self-Protection Suite of flares and armour for the Bayraktar, Akinci and Kizilelma at the Airfield, Fortification (every base building and Hisar a quarter tougher) at the Headquarters, Export Contracts at the Grand Bazaar and Domestic Warheads, 3000, at the Operations Center: a quarter more damage from the artillery, the Altay's gun, the Alpagu, Sungur and Kizilelma missiles, the Bayraktar's munitions and the Akinci's bomb. Two are bought on a single vehicle, the way America buys a drone: a SARP machine gun station on an Altay's turret for infantry, and a Field Repair Kit on a Kirpi that mends vehicles within 150 at 10 a second.
- Mark and rain. When an enemy dies where one of your eyes holds it (a Spotter Team, a Cobra, a Bayraktar or the Maroon Beret looking at it, or any Turkiye radar circle over it), every Firtina, Sakarya and Alpagu that reaches the spot fires half again as fast for 6 seconds, and their shells and rockets land on the target instead of going wide. Every kill like that starts the 6 seconds over, so a line that keeps finding targets keeps its tempo. Nothing to click: a gun sparkles as its burst starts and glows red until it ends.
- The guns keep up. The Firtina drives at 22.5 instead of 18 and the Sakarya and the Spotter Team at 24 instead of 21, against the Altay's 30, so the artillery no longer falls a screen behind the tanks it covers.
- Dig forward, shoot further. The Firtina, the Sakarya and the Alpagu reach a tenth further within 400 of a standing Siper: 660 for a Firtina instead of 600, 759 with Extended Range. Each Siper you dig closer to the enemy carries the guns' reach with it.
- The Firtina fires a shell now. It went up as a Tomahawk missile before, and a Paladin's laser or an Altay's AKKOR could pick it out of the air; the shell flies an arc in 2 seconds to 600 with the Nuke Cannon's bang and whistle, and nothing shoots it down.
- You can see what you bought. A SARP Altay carries the machine gun station on its turret and its bursts come from that gun, a Kirpi with the Field Repair Kit has tool chests and a crane on its roof, and every Siper raises a radar mast once it is dug in.
- Turkiye's eight new upgrades have buttons of their own. They used to borrow EA's pictures, so MPT-76 Rifles showed a tank shell and the SARP station a Gattling gun. The whole Barracks bar is photographs now, cut and coloured like EA's own Ranger and Red Guard: six soldiers in today's Turkish pixel camouflage with the flag on the sleeve, each with the thing that names him (the engineer's sapper pack, the Sungur's launcher, the spotter's binoculars, the Maroon Beret's beret, the Alpagu's drone), and the five Barracks upgrades as a rifle on sandbags, a gas mask, a landmine, a thermal sight and a sandbagged trench. They used to be flat renders of the models in red vests, and Mine Kit, Thermal Sights and Reinforced Siper showed GLA boots, an American sniper and barbed wire. The small upgrade marks beside a selected soldier's portrait are Turkiye's own too: the engineer shows the Mine Kit, the spotter Thermal Sights and Laser Designation, the Sungur and the Alpagu Domestic Warheads, and every soldier the CBRN Kit. They used to show America's Advanced Training and chemical suits and the GLA Worker's shoes, none of which a Turkish player can ever buy, so they never lit. Precision Guidance and Domestic Warheads have pictures of their own as well, a missile's seeker and a row of shells.
- Replays of games with Turkiye recorded before this version play out differently now. The guns fire faster after a spotted kill, reach further by a Siper and shoot shells, so the battle the replay remembers is not the one it replays.
- The computer plays it. A first 30-match Hard batch had Turkiye buying every new upgrade but Export Contracts and leaving SARP and the Field Repair Kit to a button America's scripts almost never pressed. It now buys all three itself, trains a spotter for every two guns that wander off without one, replaces a team's dead spotter, and puts up a Barracks when it has nowhere to train them. In 24 Hard matches against America, China and the GLA, both seat orders, it bought Export Contracts in 11, SARP on 21 Altays and the kit on 42 Kirpis, and won 12, lost 10 and drew 2: 5-2-1 against America, 3-5-0 against China, 4-3-1 against the GLA.
- Turkiye's soldiers talk like Turkish soldiers. Every unit that takes orders used to answer in the voice of the foreign unit it was built from, so a Mehmetcik spoke as a Ranger and the supply truck in Chinese. Now each of the twenty has a man of his own, speaking English with a Turkish accent: an eager young rifleman, a cold and quiet Maroon Beret, a gruff engineer foreman, an old truck driver who calls you son, a tank commander who roars when the gun fires, drone and jet operators talking over the radio, and the pilot who climbs out of a wrecked Altay. 291 new lines, each a second or two long, at the loudness of EA's own. The tanks, trucks and aircraft also cry out when they are hit hard, which no vehicle in the game did before.
- Turkiye's base has its own announcer. A Turkish player used to hear America's officer report low power, a lost unit or an incoming nuke, and a Ranger shout that the base was under attack. Now a woman's voice with a Turkish accent says all 36 of the lines America's announcer has, from "Power levels low" to "Warning! Enemy nuclear missile launched!", and calls you komutanım when you are promoted. When the Maroon Beret is spotted she names him, and an enemy Burton or Maroon Beret is an "enemy commando".
- The Mehmetcik fires his own rifle. He used to shoot with the American Ranger's sound, and that sound is a whole burst played for every round, so his three-round bursts came out as a smeared rattle. Now every round is one sharp shot, four takes picked at random, so you hear the three rounds his rifle kicks. Buy MPT-76 Rifles at the Barracks and the shot gets heavier and deeper, the 7.62's bang, so you can tell an upgraded squad by ear. A clip of either is as loud as the Ranger's burst and keeps its cap of three at once, so a firefight sits in the mix where it always did.

## The game plays half as fast again

- Everything in a match runs 50 percent quicker than in the original: units drive and walk faster, buildings and units come off the line sooner, weapons reload sooner and animations play quicker. A tank that crossed a map in 40 seconds crosses it in about 27. The clock on the wall did not change, so a match is simply shorter, and the countdowns on screen (superweapons, timed powers) still count real seconds.
- You pick the speed. The skirmish lobby has a Game speed box with four choices, 1.0x, 1.25x, 1.5x and 2.0x of the original game, and 1.5x is where it starts. Campaign and Generals' Challenge missions take theirs from Game speed in missions in Options, read as each mission starts.
- Every speed now steps the world 30 times a second. Picking 1.0x used to slow the whole game down to 20 steps a second, so units moved in visible hops and an order could wait 50 milliseconds for the next step; 1.25x took 25. Now the speed decides how much happens in each step, and a match at 1.0x answers your clicks and moves as smoothly as one at 1.5x. At 2.0x the game no longer asks your computer for 40 steps a second either, so a big late battle costs it what the same battle costs at 1.5x.
- A step at 1.0x covers less game time than one at 1.5x, so the speed is now part of the match: the replay records it and plays back at it. Replays and saved games from the previous version still load, at the speed they were played.
- Custom online rooms play at 1.5x and LAN games at 1.0x, the original game's own pace, until the host picks another speed. Play vs AI plays the speed you pick on its card, and a ranked Quick Match plays the speed both players agree on (see Play vs AI online). Everyone in a match sees the same game at the same pace.
- Turbo is gone. The tick box in the skirmish, LAN and online lobbies, Turbo Mode in Missions and the TURBO mark in the corner readout were replaced by the game speed above, and 2.0x is what turbo used to give a skirmish.
- Sound, music, menus and the network stay on the real clock; only the world on the map speeds up.
- Sound no longer changes with the game speed. A jet or a tank passing the camera bent its pitch by how fast it crossed the screen, so at 2.0x every flyby whined twice as far as at 1.0x, and at the default 1.5x half again as far as it was tuned. A cruising Aurora set off its sonic boom on passes made well under attack speed. Now a unit is heard at its own speed whatever pace the match runs at. Sounds fading out and the music's crossfade between tracks were cut short at the faster speeds, to half their length at 2.0x, so sounds stopped abruptly; every fade runs its full length on the real clock now.
- Mission cutscenes keep their original pace, so the voices fit the pictures again. The second half of China's second mission intro had its camera cutting away before the lines were spoken, done in 27.5 seconds where the voices need 34. While a cutscene holds the controls the game now runs at the original speed, and the faster play comes back the moment you get control.
- Replays and saved games from the previous build will not load, and everyone in a network game needs the same build.

## The game steps 30 times a second again, and the picture glides

- The game's simulation is back at 30 steps a second, as in the original Generals. It ran at 60 from version 3.0.0. On its own this step leaves game speed, unit speeds and every timing as they were (the faster play above is a separate setting); only the work behind them is lighter, which leaves more room in big late-game battles and on slower machines.
- Smooth Motion keeps the picture from showing it. It draws units between their last two positions, so movement glides at your screen's full refresh, a 60 Hz screen included, and it is on unless you switch it off in Options.
- Replays and saved games from earlier versions will not load, and everyone in a network game needs the same build.

## Your whole production from three tabs

- Three tabs now stand on the command bar's top edge, over the left end of its button grid and beside the money. Buildings puts your builder's page on the grid without you hunting for a dozer first, even with Build Without A Worker switched off, and a click on a structure starts placing it as usual. Ground units lists every unit any of your working factories can train right now, from the Barracks and the War Factory alike, and Aircraft does the same for everything with wings or rotors. Click a unit and it goes into the queue of the factory with the shortest line; shift and ctrl queue five or more at once as they do on a factory's own page. A list longer than the grid scrolls: the grid's right end turns into two square arrow keys, the top one moving the list right and the bottom one back, one column at a time, so with units 1 to 12 showing a click brings in 13 and 14 and drops only 1 and 2 instead of flipping the whole grid. The mouse wheel over the grid steps the same column, and the list stops at either end: the arrow with nowhere left to go greys out and ignores clicks until there is something to scroll to again. The grid's own hotkeys stay off while a tab is open. A tab stays open until you press it again or pick something else. Your hand never has to leave the keyboard for them: Ctrl+Q, Ctrl+W and Ctrl+E open Buildings, Ground units and Aircraft and close them on a second press, and Options > Hotkeys puts each on another key or on none. Each tab's tooltip names its key, "Ground units (Ctrl+W)", and follows a change made in the middle of a match. Each side's bar dresses them in its own steel; Classic Graphics lends them the idle worker, vehicle and aircraft pictures.
- A captured factory, or one of another army or general you built, adds its units to the tabs. Take the Laser General's War Factory as plain USA and Ground units gains his Laser Tank, while his Humvee stays off the list: it is your Humvee under another name, and a unit two of your factories make is listed once, your own army's copy. A captured Airfield puts its planes in Aircraft the same way, so a China Airfield brings the MiG and the Helix beside your Raptor. A captured dozer or worker brings its structures to Buildings, which then scrolls by the column as the other two do: USA plus a China dozer is 23 structures, each once. Click a unit or a structure only a captured building can make and the job goes to one that can.
- Layout under Options > Interface puts a Red Alert style sidebar down the right edge of the screen. Every factory you own builds from it without being selected first: Buildings, Upgrades and powers, Infantry and Vehicles each list what your base can make right now, and Q, W, E and R open them from the keyboard, since the sidebar comes with the Red Alert keys. A cameo in production fills with its progress and carries the number still queued, so you see what your base is doing without clicking a single factory. Upgrades and powers lists every research your buildings offer, and a click starts or cancels it without selecting the building. The selected units' commands move to a strip along the bottom, and the corner beside it holds the selection: the unit's portrait in a medallion, a name plate with its health under the name, and one tray that shows a single unit's upgrades, the types in a mixed selection or a factory's queue. Each side wears a sidebar of its own, America's machined steel, China's lacquer and rivets, the GLA's welded scrap and Türkiye's faceted armour; the bottom strip keeps Attack, Stop and Guard at its right end while the unit's own orders fill in from the left. With two or more factories, a row under the tabs lists them, All, 1, 2 and on, and each numbered chip shows what kind of building it is beside its number, so an Airfield never passes for a War Factory: pick one and the sidebar builds there, while All hands each unit to the factory with the shortest queue. Buildings does the same with your Dozers or Workers: pick one and the structure you place goes up by his hands, selected or not. Click one of your factories or builders on the battlefield and the sidebar follows, opening its tab with its chip lit. Select several and every one of them lights: three Barracks share a cameo click, each unit going to the one with the shortest queue, and with three Dozers lit the structure you place goes to the free one nearest the spot. A plain click on a chip lights that one alone, and Shift-click adds a chip to the lit ones or takes it back out. Cameo pictures keep their own shape instead of being stretched across the cell, and the tab icons and the factory pictures on the chips fill their buttons where they used to sit small in the middle. Sell and Repair sit under the radar the way Red Alert 2 had them. With your own buildings selected, Sell sells them at once; with none, it turns the pointer into a sell cursor, and every one of your buildings you click goes, one after another, until a right click, Esc or the button again. Repair works the same way without selecting anything: click a damaged building and the nearest free Dozer or Worker drives over to fix it, or the nearest busy one when none is free, and over a building no builder of yours can mend the pointer says so. Reforged keeps the bar you know and stays the default. HUD Width beside it pulls the whole interface into a centred 16:9 or 21:9 area on an ultrawide monitor, so the bar stays in front of you instead of out at the far edges of a 32:9 screen, while the battlefield still fills all of it.
- Nothing on the Red Alert style sidebar is stretched any more, whatever the screen's shape or the HUD Width. The build grid is three cameos wide and seven deep, 21 where it showed 12, and every well is cut to the cameo's shape. The commands along the bottom strip were squeezed into squares; they keep their pictures' shape now, and so do the portrait and the tray's tiles. On a 21:9 screen the strip's plain middle repeats to fill the extra width instead of the whole plate being pulled sideways, and on a screen narrower than 5:4 the sidebar grows the same way.
- The Red Alert style sidebar lines up. Down to the tabs it stands on one grid of four columns: the menu, the money and diplomacy above the radar, Sell, Repair and General under it and the four tabs below meet at the same edges, and the power bar starts under the tabs, beside the build grid. Every key letter, on a tab or on a command in the strip, sits on the same small plate in the button's top left corner at the same size; the tabs' letters used to sit half on their frame, and at 1080p the commands' letters were half again as big and rode off the top of their plate. The power bar works like Red Alert's: it fills up to what your plants make, the part in use green, yellow close to the limit and red past it, a white mark at what you use and the shortfall blinking red when you are over, all on one scale that keeps the two readable against each other however much power you have.
- The Red Alert style sidebar's tabs are sorted the way you play. Q holds every structure, base defences with the rest, so a Patriot is no longer a tab away from the Power Plant. W holds what you spend on instead of build: your research, the General's powers you bought and your superweapons, each firing from its cameo with its countdown drawn over it, a captured silo's included. A tab shows only what you have unlocked: a tank appears once the War Factory stands, and something you simply cannot afford yet stays in place, greyed. Each new unlock joins the end of its own country's group, so nothing you already know shifts under your cursor; your own side's cameos come first and those of a captured Dozer or War Factory follow, country by country in the order you took them.
- A replay in which a unit was queued from a tab will not play back on an earlier version.
- Smoke signals have buttons now, three keys on a plate over the minimap's top edge: attack, defend and look here. Press one and your next click on the ground or on the minimap drops that smoke for your allies; press it again or right click to call it off, and the key stays down until you do. They work where the signal hotkeys work, in skirmish and online, and the tooltip names the hotkey you have for each. Grow the minimap with Minimap Size and the keys ride up on its top edge.

## The Angry Mob in one crowd, and orders you can see land

- The GLA Angry Mob marches as one tight crowd at one pace. Its men used to string out behind the leader, with one breaking into a sprint past the rest every time he fell a step behind while another dawdled at two thirds of the pace; round a corner each found his own way and the mob arrived in pieces. Now they keep their places round the mob's own route, walk between 17 and 21 where they ranged from 12.6 to 32, and the furthest man stays 6 to 25 from the middle on the march instead of 18 to 31. Stopped, the ten of them stand within 23 of the middle, where they stood 28 out.
- Shoot one man of an Angry Mob and the attack carries on to the rest until the whole mob is dead, nexus and all; eight Crusaders set on one rioter leave nobody standing.
- A replay recorded before this change that has an Angry Mob in it will not play back.
- A group goes where you click. It used to pile up short of the spot on the side it came from, and tanks on the flank swung sideways into one file before they set off. Now every unit heads straight for the click and the group settles round it. A replay recorded before this change with a group move in it will not play back.
- Every selected unit stands in a thin glowing circle in its owner's colour, and where circles touch they merge into one outline, so five soldiers standing close wear one scalloped ring and not five rings through each other. A selected building gets the same line traced round its footprint. Give an attack order and the ordered units' rings pulse up off the ground; the unit or building you aimed at, or the one you sent them into, flashes red twice the instant the click lands. EA's red box round a building under your attack is gone, since the flash says it now.
- Every order now wears one colour from the click to the spot the units stop on: green for a move, red for an attack or a shot at the ground, orange for an attack move, gold for a guard, and cyan for anything you send a unit to do to something, such as entering, docking, repairing or capturing. A colour that would match your own seat's takes a second shade instead, so an orange player's attack moves show magenta and never pass for his selection rings. Where you click, the cursor's own mark lies on the ground at about the cursor's size and closes on the point: four arrowheads of the order's colour for a move, four triangles for an attack, gone in three quarters of a second, and the cursor's yellow dot in the middle, which stays for a second and a half. The steel ring it replaces reached about five times as far from the point. On a unit you attack the triangles stop just outside its body, a building's or a big vehicle's too, where they used to close under the model and never show. The click mark, the dots, the lines and their rings, the rally point and every power's and guard's targeting marker now have one size on the ground, the size they show with the camera closest, so they keep their shape at every zoom and shrink on the screen with the ground as you pull back; they used to grow fatter on the ground the further out you went. EA's rising green model looked the same for every order and never showed on a formation line, which now gets a marker on every station. The line to the destination takes the colour too, thinner and steadier than the blue laser it replaces, and ends in a small ring of the same colour where the puck sat: a larger one on the ground the unit is heading for, a smaller one on a target or a stop in a shift list. Eight tanks sent together share one line, and its rings now sit on the spots you clicked; they used to land on the middle of the tanks' own parking places, a tank's length or more off the marker. The stops of a shift list sit on their clicks too; a big group's joints used to spread over four or more spots round each one. A ring now means a spot you clicked or a target you picked, and units whose own routes happen to meet somewhere else leave no ring there. Each unit's own stopping place is a small dot of the same colour, a fifth smaller again under the Reforged look, as are the rings at the line's ends. It was a ring the size of the unit, and a group move drew a grid of what looked like a second selection. Each of these marks carries a dark rim, and so do the selection circles, which are a little bolder now, so a white circle holds on snow and a green line on sand at the opening zoom and zoomed out. On water the click marker and the dots lie on the surface in their own colour; they were painted under it and came out tinted. Four units parked in a square no longer show a small diamond of their colour in the gap between their circles. Classic Graphics keeps EA's ring where you click.
- The click marker, the dots and the building grid lie on the ground and nowhere else. They used to be painted over everything the ground pass had drawn: through a hill standing between you and the spot, on top of a bridge deck when the spot was on the riverbank underneath, and bright on black shroud where the ground itself showed nothing. A hill or a deck in front of the spot now hides them, and the fog darkens them as much as the ground they lie on, black shroud to nothing. The order line, the small rings at its ends and corners and the marker on water go dark with the fog the same way, so a line sent into black shroud fades out where the ground does, and under Classic Graphics EA's ring no longer lights up a click into black shroud. A click marker on a hillside used to lie on one flat plane and sink into the slope where the ground curved under it; it follows the ground now. The concrete pads round buildings darken in the fog with the ground too, where they used to sit bright on black shroud.

## A general's rank goes to ten

- The general's rank no longer stops at five stars. Ranks 6 to 10 bring no general's points; each brings a pick of two talents instead, and the one you leave is gone for the match. Rank 6 needs 12,000 points, about 120 tanks killed, and rank 10 needs 56,000.
- Turkiye has its tree first. Rank 6: buildings or infantry cost 15 percent less. Rank 7: Altay Tanks take 744 damage instead of 620, or Bayraktar and Akinci UAVs see a quarter further. Rank 8: a Siper stands 1950 instead of 1500, or a Sungur Gunner 200 instead of 160. Rank 9: the UAV Swarm sends two more munitions, 3, 5 or 7 by the swarm's tier instead of 1, 3 or 5, or the Gokbey Landing drops four more soldiers, 10, 14 or 18 instead of 6, 10 or 14. Rank 10: the Tayfun's warhead reaches a quarter further, full damage out to 62.5 and the outer blast to 112.5 instead of 50 and 90, and the targeting circle grows to match; or every new Maroon Beret is a veteran. A power card adds to the tier you bought and never hands you a tier you did not.
- The four China generals have theirs. Two rows are shared: at rank 6 Hackers cost 40 percent less or every soldier 20 percent less, and at rank 9 the Artillery Barrage fires another wave of 12 shells, 24, 36 or 48 by its tier instead of 12, 24 or 36, or Cluster Mines cover a third more ground. The China general's own picks are a Battlemaster at 480 instead of 400 or a Gattling Tank at 375 instead of 300; Bunkers and Gattling Cannons a quarter tougher, or an Inferno Cannon 15 percent faster on a quarter more armour; and at rank 10 Overlords that come off the line as veterans, or an EMP Pulse that keeps vehicles and buildings dark for 45 seconds instead of 30.
- The Tank General can have his tanks repair 1 percent of their health a second once nothing has hit them for 10 seconds, send his Emperor Overlords out elite, drop 3, 4 or 6 Battlemasters instead of 1, 2 or 4, and armour up his Emperors, Battlemasters, Dragons and Gattlings by a fifth or a quarter. The Infantry General's Minigunners can run a fifth faster and his soldiers heal 2 a second out of combat; his Infantry Paradrop can bring five more men, 10, 15 or 20, and his Assault Troop Crawler can drive 15 percent faster on a quarter more armour, with tougher Tank Hunters and Fortified Bunkers on the other side of those rows. The Nuke General's Overlord can take a fifth more or repair 11 a second out of combat. His Nuke Cannons can come off the line elite or take 30 percent more, and his Nuclear Reactors and Bunkers can stand 1950 instead of 1500 if he passes on tougher MiGs.
- The four American generals have theirs. At rank 6 every vehicle and aircraft costs 15 percent less, a Crusader 765 instead of 900, or every soldier, vehicle and aircraft gains experience half as fast again: in a staged test a Crusader made veteran on its third Ambulance, where without the card three left it short. At rank 9 the A-10 Strike sends one more plane, 2, 3 or 4 by its tier, or the Paradrop brings four more Rangers, 9, 14 or 24 instead of 5, 10 or 20, each general's own Rangers as before. The USA general's own rows: Crusaders at 576 and Paladins at 600, or Rangers at 225 and Missile Defenders at 125; Patriots and Fire Bases at 1250, or Comanches at 264 and Raptors at 192. At rank 10 his Fuel Air Bomb kills a quarter further out, the MOAB too once he has it, and the targeting circle grows with it; or his vehicles, the dozer included, repair about 1 percent a second once nothing has hit them for 5 seconds. In a staged test four Rangers 115 from the aim point walked away from the plain bomb and died under the card's.
- The Superweapon General picks between a tougher Aurora Alpha (100 instead of 80) and tougher Humvees and Avengers, then between EMP Patriots at 1300 and a Tomahawk that drives 15 percent faster on a quarter more armour; at rank 10 his Particle Cannon costs 1875 instead of 2500, or his defences repair 6 more a second on top of their own. The Laser General's Laser Tank can take a fifth more, drive 15 percent faster or leave the factory a veteran, and his Avengers and Laser Defense Turrets can take more; or his turrets and Fire Bases cost 700 instead of 1000. The Air Force General's Comanches go to 275 and King Raptors to 288, his Airfields stand 3250 instead of 2500 and his Patriots 1300, or his Combat Chinooks fly 15 percent faster on a quarter more armour; at rank 10 King Raptors leave the Airfield as veterans, or every aircraft and helicopter he owns repairs about 1 percent a second, under fire too.
- The four GLA generals have theirs. At rank 6 every building costs 20 percent less, a Barracks 400 instead of 500, or every soldier runs 15 percent faster, the Angry Mob too; the Worker keeps his own shoes. At rank 9 the Rebel Ambush brings four more Rebels, 8, 12 or 20 by its tier instead of 4, 8 or 16, or the Anthrax Bomb's blast and poison cloud reach a quarter further, the targeting circle with them. The GLA general's own rows: Technicals and Rocket Buggies 15 percent faster, or RPG Troopers at 125; Stinger Sites at 1300, or Scorpions at 444 and Marauders at 600. At rank 10 his Scud Storm spreads its nine missiles a quarter wider and every blast and poison pool reaches a quarter further, or his Marauders leave the Arms Dealer as veterans.
- The Toxin General's Toxin Tractor can drive 15 percent faster on a quarter more armour, or his Marauders take 625; his Tunnel Networks stand 1950, or his Scud Launchers get the Tractor's treatment; at rank 10 the pools his Scud Storm leaves last 67 seconds instead of 45, or his Toxin Tractors come out veterans. The Demolitions General's Combat Cycles go to 125, or his Bomb Trucks drive 15 percent faster on a quarter more armour; his Demo Traps cost half, 80 with the cheaper buildings, or his Rocket Buggies take 156; at rank 10 each Scud Storm missile hits 660 at the centre instead of 600, or his Scud Launchers come out veterans. The card made it 720 at first, and one salvo then flattened a full-health GLA Command Center, the only storm in the game that could; at 660 the same salvo leaves it about 250 health. The Stealth General's Jarmen Kell goes to 260, or his Technicals to 216 and Rocket Buggies to 144; his Tunnel Networks stand 1875 and Stinger Sites 1250, or his Bomb Trucks get the faster, tougher chassis; at rank 10 his Technicals and Rocket Buggies hide like camouflaged Rebels whenever they hold their fire, or his GPS Scrambler hides units out to 150 instead of 100.
- The promotion window is twice as wide. Your general's powers stay on the left and the five talent rows stand on the right, two cards a row. A row you can pick from is framed in yellow, the card you took lights up and the one you left is hatched out. The star button flashes while a pick is waiting, and the old exit corner now shows your rank. Each card says what it does in a short line under its name ("Altay Tanks tougher", "2 more drones in the swarm"), and its full tooltip opens the moment the mouse is on it; players never found the old one, which waited most of a second. The window now fades in whole: both halves, the cards and the power pictures come up together, where the opening used to stretch the powers half across the whole window and drop the talents in after it. It also starts the moment you press the button: opened right after a promotion, it used to stay invisible for up to three quarters of a second while the arrow pointing at the general's button finished its drop.
- The computer picks its talents as it ranks up, a coin toss per rank.
- Units that come out of the factory already veteran no longer get a talent health card's bonus counted twice: a Dragon Tank built after the card now has 600 health, the same as one that was standing on the field when you picked it.
- A replay recorded on an earlier version will not play back on this one.

## Your orders go before the computer's

- Your units get their routes before any computer player's. The game works out a few routes a frame and used to take requests in the order they came, so late in a big match against several computer players a move you gave could wait a second or more behind hundreds of the computer's own. Now a human player's units are answered first and the computer takes what is left of the frame.
- A big order no longer stands still behind a long line of routes. Version 4.0.0 worked routes out at one fixed pace however many units were waiting for one, so late in a match a group you ordered could wait a second or two before it moved. The pace now rises with the length of the line, up to four times. Sixty Rangers ordered while 480 enemy soldiers were being sent across Death Valley moved off after 5.7 seconds on average instead of 8.1; with nobody else waiting they still go in 1.4. Replays recorded before this change will not play back.
- On large maps a building going up or coming down no longer stalls the game for a frame. The map's areas are worked out again over a few frames instead of all at once. Small maps still do it in one frame, as before.
- A match with many computer players no longer stutters while they lay out their bases. Each one worked out the drive from its base to every corner of the map on the frame it placed its first building and again for its first guns, up to a tenth of a second at a time on a 32-player map; now that is done on the loading screen and a little each frame ahead of need. Their fighting costs the game about a sixth less as well. Thinking in general costs them a seventh less on top of that: every frame the game went through every unit on the map to find the sixtieth of them the computer players mark that frame on their maps of enemy guns, and each time one asked whether a factory could make a unit, the game looked up eighteen times whether the map's script had changed that factory's buttons, which a skirmish map never does. In a 32-player match their turns between minutes 5 and 10 fell from 5.9 to 5.0 ms a frame. The computer players make exactly the same moves as before: the same 32-player match ends on the same frame in the same state. After that they started taking their look at the battlefield on the processor's spare cores, every computer player at once before any of them moves, where each used to look after the ones before it had moved. Their turns fell again, from 5.3 to 4.4 ms a frame over the same minutes. A match no longer plays out move for move as it did before this change, but every machine in it still plays it the same.
- A big match against the computer does less bookkeeping. Each frame that ran slow used to write seven lines about where its time went, and the frame after it timed every unit's turn with a stopwatch; in a 32-player match nearly every frame runs slow, so that was all of them, and half an hour came to 150 MB of log. Now the log takes one slow frame a second and counts the others into it, and the stopwatch comes out only when a developer asks for it. The first seven minutes of a 32-computer match took 24.6 ms of game time a frame instead of 26.2 and wrote 5 MB of log instead of 23, and played out exactly as before.
- A big right click costs the game less. A tank in a group used to look round at every neighbour on every frame to keep its place on the road; now it looks fifteen times a second, every frame while it is stuck, and at once when it is given a new order. Five hundred and seventy tanks and soldiers sent across a large map in one order took 2.9 ms of game time a frame instead of 3.2, and over twenty staged marches, jams and bridge crossings the column arrived within 2% of the old times.
- Units look for targets for less. A computer player asking whether an idle unit has anything to hunt stops at the first enemy it finds instead of measuring the whole map, and a unit deciding whether it can see an enemy asks the cheap questions first, whether the enemy is in reach and whether it can hurt it, before it walks the line across the hills and buildings between them. Every unit picks the same target on the same frame as before, garrisons, bunkers and Stinger Sites included. In a 32-player match against the computer, units spend about a quarter less time looking for targets by minute 9, and the frames where idle units are sent hunting spend a quarter less time on the computer players' turns.
- A hidden unit showing itself costs the game a fraction of what it did. When a camouflaged Stinger Site's soldiers fire, or a Pathfinder or a hidden Rebel takes a shot, every idle enemy that can see them turns on them, and the game used to find those enemies by going through every unit of every opponent, three times a frame for a Stinger Site in a fight. Now it looks around the unit that showed itself. In a 32-player match that work fell from 1.4 to 5.7 ms of every frame to 0.1 to 0.4 ms, measured side by side, and the match plays out frame for frame as it did.
- Supply trucks and factories cost less in a big match. A truck at a depot asked the building for its docking part several times a frame, and the building went through every one of its parts to answer; a unit checking whether a building stood in its line of fire did the same at both ends of the line, and every factory looked its unit's name up again each frame to read the build time. Each answer is found once now and kept. In a 32-player match against the computer the units docking at depots and the units standing ready took about a tenth less time, factories a sixth less, the whole unit pass 4% less, and the match ended on the same frame in the same state.
- A unit hunting across the whole map shares its search out over the processor's cores. Every hunter looked over each corner of the map once a second on one core, a few milliseconds of a single frame late in a big match; with eight more cores to help, that look takes about a quarter of the time, and it finds the same target. The same 32-player match ends on the same frame in the same state on one core or sixteen.
- Computer players get through their checklists faster. Every frame each one asks whether an enemy army is standing in its base and how many tanks or soldiers its enemy owns, and every answer went through the enemy's units one by one, looking each kind of unit up by name again on the way. The answers now come from units kept grouped by kind, and each list of kinds remembers what it matched. In a 32-player match against Brutal computers the scripts took 1.8 ms of a frame on average instead of 2.3, and 2.1 ms instead of 2.9 on the busiest tenth of frames. The match ends on the same checksum.
- Units get their turns for less. The game keeps every unit waiting for its next turn in a sorted queue, and each time one took its turn and went back in, every step it moved down the queue wrote its new place into the unit itself, a slow trip to memory each step and half the cost of the sort. The places now go into a small table of their own. Units act in exactly the order they did before; a 32-player match ends on the same checksum.
- Moving units cost less. Every time a unit crossed a whole map unit it asked every scripted area of the map whether it had just walked in, and nearly all of them said no by their outline alone. Now it asks only the areas whose outline reaches its spot. In a 32-player match against the computer, moving the units took about a tenth less time and the match ends on the same checksum.
- Hunting units find their target for less. Late in a big match every unit sent hunting looked at every unit and building on the map once a second to pick one, and in a 32-player match that was four fifths of all the looking units do. A hunter now looks outward from where it stands and stops as soon as nothing farther off could outrank what it has found. Run side by side against the old build, from minute 7 to 23 of a 32-player match against Brutal computers, hunters looked at 306 things a frame instead of 13,837 and took 1.0 ms of a frame instead of 3.3. The match plays out exactly as before: the same target on the same frame, and the same checksum at the end.
- Standing units and units on an attack move look around on all of the processor's cores. Each frame the units due to look for a target now do it together, spread over the cores, before their own turns come round, and each one keeps the answer only if its target is still alive and still in sight when its turn comes. Late in a 32-player match against Brutal computers that took 1.7 to 2.8 ms off a frame of 30 to 40 ms on a busy machine with eight cores helping. About one answer in 27,000 sees the field a moment earlier than the unit would have, so a match plays out a little differently from before, and the same way on one core or sixteen.
- A computer player's base guns no longer go up in a lump. Its script could ask for three defences in one breath, and each one weighed 96 spots against the whole map on the same frame, 20 to 40 ms of it at 32 seats. They now go up one a frame, a frame or two after the script asked. In a 32-player match the frames where the scripts ran over 33 ms fell from 143 to 117, and across 96 even-against-odd 4v4 matches each side won 17. The computer's guns go up a little later, so its matches play out differently from before.
- What your screen shows can no longer pull a network match apart. The game measures how high a unit stands above the ground and keeps the answer until the unit moves, and the drawing asked too: a jet's nose, a truck's bounce, a tank's track marks and the camera following a flyer each asked a unit's height, and the answer stayed in the unit on that player's machine only. A few kinds of move then shift a kept height instead of measuring it again, so the player who had watched could carry a slightly different height than the one who had not. Heights the drawing asks for are measured and never kept now. A match against the computer plays out exactly as before.
- Your own standing units look around on all of the processor's cores too. A player's unit only takes what it can already shoot from where it stands, and that question could not be asked away from the game's main thread; now it can, unless the unit fights hand to hand. Thirty tanks holding a crossing took every one of their 217 looks from the shared work in a staged test, against 12 before, and picked the same targets.
- Wrecks and passengers stop costing the game while they lie still. A soldier riding in a transport kept the speed he boarded at, and a wreck kept a sliver of downward speed the ground left it, so the game moved each of them by nothing every frame for as long as they lasted. Now a body whose last step changed nothing sleeps until something touches, moves or kills it, and wakes in time to take the step it would have taken. The order units take their turns in a frame is now fixed by unit rather than by the order they happened to be queued, which is what lets a sleeper skip its turn without moving anyone else's. By minute 7 of a 32-player match, about a hundred bodies a frame sleep.
- Idle factories, oil derricks between payouts, minefields that have nothing left to upgrade and the gun of every unit that is not fighting stop taking a turn each frame. A factory with an empty queue still checked its doors and its repeat order sixty times a second, and every armed unit on the map asked each of its weapons whether it had just fired. Each one now waits until there is something to do: an order in the queue, the next payout, a shot, an attack. Matches play out exactly as before, to the same checksum at 8 and 32 players.
- Units looking for an enemy close by skip their own side without reading it. Around a unit most of what shares its patch of ground is its own army, and each search used to open every one of those soldiers and buildings before turning it down. A unit that shuffles within one patch also stops telling the map's index that it moved. Same targets, same checksum.
- A saved game keeps its units' groups. EA's save left out every group units move in, so after a load a column that had been ordered across the map as one forgot it was a column, and the next group made took number 1 again. A supply truck saved halfway through unloading also unloaded on the first frame after the load instead of when its timer said. Both now come back as they were. A loaded game still drifts from the one that was saved after a frame or two, because the computer players work out their routes again from scratch.
- A replay recorded on an earlier version will not play back on this one.

## Ratings, a ladder and your opponent's name before the map loads

- The online hub has a Ladder button where Buddies stood. EA's hub never had one, and nothing answers Buddies on this service. The hub stops asking a new profile for its locale, the player card stops saying "from Unknown" under every name and loses its Set Locale button and Asian text boxes, the lobby and room tooltips drop their "Region: Unknown" line, and the twelve generals' win percentages, which read "%d%%" for want of figures, now come from games played on this service, worked out the way EA's hub worked them out. A day with no figures leaves the panel off the screen. EA's yellow "Welcome to Generals Zero Hour Online." no longer sits over the server's own message, and the panel's tooltip no longer pops up wherever the cursor rests, nor does Quick Match's over the opponent you were just paired with. Quick Match's buttons are lettered in capitals like every other online screen; Stop was the one in small letters.
- Online opens the sign-in screen at once. EA's "Checking for Updates" box in tiny letters is gone (the launcher already checked), and the screen says it is connecting until the server answers; when it cannot reach it, it says so and Sign In tries again. The online sign-in screen is ours now. It says Zero Hour Reforged Online instead of another service's name, explains that your zerohour.gg email or nickname signs you in, and closes the gap the old nickname and birth date rows left behind. Forgot Password takes the place of EA's 2003 terms of service and the ESRB box is gone. Keep me signed in stores a sign-in, never your password, and the screen tells you when that saved sign-in will be used. A line under the fields says what is happening: signing in, a page opened in your browser, or in red what went wrong, worded honestly: a wrong password, too many attempts and how long to wait, the account service being down, a password changed on the site, a ban, or a sign-in from another computer. EA's box that asked for a nickname field you could not see is gone, and after a failed try the password is cleared and ready for the next one. Tab now goes from the email to the password, the checkbox and Sign In (Shift+Tab goes back) instead of into the hidden nickname box, Enter in either field signs you in, and Keep me signed in finally keeps you: typing your email no longer quietly unticks it, and the next start signs you straight in.
- Quick Match counts your search up next to the queue: "Searching for an opponent: 1:23, 4 in the queue", and EA's "There are 1 players currently attempting to match" no longer repeats it underneath. Back takes you out of the queue as well; it used to leave you in it, and whoever the server paired you with loaded against nobody. Once you are paired, the opponent's name, rating and server stand on screen for three seconds before the map loads. If he drops out in those seconds you go back into the queue instead of into an empty match. The settings this service never read are off the screen: number of players, maximum ping, disconnects and ladder.
- The online lobby lists each player's rating and round trip to the server after the name from the moment you walk in, and the tooltip names his rank. The game list's ping column shows the host's own round trip. It used to say 1 ms for every game.
- Your orders in a network match go straight from your machine to every other player's. Every player but the host used to send them to the host, who passed a copy to everyone else, so an order made two trips, and online through our relay that was four legs of internet where two will do. The delay the game builds in to cover the trip follows one trip now: the room waits on its single slowest connection, where it used to add the two slowest together, so a match of three or more answers your clicks sooner. What it adds on top of the trip follows how steady the connections are instead of a flat 100 ms: a steady ping stays where it was, and one that jitters by 30 ms waits a frame longer. A match with real ping runs at full speed now. Every order goes out three times to beat packet loss, and the game judged how close it was to waiting on someone by the last copy to arrive, 60 ms after the first, so on anything slower than a LAN it slowed itself 10% for packets that were already there. Three players at 200 ms of ping played whole matches at 55 frames a second; they hold 59 now, and 58 with 5% packet loss. The ping on the Tab screen is that player's slowest link to anyone, and the host gets a number there too instead of a dash. Your clicks are answered sooner as well. The game held every packet up to a frame before sending it, replies included, so it measured each connection about 15 ms slower than it was and padded the delay to match. Under that sat a floor of 133 ms for every match, a LAN too, sized for a safety brake that cut in four frames early where two do. Both are gone. Two copies on one machine answer a click in 83 ms instead of 133, three players at a 50 ms ping in 100 to 117 ms instead of 150, at 100 ms of ping in 133 instead of 167, and at 200 ms in 200 instead of 233. Every one of those rooms still runs at 59 frames a second, slows itself on fewer frames than before (at 50 ms of ping, 0 to 2 % where it was 8 to 13 %; with 3 % packet loss on top, 7 to 8 % where it was 12 %), and none of them stalled. The price is packets: each player sends about 130 a second in a three-player room instead of 56, which is 18 KB a second for the whole room. Those numbers were taken with no frame rate cap, and most of you play with one. Under a cap the game read and answered its network traffic once a picture and let it sit for the rest of that picture's time, up to 17 ms on every leg at 60 frames a second. It keeps reading and answering while it waits now. Two players at a 50 ms ping on a 60 cap measured an 86 ms round trip and now measure 58, and their clicks land in 100 ms instead of 117; three players at the same ping measure 58 to 72 ms instead of 84 to 90. On one machine with nothing on the wire the round trip fell from 13 to 15 ms to 4 to 9. The rooms still run at 59 frames a second, and a game with no cap behaves exactly as before. Then the delay itself came down again. The game counted the same sliver of the trip two or three times over, and kept two frames in hand for a safety brake that only needs one. A LAN match, or two copies on one machine, answers a click in 50 ms instead of 83; a 50 ms ping in 67 to 83 ms instead of 100; a 100 ms ping in 100 to 117 ms instead of 133. Two and three players on each of those links ran at 58 to 60 frames a second, with and without a frame rate cap, slowed themselves on 2 % of frames or fewer, and never once disagreed about the game.
- Every player's game now keeps an eye out for a map hack and a doctored game, and tells our server with the match result. An order aimed at an enemy you had no way of seeing, nothing of yours or your allies' anywhere near it, is counted against whoever gave it; clicking a tank that drove out of sight a moment ago is not, because the click left while it was still there. When three or more players go out of sync, the game names the ones the rest outvote. The server judges what that means, and the match itself is untouched: nothing it counts changes a single shot, so a replay plays back exactly as before.
- The player card shows the site's wins and losses, rank, rating and place on the ladder, and says so when the player is not online right now.
- The Ladder screen lists 20 players a page with rank, rating, wins and losses, your own row underneath, and Previous and Next to page through. It was an empty frame where EA's web page used to load.
- After a ranked Quick Match your game sends the replay to our server, so anyone can download the match from its page on the site. Custom games, LAN and skirmish replays stay on your machine, and so does a match that went out of sync. Until our server says it has the result and the replay, the score screen holds a "Sending Results" box over itself, because closing the game then could lose the match's result; it goes away on its own the moment the server answers, after 30 seconds at the latest.
- After a Quick Match the score screen's chat box tells you how your rating moved, "Rating +1.3 -> 22", or why the match did not count: a custom game, a desync, a player gone in the first moments, two reports that disagree.

- Started from the launcher's Play or straight from the exe, the main menu's Online button used to open a screen that only said it could not reach the server. It is now greyed out, and hovering it tells you to go online through the launcher's Online page instead.
- Some players could join anyone's online room but could not keep anyone in their own: a friend showed up in the room for a moment and was gone again. The friend's game had mistaken the host for a computer player and left the room on its own. It no longer makes that mistake.
- When a joiner leaves your online room on his own game's say-so, your room's chat tells you why: he could not find you as the host, your seat list never reached him, or it stopped listing him. Before, he just vanished.
- "Could not join - other game version" now says which half differs. A different build of the game means the host or you need the update; the same version with different game data files means a repair or reinstall, or a loose file you put in the Data folder, and the message says so.
