- A file left behind in the game's folder under Documents by an earlier install could make a healthy copy of the game look like a different version to everyone else online, and a reinstall did not clear it. The game no longer trusts that file: one written by another version or another install is thrown away and made again, which costs the first start after an update a little longer.
- Surrender from the menu and stay on to watch, and the match used to go on as if the menu were still open: chat and diplomacy would not come up, a left click selected nothing, and only opening and closing the menu with Escape brought them back. EA's game had it the same way. The menu now takes all of that with it when it closes.

## Wrecks keep the speed they died at

- Vehicles, tanks, jets and helicopters die with their momentum. Anything killed on the move used to stop on the spot where the shot found it, and even a jet lost its speed on the way down: the dead engine braked it back to a stall, so a jet shot down at full tilt crashed nearly as close as one caught on a slow pass. Now a fast jet holds its height a moment, glides on and comes down far ahead of where it was hit. A slow one drops close.
- A car or truck killed by a rocket, a missile, a tank shell, a bomb or a mine while driving is thrown up by the hit and comes down about a second later, and how it turns is worked out from where the shot struck the hull. Shot from behind, the tail kicks up and the nose dips; from the side it leans away from the gun; head on it rears back. It never flips over, however hard the hit, and it explodes where it lands. A car that comes down nose first tips back onto its wheels before it blows; until now the burnt hull appeared on the ground the moment its bumper touched, under a car still drawn up to eight units in the air. A parked one caught by a blast hops and tips away from it. One killed with no shot to throw it, by poison or fire, rolls on and slides to a stop.
- A tank killed on the move keeps sliding and brakes to a stop before it goes up, and a hit from behind sends it further.
- A helicopter shot in flight carries on along the line it was flying all the way down, spinning, instead of dropping under the spot it was hit. With its rotor gone it keeps three fifths of its speed: a Comanche shot at full speed comes down about 390 on from the hit.
- A wreck hits the ground as hard as it fell. A helicopter that dropped off its hover used to raise the same small puff as a jet going in at full speed; now the dust and the shake follow the speed of the impact. A soft landing kicks up a little dirt, a car thrown at speed or a slow jet throws a dust cloud and debris, and a helicopter or a jet shot down flying fast sends up a wall of dust with a ring rolling out from it and shakes the screen. A helicopter that came in fast also ploughs on along the ground about its own length before it stops. If you can see a wreck lying in the fog, you now see it blow up too, and the hull it leaves.
- The Technical, the Rocket Buggy and the Combat Bike had death throws of their own already, and keep them.
- A wreck sliding or flying through a crowd no longer crushes the soldiers and vehicles in its way.
- A replay recorded on an earlier version will not play back on this one.

## Matches up to 32 players

- A match holds up to 32 players now, up from EA's eight, in skirmish, on a LAN and online. Generated maps grow with the number of players, so thirty-two start positions get room instead of a crowd on an eight-player map. Saves and replays from earlier versions do not load in this build, and it cannot play online with an older version.
- A lobby full of computer players no longer grinds down as the match goes on. Past about fifteen computers, the later ones shared a single set of the notes their scripts keep, so every one of them believed an attack was under way, all the time, and kept stacking up attack orders: a 32-computer match ran at 19 logic frames a second by its tenth minute. Each computer keeps its own notes now.
- The skirmish room only ever showed eight seats, so the 32-player skirmish could only be started from the command line. Its seat list runs down to the foot of the room now, fourteen rows where it had eight, and scrolls: your own seat stays at the top and the scroll bar beside the thirteen under it, the same bar the game's lists use, takes you through all 32. The lowest seats open their lists upwards so none runs off the bottom of the screen. No shipped map has more than eight start positions, but a custom map can: past eight players the map picker lists only the official and unofficial maps with a start position for every seat, a custom 12-player map included, and the Random tab builds one for any number. Seating a player the room's map has no start for builds a generated map from your last Random tab choice. LAN and online rooms stay at eight seats for now.
- Setting up 31 computers seat by seat took a few hundred clicks. Presets, beside Record, sets up a game in one pick from 25 grouped by size, 8, 12, 16, 24 and 32 players: one against all on Hard, two even teams, a free-for-all with mixed computers and three or four teams at every size, and at 32 also an all-Brutal 16 v 16, eight teams of four, a last stand of two against 30, you and three allies against 28 Easy and a three-way war of 11, 11 and 10. Your own seat, army and colour stay as they were and every computer gets a random army and colour. The room keeps your map when it has a start position for every seat and otherwise moves to a generated map sized for the crowd. Four Custom slots at the top of the list keep a room of your own: click an empty one to save the seats, map and match rules as they stand, pick a saved one to load it, save over it or clear it. They live beside your other skirmish settings and survive a restart, and a saved game whose map has too few start positions for it loads onto a generated map.

## America, built again

- Every American unit and building has been modelled again on EA's own shape: the same silhouette, the same footprint, the turret and the barrels where they always were, with the detail modelled in where the 2003 boxes had it painted on. Each one comes in four levels of detail, the full model up close and lighter ones as the camera pulls away. A tank's road wheels turn with its tracks; EA's stood still. The campaign's own infantry are not done yet.
- It is the Reforged picture. Classic Graphics keeps EA's 2003 models, and a Classic player and a Reforged player still share a match: every bone a weapon fires from or a turret turns on sits exactly where EA put it, which we checked on all 508 models before they went in, so both looks play the same game.
- Composite Armor shows on the tank now. Once the Strategy Center finishes it, every Crusader, Paladin, Avenger and Microwave Tank you own has riveted plates bolted onto its hull, the ones already in the field and every one built after, and the plates stay on as the tank takes damage. EA's upgrade added 100 health and changed nothing you could see, so you had to guess whether the tanks rolling at you had it. The plates belong to the rebuilt models: Classic Graphics, or the Reforged picture without the model download, shows EA's tanks as they were.
- The rest of America's upgrades show on the units they change too. Chemical Suits show on Rangers, Missile Defenders, Pathfinders and Colonel Burton, and a Ranger carries the Flash-Bang Grenades and the Capture Building kit once you have bought them. Drone Armor puts armor on the drones and Supply Lines loads crates onto the Chinook. Countermeasures fits flare dispensers to every jet, bomber and gunship and to the Comanche; Laser Missiles hangs its pods on the Raptor and the Stealth Fighter, Bunker Busters its bombs on the Stealth Fighter, and the Air Force General's Stealth Comanche wears its panels. Chemical Suits used to jam a bulky hood over the soldier's head; now a gas mask sits under his helmet, on Rangers, Missile Defenders, Pathfinders and Colonel Burton. Advanced Training used to change nothing you could see, and now every American unit that gets it shows it once it is bought. Soldiers wear gold shoulder boards with dark chevrons, ground vehicles carry a gold chevron plate on the hood or the front of the hull, and aircraft carry gold chevron bands on top of the wings (the Comanche, on its engine pods). Flash-Bangs are chunky silver canisters, three on the chest and two on the back. The Stealth Comanche's panels run the width of each stub wing, and the Air Force Comanche's flare dispensers shrink to one box a side to make room. Jets that go down keep their kit: a Stealth Fighter or an Aurora falling out of the sky, and the hulk it leaves, still carry the flares, laser pods and bombs you bought. A Ranger capturing a building no longer raises a second small flag beside the big one. Like the armor plates, these parts come with the rebuilt models. China and GLA get the same treatment. Nationalism flies a team pennant over Red Guards, Tank Hunters and Mini-Gunners, and Fanaticism raises a taller standard with a crimson sash. Subliminal Messaging bolts a horn cluster onto the Speaker Tower, the Listening Outpost, the Troop Crawler and the Emperor, and the Overlord and Helix carry speakers too. Tank AutoLoader, Uranium Shells, Nuclear Tanks and Isotope Stability each add their own part to the Battle Master, Overlord and Emperor, Chain Guns hang a brass ammo can on the Gattling Tank and Gattling Cannon, Neutron Shells rack up on the Nuke Cannon, and Black Napalm wraps the Dragon, Inferno Cannon, Helix and MiG in jackets and canisters. On the GLA side a Rebel wears a camouflage mantle, an ammo bandolier or a suicide belt, the Jarmen and Stinger carry their own gear, the Worker gets new shoes, every vehicle drags Junk Repair scrap, and Camo Netting drapes all the GLA buildings, damaged and snowy ones included. Anthrax Beta fits light blue canisters to the Toxin Truck and the Scud Launcher, and one across the Bomb Truck's front bulkhead. Anthrax Gamma does it in violet for the Toxin General: a lid on every drum of the Toxin Truck and the Tunnel Network, canisters on the Scud's forward deck and either side of the Combat Bike's tail, and a small glass canister on the back of the Rebel, the Stinger soldier, the Tunnel Defender and the Terrorist. Beta's drum lids on the Toxin Truck wear a black and white hazard ring, so they still stand out on a blue player colour. The computer picks its research the way it always did: a part drawn for an upgrade never makes the upgrade look more worth buying. China and GLA upgrade parts come with the detailed unit and building models add-on, so a player without it sees the upgrades work and nothing more.
- A GLA Worker who had carried a single crate wore the Demolition General's dynamite vest and the Worker Shoes boots for the rest of the match, bought or not, on every general. Picking up the crate showed every hidden piece of his model along with it. He now wears them only once the upgrade is yours.
- A General's Power you buy now shows on its building. Strikes, drops, cash and repair appear on the Command Center, a unit you unlock or train as veterans on the building that produces it, and a power with three levels adds one piece for each. It works for America, China and GLA, Fake Command Centers included. Capture a building and the pieces on it change to the new owner's powers. Upgrades show the same way: research one and a part appears on the building you researched it in, 43 of them across the Airfield, Barracks, Strategy Center, War Factory, Nuclear Missile Launcher, Propaganda Center, Arms Dealer, Black Market and Palace, so a glance at a base tells you what its owner has bought. A save made before this update shows nothing for powers already bought, and old replays and players on an older version cannot join. Like the other parts, these come with the rebuilt models.
- The rebuilt models are an optional download of about 8.8 GB, and you play with anyone whether you took it or not. A match checks the models the game shipped with, and the rebuilt ones keep every bone where EA put it, so a player with them and a player without fight the same battle: an eight-army computer match played fifteen minutes with them and again without ended exactly the same. In a big battle they cost about 1.2 ms a frame, so Detailed Models under Options, Display switches them off for frame rate and keeps the rest of the Reforged picture. That was 1.6 ms until every armed unit stopped setting the missiles on its rack again every frame; it now does it only when a missile leaves or comes back. Classic Graphics never loads them, and a game folder without them starts as if they had never existed.
- The textures at twice EA's detail and the sharper ground are an optional download the same way, and HD Textures under Options, Display turns them off on a card short of video memory. Without them the Reforged picture draws EA's own textures and ground and keeps the rebuilt models' own paint, and you still play anyone, with them or without.
- The Avenger is the one that waits. Its new model was built from the copy EA shipped before the 1.04 patch and lacks the turret a GLA Bomb Truck shows when it disguises itself as one, so it keeps EA's patched model until that is fixed.

## A cursor for every order
- The mouse pointer says which order a click will give, and it looks like Generals again. Our first set was polished metal, and players told us it was pretty and no longer felt like Command & Conquer. Every cursor is now drawn in the 2003 game's own marks and its own sixteen-colour palette, flat colour inside a one-pixel black line: four green arrowheads closing in for a move, four red triangles round a yellow dot for an attack, red and green together for attack move, white corner brackets for select, the white dart pointer, the green arrows at the screen edge, stacked triangles for entering a building, and a red ring for an order that cannot be given. The unit abilities are small pictures with the original white arrow tip: the knife, the dynamite, the field laptop, the wrench, the brick wall that fills in row by row while a building resumes. They move the way they used to as well. The attack triangles spread, the out-of-range arrows fill red to green, the sniper's ticks turn yellow as it locks on, and the timed charge counts down from nine.
- Orders the original never drew a mark for get one in the same hand. Guard shows a white shield, unloading shows green chevrons rising off a hull's floor, garrisoning and boarding show the green triangles dropping into a building or onto a transport, hijacking drops red ones onto a car, a car bomb carries a red bomb on its roof and sabotage is a yellow lightning bolt. Placing a building shows the original's yellow placement cross; where you cannot build it turns grey under the red ring. Sell mode on the Red Alert sidebar has its own: a gold coin struck with a dollar sign that flips over about once a second, and over anything you cannot sell, the same coin under the red ring, so the pointer never jumps as you sweep across your base. Each cursor is drawn twice, and the game shows the one that matches your Windows pointer: 32 pixels like the original at normal scaling, 48 on a desktop scaled to 150 % or more, and the 48 is drawn pixel for pixel at that size rather than blown up from the 32.

## A shot from the fog gives the shooter away

- When something you cannot see hits one of your units or buildings, the fog opens around the shooter for two and a half seconds: a small circle, just wide enough to show what fired and not the ground around it. Artillery behind a ridge or a jet out of the dark shows itself the moment its shot lands. Your allies see it too, as they see everything else you see. A stealthed unit nobody has detected stays hidden, and a shot from something you can already see opens nothing. A replay recorded before this change plays out differently.

## Sight without holes

- What a unit sees used to come out dotted. Each square of ground is checked for a hill or a tree between it and the eye, and a single tree or a bump no taller than a tank hid one square here and a thin streak there, so the fog inside a unit's sight was full of pinholes. A hidden square now comes into sight when at least six of the eight around it are in sight: the pinholes and the one-square streaks open, while the shadow a real ridge or a building throws, two squares wide or more, stays dark, and nothing is seen further away than before. A replay recorded before this change plays out differently.

## The command bar fits the map

- Every side's bar is painted again with the depth of the 2003 bar it grew out of: dark steel in three tiers, in three boxes that sit flush on the screen's edges. The radar has a box of its own under a ledge, the command grid sits under a rail that rises into the money tab with the power bar sunk along it, and your selection carries the minimise and promotion buttons on a mount above it. Each side is built its own way. America's plates are cut like an aircraft's, China's carry upturned eaves, red lacquer and gold studs, the GLA's are scrap welded on crooked, and Turkiye's are modern armour with turquoise lights and no national sign. The money is larger and bold behind a gold dollar sign, with a comma every three digits, and the minimise and promotion buttons wear the side's colour.
- The radar sits in a low wide box of its own and puts black bands beside a map of any shape. The production queue and the card for a build button stand over the box's ledge instead of on it. A click on the radar still lands where it always did.
- The selection keys stand together at the right end of the command grid, top to bottom: Select Army, then the idle infantry, vehicle and aircraft buttons. The idle worker button sits in the column on the left, between the "!" and chat. Each idle button picks the next unit of its kind standing with no order; the infantry, vehicle and aircraft buttons leave the camera where you put it, and the worker button brings it to the worker unless Jump to Idle Worker is off; Shift-click takes every idle one of that kind on the map at once. Right-click on the infantry, vehicle or aircraft button takes every one of that kind, busy or not, the ones on screen first and the whole map on a second right-click. Select Army, three soldiers in a selection box in your side's own frame, selects every fighting unit on screen, then your whole army on the map with a second click, and never a worker, a supply truck or a building. The "!" used to place a beacon, in multiplayer only, and did nothing against the computer; it turns the camera to the last radar alert now, your base under attack or a building lost, in every kind of game, and a second click soon after steps back to the alert before it. The beacon keeps its key. A button glows while one of its kind stands idle, wears its plain face while you have some but all are busy (the right-click still works then, and a left click leaves your selection alone), and goes dark only when you have none of that kind at all, so a dark button really does nothing. The worker button has no right-click, so it glows or goes dark. Each tooltip names the key that does the same. These tooltips and the two new keys read in German, Russian and Ukrainian too. The worker button used to light two to five seconds after the other three, because it waited on the worker to report itself idle; all four now look at your army on the same frame, and the worker button and its key cycle through the same workers that lit it.
- The general's powers stand three to a row again, on the right edge above the general's tab. When the top row is short it leaves a step on the inside, and the tray's plate follows that outline.
- The promotion window's close button is your side's own now, cut to fit the window's corner. It was the last piece of the old bar's art left on any side's screen.
- On a very wide map the minimap stops at 4:3 and shows the rest with black bands.
- The minimap is sharp at any HUD Size. Every unit and building used to be the same blurred dot that jumped every twelve frames; units now glide across it as crisp dots, and buildings show their real footprint, turned the way they stand. The ground is drawn at twice the detail, and the edge of the fog fades over about two cells of the map instead of climbing in stair steps, the same picture under Direct3D 9 and 11, which EA's own note asked for in 2003: "this really needs to smooth the display!"
- What you have selected is white on the minimap, so the dot you just picked out of a crowd is the one you can find again. A selected factory draws a thin line to its rally point, and selected units draw every leg of their queued orders, so a shift-queued raid across the map can be checked without scrolling there. F11 turns the minimap into three colours: your own things green, your allies blue, your enemies red, everyone else in their own colour. Press it again for the players' colours back. The key can be moved in Hotkeys.ini as TOGGLE_RADAR_COLORS.
- A unit walking to its number-key group no longer hides the ones already there. The white square at the group's gathering point covered the dots of every unit that had arrived; they are drawn over it now.
- Right-click an enemy dot on the minimap and your selection attacks that unit or building, the same order a click on it in the battlefield gives, under the Alternate Mouse Setup too. It used to send them to walk to the spot. Only what your minimap shows can be picked: nothing in the fog, no stealth unit you have not detected, and a disguised unit still reads as the friend it pretends to be.
- Minimap Size under Options > Interface runs from 100 to 200 percent. The minimap grows up from the bottom left corner over the battlefield and the rest of the command bar stays where it was. 100 is the minimap as it always was.
- A grown minimap wears your side's own steel. Above 100 percent it used to sit in a flat grey border with a sliver of the old painted box showing beside it; now the frame is the bar's own art, laid round the bigger picture from the screen's edge to its foot, and it reddens with the under-attack lamp the way the box does. Classic keeps the plain border. Its corners now meet the same edge at every size, where before the length of each side decided which slice of the edge ran into the corner, a bolt cut in half one size and a step in the rim the next. The rim itself is redrawn to run straight along each side and turn the corner as one line, where the top edge used to drop a pixel or three into the corner piece, and the edges repeat without a visible joint. The signal keys' plate stands on the frame as part of its ledge now, instead of on a lit rim that ran under the keys. At small sizes a near-square map no longer leaves a strip of empty glass down the minimap's right side, and with a narrowed HUD Width the frame starts at the HUD's edge instead of the screen's.
- A grown minimap no longer drags the game down. Its dark glass was laid in tiles four pixels by two, some 24000 of them a frame at 200 percent, and a match that ran at 4 ms a frame took 38 with a frame of 194 in it. It is one sheet of glass now, and 200 percent costs what 100 does.
- The camera box on the minimap is a bright line on a dark edge, and it thickens as the minimap grows. EA's thin yellow line, darker along the bottom, all but vanished into the sand of a desert map, more so the bigger the minimap. Classic keeps EA's line.
- The mouse wheel zooms the minimap. On a big map the whole battlefield squeezed into the radar box left a base a few pixels wide; four notches over the minimap now take it to four times as close, around the spot under the pointer, and the wheel back out returns the whole map. Zoomed in, the minimap follows your camera as you scroll, and every dot, footprint, order line, alarm and the camera box sit where the ground under them is, so a click or a right-click on what you see lands on it. The wheel over the battlefield still zooms the camera, and every match starts on the whole map.
- Radar alarms read at a glance. Every alarm used to be the same huge triangle spinning down over half the minimap for a second and a half, told apart only by its colour. Each kind now has a small mark of its own: an attack is a red ring with a pulse rolling out of it, a building you lost is a cross where it stood, a finished building or upgrade is a tick and a stealth unit found is a diamond. A building's mark is bigger than a harvester's, a harvester's bigger than a soldier's, and an ally's signal draws a square with a dot. The attack ring stays up for as long as the fight goes on and goes out a few seconds after the last hit, where it used to vanish four seconds into a long fight and leave the spot blank for the next six. Losing a building marks the radar now as well, with a ping under EVA's line. Space goes to the last alarm as before; pressed again within three seconds it steps back through the four before it, never to the same spot twice. When an attack, a lost building, an infiltration or one of your hidden units being found happens off the screen, a chevron at the edge of the battlefield points the way. A unit under attack sounds the warning EA wrote for units, quieter than the building's one it used to borrow.
- Watching a match gets a bar of its own in plain dark steel with the same three tiers as the players' bars, square where it meets the screen's edge. The watcher belongs to no side, so each of his boxes is built the way one side builds: the radar and the column of players are one American box under a ledge that ends in an arrow point, the watched player's panel is China's, with a stepped rail and a row of rivets, the selection box takes Turkiye's wide chamfer and range ticks under a mount that holds the on-air lamp, and the drawers on the right are GLA scrap with welded patches and odd bolts. The panel now reaches the bottom of the screen, and a click anywhere on its steel stays on the panel. Its radar takes the map's shape, and the column of players stands against the radar's edge on a tall map instead of leaving a gap. A lamp in each player's colour sits beside his button, with a ring round the one you point at and a brighter one round the player you are watching.
- While you watch, a rack of drawers hangs from the right edge under the superweapon countdowns. The whole rack wears the command bar's steel. The top drawer holds three plain buttons for the camera, Free, Director (it goes to the biggest fight by itself) and Player (the followed player's own screen), a button for that player's fog of war and one that slides the armies drawer out; they used to be a three-stop lever and two rockers. Under it every player is ranked by one of seven numbers: net worth, cash, income a minute, army value, kills and losses, general's rank and power. A row of seven buttons picks the number, each with a picture (a stack of coins for net worth, a tank for army value, a gunsight for kills) and its key in the corner; Q, W, E, R, T, Y and A and the wheel pick it too. The number's name stands over the list in plain words, the column head says what it is counted in, and pointing at a button names it before you click. It used to be a dial with seven letters round it and nothing to say which letter meant what. Each row carries the player's place, his colour, his side's picture and a bar of his share of the leader's number; the row under the pointer lights gold and the player you follow is framed in blue. A click on a player's row, or the tab out of it, puts his own screen on yours in one go, and a second click or Esc gives you back the camera you had before; scroll away from him and a click on his name takes his screen again. Viewers used to follow a player and then hunt for the lever to see what he saw. Each row's tab carries the player's eye in his colour, and its red lamp lights while his screen is on yours. The top drawer is called Camera now and says in words what the camera is doing, Free camera or Screen of and the player's name in his colour, and under it what to do next, "Click a player's name to see their screen". Point at a button or a row and that line tells you what it does before you click. The red lamp in the drawer's head lights only while a player's screen is what you see, and a steel name plate at the top of the picture carries his eye and his name and says Player camera. A computer player has no screen to show, and the drawer says so: the director follows his fights instead. The fog switch stays where you put it. The armies drawer lists the six kinds of unit he has most of, with how many. A click on the rack never reaches the battlefield.
- The superweapon countdowns stand where they do in a player's game while you watch, in their tray. The observer's bar named no tray for them, so they used to sit bare and higher up.
- The card that rises when you point at a build button is drawn in your side's own art now, with the price and the build time beside the name behind a coin and a clock. Under them one row of icons says what you are buying: health, armour class, damage, damage a second, range and speed for a unit, health, armour and the power it adds or draws for a building. The six lines of figures that used to pad out the description are gone, and so is the "Power Required" line EA wrote into every building's text, in every language. The small tooltip beside the pointer sits in a framed well of the same art in a match and of the watcher's steel in the menus. Both are cut from the bar itself: the same near-black shell, bevelled lip and sunk glass, the card's corner shaped like the side's bar (America's 45 degree cut, China's two steps, the GLA's bitten scrap, Turkiye's wide chamfer with its turquoise light), open on the side that meets the screen's edge.
- EA's own faction pictures are back on the army screen, in the lobby's game list, on the player card and on the score screen. The generals' faces and the side logos you know from 2003 replace the steel cards and emblems that stood there since v3.6.0, and the score screen's rows start with the player's name again, with no emblem before it and no faint card behind the table. Turkiye keeps its own picture on the army screen. Watching, the player buttons and the board's rows carry EA's observer pictures again, one per side as in 2003, where we had drawn a badge for every general; Turkiye wears America's there, as it does in the lobby. America, China and the GLA show there in full colour now. Their logos came out grey, because the picture EA gives each army is a greyed copy; the screen takes EA's coloured faction logos instead.
- The Tab screen, with the players, their teams and the chat buttons, is painted in your side's bar now instead of EA's see-through black with a blue rule. It stands in the top left corner on the same dark steel in three tiers, square on the screen's two edges and cut at the corner facing the battlefield, every player's row in a sunk well with alternate rows a shade lighter so a name lines up with its team at a glance. Its buttons are cut from the same metal: the mute switch carries a speaker that is struck through once you have muted someone, the money's minus, plus and Send sit in bezels shaped like the side's toolbar buttons, and Main Menu stands in a socket of its own. In a campaign the mission's briefing fills one clear well of dark glass, without the empty player rows, the grey veil and the blue frame it used to wear, and its scroll bar's arrows and groove are cut from the same steel. Signed in online, the In Game and Buddies tabs over the list are keys from the command bar's own tabs: dark glass in the side's bezel, the open one lit in the side's colour, the label gold under the pointer, where EA's orange and yellow outlines used to sit. The Communicator page behind the second tab stands on the same steel: your buddy list, the chat and the line you type each sit in a well of dark glass below the tabs, with the scroll bars cut from the side's metal, instead of blue outlines and a bright cyan box laid over the In Game page's column titles. The watcher gets it in his own steel. The panel is solid, so the battlefield no longer shows through the list. The Classic interface keeps EA's screen.
- An army standing guard no longer slows the game down. Each shield over a guarding unit's head was painted a line at a time, 60 to 180 little pieces a unit, and three hundred Rangers on guard took the picture down to 12 frames a second. The shield is now one picture, the same shield, and the same three hundred draw at about 240.
- Eight new player colours after the original eight: Teal, Lime, Navy, Magenta, Brown, Lavender, Coral and Olive, for players and AI in skirmish, LAN and online. They replace Crimson, Azure and Salmon.

## Your queue in pictures again

- What your base is building stands over the radar as pictures again, not lines of text: one row of four, no wider than the radar's box, the next to arrive on the left, together in one steel tray hard against the left edge of the screen, built like the tray that holds the general's powers, each picture in its cell with the coloured edge a power button wears. The seconds left sit in its corner on a dark plate, an x4 marks four of the same thing queued back to back, and a dark sweep comes off the picture as it builds. Past four, a tag sticking up from the tray says how many more are coming. Click one and the camera goes to the building making it; right-click it, or click with Ctrl held, and the newest of it comes off that building's queue, the picture turning red under Ctrl first so you see what you are about to cancel.
- Your hero gets a cell of his own on top of the queue, in the same steel against the left edge: Burton, Black Lotus, Jarmen Kell or the Maroon Beret, with an upright bar beside his picture that drains from the top as he takes hits, in the colours of the bar over his head. One click on it selects him and brings the camera to him, as the hero key does, and if he is riding in a transport it selects the transport. The cell is there as long as he lives, with or without anything in the queue, and it never moves when the "+N" tag comes and goes.
- Superweapon countdowns in the top right are pictures too, yours first and then everyone else's, each soonest first, six to a row and two rows at most in a tray of their own against the right edge of the screen, a little under the info strip, with a tag hanging below it for the rest. A thick border in its owner's colour runs round all four sides of each one, edged in light under a dark colour and in black under a bright one, so a navy or olive player stands out from the tray as clearly as a yellow one. A dark sweep shows how far the charge has come, and once one is charged its owner's colour rises up over the picture like light off a lamp, brightest at the foot, breathing slowly so a ready superweapon reads at a glance. Clicking one of your own takes the camera to it.

## Air that shimmers over fire

- Heat Haze, under Options, Display, is a new setting, off by default until it has been played. The air above a burning building wavers, a laser's beam bends what lies behind it, and a missile leaves a ripple behind its exhaust, the way hot air does in Command and Conquer 3. Only the ground behind the heat moves: a tank parked in the fire keeps its outline. The Performance / Quality slider turns it on one stop past High, with ambient occlusion, and you can still tick it by hand at any stop. Your opponent's setting is his own, because nothing in the game reads it. Direct3D 11 only, and off under Classic Graphics.

## EA's four ranks are back

- The rank ladder is gone, every grade, perk and aura of it. A unit is Regular, Veteran, Elite or Heroic again, on the kills and the bonuses the 2003 game gave them, with EA's chevrons over the health bar and on the portrait. Six kills of its own kind make a Crusader Heroic, where an American one needed 66 on the ladder.
- What EA built a level up is built a level up again. Red Guard Training makes a Veteran and Battlemaster Training an Elite, the Tank General's tanks and the Infantry General's men leave the factory Veteran, and the tooltips and general bios say so. A veterancy crate gives one whole level, and a hacker earns experience at EA's rate.
- The rings under leaders went with it, and so did GLA's faster, self-mending veterans and each side's own bonus table. Turkiye, still an experiment, ranks up on EA's four levels too.
- Replays recorded before this change play out differently.

## Five more colours

- Crimson, Azure, Salmon, Teal and Lavender join the colour box in every room. EA's list stopped at eight, so the last player into a full room took the one colour left; now he has six to pick from, and everyone's old colours stay as they were. A replay recorded before this change, with a random colour in it, plays out differently.

## A handicap for every seat

- The skirmish, LAN and online rooms have a Handicap box at the end of every seat's row, from 100% down to 10%. At 50% that player's units and buildings have half their health and his weapons and superweapons deal half their damage: his Crusader reads 240 where the same tank reads 480 across the map. Building, research and every special power's recharge take twice as long, and flat healing is halved so a smaller body refills no faster. Rate of fire, income, speed, sight and prices stay as they are. A demo truck still dies in its own blast, and a sniper's shot or a pilot kill works as ever.
- You pick for your own seat and the host picks for the computer seats, the way colour and team already work. The pick is in the replay and the saved game, and a room that leaves the column at 100% plays and replays as it did.
- Promotions and armour research still come on top, at the seat's share: an Elite Paladin with Composite Armor reads 364 at 50% against 728 at 100%. A vehicle stolen from a handicapped player moves to its new owner's column and keeps its share of health, so a Humvee at 80 of 120 becomes 160 of 240 with no damage dealt and no repair given.

## Long routes in big computer matches

- A unit looking for a long way across a crowded map no longer stops mid-search and gives up. A search that runs out of its share of a step waits for the next one and carries on, and the limit on how much ground one search can cover is doubled. In eight Hard computer players on Twilight Flame, six matches a side, the pathfinding cost 34.9 seconds a match where it cost 42.8, with 28% fewer cells searched, and fewer units sat wedged. The worst frames of those matches did not get measurably shorter. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- Before a long search the pathfinder sketches a rough corridor over the map in blocks of ten cells, and two kinds of sketch were pure waste. One was drawn for a unit whose destination turned out to be taken, which then had to look for the nearest free spot instead. The other was a worker a step from his own building site: the half-built walls split the blocks the sketch walks while the ground he walks stays open, so it covered the whole map, 4 to 7 ms of a single frame, and found nothing. Now the sketch is drawn only for a search that will run, and it gives up past 5,000 cells, a size no sketch that found its corridor reached in three long matches. Every unit is handed the route it was handed before. Eight Hard computer players on Twilight Flame, one match at a time on three seeds: frames where the pathfinder's own queue took over 5 ms went from 13 to none, and over 3 ms from 337 to 139, fewer on every seed. The pathfinder's total time stayed where it was, and the few frames over 33 ms are the opening's scripts, the same frames in every build. Which frame works a route out has moved, so replays recorded before this change play out differently.

## Computer players earn half as much again, and more when they fall behind

- A computer player in a skirmish or a network match earns half as much again as you would, on every difficulty, where it used to earn double. A truckload worth 75 banks 112, and the 1000 for capturing an oil derrick is 1500. It counts everything the computer makes by playing: supply docks, oil derricks and other tech buildings, black markets, drop zones, hackers, bounties, crates, salvage and stolen cash.
- A computer that falls behind earns more. Every thirty seconds it weighs its team against the strongest enemy team still in the match, each team's armies, bases and banks at their prices, divided by its living players, so a team of three does not look rich next to a lone enemy just for having three bases. Its human allies count toward its team, and in a free-for-all every enemy is a team of one. Level or ahead, it stays at half again. Behind, it gains up to 25 points of income at each weighing, toward double at three quarters of the enemy team's worth and triple at a quarter and below, so a computer that is being crushed reaches triple in three minutes. It gives the points back the same way as it catches up.
- The score screen and its charts show what the computer would have earned without the bonus, so its money earned reads against yours on the same terms.
- Money it gets back stays what it was. Selling a building or cancelling a queue returns the same sum as yours does, or a computer could queue and cancel its way to a fortune, and cash from a map's script or from an ally gets no bonus either. The money figure floating over a computer's truck or building shows what it really banked.
- Your own income does not change, and your cut of a computer ally's income under Share Income is the plain cut. Campaign missions and Generals' Challenge opponents earn what they always did.
- Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- It also goes for that money from the start. A computer used to buy the capture research only once a soldier stood idle at home, and by then its opening had often spent the bank. Now the first barracks trains the soldier and starts the research within five seconds of standing, and he walks to the nearest oil derrick while it runs. The same four-player match on Twilight Flame: Hard's first derrick fell at 2 minutes 20 seconds where it had taken 4 minutes 40, Medium's at 2 minutes 35 against 3 minutes 10, Easy's at 2 minutes 50 against 4 minutes 11. Script teams also stopped recruiting that soldier off a half-captured derrick. During the first six minutes a computer that can expand looks for a new supply dock every 15 seconds instead of every minute and will spend its last dollar on the building, where it used to want twice the price in the bank. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.

## Missions keep the time their script wrote

- EA's cinematics slow the game on purpose, so the radio lines fit and the camera lands where the next shot starts. This build had stopped honouring that on 18 October. Every mission's cutscenes now run at the pace their script asks for. China's parade had 16 seconds of radio talking over itself, and has 11 now: what is left is EA's own script, which starts the tank crews' lines two thirds of a second apart.
- Parade tanks drive the road. A mission's waypoint route had been handing out a lane per vehicle, which put China's column up to 82 feet off its line. The furthest any tank strays now is under a foot.
- China's first mission could hang in its opening shot. Your own idle tanks opened fire on the bomb truck during the cutscene and killed it before it reached the crowd, and the scene waited for a blast that never came. Nothing you own starts a fight on its own until the script hands you control, as in EA's game.

## Classic first, Reforged when you ask

- A first start now opens the game EA shipped: its own textures and ground, the hard stencil shadows, the flat 2003 light, no glow, bilinear filtering, the original sound mix, health bars only on what you select or point at. The HD art stays on your disk, unmounted. Every setting this build added to the picture, the sound and the controls starts off, and each one is a box in Options.
- One click brings the other game back. Options, Graphics, untick Classic Graphics: the High preset fills in every Reforged box on the page, you can move the quality slider from there, and Accept saves it for the next start. Tick it again and the same boxes go off.
- Defaults in Options now means this game too. It used to leave every setting this build added where you had put it, so a Reforged page stayed Reforged after the click. Now it ticks Classic Graphics and puts every row back where a first start has it, the controls and the sound included. Your language, window mode and resolution stay, and unticking the box still gives you High.
- Classic now means EA's picture in a fight too, checked side by side against the real 2003 game on this machine. Every explosion, every muzzle flash and all the black smoke this build retuned goes back to EA's own numbers under Classic: 132 effect lists and 235 particle systems stand as shipped, and the 51 particle systems this build invented draw nothing. So do the slow water, tank barrels that tilt to the target and the grade insignia on units, which return to the three chevrons, and a match opens at EA's camera height. Tick off Classic and Reforged has all of it, down to the pixel. Two players on different looks still share a match, and we ran one 3000 frames with no mismatch.
- Classic was the slower look in a big fight, and the picture never asked for that. Every explosion's light tested every patch of ground for every light on the map, and each shadow was copied a second time for a graphics device that draws nothing. Both are gone and the picture is the same. In a late 8-player match the drawing behind one frame falls from 9.6 ms to 5.4 ms, and the slowest frame in a thousand from 21.25 ms to 17.75 ms.
- The Performance / Quality slider stopped short of this version's own looks: you had to find each box by hand. Now it reaches all nine. One stop past High brings tone mapping, the sky and ground light, ambient occlusion and water splashes, the next adds battle marks and weather, and Ultra adds firelight, atmosphere and collapsing buildings. All nine together cost 1.4 ms of graphics card time a frame on an RTX 2060 in our chaos fight, 9.36 against 7.99. High is the picture it always was, and under Classic Graphics the slider leaves every one of them off at any stop. Firelight, atmosphere and collapsing buildings carry known faults, a stall, a black smear at a flat camera and a hitch, which is why they wait for Ultra.
- The launcher's Options page has the same slider, with every new box beside it. Move it there or in the game and each opens on what the other saved.
- A detail preset now means EA's detail settings. Before this, a preset in your settings file switched on team glow, water foam and 4x multisampling behind any box you could see, and not on the very first start, so the first start and the second drew different pictures. Now a Reforged setting comes on from its own line, which the menu writes when you accept.
- The Classic stencil shadows no longer crash the game under a model with a very large shadow outline. The room the game kept for a shadow's outline ran out at about 680 edges, and a building past that took the match down. That room is sixteen times larger now.
- Smooth Motion, the blending that made units glide on a fast monitor, had no switch at all. It is a box in Options, Display, off until ticked, and a 60 Hz screen shows no difference either way.
- Already playing? Nothing in your settings file gets rewritten and every line in it still wins. A setting you never touched has no line, so it takes the new default, which for most of you means Classic on your next start. Untick Classic Graphics once and you are back. The settings can differ between players in one match: none of them reaches the game's logic.

## Buildings go down

- Collapsing Buildings, under Options, Display, is a new setting, off by default until it has been played. EA's building stands until the frame it dies, then it is gone or it is a pile of rubble, with a cloud thrown over the moment. With this on it holds for a beat, shudders, leans about seven degrees and goes into the ground, a second for a small one and up to two and a half for a tall one. Most of the fall happens inside EA's cloud, so the part you see is the first half second, the roof dropping as the smoke comes up. It blocks nothing and nothing in the game reads it, so two players in one match can have it set differently. Direct3D 11 only.

## A sky over the map

- Atmosphere, under Options, Graphics, is a new setting, off by default until it has been played. Tilt the camera flat or fly it low in a replay and EA's game ran out of world, black above the skyline and a far plane that cut the ground off in a line. With this on there is a sky, EA's own art for the map's hour, the ground far from the camera fades toward its colour, and the black ring past the map goes into the same haze. Your fog of war stays as dark as it was, the ground near the camera stays clear, and nothing moves but your camera. Your opponent's setting is his own, because no part of the game reads this. A battle of three armies and three superweapons takes the graphics card's frame from about 8.0 to 8.2 ms. Direct3D 11 only, and off under Classic Graphics.

## Shells land in water

- Water Splashes, under Options, Effects, is a new setting, off by default until it has been played. EA's shells burst on a river as they burst on sand: a fireball and nothing on the water. With this on, a shell or a bomb that comes down in water throws up spray, leaves a patch of foam and sends two rings across the surface, dimmed by the map's light at night. On the wet sand at the water's edge you get the spray alone, since a ring lying on a beach looks like glass. Your opponent's setting is his own, because no part of the game reads this. Fifteen guns shelling one channel without a pause, more than a match ever puts in water, take the graphics card's frame from about 2.45 to 2.64 ms and the slowest frames from about 13 to 15 ms. Direct3D 11 and Classic water only, and off under Classic Graphics.

## Weather, if you want it

- Weather, under Options, Effects, is a new setting, off by default until it has been played. A green map gets rain, and a desert map gets blowing sand over a still tan haze. A snowy map with no flakes of its own gets them. The trees lean and sway harder and smoke drifts gently downwind, and rain, sand and snow blow at a quarter of the speed they first flew at; a map that already rains or snows, Flooded Plains or Bitter Winter, keeps what EA gave it and takes only the wind. The weather is much lighter than it first was, so the field stays readable in rain, sand and snow. No part of the game reads any of this: what a unit sees and hits stays what the map says, so you and your opponent can have different weather in one match. A sandstorm over a battle of three armies and three superweapons takes the graphics card's frame from about 7.9 to 8.5 ms. Direct3D 11 only, and off under Classic Graphics.

## Fire keeps its colour

- Internal HDR Tone Mapping, under Options, Effects, is a new setting, off by default until it has been played. The name is exact: the game's picture has held light past white for a long time, then squeezed nearly all of it into one white on the way out, so a Strategy Center going up was a blown patch with no shape. With this on that fireball stays orange and yellow, a night fire shows its flame tongue, and the white heart of a nuke shrinks, about 54,000 near-white pixels down to about 24,000 in the same shot. Team colours hold a little more colour, and ground lit by a blast leans more orange. Ground and walls away from a fire do not change. Your monitor still gets a normal image: an HDR screen gets no HDR signal, and no HDR screen has seen this. In a battle of three armies and three superweapons the graphics card's frame reads 7.95 ms on and 7.78 and 8.12 ms off, which is no cost anyone can measure. The Direct3D 9 picture and Classic Graphics keep the old look.

## Tanks sit on the ground

- Ambient Occlusion, under Options, Effects, is a new setting, off by default until it has been played. EA gave a unit one shadow, the sun's, so on its shaded side a tank met the sand with nothing between them and read as hovering. Now the ground at the tracks of a tank on Golden Oasis loses about 40% of its light and has it all back 130 pixels out, the foot of a War Factory's wall and the crease under a turret go dark the same way, and open ground stays exactly as it was. The water and the fog of war stay out of it. In a battle of three armies and three superweapons the graphics card's frame goes from 7.9 ms to 8.2 ms. The Direct3D 9 picture and Classic Graphics keep the old look.

## Shadows reach the far ground

- Pull the camera right out, tilt it flat, and shadows used to stop along a line across the far ground. On Twilight Flame a whole base stood past that line with its power plants, trees and tanks on bare lit earth, each with no shadow under it. They were drawn for 2400 units round the spot you were looking at, while the far corner of that view is 3343 away. The shadows now go round what is on the screen and reach the top of it.
- Zoomed right out at the usual tilt, the same shadow picture covers less empty ground, so a shadow's edge is about a fifth finer: 1.44 units a dot down to 1.12 on Tournament Plains. In a crowd battle at that zoom the slowest frames read 14.00 ms with the change and 14.12 without it, which is no difference at all.

## Sky above, ground below

- Sky And Ground Light, under Options, Effects, is a new setting, off by default until it has been looked at on more maps. EA gave every model one flat ambient colour, so the shaded side of a tank was the same dull tone from deck to belly. Now a face looking up takes the map's ambient lifted and bluer, and a face looking down takes it lowered and warmer. By day it is quiet, since the sun does most of the lighting: a War Factory's roof reads 4% brighter and 8% bluer on Golden Oasis. On Winter Wolf that roof goes from cream to frost, 11% bluer, and on Dark Night it gains 8% while the ground beside it stays the same, so a night map stays a night map. In a battle of three armies and three superweapons the graphics card's frame reads 8.0 ms with it off and 8.15 with it on, less than two runs of one setting differ by. The ground and the batched trees keep their light, and so do the Direct3D 9 picture and Classic Graphics.

## Fires light what stands around them

- Firelight, under Options, Effects, is a new setting, off by default until it has been played. A burning building, a wreck or a blast throws a flickering orange light on the ground around it, where before only the one-off flash of an explosion lit anything and a town could burn all night over unlit paving. On Dark Night the moonlit ground beside a fire goes from cold blue-grey to warm tan. Twelve fires at most are lit at once, the strongest in view, and with all twelve going in a battle of three armies and three superweapons they add about a millisecond to a frame already at 18. The Direct3D 9 picture and Classic Graphics keep the old light.

## The ground remembers the fight

- Battle Marks, under Options, Effects, is a new setting, off by default until it has been looked at on more maps. Tank shells and missiles landing on open ground leave a burn, where only fifty of the game's 431 effects ever marked the ground and a tank shell was not one of them. A building that falls leaves a dark stain with cracks in it. A nuke, a MOAB or a Daisy Cutter burns a ring of scorched earth round its crater, and a tank's track stays dark for three quarters of its length instead of a quarter.
- Marks hold for a minute and are gone three minutes after that. There are never more than 256, the oldest going first, so a two hour match carries no more than a ten minute one, and a nuke's ring takes room enough that one after another clears the older marks early. A gun firing at one spot renews one mark instead of stacking them into a black disc. A blast in the air or over water leaves nothing, and neither does one you could not see, so a mark never gives away a fight in the fog. The Direct3D 9 picture and Classic Graphics keep the old ground.

## The ground a defence can hit

- Click one of your defences, or put a new one on the cursor, and the ground it fires on is painted on the terrain in your colour: a quiet wash with a clean line round the end of its reach, lying over the hills and down the slopes, under your units and buildings. Only what you clicked or what you are placing is painted: a base of ten defences no longer floods the ground in colour the moment a dozer picks up a building. Where a cliff, a building or the fog cuts into the ground, the wash fades in softly instead of ending on a line, so you can tell at a glance whether a gap is out of range or out of sight. A faint pulse leaves the line every few seconds and runs inward. The enemy's defences show nothing. This came back after the one-interface change took the old range ring away with the Reforged interface.
- Only ground the defence really hits is painted. Every spot is put to the same questions the game asks before a defence fires on its own: is the target in reach, with the extra reach high ground gives; does a hill or a building stand in the line of the shot; can you see the spot at all; is it too close, the way the patch under a Fire Base's walls is. A spot is painted only if the answer is yes for the lowest raider and the widest tank in the game, and for every gun the defence might pick for it. The shot is decided square by square, and the first version drew those squares: the edge stepped round every building and down every brow in hard little stairs. The edge is smoothed now and drawn a hair inside the squares, never outside them, so it still paints no ground the defence cannot hit. The old ring was drawn flat on the screen, over the units, and for weeks it ringed a Patriot at its 450 assist missile when it shoots tanks out to 225.
- A Patriot battery shows where it shoots ground targets by itself. The long missile it fires only when another Patriot calls for help is left out, so is its anti-aircraft missile, and so is anything in the air. A defence with no power, or one that has been hacked or hit by an EMP, shows nothing, because it fires at nothing.
- Checked against the game itself. On Twilight Flame's hilly south-west plateau a Patriot, a Fire Base and a Gattling Cannon had their painted ground sampled at 3,411 random spots, with a Combat Cycle, a Rebel or an Overlord standing on each and the game asked whether the defence would fire: it would, on all 3,411, and on all 2,596 of the spots painted for the same defences on the placement cursor. Leave the hill test out of the painting and the same check finds 51 to 338 painted spots per run the Patriot never shoots at.

## What a rank gives

- America, China and GLA units now get what their rank ladder on the website promises. Rank has always raised a unit's stats; now certain grades also add a perk of their own, and the officers and leaders further up the ladder carry an aura that helps friendly units around them.
- Perks work on the unit itself: a GLA Fighter starts mending itself at 0.5% of its health a second, a Hardened Raider carries 8% more health, an American Private First Class the same. Aura kinds are rate of fire, damage taken, mending, sight, speed, experience, detection, resistance to EMP and paralysis, capture time and a share of kill value. They never touch the leader, and auras of one kind do not add up: a unit near three leaders takes the strongest of each kind.
- Auras start at the Elite rank: an American Warrant Officer (grade 13), a Chinese Second Lieutenant or a GLA Raid Captain (grade 10). Below that, whole squads of corporals and sergeants carried rings and buffed each other. A sergeant's old aura is now the same bonus on himself: a Chinese Master Sergeant Second Class (grade 8) takes 7% less damage while he holds his ground, an American Command Sergeant Major (grade 11) fires 10% faster, a GLA Squadhand (grade 6) runs 8% faster. Drill, steady and spoils have nothing to turn into and are gone below the officers; America's steady aura moved up to the W-2 Chief Warrant Officer (grade 14).
- Red Guard Training lifts a new Red Guard three grades, to Corporal, where it used to make him a Veteran Sergeant with the horde bonus from his first second. Every other unit that came off the line a level up now comes three grades up for EA's Veteran and six for its Elite: Technicals and Inferno and Nuke Cannons with their trainings, a Battlemaster with Battlemaster Training on grade 6, and the Tank General's tanks and the Infantry General's infantry, who start three grades up. Two on one unit add up, so the Tank General's trained Battlemaster starts on grade 9 and the Infantry General's Mini-Gunner with Mini-Gunner Training on grade 6, both still Veteran where EA made them Elite.
- An American Second Lieutenant (grade 18) gives every friendly unit within 140 of it +12% rate of fire; a Captain two grades later heals them 1% of their health a second. A GLA Field Commander (grade 13) heals 1% a second at a radius of 140, and a Warlord (grade 15) speeds up every unit near it by 12%.
- Every aura a ranked leader gives draws its own ring on the ground, out at that aura's radius, so you can see which units each one covers. The rings are always there, nothing to select, under your leaders and the enemy's alike, and an enemy leader hidden in the fog, or stealthed and not detected, shows no ring. The rings borrow Turkiye's five patterns and tell the kinds apart by tint where two share a pattern. Detection draws none.
- Hackers give no aura and draw no ring, whatever their rank. A hacker climbs on its hacking payouts alone, so a row of them at the back of a Chinese base reached Second Lieutenant and up and laid a stack of officer's rings over the whole base without ever leading anyone into a fight. Their own rank bonuses stay.
- The full tables, grade by grade, are on the Rank ladder page of the website.

## French

- The language box under Options, Gameplay now offers Français after Русский. All 4722 lines the game shows are in French: menus, tooltips, briefings and subtitles in the words of EA's own French release, so unit names and orders read as French players have always known them, and every line Reforged added, its options, hotkeys, lobby, score screen and Turkiye included, translated to match.
- An English install can pick it too. A French install that picks it reads the new options, hotkeys and lobby in French, where they used to stay in English. `-language french` picks it for one run.
- Lines EA left unfinished in French, such as the Dragon Tank's and the MiG's fire buttons, which showed a lone full stop, are written out.

## A Random tab in the map list

- Select Map has a third tab beside Official and Unofficial. Pick a map type from the official maps, listed in the Official tab's order, or Surprise me, and a size from Tiny to Extra Large; the preview shows the original map with its start positions, the way the Official tab does. Accept makes a new map from that choice for everybody seated, in the skirmish, LAN and online rooms alike, and every Accept rolls a fresh one. Extra Large still seats eight.
- There is no player count to set. A generated map is for the players in the room, humans and computers, observers left out: add a computer seat or let a friend join and the host's room makes the same map again for one more, its start positions and preview following, and every other machine rebuilds it from the new name. A room on a generated map keeps all eight seats open.
- A map built from an official map takes its sizes from that map. Medium is the original's own size for as many players as it seats, the room they would have on it: a Twilight Flame map is 477 cells a side for two to eight players, where four used to get 304 and eight 416, and each player past the original's seats adds one seat's ground. Extra Large is 708. Surprise me keeps the sizes it always had.
- Bases on raised ground, as on Twilight Flame, now share one stretch of high ground the way the original's do, and each has its ways down widened and one more running straight toward the middle. They used to stand on separate plateaus with a narrow gap between them, and armies queued in it. Over three eight-player matches at Medium size, units stood blocked on the way 163 times per thousand frames, against 205 on Twilight Flame itself and 319 before; four players over five matches 80 against the original's 67, where they used to block twice as often.
- A map built from an official map no longer has slopes that look like cliffs and drive like hills. A slope between about 10 and 15 height steps a cell is drawn as rock and walled off now, so what reads as a cliff is one. Over 570 test maps from all 64 official maps, the median map had 853 cells of that kind of slope and now has none, and the one-corner spikes in the ground fell from 1,323 to 77. Its roads follow the ground: they go round a crest, are cut through one they cannot avoid and climb at most 5 steps a cell, so on nine maps in ten the worst step fell from 21 to 8 and the road cells that top a hill or ride a ridge from at most 109 to at most 11. A base's own road that would run down a cliff the new ground made is left out instead of drawn over it. Every one of the 570 maps lets every player walk to every other and to all the money on it, where 9 used to cut someone off: a dock across a river with no bridge gets a ford, and a derrick no ramp can reach is not placed at all.
- On a Surprise me map, the ways cut between the bases and to the money are drawn as roads. They were only shaped into the ground before, so nothing told you where the easy way across the map ran.
- A map built from a river map keeps a bridge over its river at every size. The smallest two-player Silent River map had none: the bases left no clear ground for one, so now the crossing that runs least into a base takes the bridge.
- Random maps took a long list of repairs this version, from a run through 62 reported defects, each fix measured on the maps before and after. The price is plain: a random map is built from its name, and this build builds different maps from the same names, so it refuses the names an older version made. A replay recorded on a generated map in 3.5.1 or earlier will not play on this build, and a lobby or saved game that names one cannot rebuild it.
- Towns on a river keep their houses. A map copied from Heartland Shield cut its river town round the middle of the water instead of round the houses, and kept 12 of the original's 42. The same map now holds 17 houses on the crossing, a 4-player map that had 4 holds 22, and an 8-player map holds 42. The bridge ends stay dry, and a town that still has to lose houses says so.
- Roads run like roads. A copied map laid its roads in short pieces that jogged along a 45 degree grid and stopped three cells short of the road they were meant to meet, and every end was cut square. On one Heartland map there are 61 pieces where there were 104, each nearly twice as long (19 cells against 11), the 21 grid jogs are gone, no end is cut square (42 before) and four proper junctions appear where there were none. A road no longer starts in the open from a copied base.
- No more seams in the ground texture. Where a copied map met two grounds, the edge between them was cut square, 16% of all edges on Heartland Shield, Twilight Flame and Silent River. It is 3.7% on Heartland, 0.8% on Twilight, 1.7% on Silent River and 2.4% on Tournament Island, below what the shipped Heartland has (5.9%). Rocky river banks with no water in them are mostly gone too: 868 stray bank cells on a 4-player Heartland map are 91, and the sea floor on Bombardment Beach is sea floor in 87 to 97% of its wet cells, where it was 8 to 18%.
- Cliff faces are drawn as rock. A cliff used to be the ground texture stretched down the slope, a grey stripe. It now carries the stone's own texture, laid the way the shipped maps lay it: about two steep rock cells in three on a Twilight-style map and on a map copied from an original. A cliff that stretched its texture more than twice as far as it should came to 28% of the faces on a Twilight-style map and 19% on a copied Twilight Flame, and now to 9% and 5%.
- Seas come back at their share. Bombardment Beach copies had no sea at 4 players (a message said no coast was clear) and now have 17% water against the original's 18%, with 2 and 8 players at 18%. Tournament Island at 8 players went from 37% water to 45% against the original's 47%. The smallest 4-player island is still short at 37%.
- Docks and oil derricks stay on dry ground inside the map. Island maps stranded them in the sea, and copied maps put some past the edge: on Tournament Island a player's own dock was 117 cells away and is 23, on a 4-player Heartland map 98 and now 24, and no dock on the Twilight Flame test maps stands off the edge. Rivers no longer dam up against a dock or a derrick: 663 cells of river bed left dry round the money on one Heartland map are 18.
- Every seat gets the same base and the same money. A Twilight Flame copy gave every other seat a lower base than its neighbour's, a different one from the original, and no oil derrick at all; all eight now stand on the same base at the same height, every player has 2 derricks and every gap between two bases has 4 supply piles, where seven of eight gaps had none. On plain maps the contested docks are shared out by bearing round the middle: a 4-player seed that gave 3, 3, 1 and 1 docks to the nearest seat gives 2, 2, 2 and 2.
- Woods are woods. Trees on generated maps stood in a solid grid, a quarter to a third of them ringed by other trees on every side. The ringed share is down to 5% and the edge of a wood is ragged.
- Random maps from Surprise me look like ground now. A river map's river was a straight pipe of one width that stopped short of the map's edge; it now bends, narrows and widens, runs out past both edges, and its banks close in on each ford. With six or eight players the bases are now spread by the walk to each ford, so on a six or eight player river map the player furthest from a fight walks at most 10% further than the closest one on nine maps in ten, where the old straight river allowed 30%. The mountain in the middle of a massif map was the same round table on every seed; it now leans off the centre, bulges and pinches into an outline of its own, splits in two on about a third of seeds, rises to a high end on top and has walkable slopes in its rim beside the cliffs. Canyons are valleys with a floor between their walls instead of thin scratches. Lakes come out whole, as ovals lying every which way, and the fat streams that lay along the map's edge are gone: over 800 test maps the water too thin to call round fell from 818 patches of 1980 to 26 of 1419. A town on a hillside sits on a few broad shelves that follow the slope, with a ragged edge that reaches along the hill and stops short up it, instead of a staircase of house lots or one flat pale square, and a map that found no room for a town now always gets one. Ground you can walk on no longer looks like a cliff: over 800 test maps the slopes steep enough to pass for a cliff wall while units walked straight up them fell from a median of 168 cells a map to 3, and the lone one-corner spikes from 404 to none. The ways cut between bases and to the money now go round a hill or through a saddle the way a road would, climb at most 5 height steps a cell where they used to take 8 and more, and the worst map's ways run over a crest or along a ridge top for 9 cells where the worst used to for 50, and a supply dock or oil derrick no longer sits across one and leaves a step in it. On open ground they bend in long easy curves to the low side instead of ruling straight lines and 45 degree corners across the map, and a ramp off a massif's table curves round toward the base it serves and sits in the rim, where it used to leave the table as a straight spoke with a lip at the top. A base no longer sits in a tray cut into a hill, its level is taken from the ground around it, and the median gap between a base and the land 30 cells out fell from 6.7 to 3.0 height steps. Every one of the 800 maps still lets every player walk to every other and to their money, as before. These maps are new, so a random-map name or replay from an older build builds a different map and is refused.
- A random map's picture is the right way up. It was drawn upside down, so in the lobby, on the load screen and on the score screen the numbered start spots sat at one place and the white base marks in the picture at the mirror of it, and the lakes and cliffs you saw lay on the wrong side of the map from where they were. The map itself, its name and its replays are untouched; only the picture is turned over.
- The deepest pits on Twilight-style maps are pits. They could wrap past the bottom of the height scale and come out as a needle of mountain, 97 cells of them on one 8-player map; none now. A lake no longer sits under the flat ground of a base (119 cells on one 2-player map, none now), across 30 test maps the closest town building to a base is 44 cells away where it was 14, and a pond left behind a river ford is dry ground.
- A map copied from an original can no longer come out smaller than that map's smallest size, whatever the player count.
- Every player starts on dry ground of their own. A map with little flat ground ran out of good spots and put the rest of the players on a plain circle, which could drop a base into a lake or onto the river, and with fewer spots than players two of them got the same one. The players left over now go to the driest ground the map has, as far from the other bases as it allows.
- Two bases count as joined only when a unit can drive from one to the other. The strip round the outside of the map, which no unit can enter, was taken for open ground, so two bases could count as joined through it and get no ramp between them, and each player's money was placed by walks measured across it.
- A ramp the game cuts to open a base or reach a dock stays open. The cuts used to come after the towns and woods were down, under a building or a rock that then stood in the way. Now they come first and the towns and trees keep off them; once everything stands the map is walked again, and a cut made at that point clears whatever is on it.
- A Twilight-style map asked for smaller than its bowl allows comes out at the smallest size that holds it, 214 cells across. Asked for at 64 cells for eight players, it was one plateau with the starts five cells apart.
- On a map copied from an original, every seat gets as many docks and oil derricks as the next.
- The same number makes a different random map in this version, so a random-map replay from an earlier version does not play in it.
- The player count starts at the number of seats already taken in the room. The tab, the map type and the size you used last are remembered for the next time.
- In a LAN or online room the other players do not download anything: the map's name carries its recipe, and their own game builds the same map from it and checks it against yours. A room that records stats keeps to the official list.
- Random maps used to be reachable only by a hidden command-line switch that added five rows to the skirmish list.
- Leaving the skirmish room for the main menu no longer crashes the game. In 3.4.0 it did every time, whatever map was picked: the room went on refitting its random map to the seats for a moment after Back had already thrown the seats away.
- A LAN match on a random map no longer crashes the host as it starts. The room waits behind the battle with its window taken down, and it went on refitting its map to the seats there: one host's game rebuilt a two-player map for three on the match's first frame and died. The online room had the same habit while it slid shut.
- A LAN or online room on a random map no longer starts when another player's game built a different map from the same name. The room noticed the difference and then let the host start anyway: it sent the host's copy across, the other game went on playing its own, and the match fell out of sync at its first check. Start now stays shut while any seat's map differs from the host's, and the chat names the player, so the two of you know to get on the same version first.
- Ranked Quick Match checks the map too. Before the match loads, each game tells the others what its copy of the generated map came out as, and one that disagrees calls the match off with the player's name instead of loading into a desync. A game that says nothing within 20 seconds, an older version say, calls it off the same way rather than leaving you on a load screen.
- Back from a match on a random map, the skirmish room still has that map picked. It used to show some other map, usually the first of your own downloaded ones, because the room wrote the map's name down in a way it could not read back. The room also picks up a random map remembered from your last session, building it again from its name.

## An army screen in every lobby

- Click a seat's army in the skirmish, LAN or online room and a full screen opens in place of the drop-down list. Every army stands on it under its side's heading, USA, China, GLA and Turkiye, with a large portrait of the one you click, its name across a banner, what it is built to do and what it brings. Confirm takes the army; Back or Escape leaves the seat as it was. The host picks for the computer seats the same way, and nobody can open another player's seat.
- Random gets a pool you choose. Custom Selection puts a tick box on every army, and Random then draws only from the ticked ones: tick China and its three generals and you play Chinese every game, which one is a surprise. Each side's heading carries a box that ticks or clears the whole side, and a click on the side's name leaves it alone in the draw, so "Random USA" is one click. With Random focused, the portrait shows every army it can be, lit when it is in the draw and dimmed when it is not. Everyone in the room draws from the same pool, the replay too, so a game never splits over it, and the skirmish room keeps your pool for the next match.
- A plain Random no longer hands you Turkiye. The side is an experiment and a player asking for any army should not get it unasked; tick it into a Custom Selection to have it in the draw. A replay recorded before this change, with a Random seat in it, plays out differently.
- The army screen answers the mouse. Back and Confirm are drawn in the lobby's own button art now, and under the pointer they take its lit blue and letter their label green, the same as Play Game beside them. The two tabs do the same, with the open tab showing the pressed button instead, so you can still tell which one is open. An army tile under the pointer turns blue, as does the scroll bar's handle, and a side's tick box gets a bright edge. The tile used to get a one-pixel line nobody could see, and everything else stayed dark until you clicked. The map picker's Official, Unofficial and Random tabs and the random map's size buttons light the same way now, in skirmish, LAN and online.

## Music that follows the fight
