- In a skirmish or an online match the music now answers the battle. While nothing happens one of your side's calmer tracks plays; once guns open up near the camera or on your own forces it crossfades to a harder one, and to the hardest when the fight is big. Six Crusaders against six Scorpions and four Technicals: the first shots brought in a tense track, the battle track followed four seconds later, and twelve seconds after the shooting died down a calm one was back. Two Rangers against three Rebels only gets the middle one.
- The tracks are the game's own: each side's ten or eleven skirmish pieces were measured for loudness and pace and sorted three calm, three or four tense and four for battle. One track plays at a time, a change is a two-second crossfade that keeps the loudness even through the middle, and a track keeps the floor for at least twenty seconds, so a skirmish that flares and dies does not make the music lurch.
- Music Follows the Fight is on by default and sits under Music Volume on the Audio page. Off, the music plays as the original game had it.
- When a mission changes its music, the new track now fades in under the old one instead of cutting in at full volume.
- A Master Volume slider heads the Audio page and turns the whole game down at once: music, effects, voices, ambience and movies. At half it put the music exactly 6.0 decibels lower. Unit replies keep their lift over the battle and are turned down with everything else, and at full volume the loudest moment of a tank fight still stops at the limiter's ceiling.

## Sound in the open air

- The tunnel is gone. A player told us the game sounded like standing in a tunnel, and had it right: every map carried an echo up to 2.6 seconds long with a slap off the buildings, and a far sound was mostly that echo. Distance dulled it on top of that, a hill in the way muffled it again, and each one reached you late, by up to a second, while a big blast sank the rest of the battle to a sixth of its volume for four seconds. All of it is out of the game. A gun across the map now loses level with distance and keeps its crack, and when a sound stops, nothing is left ringing after it.
- Legacy Sound, under Options, Audio, Output, brings back the original game's sound for anyone who misses it. It turns off everything below: the pitch bend, the Aurora's boom, the cap on battle sounds and replies, the zoom mix, the map's ambience, the limiter and the music that follows the fight. Master volume, the output device and the speaker setup keep working, and the change is heard the moment you press Accept, in a match too.
- Jets, helicopters and the Nuke Cannon's shell rise in pitch as they come in and drop as they pass, by how fast they move towards you. Units cross the map far slower than the real machines would, and the faster the unit the bigger the gap, so the bend is worked out at three times a tank's speed and more for anything quicker: a Raptor or a MiG is heard at five times its speed and comes in several semitones high on a normal pass, up to an octave dead overhead, and an Aurora screams in a full octave up.
- An Aurora on its attack run now cracks past you with a sonic boom. EA recorded that boom, shipped it in the game's own sound archive and used it only in cinematics; no unit ever played it. It goes off as the bomber passes the camera at speed, louder the closer it flies, and a damaged Aurora limping home at cruising speed stays quiet.
- Nothing clips any more. A dense tank fight in a city used to drive one sample in twenty past full scale; a limiter at the end of the mix now looks two milliseconds ahead and turns the whole mix down just enough, so the loudest moment is as loud as the speakers go and no louder.
- A big battle no longer fills every channel with gunfire. At most 16 battle sounds play at once, and when a seventeenth arrives the quietest, furthest one gives way, or the new one is dropped if it matters less than all of them. The same shot fired by several tanks side by side in the same moment is one louder sound instead of a stack. On a 290 unit crowd fight the busiest second went from 25 voices to 17, with the same peak level. Replies, EVA, the interface and looping sounds are never cut for it.
- Zoom out and the fight takes a step back. Unit and weapon sounds drop to 75 percent while the camera is high, and the wind, birds and city hum around them do not, so the whole map still sounds like a place.
- A fight anywhere on the screen is heard now, zoomed out as well. The camera goes nearly three times further out than the original's, but every sound still carried only as far as it did at the original's zoom, so at full zoom the side of the screen was 700 units from the microphone and its top 1000, past the 800 most sounds reach: the top quarter of the screen was silent and a fight at the edge came through 14 decibels down, against 9 decibels down for one in the middle. Every sound's reach now stretches with the zoom, so the screen falls off from its middle to its edges the way it does zoomed in: at full zoom a fight in the middle plays 2.5 decibels down and one at the edge 3.
- Every map has a bed of ambience now: snow, town, desert or field, chosen from the terrain the map is made of and played from the game's own ambient loops. It sits under the battle and swells as you zoom out.
- The music crossfade is real. The old fade counted drawn frames, so it ran at the speed of your graphics card; it now runs on game time, two seconds, with no dip in the middle.
- Headphones mode, under Options, Audio, Output. Each ear gets its own delay, level and muffling from where a sound is, so a gun to your left is on your left and one behind you is dull. The same page offers 5.1 and 7.1 surround on Windows, and a list of output devices.
- Mute in Background is an option now and works on Linux and macOS too. Turn it off and the game keeps playing when you click another window.
- Unplug your headset mid-match, switch Windows to another output or start with no sound device at all, and the game picks up the new device or waits for one, instead of going silent or dying. This may also be the cause of the crashes inside xaudio2_9.dll in our crash reports.
- One rare audio crash is closed. A broken pitch value could reach Windows' sound mixer and take the game down; the game now catches it first and plays that sound at its normal pitch.
- A Turkiye rank perk that detects stealth now behaves like a detector: the radar pings the spot, the discovery sound plays and EVA says so.
- Clicking through your army no longer stacks a dozen replies on top of each other. A unit that just answered stays quiet for a second and a half, a new reply waits until the last has had four tenths of a second, and no more than two talk at once.
- macOS and Linux hear the same, and so does the sound the game records for a video, in step with the picture frame for frame.

## Ukrainian and Russian

- The language box under Options, Gameplay goes on past Deutsch to Українська and Русский, each written in its own alphabet, so a player finds their language without reading a word of English first. All 4684 lines the game shows are translated in both, menus, tooltips, briefings and the fork's own options included. The launcher's game language box offers the two as well.
- The command bar's one-key shortcuts used to go dead the moment a Russian or Ukrainian keyboard layout was on: the key marked C typed с, and no button answers to с. The game now reads a key from a non-Latin layout by where it sits on the keyboard, so C is C whichever layout Windows has active, in every language.
- The check that refuses a broken Turkish or German line reads both new files on every build. A tooltip whose blanks would not match the English one is turned away before it can crash the game.

## Trees cast the shadow of their own crowns

- A tree's shadow used to be its outline laid flat at the foot of the trunk, which sank into the ground on a slope and never darkened a tank parked under it. Now every tree, the palms included, puts its real leaves into the sun's shadow, gaps between the fronds and all, and that shadow falls over the hillside and over the units standing in the wood. Direct3D 11 on Windows and Linux both draw it; the Direct3D 9 renderer keeps the old flat shadows.
- Linux gets the sun's shadows Windows already had, soft under a helicopter and hard under a tank, and the smoke shadow that darkens a battlefield under a thick plume. Your own cloaked units still cast only a faint part of theirs.

## Modern water

- Options has a Water Style box. Modern rolls the sea in waves whose crests catch the sun all the way into the shallows, and at the shore they turn along the bank and pile up foam. Boats push foam off their hulls. Classic stays the default, and either way a map keeps the water colour and depth its maker gave it.
- Windows has it now on the default renderer, and the box switches it in the middle of a match. The Direct3D 9 renderer and macOS keep the Classic water and hide the box. Linux still draws one thing Windows does not, a second band of foam laid over the surf where waves break on a beach. The first Modern frame on a fresh install stops for about ten seconds while its two water shaders compile; every match after that loads them from the cache.
- The main menu runs smoothly again. 3.4.0's quality slider switched Modern water on for every detail level from Medium up, and for anyone who had never touched the Water Style box, so the sea under the menu cost a pass 11 to 45 ms where Classic water takes 3 to 6 on an RTX 2060. Modern water is your pick again: the slider and the detail presets leave the box as you set it, and Classic is what you get until you choose otherwise.
- Classic Graphics always draws the original water. With Water Style on Modern, which 3.4.0's slider and presets set for you, the sea under the main menu and in every match came out as the new water, smooth and deep blue, beside the 2003 art and its textured teal sea. The box keeps your pick for when Classic Graphics is off again.

## Volumetric hazard clouds

- Options has a Cloud Style box. Volumetric draws toxin, anthrax and nuclear fields as moving smoke at the size and for the time the hazard really lasts: low smoke hugs the ground and curls around infantry walking through it, and a nuclear field fades in across its whole width with dark billows and embers rising through the heat shimmer. The damage is exactly what it was. Classic stays the default until the cost in a big battle is measured.
- You can see into a toxin field. The cloud was thick enough to hide the soldiers and the ground inside it, which is the one thing you need to read when deciding whether to walk in. Toxin, Anthrax Beta and Anthrax Gamma now share one thickness, 42% of plain toxin's old one, and the Classic puddles glow half as hard on Direct3D 11 and Direct3D 9 alike. Radiation looks as it did, and each field's damage, size and time are unchanged.
- Windows draws them too, on the default renderer, and so do Linux and macOS. The Direct3D 9 renderer and the Classic graphics setting keep the original puddles whatever the box says, and turning heat effects off takes the shimmer off a nuclear field as well. A cloud that only drifts redraws its smoke twenty times a second rather than every frame, and the second match of a session no longer stalls on the first toxin shell while the clouds' shaders are built again.
- The first toxin cloud of a fresh install no longer freezes the game for three and a half seconds: the clouds' shaders come with the game now, and are made ready when a match starts or the box is switched rather than when the first field opens. A toxin field also no longer comes back at full strength for ten seconds after it has run out; it fades with the hazard.
- A fresh install's first Scud Storm landing, Particle Cannon, nuke and general's air strikes no longer catch a picture for 110 to 130 milliseconds each, whichever cloud style is on. The explosion and lit-smoke shaders those strikes draw with come with the game now, where each one used to be built the first time its blast showed up; a superweapon battle on Twilight Flame from a fresh install now builds nothing at all.
- A blast the game has no shader for yet, a combination nobody recorded, no longer stops the picture while one is built. The shader is built beside the game, and the blast's pieces that need it appear when it is ready, about a sixth of a second later at worst; before, the whole frame waited 110 to 130 milliseconds for each one. With a shader file missing twenty-two of them, a superweapon battle drew on with no pause and the longest any blast waited was 153 milliseconds. The interface, the fog of war and anything drawn into a picture of its own still get their shaders at once, on the match's first frame.

## A rank ladder for every army

- Three chevrons are now a whole army's ladder. An American unit climbs 28 promotions from E-1 Private to General of the Army, a Chinese one 19 from Private to General, a GLA one 20 from Recruit to Supreme Liberator. Every unit starts unranked with a bare health bar and no bonus; from the first promotion on, each grade wears its own insignia beside the health bar and floats it up over the unit's head the moment it is earned. Hover the portrait for the rank's name and how far the next one is: "Next rank 340/420 XP".
- The climb is long. The first promotion is one kill of a unit like your own, every step after costs a fixed share more, and the top is 120 such kills on every side: 12,000 experience for a Crusader. One kill lifts a unit one grade at most, so a Ranger who kills a tank early gets two grades out of it, not five. Six kills used to make a tank Heroic; now they make it an American Corporal, a Chinese Staff Sergeant or a GLA Hardened Raider.
- Every grade makes a unit a little better, on one curve for all three armies: rate of fire times damage times health is 1.13 times a regular's after the first kill, about 1.25 at Veteran, 1.6 at Elite, 2 at Heroic and 2.4 at the very top, where EA's Heroic gave 3.1 after six kills. Each army takes it its own way: America in rate of fire, health and up to 7% more range, China in health and a 10% faster horde, GLA in rate of fire, up to 14% more speed and up to 2% of its health mended a second once it has gone five seconds unhurt.
- Veteran, Elite and Heroic still exist and still bring their weapons, voices and upgrades: America turns Veteran at Corporal, Elite at Warrant Officer and Heroic at Lieutenant Colonel; China at Sergeant, Second Lieutenant and Colonel; GLA at Raider, Raid Captain and Warlord. A pilot climbing into a vehicle, map-placed veterans and the Heroic cheat land on those ranks. A veterancy crate is worth three grades, never past Heroic, since one EA level is up to 42 kills on this ladder.
- Burton, Black Lotus and Jarmen Kell climb like everyone else but wear high rank from the start: Burton is a Colonel on his first day and a General of the Army at the top, Lotus goes from Colonel to General, Kell from Warlord to Supreme Liberator.
- Every general's army takes its side's ladder; civilians and other armies keep EA's three ranks. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.

## A new loading screen

- Skirmish, LAN, online and replay loads show every player on a card: the general's portrait, or the side's crest for a plain side, the name in the player's colour, the army, and for a computer seat its difficulty and personality. Teams face each other in two columns with the map between them, its start spots drawn as the room draws them: the blue ring, filled with the player's colour and his seat number where the others may see who starts there. Each card wears that same numbered spot in its corner, so you find a player's base on the map without counting colours.
- The teams are the score screen's. A 2v2v2 or a 3v2v1 fills the two columns with whole teams, never half a team on each side of the map, and every team stands under a band with its lobby colour and "Team 2", as it will on the score screen afterwards. A game where everyone plays alone keeps plain cards. The header says what is played the way the score screen will: "Skirmish · 4v4 · $10,000", "LAN game · Free for all (6) · $10,000". A team keeps its number from the load to the score screen, a player alone included, where the score screen used to count the loners in the order they finished.
- In a LAN or online game each player's card carries his own load bar, so you see who the match is waiting for. A crowded column gives up the computer's third line first, then puts each player on one line, the side's crest, "name · general" and the bar under it. Past sixteen to a side, as a 32-player game can be, the side splits into two narrow columns of one-line cards, and where even those run short the bar gives way to the percentage beside the name. Seats from 9 up carry their own number on the map and the card, where the old lookup stopped at 8. Nothing runs into anything: a general's name is shortened the way its language does it, a player's name only ever ends in an ellipsis.
- The map sits in its frame at its own shape, the way the score screen shows it, so a wide map no longer floats in a black square, and only the start spots someone starts on are drawn. Under the map a box lists the rules the lobby set, with the lobby's own words: game speed, starting cash, superweapons, income sharing, the supply pile limit, tech building respawn and the unit limit. The observers sit under it, you too when you watch the match yourself, as many names as the room holds and then "+3". The small type on the screen grows at 720p until its capitals stand 12 pixels tall, so the rules, the header and the team names stay readable on a small monitor.
- Along the bottom the tip has a panel of its own over the load bar, two lines at most; a tip too long for two lines on your screen is skipped instead of cut off. The bar reads "LOADING 81%", in Turkish "YÜKLENİYOR %81".
- Enemies who picked a random side, colour or start stay hidden as they were in the lobby. Observers and replays see every side as it is.
- A campaign mission keeps its own picture and briefing movie. Once the movie ends, the mission number, campaign and difficulty sit above it and the same tip and bar sit below it. Generals' Challenge is unchanged.
- It is the lobby it came from: the same see-through panel in the same blue ruler frame over the menu's battle picture, the map's name in capitals where the lobby says SKIRMISH, cards framed like the lobby's seat rows, the map preview in a button's blue edge, and the load bar a wide button along the bottom that fills as the game loads. A mission's header and foot are strips of the same panel over its own picture.

## A summary and graphs on the score screen

- The old score table with its rows of icons and the Tactical Analysis box is gone. Every score screen, skirmish, LAN, online, replay and campaign mission alike, opens on its Summary page: a large row per player with its side, units built, lost and destroyed, buildings built, lost and destroyed, and money earned. The winners carry a gold Winner tag, and the best number in each column is gold too, the fewest where fewer is better. In a campaign mission your enemies share one row per side, as they did in the old table. Generals' Challenge keeps the general's portrait and verdict it always had.
- The tabs beside Summary give a chart the whole screen, one line per player over the whole match: money earned, army size or buildings standing, with each player's colour named along the top. Army size counts infantry, vehicles and aircraft; workers and supply trucks are left out.
- A single row of small pictures above the chart marks superweapons built and fired, general's powers and promotions, framed in the player's colour. Moments that fall close together share one picture with a count on it. Hover over it for the list, each line with its time, and a faint line down to where each one falls on the chart.
- The Build order tab puts the first of each structure and unit each player made on a timeline whose first five minutes take over half the width, so an opening reads at a glance. Show every build adds the rest; hover over a picture for its name and time. With the whole page to itself a 4v4 keeps two strips of pictures per player, even at 1280x720.
- The map's name heads the page in capitals, where the lobby puts its title, and a campaign mission's page is headed with the mission's name or number rather than the map file's. The pages sit in boxed tabs like the options screen's, and the open one is lettered green. Save Replay, Exit, Continue and Play Again stand in the lobby's button row inside the panel, and after a network game the chat sits just above them. Dark blue and purple player names are lifted so they stay readable on the panel.
- The game records all of this as the match plays, a sample every five seconds, and it changes nothing in the match itself. A game loaded from a save only graphs what happened after the load.

## Computer players have personalities

- Every computer seat in the skirmish, LAN and online lobbies has a new Personality box beside its team. It says how that player plays, and the difficulty still says how well, so a Hard Turtle and an Easy Turtle play the same way at different strengths.
- Point at the Personality box and its tooltip says what the picked personality does, in one line, where every box used to give the same vague sentence. With the list open, each line explains itself as the pointer passes over it. In English and Turkish.
- Normal is the computer player you know, unchanged. The others:
  - **Attacker** goes out early and often with smaller waves and spends everything it earns.
  - **Turtle** finds the narrow stretch of each road into its base and packs its defences there so they cover each other, rather than ringing its command centre. China mines the guns on that line, GLA lays demo traps in front of it and America leans on Fire Bases. It holds its army back for a few big late waves and pulls out of fights it is losing.
  - **Economist** puts income and upgrades first and keeps a fatter bank before it spends on the army.
  - **Air Force** puts up several airfields early and fights mostly from the air, switching aircraft rather than giving up when it meets heavy anti-air. GLA has no airfield, so a GLA Air Force fields rockets instead: Quad Cannons, Rocket Buggies, Scud Launchers and an early Scud Storm.
  - **Rusher** throws everything into one attack in the first four minutes, then keeps pressing.
  - **Raider** sends its fastest vehicles after supply trucks, workers and depots the enemy has left unguarded.
  - **Tech** goes for its tech, general powers and superweapon, and defends until they stand.
  - **Infantry** fields a crowd of foot soldiers from two to four barracks, cheap ones mixed with whatever beats the army it has seen, and fills buildings with them.
  - **Armor** builds tanks from several war factories and comes at you in big slow waves.
  - **Sneaky** prefers stealth units and comes in by the back door or the flank.
  - **Opportunist** goes for the weakest enemy, and for whoever is already busy fighting someone else.
  - **Supporter** attacks what its ally attacks and sends its army home to its ally when the ally's base is hit.
  - **Counter** studies what you field and builds the answer to it.
  - **Random** picks one of the above when the match starts and does not tell you which.
- Computer allies with a personality answer their team. When an ally's base is hit, an Air Force strikes the attacker, a Supporter comes home to defend, an Attacker or Rusher hits back at the attacker's base and a Tech turns its powers on him. An Economist sends money to an ally who runs dry.
- Allied computer players join the attack a teammate has started, so a team hits one enemy together.
- Seven computers against one strong player now count each other. Each used to weigh its own army against all of yours, decide it was outmatched and go on the defensive. When a computer now decides whether to defend, it adds its allies' armies, Hard all of them, Medium three quarters and Easy half, and counts your allies against it the same way. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- You can call them too. A beacon you place asks your computer allies to attack there, and typing `help`, `attack` or `money` in chat (`yardim`, `saldir`, `para` in Turkish) asks for help where you are looking, an attack there, or cash.
- Or without typing a word. Alt+Z asks your allies to attack the spot under the pointer, Alt+X to come and defend it, and Alt+C only marks a spot to look at. The pointer can be on the radar as well. People on your team see the smoke, the radar ping and a line in the chat; computer allies with a personality act on it, in a skirmish against the computer too, where the keys used to do nothing. The keys come from the launcher and move on its Hotkeys page like any other. Request money has no key by default, since Alt+V evacuates a transport; set one on the Hotkeys page, and a key you already gave it stays.
- A personality is a preference, never a bonus: every computer earns the same half-again income and the same catch-up bonus, and no personality adds money, faster building or tougher units to it.
- Computer players with a personality now and then say something in chat, in their own voice, at most once every two and a half minutes. Normal ones stay quiet.
- An Infantry computer player no longer crashes the game while one of its factories researches an upgrade. Shopping for a troop carrier, it read the upgrade in the queue as if it were a vehicle.
- The choice travels with the game to every player in a LAN or online match and into the replay. Replays and saves from earlier versions load with every computer player on Normal; a save made with this version does not load in an earlier one.

## Turbo mode instead of a speed dropdown

- Every match plays at normal speed. The skirmish lobby's game speed dropdown is gone, and with it x0.5 and x0.75.
- Turbo mode is the one choice left: a box in the skirmish, LAN and online lobbies, off unless you tick it, that plays the match twice as fast. It is the old "skirmish at 60 fps". The original game moved the battle one 1/30 s step per frame, so a skirmish run at 60 fps played at double speed. Since the battle moved to 60 steps a second, normal play already runs at 60, and Turbo gives back that double speed: two seconds of battle in every second. The battle itself is the same one, step for step, only more of its steps run each second; the screen still draws as often as it did.
- In a network game the host ticks the box and every machine in the room plays at that speed, so nobody falls out of step. A recorded stats game online plays at normal speed. A replay plays back at the speed its match had, and its speed buttons still work from there.
- Campaign and Generals' Challenge missions have the box in Options, under Interface: Turbo Mode in Missions. Ticked in the middle of a mission, it speeds that mission up at once.
- A skirmish lobby or a saved game left on x0.5 or x0.75 comes back at normal speed. A map script can no longer change how fast a match runs, and the speed console command picks between normal and turbo.
- In a turbo match the corner readout says TURBO 60hz with the frame rate beside it, where it said 120hz. The battle still steps 60 times for every second of battle; turbo fits two of those seconds into each real one, and 120hz read as if the step itself had changed.

## A lobby built for your screen

- The skirmish, LAN and online rooms are laid out again from scratch, the same way in all three. Each seat is one row: a bar in that player's colour, the player or the computer's level with its personality beside it, the army, the colour and the team, with the colour swatches framed and sized like the check boxes under the map. In LAN and online games a player who is ready turns his whole row green and the host's row wears a gold edge, so you see who you are waiting for without hunting for a little light.
- Teams have colours of their own: white, black, brown and teal for teams 1 to 4, none of them a colour a player can pick, and four different greys even to an eye that sees no colour at all. A swatch beside the team box shows it, and on the map preview a taken start spot keeps its blue ring and its dark middle turns its team's colour, or the player's when he has no team, so you see who starts beside whom before the match. The colour runs right up to the ring and takes the soft inner edge EA painted for the black, instead of a smaller disc with a black gap round it. The seat's number stays on it, in black or white, whichever reads better on that colour.
- The map preview is square at last, 410 pixels a side in the skirmish room at 1080p where it was a 422 by 266 oblong of a square map, and the match rules sit under it the whole time. The Info, Chat and Lobby Settings tabs are gone: the match rules never hide behind a click. In the skirmish room the seats get the whole height and your medals and career record open from the Record button beside Back, over the room dimmed behind them; Escape, Close or a click beside them puts them away. The network rooms keep their chat under the seats.
- The rooms used to be a 4:3 screen pulled out to fit a wide monitor, so every emblem, start spot and the map itself came out a third wider than tall. They are drawn for 16:9 now and keep their shape on any screen: exact at 1080p, twice that at 4K, and centred between bands on a 4:3 or 16:10 monitor instead of squashed.
- The Limit Armies box is called Original Armies Only now, Sadece Ana Ordular in Turkish. It always meant that: the original USA, China and GLA, no generals' armies. Players kept reading it as a cap on units and mixing it up with Unit Limit. It does exactly what it did.
- A colour left to chance says Random in the colour box. EA's word for it was three question marks, which looked like a name that failed to load on every seat nobody had coloured.
- Online chat shows Turkish and Russian lines. EA's filter for Asian text counted every letter past the Latin alphabet as Asian and was on for English players, so a line with ı, ş or ğ, or any Cyrillic, never reached the chat box.
- The personality list opens eight lines tall with a scroll bar. Opened from a lower seat, its sixteen lines used to run off the bottom of the screen.
- The personality column lost its heading. A computer's row shows its level and its personality side by side; a player's row, and an open or closed seat, gives the name box the personality's room as well, so long names fit and no empty gap sits in the middle of the row.
- The record and the map list stay on top of the seats. Once you had picked an army, colour or team, those boxes drew over the open record; and the seat rows, their colour boxes and the personality list showed through the map list. The whole seat table now steps aside while the map list is open, in the skirmish, LAN and online rooms alike, and comes back as it was. The record's Close button closes it; it did nothing before.
- Select Map swaps the seat table for the map list instead of laying a small 4:3 window across the room. The list fills the seat table's whole panel under Official and Unofficial tabs in the room's own blue-framed style; its preview stands exactly where the room's map stands, and Accept and Cancel take the row of the map's name and Select Map. The map column and the match rules beside it keep their size and place.
- The map list shows every map in your Maps folder. EA's list stopped at 100 maps in a LAN or online room and 300 in skirmish, and since it fills two-player maps first, a folder of a couple of thousand downloaded maps never got as far as the six- and eight-player ones in a network game. It holds 4096 now.
- The colour and team swatches sit in the middle of their boxes, with the same dark border on all four sides. The colour used to sit two pixels low, over the box's bottom edge, with a dark band along the top only.
- The three rooms wear the same frame as the loading and score screens that follow them: the score screen's blue ruler and grid around the edge of the screen, with the panel sitting on its bright line. The LAN and online panels get the blue edge the skirmish one had, under the same blue rule; the seat rows sit on the panel's black in that blue; the colour bar is a little wider. Record and Close are in capitals like every other button, the record's heading is lettered green, and the darker names in the colour list are lifted toward white so they read on black, the way the score screen lifts them.
- The menus no longer make you sit through their animations. A click or a key while buttons are still sliding or flashing in puts them where they were going, and the click counts: Solo Play pressed while the main menu is still coming up opens its list straight away, where it used to be ignored. A screen on its way out goes the moment you press anything, so Skirmish then a click reaches the skirmish room in about 100ms instead of half a second, and Back to the main menu in 10ms instead of 380.
- A long army name in a room now shrinks to fit the field, and only that name.

## Every campaign mission is open

- Picking USA, GLA or China now opens a list of that campaign's missions, every one of them open. Pick a mission, then the difficulty, and it starts with its briefing and movie as it always did; win it and the campaign carries on to the next one. Every campaign mission starts at the same rank however you reach it, so starting at the fourth is the same game as playing through to it.
- The original Generals campaigns from 2003 are back beside Zero Hour's, seven missions a side, each with its spoken briefing and the voices its script cues during the fight. Zero Hour has always read the base game's archives for art and maps, but its own data dropped the 1355 lines of mission speech and the 29 movies the old campaigns call for, and its own campaigns took their names. The movies play when your Generals install has them. Finishing one earns that side's campaign medal, as Zero Hour's does.
- The "Mission Start" saves the campaign makes after each victory load again, from the original game and from every earlier version of Reforged. They hold only the campaign, the mission and the difficulty, none of which the 60-step battle changed. A game saved in the middle of a mission on an earlier version still does not load, and the message that refuses it now says which saves do.
- A mission with moving water (China's third, GLA's first, America's sixth) loads from a save with its water still running and at the height the mission had raised it to. A load used to freeze the water until the next wave came through and drop it back to the level the map started at, and saving while a script was raising it tore the game down.
- Load the same save twice and the same battle plays out both times. The dice, the paths units were waiting for and the computer players' calls to each other are saved now, so two loads no longer drift apart within a minute. A load also stopped switching a powered player's radar off, stopped forgetting which targets a mission's computer player was told to go after, and no longer counts every unit's sight twice for the first seconds. Saves from earlier versions still load; a save from this version does not load in an earlier one.
- Zero Hour's second GLA mission leaves its opening scene again. The scene ends only when the three terrorists have blown up all three American tanks, and the tanks shoot at the tunnel the terrorists climb out of as they drive past it. From 3.2.0 to 3.4.0 a tank shell did its full 60 to a soldier, so two shells kill one: two shots at the tunnel took out two terrorists as they came out, the third was shot down on his way in, the tanks then wrecked the tunnel and the scene waited for ever. At 18 a shell the terrorists reach the tanks with 102 of their 120 health, and the scene hands you the controls on all three difficulties.
- The original America's fourth mission ends the way it did in 2003. Once the Tomahawks take out the Stinger sites, the B-52s carpet bomb the GLA base and nothing else. A map can retune a weapon for its own mission, and EA's game always threw those edits away, so the campaign was played and balanced without them. Reforged started honouring them in 2.2.0, and this mission's file asks for bombs that hit for 1000 across a 1000 radius, where the real ones do 300 across 50: the cutscene wiped every unit on the map, yours with it, and either ended the mission in defeat or handed you a victory with the rest of it unplayed. Map edits to weapons are dropped again, as in the original.

## Health bars you can read at a glance

- The bars over units are a third thinner, so a big fight no longer looks like a sheet of red and green stripes over the units underneath.
- Health a unit has lost now shows as a dark stretch at the end of its bar. It used to be bare ground, so a red bar over red ground, or any team colour over the wrong terrain, looked full when it was half gone.
- A factory's white bar now says how much is waiting behind it. One small square sits over the bar's right end for each order in line, so a barracks with four on order wears three and one on its last wears none, and a glance across the base shows which factory is busy for the next minute. The seconds written on the bar are gone; the build button and the queue still count them down.
- Seats and rounds are small flat chips in a row that starts at the left end of the health bar, three pixels below it, so they never touch the bar or read as part of it. A seat is a little square with its corners cut: green with a soldier in it, blue with a vehicle or anything else aboard, and hollow while it stands free, a light edge round a dark middle. Rounds are upright amber slugs that go hollow as they are fired. Every lit chip has a thin dark edge, so it shows on snow and on sand. They are drawn pixel by pixel instead of stretched from a picture, so they stay sharp on any screen: the same size at 1920x1080 and 2560x1440, exactly twice that at 4K. EA's pips showed only while you had the unit selected or under the cursor. Your own transports and garrisons show their load all the time, your aircraft their rounds, and a building held by the enemy shows how many are inside, because that is what you want to know before you shoot at it. An enemy transport's load stays hidden. A unit carrying both keeps its seats under its rounds. A veteran's rank chevrons stand just past the bar's right end, and the clock over a building being captured hangs below the chips. When the bar is not showing, the chevrons sit centred over the unit instead: a bar on a big screen is far wider than a soldier, so an ejected pilot nobody had selected wore his rank floating off to one side of him.
- Signs over units keep one size when you zoom. The heal cross, the promotion chevrons, a crate's dollar sign and a planted bomb's icon were scaled with the camera: zoomed in they ballooned over a tank, zoomed out they shrank to specks. They all draw at the size they have at the opening camera now, still pinned to their unit. A supply pile's cash and the group number were already drawn in screen pixels and stay that way. The health bar and the capture clock under it still follow the zoom, because the bar is there to span the unit it measures. The seats and rounds under the bar now shrink with it once you pull back past the opening camera, down to dots two pixels across: zoomed all the way out, a Troop Crawler's eight seats used to run twice as wide as its health bar and a garrisoned Bunker's five past the end of its own. Up close they keep the size they had.
- The "+$" that rises where cash lands looks like the 2003 game's again: the plain lettering of a unit's name in the earner's team colour, one black shadow under it so a pale colour still reads on sand and gravel, drifting up and fading out over nearly three seconds at any game speed. The bold, white-flashing figure that leapt up and stopped dead read like a sticker on the battlefield, and it is gone. You no longer see what your enemies earn. The old game showed an enemy's income over every truck and derrick you could see, so one look across the map told you how his economy ran. Now only your own money and your allies' shows, each in its owner's colour, so in a team game you know whose truck just unloaded. A colour too dark to read on the ground, navy or purple, is lifted toward white. Money stolen from you or an ally shows in red. Watching a match or a replay you see everyone's. It is the same size at every zoom. The money on the command bar counts to its new figure instead of jumping, the way Red Alert 2's did. A 100 supply drop ticks up over a fifth of a second; a 100,000 windfall rolls in under one.

## Jets fly like jets

- The Raptor, King Raptor, MiG, Aurora and Stealth Fighter turn the way a plane turns. The faster a jet flies, the slower it comes round, so at cruise it sweeps a wide arc and only a slow jet turns tight. It no longer slides sideways through a turn. A Raptor's half circle at cruise takes about 3.2 seconds, where it took about 1.7.
- A jet banks into every turn and rolls through level when it swings from one turn into the opposite one, so you can read where it is going from its wings.
- Jets no longer rock their wings. A 2 degree nudge on a chase or a path corner flicked the wings 15 degrees over and back inside a third of a second, and a fighter did that every few seconds, so it looked like it was shaking the whole way. Measured over a four-player Hard match, flicks of 8 degrees or more that barely turned the nose came 1.8 times a minute per jet; now 0.2. A full turn still reaches the full bank. A jet that flies into view mid-turn also shows its bank straight away, where it used to snap level and roll back in, up to 42 degrees out.
- Attack runs take longer, and against a target that moves that is a real nerf. A jet cannot snap round onto a tank that drives out from under it, so it flies a wider loop to come back for another pass. In a test a Raptor's pass on a moving Overlord took about 14 seconds where it took about 4. That is the price of a plane that turns like one.
- Takeoff has a runway in it. The jet rolls at full throttle, rotates its nose up, lifts its wheels off the tarmac and climbs out at a steady angle, where it used to hop off the end of the runway.
- Landing has a circuit in it. The jet turns down in a descending curve onto a straight final, glides in, flares and touches down on the centreline, then rolls out and slows. It used to corkscrew down and stop dead.
- A jet flies its landing circuit once. Coming round onto the final from beside the runway, it could pick the turn away from the runway, drift back inside where the turn starts and set off round the whole circuit again, holding the runway the while: 13 of 54 test landings did that, one of them turning through 771 degrees before it touched down. It now turns towards the runway and, once the turn in has begun, stays on the final. A jet that would reach the turn too high to make the glide flies the circuit a little further out, coming down on the way, instead of turning in high and going round. The Aurora, which comes home from a sortie faster and higher than the rest, went round on those landings: it flew its circuit out level, turned in still 99 high and crossed the runway end 13 too high to land. A Stealth Fighter did it now and then too. Both come down on the way out now and land in one circuit; an Aurora back from a sortie is rolled out about 9 seconds after reaching the airfield, where it took 18. Over 92 test landings at two game speeds, Raptors, King Raptors, Stealth Fighters and Auroras, none went round, and the longest from reaching the airfield to rolling out, waits for a busy runway included, fell from 21.3 seconds to 17.6. Replays with jets in them recorded before this change play out differently.
- A landing jet takes the runway when it turns onto its final, not when it reaches the airfield. It used to book the runway before flying its whole circuit, and every jet waiting to take off from that runway sat on the ground for it. A landing now holds the runway about 7 seconds instead of 10, and at most 7.8 instead of 11.2. With takeoffs and landings mixed on one airfield, the average wait to take off fell from 1.2 seconds to 0.4, and the longest from 5.5 to 3.2. If the runway is still taken when a jet comes to turn in, it circles at the turn in until the runway is clear, or goes round when it was already lined up on a short final; in the last 92 test landings that go-around never happened. No landing or takeoff failed, and no two jets were ever on one runway together. Carriers book their deck as they always did.
- On the ground a jet taxis on its wheels. It rounds the taxiway corners, rolls straight out of the landing into the taxi and turns into its parking spot in one smooth sweep.
- A jet puts its whole clip out on a pass again. It used to turn away with a round still loaded: the Stealth Fighter fired one missile of its two and went home.
- Helicopters are untouched and fly as they did.

## A plane that is shot down hits the ground hard

- A shot-down jet now hits the ground with a blast: 80 damage in a small radius. A B-52, a B-3, a cargo plane, the carpet bomber or a Spectre does 160 in a wider one.
- The wreck leaves fire burning for about 6 seconds, and the fire sets infantry alight. A big plane leaves a line of fires along the length of the wreck.
- The blast and the fire spare the plane's owner and allies, and still hurt enemies and neutral buildings. A Supply Drop plane shot down over your own base used to wreck it; in a test the same crash that cost your own side 10 men and 136 health off two power plants now leaves them untouched, while the enemy beside them loses the same 10 men.
- Bombers and cargo planes no longer vanish silently when they hit the ground. A jet destroyed while it sits parked is unchanged.
- A missile whose target dies before it arrives flies on and blows up where it comes down. A Stinger chasing a jet that another shot brought down used to wink out in mid-air, with no blast and no damage; it now drops like a spent rocket, motor cut, still travelling forward while it curves down with its nose following the arc, and goes off where it hits the ground, hurting whatever stands on that spot. Over a Stinger site shooting down drones, 22 such missiles flew on for 1.9 to 3.3 seconds and 260 to 620 units before they came down. A missile that runs out of fuel falls and goes off where it lands, where it used to vanish the same way. Either one keeps a thinner smoke trail all the way down: the moment its target died or its fuel ran out, the trail used to be cut off and it flew its last seconds clean.

## A tank shell hurts the man it hits

- A cannon shell did 6 damage to a soldier. A Ranger has 180 health, so thirty shells that actually hit him left him standing, a full minute of fire from a Crusader, while the same shell does 60 to another tank. It now does 18 to him. Ten hits kill a Ranger, seven a Red Guard or a Rebel.
- 3.4.0 let the whole 60 through, and players were right that it went too far: an Overlord cut a Red Guard down in under a second and a tank column no longer had to care what infantry stood in front of it. Tanks keep three times the damage Zero Hour gave them and lose the rest. In staged fights for equal money, Red Guards beat every tank at Zero Hour's 6 and lost to Crusaders every time at 3.4.0's 60. Now the two split, and the side of the field each starts on decides it.
- The gun still throws the shot wide of infantry, and the blast is small, so a shell that bursts beside a man still misses. A Gattling Tank does not throw wide, and it is still the gun that cuts a whole squad down.
- A chemical suit still stops toxin, radiation and microwaves, and a cannon shell goes through it the same as through a bare uniform. The Infantry General's men, the Toxin Rebel, the biohazard suit and the Demolitions terrorist each had their own copy of that shrug, and a shell goes through those too. The men on a Stinger Site keep theirs: that armor belongs to the site. The Missile Defender's laser-guided missile is the same kind of round, so it does 12 of its 40 to a soldier, and he fires that one at them. An ordinary rocket still barely scratches a man.
- A replay recorded before this change plays out differently.

## The battle runs at 60 steps a second

- The game now works out the battle 60 times a second, double the 30 Zero Hour has run at since 2003. Each step is 17 milliseconds where it was 33, so an order you give waits half as long for the step that carries it out, and a unit turning, braking or firing moves in steps half the size.
- The match plays at the speed it always did. Every speed, delay, reload and build time in the game's data was converted to the shorter step, so a Crusader still fires every two seconds. The balance is the one you know.
- Mission timers keep EA's clock. A map's countdown still ticks 30 times a second, because the missions read a running timer's number and act on it: the second American mission declares victory when its "Win" timer drops below 1700, and on the first 60-step builds that came after 38 seconds instead of 10. The cutscene cues, the random music pick in the campaigns and the generals' challenges, the shell map's camera loop and the lightning on Eastern Everglades and Rocky Rampage were off the same way, 30 maps in all, and run on their original timing again. Custom maps get the same.
- Normal speed is 60 steps a second. Turbo mode, the one other speed a match can have, runs 120 of the same steps a second (see Turbo mode above). Replays still play as fast as you ask.
- On a screen faster than 60 Hz the armies glide. The battle moves in 60 steps a second, so a 144 or 240 Hz monitor showed every step two to four times over and a tank crossing the map moved in small hops. Now each picture draws every unit part of the way between its last two steps. The picture runs one step, 16.7 ms, behind the battle; the battle itself does not change, and a replay drawn with it, without it and with no picture at all ends on the same checksum. A 60 Hz screen gets nothing it did not have. `-nosmoothmotion` turns it off for a run, `-smoothmotion` turns it on whatever the screen.
- Helicopter rotors used to jump between thirty poses a second. On a 60 Hz or faster screen they now turn through the poses in between, and so do other model parts moving at an ordinary pace. A part the art cuts from one spot to another, or one moving very fast, still jumps, and the extra pictures a heavy battle draws between steps hold the blades still.
- The battle's arithmetic runs on a thread of its own, beside the drawing, on Windows. The game used to work out a step and then draw, one after the other, so a heavy step stalled the picture; now the screen keeps drawing while the next step is worked out, which pays most in the late game, where the steps are heaviest. In a late 4-player match, uncapped, frames slower than 16.7 ms (one 60 Hz refresh) fell from 23% to 0.8%, the slowest one frame in a hundred fell from 24.0 to 16.5 ms live and from 16.0-16.5 to 10.6-12.5 ms in a replay, and the average frame went from 15.2 to 11.8 ms. The battle still takes 60 steps a second, no more and no fewer. A match too heavy for its clock used to pay for the thread: the catch-up steps after the picture ignored the step already run beside it, so each frame ran one step more than without the thread. Eight Hard AIs on Twilight Flame at minute 20, run at four times normal speed so they cannot keep up: one frame in a thousand took 26.8 ms with the thread and 24.0 without. Both now spend the same budget, and with the thread that frame is 21.5 ms and the average frame 11.9 ms against 13.9 without, at 12% more steps a second. Nothing turns the thread off, not a menu, a saved setting or the command line, and Mac and Linux run it too. Network games now draw beside the step as well. Two seats at 240 ms of ping and 5% packet loss, with 400 units fighting: one frame in a thousand went from 18.5-21.5 ms to 10.3-12.5, one in a hundred from 13.0-14.8 to 8.3-9.0, and frames over 16.7 ms from 44-95 a match to 6-9. An order reaches the battle and the screen as fast as it did, and a seat with the thread off still agrees with one that has it on. A seat whose drawing takes longer than a step keeps the old order, so a slow graphics card holds the room no lower than before. Network machines compare checksums every 10 steps where they used to compare every step, so nine steps in ten skip a pass over the whole world, and a desync is caught at most 10 steps late. A step too long for one refresh no longer freezes the screen in single player: the game waits for it as long as a picture can still arrive on time, then draws one more, timed to finish as the step does. Eight Hard AIs and 2000 objects at minute 17, two copies racing on one machine so both met the same noise: one frame in a thousand went from 64.0 to 19.0 ms, frames over 16.7 ms from all of them to 1.6%, and the battle took 29.1 steps a second against 29.7. Those extra pictures move the camera and the effects; units still move once a step, so this smooths a heavy match without making it faster. The game also stopped asking the disc drive for its disc every five seconds during a match, which cost 7 to 11 ms a time on a machine with an empty drive.
- That thread went off after 3.3.0, whose crash reports traced the random crashes in the middle of a match to the drawing and the battle writing to the same memory at the same moment. It is back because those collisions are closed. A model or animation the battle loads for the first time now waits for the picture to finish, the trees a unit pushes through move between frames, the team colours and the list of every object stay put while a picture is drawn, and the shadows thrown on units stop asking the battle where things stand while it is moving them. The test that decided it is a 4-against-4 match of 18000 steps, drawn with the thread on, drawn with it off and run with no picture at all, ending on the same checksum each time with the counter that flags the drawing reading the battle at zero.
- Opening the pause menu no longer makes boats snap to a different angle or parked aircraft sink into the carrier deck. Boats keep their rocking angle and aircraft remain above the deck while the game is paused.
- Replays and games saved in the middle of a match from earlier versions will not load in this one. The "Mission Start" saves a campaign makes between missions do, and every campaign mission can be picked from the campaign menu. A player on an earlier version cannot join a match with a player on this version, whichever of them hosts, so a LAN party needs everyone on the same build.
- Guns fire at their 2003 rate again. After a shot the game goes back to aiming for a step before it can fire again, which at 30 steps put a 100 millisecond Quad Cannon on a shot every 0.133 seconds; at 60 the same loop fired it every 0.100, a third faster. Shot delays and reloads are rounded to the old step and a gun's next shot is held to the old rhythm, so every weapon fires on the frames it did in 2003. A turret with no turning speed in its data rose twice as fast as it should, aircraft weighed their thrust against gravity at half strength, and a unit hit on the step before still counted as untouched for stealth. All three keep EA's timing now.
- Shells fly the arcs they flew in 2003. A shell that arcs high but flies fast was only ever put at the muzzle and on the target by the 30-step game, and at 60 steps it stopped partway up that arc. A shell now passes through the points it passed through in 2003 and flies straight between them. A shell fired point blank, close enough to arrive in one step, used to fly to the corner of the map and explode there, a bug since 2003; it hits its target now.

## Turkiye joins the fight, as an experiment

- Turkiye is a fourth side in the skirmish and multiplayer lobbies, listed as Turkiye (Experimental), Türkiye (Deneysel) in Turkish. The label is there because the side is not finished: its powers and abilities are still being worked on and will change. It has an army of its own: Mehmetcik riflemen, Sungur missile teams and Maroon Berets from the Barracks; the Altay tank, the Kirpi carrier, Korkut air defense, Firtina howitzers and Sakarya rocket launchers from the Factory; Bayraktar and Akinci drones, the Gokbey helicopter and the Kizilelma fighter from the Airfield. Every name and tooltip reads in English and in Turkish. The Detailed Models add-on now redraws every Turkish unit and building in high resolution, with distance levels like the other sides' models, and a player without the add-on sees the plain models and still plays in the same match.
- Turkiye kills from range and cannot see for itself. The Firtina throws a shell 600 and sees 100, so it waits until a spotter team, a Bayraktar or a Radar Tower finds the target, then fires on its own. Extended Range at the Factory pushes the guns further.
- Turkiye's rockets fly on radar. Every rocket and missile the side fires, from the Firtina, the Sakarya, the Bayraktar, the Sungur team, the Kizilelma and the Patriot Battery, hits as aimed when the target stands inside the radar circle of a Command Center (600), a Radar Tower (1000), a Koral (650) or an Akinci (750), yours or an ally's. Past every circle only one shot in five keeps its lock; the other four come down on the ground beside the target and miss, and against aircraft that means they miss altogether. A radar under construction, out of power or knocked out by an EMP covers nothing. Inertial Guidance at the Factory, which replaces Precision Guidance, makes it two shots in five. The old blind spread is gone, and so is the Sakarya's fixed spread of 25. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- Turkiye's radars now see what moves under fog. Every sweep of a Command Center, Radar Tower, Koral or Akinci marks the enemy units walking inside its circle that nobody can see, as a red ring on the ground and a mark on the minimap. A unit that stands still draws nothing. A Firtina or other gun with long sight fires on a ringed target without waiting for a spotter, and a right-click on a ring sends your selected units to attack it. The rings never name the unit, so neither the cursor nor the unit's voice gives away what is under one. The circles grew with it: Command Center 600, Radar Tower 1000, Koral 650, Akinci 750.
- Once something sees for it, the artillery is what kills. A Firtina shell does 200 where it lands and 60 out to 35, every 7 seconds, where it did 150 inside 10, less than an Altay. A Sakarya salvo is six rockets of 70 each with a 30 blast, every 14 seconds. The Sakarya never hit anything before: its rockets left the launcher level and went nowhere, and it now aims them up the way the Firtina does. Four Battlemasters or sixteen Rangers marching straight at two Firtinas and their spotter, the same 3500 in money, die before they get there. Crusaders and Scorpions get through with one to three tanks left. Come at the guns from the side with that money in tanks and the tanks win seven fights in eight, so a raid on the flank or a dead spotter is how a gun line falls.
- Sight is what Turkiye pays for. The Bayraktar is the artillery's real eye, 550 from the air, and costs 900 instead of 500. The Cobra sees 250 instead of 400 and is a fast car with five seats, no longer the cheapest spotter. The Radar Tower costs 800 instead of 400 and draws 3 power. The spotter team sees 500, has 200 health and moves faster. It no longer hides: the Pathfinder's camouflage made it an eye nobody could find for guns that hit from 600, and left the enemy nothing to shoot back at but the guns. The free Spy Satellite Scan is gone, and the Sungur gunner sees 200 instead of 300.
- Combat Engineers build the base in place of a dozer. They are infantry, so they can be shot and run over. The Barracks' Mine Kit lets them bury mines, and the Factory's Reinforced Hull, which used to be called the Armor Pack, gives the Kirpi and the Altay 20% more health.
- Turkiye pays its way. The other sides earn beside their gatherers, America from drop zones and GLA from black markets; Turkiye had only its trucks, and those cost 700 and drove 10% slower than China's. The truck is 600 and full speed now, and every Supply Center pays 20 every 2 seconds, what a Black Market pays. A Hard Turkish computer earned 77% of what America's did per minute and now earns 85%; against China it went from 50% to 72% and against GLA from 32% to 42%. In forty-minute games on Twilight Flame it now beats America six games in six, up from four in six, and China four in six, up from two.
- The engineers dig in at the front. The Siper is a bunker for five infantry, 500, that goes up wherever an engineer stands: the army moves up, digs a Siper, spots and shells. Mehmetcik inside it hold off infantry and Sungur gunners hold off tanks. It takes the place of the air defense site, a Chinese gattling cannon that fired at everything. The Patriot battery is now called Hisar and is the base's one fixed air defense.
- The Korkut is air defense and nothing else. Its cannons reach 350 into the air and no longer fire at the ground, where they used to outrange the Altay; three Korkut that cut down eight Rangers without a scratch now lose to them, and still shoot down three Comanches untouched. The Kizilelma's missiles hit the ground as well as the air, and it costs 1800 instead of 2200. It carried 380 health on a Raptor's frame and shot a Raptor down in 29 seconds while the Raptor needed 86 for it; at the Raptor's 160 the duel is even and the dearer jet loses on price. The Akinci drops its own bomb, one a sortie; it had been dropping the Aurora's. Fuel Cells and Fuel Resupply used to hang two and then four of them under it, enough for one jet to level a base, and now it carries one whatever you buy. With 420 health no ground air defense paid for itself against it. At 200 a Gattling Tank or a Missile Defender beats it for the money and a Quad Cannon breaks even.
- Every Turkish unit has its own command bar with only buttons that work: no drone buttons on the Altay and the Cobra, no TOW on the Cobra, no rocket pods on the Bayraktar, no flash-bang switch on the Mehmetcik. The Barracks sells Capture Building, so the Mehmetcik's capture button works.
- Turkiye's general buys sight before firepower. At the first rank, Laser Designation lets a spotter team or a Bayraktar put whatever it is shooting at under radar cover wherever that target stands, so every guided rocket fired at it keeps its lock. Early Warning pushes every Turkish radar a quarter further out. UAV Recon sends a drone to circle a spot for 30 seconds, and every enemy unit under it shows on the map with what kind it is, standing or moving, while the fog stays where it was.
- Rank 3 is where the tree splits. Mobile Radar lets the Factory build a radar truck that covers 900 while it stands and nothing while it drives, and Akinci AESA takes the Akinci's radar from 750 to 1000. The UAV Swarm sends loitering munitions where you point, each diving on the dearest target it finds: one at the first level, three at the second, five at the third. Gokbey Landing parachutes Mehmetcik and Sungur gunners in, six of them, then ten, then fourteen with a Kirpi beside them. Electronic Warfare blinds the radar of every enemy with a building in the circle for 30 seconds and jams the circle for as long, so drones and spotters inside it see nothing and a guided missile that crosses it loses its lock.
- The top rank holds the big guns. Satellite Guidance makes the whole map count as Turkish radar for 45 seconds, and every guided shot in that window hits where it was aimed. The Tayfun is a ballistic missile, 600 at the point and 200 out to 90: inside radar cover it always lands on target, outside it hits one time in five and the rest come down 100 to 200 away. The Commando Raid stays, a Maroon Beret and two spotter teams dropped behind the enemy's lines. The Minefield, the Spy Drone, Fuel Resupply and the Fire Mission are gone, and the Swarm Strike lives on as the third level of the UAV Swarm. The Turkish computer takes one of two roads, the swarm with Satellite Guidance or the landing with the Commando Raid, and the Tayfun at the end of both. The American Paradrop, Leaflet Drop, Spectre gunship and CIA intelligence are gone from the Headquarters and the power bar.
- Four Turkish buildings sell a new upgrade each. Target Classification at the Radar Tower, 1500, puts a mark in every radar ring that says whether it is infantry, a vehicle, air defense, artillery, an aircraft or a defense. AKKOR at the Factory, 1500, arms every Altay with a hard-kill charge that bursts one incoming missile or rocket in the air every three seconds, with the same flash the Paladin's point defense makes. Gokdogan missiles at the Airfield, 1500, give the Kizilelma 360 range instead of 280 and 130 damage instead of 100. Reinforced Siper at the Barracks, 800, adds 750 health to every Siper, half as much again.
- Turkiye has a superweapon: the Kargu Drone Base. It costs 5000, draws 10 power, opens once you have an Operations Center, counts against the lobby's superweapon limit like the Particle Cannon, the nuke and the Scud Storm, and every player watches its five-minute countdown. The base is a drone launch site of its own: three sheet-steel shelters with doors in your colour, a concrete apron with two launch lanes, olive control containers behind blast barriers and a tall mast carrying two radomes and a turning antenna. Fire it and the shelter doors swing up, and a second later sixteen Kargu quadcopters roll out, one down each lane in turn every quarter of a second, and lift off and climb; all sixteen are in the air seven seconds after you fire. Then they climb to 300, as high as the camera goes, and fly straight across the map where everyone sees them coming. Each goes for one of the sixteen most expensive things inside the target circle and comes down on it from 250 short the way a Scud Storm missile does, curving over into a steep dive, and steers onto it all the way down so a tank driving away still takes the hit, and hits for 700, 11,200 for the whole swarm. Every target in the circle gets one drone before any gets a second, and the spares go round again dearest first. A drone whose target died on the way takes the dearest enemy in the circle that no other drone is already after, and doubles up only when every one has a drone coming. Nothing can shoot them down, as nothing can shoot a Scud Storm's missiles; anti-air used to pick them off on the way in. Fired across Twilight Flame into an American base with three Patriot batteries and four Avengers, all sixteen reached their dive, and the swarm killed all four Avengers, four of eight Crusaders and three of six Humvees and took 69% off the Patriots, 43% off the two power plants, 33% off the War Factory and 21% off the Command Center. The Avengers' point defense lasers used to shoot a diving drone out of the air; they no longer see it. The Turkish computer builds and fires it on every difficulty: Hard as soon as it can pay once its Operations Center stands, Medium after seventeen minutes and Easy after thirty, the same clock America's plans keep for their Particle Cannon. The announcer calls it a Scud Storm until Turkiye has voices of its own.
- Turkiye has a technology building, the Operations Center (Harekat Merkezi in Turkish). The engineers put it up once a Factory or an Airfield stands, for 2500. It is the Strategy Center with its gun and its three battle plans, Bombardment, Search and Destroy and Hold the Line, and it researches Advanced Training and Chemical Suits, which the Turkish units take as the American ones do. The Kargu Drone Base needs it, the way the Particle Cannon needs the Strategy Center, where it used to open with a Factory and a Radar Tower. The Turkish computer builds it where America's plans put their Strategy Center.
- The Operations Center opens Turkiye's late army the way the Strategy Center opens America's: the Sakarya, the Koral, the Akinci and the Maroon Beret wait for it.
- Turkiye has a black market, the Grand Bazaar (Kapalıçarşı). It costs 2500 once a Factory stands, pays 20 every 2 seconds and sells Countermeasures for the Bayraktar, the Akinci and the Kizilelma and Worker Shoes for the engineers. The Turkish computer puts one up by itself, and Hard keeps buying them: three by minute ten against China's Easy computer on Twilight Flame, where it earned 103,450 in eleven minutes against 88,200 without them, one match each.
- Two engineers on one building put it up in half the time, three in a third.
- The Koral electronic warfare vehicle jams everything within 400 of it. Enemy drones and spotters inside the field go nearly blind, and guided missiles fired into it lose their lock and fly wide.
- The Barracks trains the Alpagu operator once a Radar Tower stands, 600. He kneels, sets a kamikaze drone on the ground in front of him and flies it with a hand controller: it goes straight up, then turns over and dives into the target nose first with its speed on, 45 to 57 degrees steep whatever the range, out to 350, a hundred past the Sungur. In the air it pulls a faint grey streak behind it that is gone within a second, enough to follow the drone across the sky without mistaking it for a missile. It flies like a real quadcopter: it turns its nose to where it is going, dips it to set off and keeps it down at speed, banks into a turn and points it down the dive like a racing drone flown into its target. It used to slide across the sky dead level, still facing whichever way he had set it on the grass, and came to a stop over its victim before dropping onto it; a close shot climbed as high as a far one and fell almost straight down. A near target now gets a lower climb, about 50 up point blank against 143 at full range. A replay recorded before the dive, with Alpagu drones in it, will not play back the same. He has a model of his own and moves like the Mehmetcik, with the drone strapped to his back: he kneels, swings it down onto the grass and steers it from one knee with its propeller spinning off into the sky. One drone every eleven seconds, and the blast kills any basic infantryman it lands on and hurts everyone within 40. It does half that to Humvees and trucks, a quarter to defences and a tenth to tanks and buildings, so it is no answer to armour. He sees only 200, so past that a spotter team, a Bayraktar or a Radar Tower has to find the target, and then he picks his own targets out to 350 the way the Firtina does. Given those eyes, two Alpagu teams against a Patriot with nothing coming out to meet them lose nobody and leave it at 40 to 47% after two minutes; one Firtina kills it in about half a minute. A drone that lands on a walking squad follows it down; a car driving away gets out from under it. Eight of them, 4800 in money, wipe the same money in Red Guards, Missile Defenders, Tank Hunters, Rebels or Rocket Buggies without losing a man, and lose every man to it in Technicals, Quad Cannons, Gattling Tanks, Scorpions or Crusaders.
- The Maroon Beret is a hero against every side. He is camouflaged, sees 350 for the artillery from inside the camouflage, and carries Burton's knife. To you and to anyone watching, his camouflage holds a steady half-glass look; it used to swell into his full colours and fade back every 0.7 seconds, which in a close view of him kneeling over the Kargu looked like the camouflage flickering on and off. He no longer hijacks supply trucks, which used him up for good and found nothing to take from America. Burton's charges are gone too; he calls in drones instead. Designate Target sends him to within 300 of a vehicle or a building, where he raises his carbine and holds a thin red targeting laser on it, straight out of the end of his barrel to a small red dot on the side of the target that faces him, and the dot goes out with the beam. The beam used to start a step in front of the barrel and stop inside the hull, and its dot was never drawn at all, and before that the spot was a yellow-green dome over the target that stayed on the wreck. A TB2 comes in behind him while he lases, drops a Kemankeş munition as it passes over him after 4 seconds and flies on out of sight; the Kemankeş glides in for two seconds and dives onto the target for 250, half a Crusader, with a tank-killer's blast, and he keeps the laser on the target until it hits. His camouflage is off the whole time he lases; moving him or killing him in the first 4 seconds calls the strike off. Once a minute. Kargu Swarm has him swing his carbine onto his back, drop to his right knee and stay down there while he takes three kamikaze Kargu off his back and sets them down one by one, on his left, in front of him and on his right; he used to straighten up between drones with the carbine across his chest, and the drone in his hands was a darker grey than the one standing on the ground a moment later. The drones are small hand-launched ones on the ground, half as wide as they were, with clear ground between them, and as the three lift off together they spread out wide around him while they grow to full size, so they no longer clip into each other on the ground or in the hover. Then he stands and they hover and dive one after another, each long enough to watch, on a spot 75 to 350 away, each with a small drone's blast, 90 on a direct hit, every 45 seconds. Replays with a Maroon Beret in them recorded before this change play out differently.
- Thermal Vision at the Barracks lets the spotter team see out to 650 and the Cobra to 320, both through stealth. The Airfield sells Fuel Cells, which double how long a Bayraktar stays over the target, and Swarm Software, which sends each Bayraktar munition at the most expensive target in reach rather than the nearest one.
- Turkish units move at their own speeds. The engineer, the spotter team and the Kirpi are slow, and the Korkut keeps up with the tanks.
- A Turkish computer player fires its powers, the Minefield included, as soon as they are ready, and pulls its spotter teams back out of the enemy's reach while keeping the enemy in sight.
- Turkish units climb the Turkish Land Forces' own ladder: 21 promotions from Er through Onbaşı, Çavuş, Uzman Çavuş and six astsubay grades to Teğmen, Yüzbaşı, Albay, the four generals and Mareşal at the top. The names read in Turkish in every language, and each grade wears its own insignia: chevrons for the enlisted men, gold bars for the astsubays, stars for the officers, the oak wreath under a field officer's stars and the crescent and star over a general's. The climb costs what it costs everyone else, a unit turns Veteran at Uzman Çavuş, Elite at Teğmen and Heroic at Albay. Its bonuses lean on health: at Mareşal a unit has 42% more of it, fires 25% faster, hits 19% harder and reaches 12% further. The Maroon Beret starts as an Albay, as Burton starts as a Colonel. Before this a Turkish unit wore EA's three chevrons.
- Turkish ranks carry more than numbers. A Çavuş sees 10% further, an Uzman Çavuş takes 10% less damage standing still, and from the sixth grade a unit patches itself up out of a fight at 1% a second. Sight grows to 20% and 30% further at the astsubay and general ranks. A Teğmen spots for the Firtina and the Sakarya the way the spotter team does, a Binbaşı's own guns spread 15% less, and a Tümgeneral finds stealthed enemies within 100 of it. Officers lead: the Astsubay Kıdemli Başçavuş makes every friendly unit within 150 fire 5% faster and the Albay 10%, the Yüzbaşı lets them see 10% further, the Korgeneral cuts the damage they take by 10% and the Orgeneral puts 5% on the artillery's range. A Tuğgeneral who falls leaves the men around him taking 15% less damage for ten seconds, and a Mareşal's leadership reaches 300. Two officers of the same kind never add up: a tank between an Albay and a Başçavuş fires 10% faster, the Albay's figure alone. Select or hover a leader and what it gives the men around it shows on the ground as one quiet dial at the edge of its reach, each gift in its own band and its own pattern: short ticks round the rim for fire, a dotted line for sight, a notched line for armour, a graduated scale for the guns' reach and a faint wash inside for the last stand, so an Albay draws two bands and a Mareşal the whole dial; the portrait's tooltip lists what the rank carries. Only you and your allies see the rings. Making those colours work fixed a mistake in how the game tints glowing ground marks, which had drawn every one of them in pure blue. The grid a spy satellite or a radar scan lays over what it reveals is now the dim grey-blue EA's data asks for, and about half as bright as before.
- Every Turkish unit and building now has a model of its own; only the voices are still borrowed from the other sides. The build buttons and selection portraits show the Turkish model too, 34 of them drawn the way EA's cameos are, the unit filling the frame against sand and a hazy sky in your side's red, where the Altay's button used to show a Crusader and the Siper's a Chinese bunker. The infantry wear today's olive helmets and plain field uniforms, and each man is easier to pick out by one thing he carries: the Mehmetcik's coyote-brown rifle, the engineer's sand pack, the Sungur's launcher, the Alpagu's lit controller. The Sungur gunner wears a model of his own on the Missile Defender's frame and moves exactly as the Missile Defender did. The Mehmetcik has a model of his own: a rifleman with a sleeve patch and a plate carrier in his side's colour, under a plain olive helmet. He moves like a Turkish soldier carrying a heavy rifle. At rest he stands at low ready, feet a shoulder's width apart and stock in the shoulder, and now and then sweeps his sector with head and rifle turning together or eases the cocking handle back to check the chamber. Sometimes he grounds the rifle at his left side, brings his heels together and salutes: right hand flat at the helmet's edge, elbow out at shoulder height, held, then cut down. He fires with his cheek on the stock and his weight forward, and each round of the burst rocks his shoulders back before he settles. He runs leaning into it with the rifle at low ready, both feet off the ground between steps and the knee taking each landing, his legs following the joint angles measured on real joggers, and closes on a target at a crouched walk with the rifle shouldered and level. Hurt, he keeps hold of the rifle, presses his free hand to his side and fires from the textbook kneeling position, sitting on his right heel with his left elbow on his left knee. Shot dead, he either goes over backwards or folds onto his knees and falls on his face, and the rifle drops beside him. A blast throws him and he lands on his back. A boot carrying his weight stays where it was put down: the run, the walk and the limp were checked frame by frame, and no planted foot moves over the ground. The parachute drop is still the Red Guard's. The flag he and the Alpagu operator plant over a captured building is their own, in their side's colour. Anyone joining a game needs the same copy of the model and animations, so they ship with the game.
- The Combat Engineers stopped being GLA Workers in a Turkish name.
