The engineer is cut from the Mehmetcik's cloth, so the two read as one army: the same field uniform, with the plate carrier and a patch on the left sleeve in his side's colour, under a plain olive helmet. On his back rides a big sand-coloured sapper's pack, the thing that picks him out of a crowd. He builds by swinging a pickaxe and sweeps for mines with a flat-headed detector. Underneath he still has the Worker's skeleton, so he runs and falls exactly as the Worker did, and his model ships with the game like the Mehmetcik's.
- Turkiye's base is a present-day army base now, every building on its American or GLA parent's footprint and at about the triangle count of the building it stands beside. The Command Center is a concrete headquarters with ribbon windows under a rim in your side's colour, an operations tower carrying the big drone ground-control dish, a steel vehicle hall round the gate, a helipad on the roof and HESCO walls, the flag and Turkiye's badge in the yard. The Power Plant is a gas-fired plant: a steel turbine hall with roof fans, a boiler and tall stack behind it and a transformer yard under steel gantries, its window ribbons lit once you buy Advanced Control Rods. The Barracks is a fenced compound of two-storey prefab blocks with solar water heaters on the roof, and soldiers walk out through a passage under its canopy instead of through a wall. The War Factory is a pale ribbed-steel assembly hall whose sectional door runs up to let tanks out, with a yellow gantry crane over the repair stand. The Supply Center is a logistics depot whose gantry crane lifts each delivery off the truck onto the loading platform. The Airfield keeps its four hardened shelters and trades the stone keep for a concrete operations block and control tower. The Operations Center is a stone-clad block with a radio mast and a dish on a hardened bunker, and each battle plan raises its own kit: Bombardment lifts a howitzer out of a hatched pit, Search and Destroy runs a radar mast out of the roof, Hold the Line throws a HESCO wall round the yard. The Grand Bazaar is a covered market hall, a barrel-vaulted steel shed with stalls under its open side. The Siper is a HESCO fighting position round a concrete shelter, the Hisar a canister launcher behind T-walls, the Radar Kulesi a concrete tower under a turning array, and all three leave ruins of their own.
- The vehicles and aircraft stopped borrowing. The Cobra is an Otokar Cobra II, the Kirpi a tall armoured carrier on a V-hull, the supply truck a BMC 6x6 whose open bed fills with crates, the Korkut an ACV-30 with the twin 35 mm mount, the Mobile Radar a six-wheeled radar truck whose antenna turns only while it stands. The Firtina is a tracked 155 mm howitzer that raises its long gun to fire, the Sakarya a six-wheeled truck with two pods of twenty rockets, and the Koral an 8x8 truck with the jammer's antenna platform over its back. In the air fly a TB2 for the Bayraktar, the real Akinci with its two turboprops, a T625 for the Gokbey, and an A400M brings the paradrops and supply drops, lowering its rear ramp over the drop zone. The Kargu swarm flies as Kargu quadcopters and the Tayfun comes down as a slim ballistic missile instead of China's neutron rocket. Every one of them dies into a wreck of its own, most throwing a wheel, a door or a blade. The spotter team is a sniper-observer in a boonie hat and ghillie mantle, the Maroon Beret a special forces operator under a maroon beret with a suppressed carbine and a demolition pack, and a bailed-out pilot wears an olive flight suit. The Altay dropped its whip antennas and the small boxes on its turret, so it reads cleaner in a crowd.
- Every Turkish soldier now moves on animations made for him, on one skeleton of their own, and no retail animation drives any of them. The Mehmetcik's case comes off his back and the flagpole telescopes out of it when he takes a building, the engineer pulls his pickaxe and detector out of his pack, the Sungur jogs with the tube on his shoulder and the Maroon Beret draws his knife left-handed from the thigh. The spotter no longer borrows the Pathfinder's sniper crouch: he drops to one knee and fires single aimed rounds, and stands again after the last. Each gait covers exactly the ground one stride does, so no foot slides. A replay with Turkiye in it, recorded before this version, will not play back.
- The Altay stopped being a Crusader in a Turkish name and is a modern Turkish main battle tank of its own. Its hull is long and low, riding on seven road wheels behind full side skirts. The flat welded turret is faced with bolt-on armour blocks at the front and armour panels down the sides, runs back into a long bustle with a stowage basket, and carries a remote machine gun on the right of the roof and the commander's sight on the left. The 120 mm gun is long, with a thermal sleeve and a fume extractor halfway out. Your side's colour runs along the skirts and the turret's side armour and rings the muzzle. It stands on the Crusader's footprint, so it fits where a Crusader fits. The gun rises and dips onto its target and kicks back with every shot, and the tracks run over exactly the ground the tank covers. Badly hurt it goes black with soot and loses its antennas. Killed, it leaves its own burnt-out hull with the turret and gun thrown clear of it, where it used to leave a dead Crusader. The model ships with the game, like the Mehmetcik's.
- The Kizilelma stopped being a Raptor in a Turkish name and looks like the real Bayraktar Kizilelma. Nobody sits in it, so there is no canopy: a long nose droops to its point ahead of a smooth hump along the spine, and a sharp edge runs back along each side with the air intakes tucked under it. Small canards sit just behind the nose, the big low delta wing grows out of that edge, and one round nozzle sits between two flat tail booms under fins that lean hard outward. It is the real jet's flat grey. Your side's colour covers the canards, runs behind the wings' leading edges and caps the fins. Its wheels stay down on the runway, parked, taxiing, through the takeoff roll and the landing rollout, and fold away only once it is airborne. Badly hurt it goes black with soot. Shot down, it loses its left wing in the air, throws a fin and a canard where it hits the ground and leaves its own burnt-out wreck. The model ships with the game, like the Altay's.
- The computer plays Turkiye too. A Turkish AI puts up a full base with radar towers, Hisar batteries and Siper bunkers it fills with its own infantry, sends supply trucks, fields the new army, artillery included, fires its own powers and attacks.
- The Turkish computer brings its guns and the eyes to aim them. A Firtina or Sakarya that comes out for one of its attack groups now sends for spotter teams, one on Easy and Medium and two on Hard, and the group waits for them before it leaves; until now the guns walked out blind and the spotters it did buy sat in its bunkers. The American battle plans it plays never put a Firtina in an Easy attack and only reach one after a quarter of an hour on Medium, so it adds a gun of its own to every Easy attack group, every second Medium one and every fourth on Hard. In three fifteen-minute matches a difficulty on Twilight Flame against America, Easy fielded 21 guns, Medium 48 and Hard 27, and all 41 that came out for an attack group sent for their spotters. The computer pays the Turkish price for them now. A Firtina used to cost it the American 1200 whenever that was all it had in the bank. A spotter team killed in the field is replaced for any group that still has a gun and none left to see for it, the men it trains for the seats of a Humvee or a bunker are no longer spotter teams, and a group whose spotters are late leaves without them instead of breaking up when its build time runs out.

## Zero Hour on a Mac, on Linux and on the Steam Deck

- On Mac and Linux the battle now runs on its own thread beside the drawing, as it does on Windows, where it used to be worked out between pictures. `-logicthread` is gone from the command line on every platform; the battle always has its thread.
- On Linux and Mac, a failed resolution change no longer discards the old picture before its replacement is ready. Pending drawing finishes before the old targets are retired.
- Linux and Mac keep the ordinary depth format when the graphics card cannot provide the depth copy needed by modern water and volumetric clouds, instead of choosing a potentially larger format for effects it cannot draw.
- The game runs on Apple silicon Macs and on Linux, the Steam Deck included, as a program built for that machine. There is no Wine or Proton underneath. It draws through Metal on a Mac and through Vulkan on Linux, from the same Zero Hour files you already own.
- The first start finds your game. It looks in your Steam libraries, `~/Games`, `/Applications`, and CrossOver and Whisky bottles, and asks for the folder only when it comes up empty.
- One command builds it. `./build-macos.sh` leaves a Mac app ready to open and `./build-linux.sh` a folder ready to start, and each checks your machine first and names the package to install for anything missing. On Linux it can make an AppImage, a .deb, an .rpm, an Arch package and a Flatpak, none of them carrying EA's files, and the Flatpak has played a full check match on a Steam Deck.
- No Windows needed to get the game's files onto a Mac or Linux either. `./extract-game.sh` takes a Zero Hour or Generals disc, an `.iso` of one, or a folder copied from a Windows install, and lays the two games out where the game finds them, Generals inside Zero Hour's folder. It asks before it writes to the default folder or over files already there, and says when a game is still missing.
- One game on every machine. A replay recorded on a Mac plays back on Linux and on Windows to the same checksum, and the other way round, and a Mac and a Linux PC have played a LAN match together without once disagreeing. A Mac or Linux game could not join a Windows one: the check every machine runs before a network game failed, because the Mac and Linux copies of the game's data files ended each line differently from Windows'. They agree now. A match between Windows and a Mac has not been played yet.
- A German, French or other non-English Zero Hour on a Mac or Linux speaks its own language. Windows' installer writes the language into the registry, and nothing does that on a Mac or Linux, so the game took English and found it in the original Generals' files beside Zero Hour: the menus came up in Generals' English with Zero Hour's own lines missing, so it looked like plain Generals. With no language set it now takes the one your Zero Hour's own files are in. A language you set yourself still wins.
- Text on the Linux menus is as wide as on Windows. Linux has no Arial, and the font standing in for it reports a wider average letter, so every menu font the game sets to a fixed width came out a quarter narrower than it should, the "Generals" lettering and the menu buttons among them. Each is measured against Arial's own figure now, and lands within one percent of Windows.
- The game no longer crashes on some Linux PCs as its window opens. The game hands out memory its own way, and on Linux the graphics driver gets its memory from the game too. Some drivers, AMD's on Debian 12 among them, need every piece lined up on a 16-byte boundary, and the game's lined up on 4, so the start died or went through depending on where the pieces happened to fall. On Linux everything outside the game's own pools now comes from the system, which lines it up as the driver expects.
- `./build-linux.sh` stopped on Linux Mint and Arch after the centred Classic interface went in: the new code compared layout names with a Windows-only spelling that GCC on Linux has never heard of. It uses the name every platform knows now, and so do the two debug-build spots with the same habit. From 3.0.0 on, `./build-macos.sh` and `./build-linux.sh` stopped again, on another Windows-only spelling and, on Linux, a file name written in the wrong case, which Windows does not mind. The log blamed the audio library because it was the last file the build had started; the real error sat higher up. Both are fixed, after Andreas Berger found them. On 3.2.0 `./build-macos.sh` got nearly to the end and stopped on four of the build's own tests of how the game reads its files, which were missing two pieces the game's job scheduler picked up in that version. They have them now, after Martin K. reported it. Since 3.4.0 `./build-macos.sh` stopped once more, this time on the save and load code: it handed the save file's name to a log line as a whole text object where the line wanted plain characters, which the Mac's compiler refuses and Windows lets through, so on Windows that line printed garbage in place of the file name. It hands over the name itself now, and the Windows build warns about the same mistake anywhere else. Martin K. reported this one too.
- Windows on Arm laptops, the Snapdragon ones, get a build made for them. Microsoft never shipped those machines the library the game loads its textures and shaders through, so the game brings its own, the texture code the Mac and Linux versions already run. Switched on in place of Microsoft's library on an ordinary Windows PC, it draws the same battlefields, with no tree, house or patch of ground going missing. Nobody has played it on a Snapdragon laptop yet.
- The Linux game has Generals' icon. The window carries it in the taskbar and in the window switcher, and `add-to-menu.sh` in the folder `./build-linux.sh` makes puts the game in the desktop's app menu with it, which is where GNOME takes a running game's icon from. It had none.
- Hotkeys you set in Options are saved on Linux and still there the next time you start.
- Building from source no longer stops at a test your compiler cannot build: a test that gcc 16 refused is fixed, after Narfmeister found it, and Apple Clang 15 builds the game again.
- Modern water runs on Linux with the same reflections as Windows: Legacy, SSR and Hybrid. Options gets a Water tab, hidden on Windows, with scene reflections, reflection detail, wave detail and refraction, all following the quality slider. The water's static mesh and the shoreline are worked out once and reused, which makes it faster. Classic water stays the default. Thanks to Shin-Aska, whose pull requests these are.
- With Cloud Style on Volumetric, more than eight toxin or radiation fields at once keep their cloud look on Linux and Mac. The ninth turned flat. Thanks to Shin-Aska for the fix.
- Thanks to ilyasakin, whose port this is.

## No more mods

- The game no longer loads mods. EA's own `-mod` switch is gone, and so are `-modpatch` and `-modfactions`; what you play is Zero Hour's data with Reforged's changes on it, the same on every machine in the room.

## One interface

- The choice between a Classic and a Reforged interface is gone. There is one, laid out the way Zero Hour shipped, and the orders Reforged added now live on the keys you already know: A attack-moves, holding Ctrl fires on whatever is under the cursor as it did in 2003 (that hold is yours to move on the launcher's Command bar page), a guard order can cover a patch of ground instead of one spot, and orders queue up one after another. Everything your base is building stands on the screen as a line of text each, the six closest to done first and "+N more" for the rest. Superweapon countdowns are listed the same way, up to eighteen. Both lists are in bold type, the build list in white and each countdown in its owner's colour. The promotion screen no longer darkens the battlefield behind it. Whether the right button gives orders, or the left as in 1.04, is a setting in the launcher.
- An attack move and a Ctrl attack fire on the left click in every mouse setup. With the right button giving orders, A then a right click attack-moved, and Ctrl fired only on a right click, so the same hands did different things depending on one checkbox. Now A, or Ctrl held, then a left click is the attack everywhere, and a right click with A armed puts the key down without an order. Ctrl with a right click gives none. Plain orders stay on whichever button your setup gives them.
- The drags followed the click there. Under the Alternate Mouse Setup the line you draw with attack move or guard armed, the Ctrl circle and the Ctrl+Shift attack line still wanted the right button, and a left drag with A armed drew a selection box instead. All of them, and every guard button, are the left button's now in every setup, and a right drag pans the map with the key still armed. On the radar a left press with A or G armed, or with a general's power waiting for its target, sends the order there, where it used to move the camera; the right button looks.
- Holding the right button on the radar now carries the camera with the cursor when the left button gives orders. The radar has looked with the held button since the last version, but only the left one ever got the drag: the right press moved the camera once and then sat there, so in the game's default setup crossing the map still meant clicking your way over it.
- Ctrl on a garrisoned Bunker fires on a unit as well as the ground, where it used to take only the ground. The soldiers inside do the shooting, and the Air Force General's Combat Chinook takes a Ctrl target the same way. Shift on top of the Ctrl hold keeps it: the pointer stays the force-fire one, and a drag draws the attack line instead of the circle. The Force Attack button 3.1.0 put on the command bar is gone again, since Ctrl already did everything it did, and each bar has its old empty place back.
- The Hotkeys tab in Options stopped listing a Force Attack button on bars that have not had one since it left the command bar. Ctrl still fires on whatever is under the pointer, and that hold now moves on the launcher's Hotkeys page alone.
- The dark plate behind Exit, Restart and the options screen in a match covers the whole picture. It used to sit in a 4:3 frame in the middle, so a widescreen left the battlefield bright down both sides. The box itself keeps the shape it was drawn in.
- Buildings select together again, which the one interface had taken away. Shift-click them, drag a box over them, or double-click one for every building of its kind on the screen; select four War Factories and each tank you click goes to whichever has the shortest queue. Double-click a unit and every one of that kind whose feet sit in the picture is taken, including the ones sitting past the camera's far clip that used to be skipped. A building and a unit still never share a selection.
- Formation lines are back for everyone. With move, attack move or guard armed, a left drag spreads the selection along the line you draw again; since the one interface it drew a selection box instead, because the line was switched off for the Classic mouse that every player now runs. A drag with no order armed is still the selection box.
- A box round your soldiers leaves the worker among them behind again. The rule that a box holding anything military drops the dozers, workers, supply trucks, Chinooks and hackers from it was switched off for the Classic mouse, which is the one every player now runs, so the dozer came along with the tanks. It holds for every box now, a Shift box added to a selection included. A box of workers alone still takes the workers, and a click or a double click on one still takes it.
- Every key is yours to move. The launcher's Hotkeys page draws the command bar of every building and unit each general can field, cameos and letters as the game shows them, and a click and a keypress gives any button a new letter or none. Two buttons on one bar that would share a letter are marked before you play. The keyboard commands are there too, from bookmarks and team keys to the camera, along with the ones Zero Hour never bound: select all your infantry, vehicles or aircraft, every barracks, war factory or airfield, the next idle worker or unit, pause, the general's promotions, the three signals to your allies and the general's powers. Your keys are yours alone; the other players in a match keep theirs, and a match never refuses you for them.
- Some keys now mean one thing on every bar: A attack move, S stop, G guard, Y rally point, V evacuate, N sell, C combat drop, and H for land mines, camo netting and the GLA worker's switch to fake buildings. Sell sits on its own key, so emptying a bunker can never sell it. The 188 buttons Zero Hour had put on one of those letters take another, kept off the 18 letters under your left hand where the bar leaves room (the Avenger is J now), and no bar gained a clash doing it. Those letters are still yours to hand out: the Hotkeys page gives A or H to any other button you pick, and marks the clash. On a bar that has the order as well, the order keeps its key: a Barracks button on A fires from A, and a tank's A is still attack move. A `FixedOrderKeys` block with `Enabled = No` in Hotkeys.ini turns the fixed keys off and gives every button the letter the game's own text gives it, the orders included, as the game shipped: in the German game guard is W and the rally point U again, and the 179 German buttons on one of those letters, the Humvee on V and the supply center on N among them, have their keys back.
- Those orders move too. Sell, attack move, stop, guard, rally point, evacuate, combat drop, the mines, camo netting and the fake building switch were locked to their letters: the Hotkeys tab refused to wait for a key on them, and a letter given to one in the file was ignored in the match. Each one now takes the letter you give it, or none, on the Hotkeys tab like any other button, and keeps it after a restart; the letters above are only where they start. A letter you set also beats the one a button had from the game: Sell moved to K on the GLA Command Center used to lose K to the Worker button, and now sells. The launcher's Hotkeys page lets them go as well; it used to show the fixed letter whatever you had set and refuse to change it. Two holds Zero Hour put on a modifier alone are on the list of commands now, in the game and the launcher: Alt queues orders and Shift adds to the selection, and either can move to a key or another modifier. With nothing selected and a worker lending you his bar, only his buildings answer a key. H used to throw a GLA worker over to his fake buildings, and S stopped him, though nobody had picked him. The launcher also stops shifting keyboard commands off those letters: it had put View command center on P because H belonged to the mines, and the next time it starts it hands H back. A key you chose yourself stays where you put it.
- The Hotkeys page is in the game as well, as the last tab of the options screen, so a key can move without quitting to the launcher: from the main menu, or from Esc in the middle of a match. Every command sits on the left with its key. On the right you pick a general and one of his buildings or units, and its command bar is listed button by button, each with its cameo and its letter. Double-click a line, or press Enter or Change, and then the key; Esc lets go. Two buttons of one bar on one letter, or two commands on one key, turn red, and the line under the lists names them. Accept writes the file the launcher writes, so a key set in either place is there in the other, and a key changed in a match works from the next press.
- Export and Import on the Hotkeys page take your keys to a file and back, for another PC or a fresh install. Before an import the page tells you how many keys it changes and how many would clash; a file with a line it cannot read changes nothing and quotes that line.
- The arrow keys scroll the camera in the German game, as they do in English. German Zero Hour put next and previous unit and worker on the bare arrows, so the arrows picked units and only Ctrl and an arrow moved the camera; those four now sit on Ctrl and an arrow, as the English game ships them. Any language that puts a command on a bare arrow gets the same, and an arrow you gave a command yourself on the Hotkeys page stays where you put it.
- Grid keys are back, keyed by the cell a button sits in. The first grid moved buttons around to give them a place's letter and still left two places without one; this one moves nothing. With the grid on, the top row of the bar is Q W E R T Y U and the bottom row A S D F G H J, column by column, so the first cell is Q on a Barracks, a War Factory and a tank alike, and the cell under it A. Upgrades take X C V B N in the order they stand on the bar, so the first upgrade of any building is X. The fixed keys step aside on the bar: attack move and stop take their cells' letters like every other button, while Ctrl still forces an attack. A letter you give a button still beats its cell, and a letter can now go to one cell alone, which is what a transport needs: its passengers' exit buttons are all one button, and with a key per cell the third passenger out can be M while the rest keep the grid. Accept on the in-game Hotkeys tab keeps the grid and every per-cell key, and the tab's list shows the grid's letters.
- Red Alert keys, if your hands learned on Red Alert 2. They come with the Red Alert style Layout under Options, Interface, one choice for the screen and the keys alike, and the Classic layout keeps the Classic keys. Red Alert puts Q W E R on the four production tabs, D on deploy, L on sell, K on repair, T on select same type, P on select all, N and M on next and previous unit, F5 to F8 on the cheer and the three smoke signals, and Z held lays waypoints the way Alt does. A attack move, S stop and G guard stay where this game has them. Every Red Alert key moves on the Hotkeys page like any other, and the page edits the keys of the layout picked on the Interface page. The two keep their own changes, so switching back to Classic finds your Classic keys as you left them.
- W no longer starts a War Factory. The launcher had moved China's War Factory onto W, which Zero Hour already gives to Select all aircraft. With a tank selected and no aircraft on the map, W dropped the tank, the idle worker's bar took its place, and the same press let go on that bar's War Factory. The launcher now keeps the buttons it moves off every letter a keyboard command holds on its own, W, Q and the idle worker's I among them, and China's War Factory sits on D. Start the launcher once and it rewrites its part of the file. A letter you picked yourself stays where you put it. The game now settles it for any letter, yours and the grid's included: a key press does one thing. If a button on the bar wears the letter when the key goes down, the button gets it and the keyboard command on that letter waits; if none does, the command fires and the bar that comes up after it is left alone. A button that loses its letter to another, on the bar or the strip of general's powers, shows no letter instead of one that does nothing. With nothing selected, the worker's buildings that the bar shows anyway step off any letter a keyboard command uses on its own: on the grid, Q selects everything and W every aircraft again instead of putting down a Power Plant or a Barracks, and the buildings on free letters keep them.
- With a transport or bunker selected, click one of your units to send it inside.
- A unit on repeat can be switched off even when it cannot be built: a lost prerequisite, the unit cap, a full queue or an unpowered factory no longer lock the button.
- Guard, Attack Move, Force Attack, Move and Hold Position have their own rows on the Hotkeys page. Command bar buttons take digit keys too.
- The launcher keeps its pages in a rail down the left side. Home, Maps, Replays, Hotkeys, Game options and Health are one click each, with the counts that matter beside them, and the gold button under them is always the next step into the game: Install until the game is on disk, Update now when a release waits, Play after that.

## The command bar moves to the middle

- ControlBar Pro is the command bar, in every match and for every side, and nothing has to be installed for it. The radar sits in the bottom left corner, the command buttons with your money and power in the middle of the bottom edge, and your selection, rank and general's buttons in the bottom right. Each piece is drawn at your screen's height and keeps the shape it was painted in, so nothing stretches on a 4:3 monitor or a 32:9 one, and the battlefield shows between the three. At 1920x1080 they stand where ControlBar Pro's own layout puts them, to the pixel. Its rank screen, power buttons, chat, quit and disconnect screens come with it. Thanks to xezon and FAS, whose bar this is.

- The command bar is one console standing in the middle of the bottom edge: a taller radar, your selection and the build grid side by side, with the power bar over the grid. The idle worker and rank keys sit in a row over your selection, and in multiplayer the smoke signals join them. The red under-attack lamp is gone: the ping on the radar, the voice and the line in the event feed already tell you where you are hit, and the lamp only blinked about it a second time.
- Your general's powers grow out of the console's right end, a column for each F key with its powers stacked up it, and only the powers you have take any room.
- A single unit's name and health stand beside its portrait, and a veteran gets his gold stars there too. The stat panel that once sat under them, with the main weapon's damage, damage a second, range and how much of the damage from gunfire, tank shells and rockets its armour stops, went out with the HTML control bar, and the build button card shows the stats now; whether the panel comes back is still open (issue 78). A Terrorist, or a Combat Bike with one riding it, used to read 999,999 damage and millions a second, the figures of the stand-in charge that kills the rider so his real bomb can go off. They read the bomb now, 500 for the Terrorist's dynamite and 700 for the bike's, and a bomb that goes off once has no damage a second. Your own units and your allies' show as they stand, so a veteran's bonus, a Composite Armor upgrade or Hold the Line shows the moment it lands. An enemy's show only what his veterancy stars already tell you, never his upgrades or battle plans. Click an enemy and his health reads as a share, 64%, because 512/800 would tell you he bought Composite Armor; the upgrade icons under his portrait stay grey for everything his side researched, where retail lit Composite Armor or Supply Lines for anyone who clicked, and light only for what the unit visibly carries, a drone or an Overlord's turret. A group shows every type it holds in the same box, five to a row. Click a type there and only those stay selected; shift-click it and they leave the selection, so the two Rangers that tagged along with your tanks are one click from gone. Watching a match with nothing selected, the empty portrait box is gone and the console is the radar alone; click a unit and the box comes back. Following nobody, the experience bar beside the radar is gone too, since there is no general's rank to fill it.
- The match clock hangs from the middle of the top edge with your money in its own box under it. Superweapon countdowns in the top right corner are as big as your general's power buttons.
- Tab is Zero Hour's again. It opens and closes the diplomacy screen the game shipped with, in its own art and layout, players, teams and mute buttons where you remember them. With a group selected, Tab used to step through the unit types in your selection instead, and the diplomacy screen wore ControlBar Pro's paint.
- Peace time counts down in red at the end of the info strip in the top right corner, PEACE 4:59, down to the last second, and nothing pops up over the middle of the battlefield any more. It stays there with Info Box switched off, alone on the strip, because the truce is a rule of the match. The strip itself was missing from the released game; it is on for everyone now.
- Superweapon countdowns and a map's named timers no longer sit on top of that strip. They started at the very top of the corner, so the strip's clock and money were written over the first countdown; they now begin under the strip whenever it is showing.
- A superweapon built, charged or fired anywhere on the map flashes its name in big letters under the clock: "Nuclear Missile launched". Yours are white, an ally's blue, an enemy's red. Each line stays four seconds and fades out. When several land at once they queue and hurry through, two seconds each with one more waiting and one second with a pile behind it, so the last news never sits stale.
- Your production queue stands on the console over your selection, five to a row, each row only as long as what is in it. The event feed runs down from the menu key in the top left corner, and the chat sits under it.
- Point at the attack, hold position or move key and a card says what it does, in English or Turkish. Those three are painted onto the grid rather than given to a unit, so the game had no card for them and showed nothing. The card stands on top of the command bar like every other button's.
- HUD Size grows the console from its middle, and on a narrow screen it stops at the size that still fits.
- The grid under a building you are placing is fainter and its lines thinner, and the red squares where nothing can stand are lighter, so the ground under them shows through. Untick grid placement on the Controls page and the lines go altogether.
- Placing a building no longer crashes the game now and then. The ground can still be marked as taken by something that has already gone, and the red squares under the building you are placing asked that missing thing who owned it. Such a square stays red until the ground is free.
- Hold Ctrl while placing a building and grid placement flips for as long as the key is down. With the box unticked the building snaps to the grid and the lines come up, so one flush row is a held key away; with it ticked you get a free hand for the odd building that has to sit between two squares. It works the same in Classic.
- The camera works the same way with Shift. Turn it with the middle button or the rotate keys while Shift is down and the 45 degree camera steps flip: with the box unticked the view clicks round the eight headings, with it ticked it turns freely, and letting go of Shift mid-turn hands back whatever the box says. A quick square-on look no longer means a trip to the options.
- Your general's promotion screen opens in the middle of the screen, in the Classic interface as well, instead of hanging from the top edge. The battlefield dims behind it, and a click anywhere off the screen closes it without selecting or ordering anything underneath.
- A group selected shows its unit types cleanly again. Under the type pictures the single unit's portrait was still drawn, a size larger than a picture's slot, so it hung below the first row and the count badges landed in the middle of it. The well is empty behind the pictures now. Each picture also uses the sharp portrait art: a group of one kind fills the whole well, and that used to be the small button picture blown up to a blur.

## Groups attack-move at their own speed

- An attack move used to hold the whole group to its slowest member when you held Ctrl on the click, and the computer's groups did that every time. A damaged truck walked the tanks in. Each unit now goes at its own speed. A replay recorded before this, of a group attack-moving that way, will not play back the same.

## Veterancy goes to everyone who fought

- A kill used to promote only the unit that fired the last shot. Two Crusaders could grind an Overlord down to a sliver and a passing Humvee's rocket took every point of it. Now the killing blow earns a quarter and the rest is shared out among everything that hurt the target in the last ten seconds, by how much of its health each one took off. A unit that died before the kill leaves its share to the killer. Healing counts too: an Emperor, or an Overlord or Helix with a Propaganda Tower, earns for every friendly unit it patches up, half of that unit's worth as a kill for a full repair and less for less. The kill on the score screen and your general's promotion points still go to the last shot. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.

## Tanks and cars move as they did in Zero Hour

- Players said the Humvee drove nothing like the original and the Dragon Tank crawled, and they were right. Since October every tank, car and bike had eased up to speed over a second, braked early for each stop and bend and backed up to a spot behind it, and even with a quarter more acceleration and turn rate on top it lost to Zero Hour over any distance. Tanks, cars and bikes drive on EA's own code and EA's own numbers again. Sent 300 east, a Crusader arrives in 9.7 seconds where it took 10.3. Sent 300 on a diagonal it arrives in 7.0 where it took 10.2, because EA measured a vehicle's speed in a way that let it run 41% faster at 45 degrees, and players have planned their raids on that since 2003, so it stays. A Humvee covers the same diagonal in 3.6 seconds instead of 5.6 and a Scorpion in 5.3 instead of 7.9. Start and stop are Zero Hour's to the frame, and a car still gains one or two frames on a short hop by sliding onto its spot a frame sooner. Soldiers keep their true speed at every heading.
- Turning is the one place they beat Zero Hour. Every vehicle on the ground swings round half as fast again as it used to and no healthy one turns slower than 100 degrees a second, a damaged one still slower than that by the same share as before, so a Crusader comes about at 270 degrees a second where it managed 180, and an Overlord reverses its heading in 1.8 seconds instead of 3. A tank sent somewhere more than 45 degrees off its nose used to stop dead and pivot on the spot first. Now it rolls through the turn, slower the tighter it is, and stands to pivot only for a hairpin past 135 degrees. Jets and helicopters taxiing on the ground turn as they did. Replays recorded before this change play back differently.
- What you see points where the tank points. Reforged's picture used to swing the hull into a turn up to 15 degrees and 83 milliseconds behind where the tank was really heading, so a fast turn looked mushy and a shot seemed to leave a hull still coming round. The hull now follows its real heading in every graphics mode, and the turret stays on its target. They still look driven: the squat as a tank pulls away, the dip when it brakes, the suspension and the moving treads are all still there, and none of it moves the tank by a step. Tanks keep firing on the move.
- A tank in a column closes up behind the one in front and moves off with it. EA's tanks stop dead, and for a while a tank behind another stopped a short gap back and then took a second, not half of one, to get its speed back, so that it would not nose into the tail in front. It did cut the shoving and it cost every queue its pace, measured at the same tank speed: twenty Crusaders over the Kandahar bridge on Golden Oasis had their last tank across seven to eight seconds later, twenty-four tanks through the streets of Alpine Assault nine and a half seconds later on average over four runs, and the Forgotten Forest trailer column 17 seconds later in the one run we made. The gap is gone and those columns keep their pace. The price is contact: tanks spend more moments pressed against the one in front, half as many again through Alpine Assault and over a third more in a block of 420 Crusaders crossing Twilight Flame, where the arrivals come out the same.
- Late in big 4v4 games units no longer stand for up to four seconds waiting for a route; the longest wait is now under two seconds, with movement and frame rate unchanged.
- Replays recorded before this change play back differently, and this version cannot join a game hosted on an older one.

## Soldiers turn and stop on their feet

- Send a running Ranger back the way he came and he used to slide backwards past his own nose for a sixth of a second while he swung round. Now his feet carry him round with the turn, and past a right angle he plants them and pivots. On a gentle bend he barely slows: through 30 degrees a Ranger keeps 85% of his pace where he used to drop to 68%, and a 90 degree corner costs him half the time it did.
- A soldier told to stop takes three short steps to a halt instead of freezing mid-stride, about one more step of ground. Arriving at the end of a move looks the same way. He still starts walking as quickly after the click as he always did.
- Infantry on attack move look before they step. A Ranger used to walk three paces toward the move point, stop and turn on an enemy that had been in plain sight, and a Red Guard came at it from the side and pivoted on the spot before he fired. Both now walk straight at the enemy and arrive facing it. A replay recorded before this change plays back differently.

## Tanks shoot on the move

- A turret that picked its own target on the move fired once and then let go of it until its next look round, two seconds later for most units. A Technical driving past four Troop Crawlers hit them twice. It now hits every 6 frames, 11 times, as fast as it fires standing still. On the same drive a Quad Cannon went from 28 hits to 53 and a Gattling Tank from 28 to 50, and an Overlord's second shell comes 10 frames after its first instead of 38.
- Told to move in the middle of a fight, a tank or car with a turret keeps shooting what it was attacking for as long as the target is alive and in range, the way helicopters already did. A Technical pulled back from four Troop Crawlers used to fall silent for two and a half seconds and no longer stops at all. A Marauder used to wait almost four seconds past its reload before the next shell and now waits half a second. A move order still never starts a new fight.
- The Marauder's turret turns. The model always had one, but the tank swung its whole body round to aim and could not shoot on the move. The turret turns 100 degrees a second, as fast as the Scorpion's: driving past four Troop Crawlers a Marauder used to fire nothing and now lands three shells, and circling them it kills all four where it never fired. The turret is slower round than the hull was, so a target appearing straight behind a parked Marauder takes its first shell most of a second later than before.
- The Gattling Tank opens fire 15 degrees before its guns are on the target and walks the stream onto it, where it used to wait until it was within 2 degrees. The Gattling Cannon defence and the Strategy Center's bombardment cannon do the same. Circling four Troop Crawlers, a Gattling Tank hit them 208 times where it hit 102, and 12 of the extra hits come from the earlier start.
- The Gattling cannon on an Overlord's back turns at the Gattling Tank's 180 degrees a second instead of 60 and opens fire the same way. A target appearing behind the Overlord is under fire 22 frames sooner and took 66 hits where it took 41.
- A replay recorded before this change plays back differently.
- Tell a tank to fire at the ground and it fires from where it stands. On any slope the game read the spot as hidden behind the very hill it was lying on, so a tank with the spot well inside its range drove off looking for a better angle, swinging its hull round under its own turret, and fired on the way. Pulled off a building to shell the ground 140 behind them, a Battlemaster took 84 frames to its first shell on the new spot and now takes 45, which is how long its turret needs to come round, and a pair of Scorpions that used to wander about 200 away over eight seconds now stay where they were put. Replays recorded before this play back differently.
- Tank shells fly straight at the target. EA's shell climbed ten over the highest ground on the way and dropped back down, so once the shells glowed, every Crusader shot looked like a lob: it left the barrel 12 degrees high, rose 7 over the line and hit coming down at 25 degrees. Now it flies the line, rising off it by nothing, and only a hill between the tank and its target still lifts it over. This goes for every tank cannon, the Battlemaster, Overlord, Scorpion and Marauder too.
- The gun lowers onto its target. Turrets used to only turn, so the barrel stayed level and a straight shell left it at an angle: a Paladin shooting a car 13 degrees below put its shell 7 degrees under its own barrel. The Crusader, Paladin, Battlemaster and Scorpion, the generals' versions and Turkiye's Altay included, now dip and raise the barrel onto the line from the muzzle to the middle of the target, down to 15 below, and the shell leaves along it: measured at the shot, a Paladin's barrel sat within a degree of its shell's line. The barrel holds that line while the hull tilts on a slope and rocks back with the shot. Hits land when they did and do the same damage: the same fight of five tanks plays out to the same health, frame for frame. The Overlord, the Emperor and the Marauder keep a level gun, because each carries two barrels that the turret cannot pitch together. A replay recorded before this can play back differently, since the shell now starts from the lowered muzzle.
- The Nuke General's Battlemaster wears its own nuclear paint again. When the guns learned to lower, his tank and the Tank General's swapped bodies, so the Nuke War Factory rolled out what looked like a plain Battlemaster and the Tank General drove the nuclear one. It was always the Nuke General's tank underneath, with his gun, his price and his radioactive death; only the picture was wrong, and every other general's units were checked against EA's for the same slip. A replay with either tank in it can play back differently.
- Artillery shells leave along the barrel. A Nuke Cannon's shell used to come out six and a half degrees under its raised barrel and jerk onto its arc; it now leaves the muzzle at the barrel's angle and the arc grows from there. Inferno and Nuke Cannon shells still lob as high as they did.
- Artillery lands on time. The Fire Base, the Inferno Cannon, the Nuke Cannon and the campaign's battleships fire like real guns now: the shell flies a true arc and comes down the same time after it left at any range, 1.2 seconds for a Fire Base and 1.6 for the Inferno and Nuke Cannons, and the gun raises its barrel to that arc before it fires. A target close in gets a steep lob from a barrel near upright (a Fire Base fires at 57 degrees on a 108 shot, an Inferno at 77 on a 55 one), a far one a flatter shot (34 degrees at 225, 49 at 235), and the drawn barrel and the shell's way out agree to under a degree. Each flight time is the old shot's average over the gun's range, so a tank has as long to drive out from under it as it had, and a shell still follows a target that keeps moving. Before this the barrel's angle and the arc came from two places and never met. The Fire Base's howitzer fires the tanks' shell, so when tank shells went straight it fired flat under a barrel 46 degrees up; the Inferno's barrel sat at 45 whatever the range. The battleships fired from a point 65 past their front guns and from under the waterline behind them, and both turrets aimed for the front gun; every shell now leaves its own drawn muzzle. A Technical's cannon shell left 17 in front of its gun and now leaves the gun. Tank shells still fly straight.
- A SCUD or a Tomahawk flies one smooth curve to its target. A SCUD went straight up, flipped over the top at six degrees a frame, glided flat for a moment and then kinked again into its dive. Now it rolls over and comes down in a single sweep that only ever eases off, its sharpest turn 4.6 degrees a frame. The Scud Storm takes the same curve and lands within half a second of when it did. Replays recorded before this play back differently.
- Machine gun fire looks fast. The tracers of a Humvee, a Technical or a Quad Cannon crawled across the field at 300 a second and took half a second to reach a target 150 away; they now cross it in a tenth of a second, at 1,500, as streaks twice as long. Rangers, Rebels, Gattling Tanks and Cannons, Comanches and the Spectre got the same treatment. Only the picture changed: every bullet lands when it always did.
- Tracers glow. Each machine gun round keeps EA's streak and adds a soft orange glow around it, strongest at the head of the round and thinning toward its tail. Glow at Off, or Classic Graphics, gives you EA's streak alone.
- The Toxin Tractor and the other stream weapons spray one straight line into a building again, not a zigzag.
- Units pick their own targets by the armour their weapon is made for. A tank goes for the tank, even with a Technical beside it that would die sooner; a Humvee shoots the infantry and the Technicals before the tank; rocket soldiers go for vehicles. Among targets in the same armour, the one that dies quickest goes first. Anything that is shooting one of your units still gets answered, unless something in range that its weapon is made for is nearly dead. Computer armies pick the same way.
- Patriot batteries shoot down Tomahawks and SCUDs again. Since 3.7.0 a Patriot locked onto the launcher sitting just past its reach, could not fire at it, and let every missile through. A defence now always takes something it can hit over something it cannot: three Patriots under two Tomahawk launchers shot down 8 missiles where they shot down none, and a lone Patriot under two SCUD launchers lived twice as long and took 4 of them out of the sky. The Gattling Cannon always fired at them; one alone is too slow to finish a Tomahawk, as it was in EA's game, and two shot down 10 in the same fight. A replay from 3.7.0 or 3.8.0 in which a defence let missiles through plays back differently.

## Point defense lasers back on the planes, in clips on the tanks

- The Air Force General's King Raptor, Aurora, Stealth Fighter, B-3 and Chinooks have their point defense lasers again, and so does the Boss General's Raptor. From 2.4.0 they dropped flares instead; the flares are gone, and the lasers fire the way they did in EA's game, with no clip and no upgrade to buy. Two King Raptors making seven passes over a Stinger Site burned down 52 and 54 Stingers and came home with 360 and 390 health of 480. A Chinook sitting on its pad shoots down missiles again too, and the laser takes on a SCUD or a Tomahawk near these aircraft, which no flare ever fooled. Countermeasures works as it did in EA's game.
- A missile a point defense laser hits now goes up in a proper burst: a bright flash, sparks falling away and a short orange blast on top of EA's red flash and scrap of casing. It is gone in a second and leaves no smoke, so a run of intercepts does not stack a grey column over the tank. This goes for every point defense laser: the Paladin, the Avenger, the Air Force General's planes and Chinooks, and the Superweapon General's drone.
- The Paladin and the Avenger keep their point defense lasers, and you can see them again. In 2.4.0 they fired an invisible charge: a puff at the hull and a missile bursting in the air with nothing between them. The beam is back, drawn from the same spot on the tank EA drew it from, and a missile it touches still goes in one shot. What 2.4.0 changed stays. The lasers fire in short bursts: a Paladin gets two shots and four seconds to recharge, each of the Avenger's two lasers gets four and three seconds. Under five Tank Hunters an Avenger stops 8 missiles where EA's endless laser stopped 14 or 16, but it dies on the same frame, because fifteen hits kill it either way. A Paladin under four Rocket Buggies stops 4 rockets of 36, as it always did.
- The Paladin's laser also burns any soldier who comes within 65 of the tank, and a soldier it kills burns up again instead of being thrown by a blast. It has a second laser of its own for that, with its own two shots, so firing at a soldier never leaves the tank empty when a missile arrives.
- Lasers glow now. The Paladin's and the Avenger's point defense, the Laser General's Crusader, Paladin, Avenger and turrets, and the point defense drone each draw a white-hot core down the middle of the beam and a soft halo in the beam's own colour along its whole length, so a pink Laser Avenger beam sits in a pink haze from the tank to its target. On the default renderer the core spills into the screen's bloom; on the Direct3D 9 one the halo carries the glow by itself. The Avenger's marking laser, the one that paints a target for the rest of your army, is not a weapon and keeps EA's thin blue line without a halo. The Glow setting decides how wide the halo burns, and Off gives you EA's plain beam back. The halo now rounds off past both ends of the beam instead of stopping in a straight cut across it. EA's own beams, the marking laser included, stop blinking: their texture scrolled half its height every frame, so at a steady 30 frames a second they were drawn on one frame and dark the next, in the 2003 game too. Now they hold the lit middle of the texture and show on every frame. Only the picture changed: damage, range and timing are what they were, and replays play back the same.
- The same lasers now look like beams of energy. EA's beam texture lights only the middle three percent of each layer, so every weapon laser in the game was a thin line, and the halo laid over it was one flat red band the width of a tank. Now each beam is a thin, intensely bright core, nearly white with the beam's colour in it, inside a narrow glow that falls away fast, with only a faint haze beyond. The muzzle shows a small hot point, the spot it hits a small burn point, and the whole beam shimmers slightly while it fires. A shot no longer appears at full length at once: it streaks out from the barrel behind a small bright edge in 12 to 30 thousandths of a second, depending on the range, and the burn point catches as it lands. Recorded footage moves the streak on every picture rather than in steps. A beam held on one target, like the Avenger's on an aircraft, runs out on the first shot and stays whole after that. Each shot dies away over its last third instead of vanishing in one frame. Off in the Glow setting still gives you EA's plain beam. Picture only: damage, range and timing are untouched.
- Laser Defense and Laser General beams no longer rebuild their glow on every shot. With Glow off, on Low, or under Classic Graphics a beam does only EA's work, about a tenth of what a shot cost before.
- A replay recorded before this change plays back differently.

## Helicopters fly like helicopters

- Every helicopter in the game, on every side and for every general, used to drive like a tank with rotors. Told to go somewhere behind it, a Comanche swung its nose all the way round on the spot and only then flew off nose first. Now it sets off at once wherever it is sent and brings its nose round on the way. Sent 300 behind itself, a Comanche turned 178 degrees before it went and was 30 out after a second and a half; now it is 30 out after one second with its nose already two thirds of the way round, and flies nose first a second and a half in. Players told us the first version of this flew backwards and sideways too much, so the nose now turns into every move longer than a helicopter's own length. A hop shorter than that is still flown sideways or backwards with the nose left alone, which is what you want when nudging one into place.
- A Comanche keeps its guns on what it is shooting at while it flies. Its cannon and missiles only fire straight ahead, so a Comanche ordered to move in the middle of a fight turned away from its target. It now holds its nose on the target and slides along beside it: one sent across in front of an Overlord it had been shooting stayed within a degree of the tank the whole way, where it used to point 84 degrees off on average. One flying past a supply truck 120 off its line now turns to it and shoots, where it used to fly straight by.
- The Comanche's chin gun turns, as the real one does, 120 degrees either side of the nose. EA bolted the cannon and the missiles straight ahead, so a Comanche had to swing its whole body round to shoot anything. Now the missiles still fly where the nose points, and the cannon tracks on its own: making a pass along four Red Guards, a Comanche turned 34 degrees where it used to turn 132, and its gun held within 4 degrees of the target while the nose stayed on the flight. A target behind the gun's reach turns the helicopter just far enough to bring it back in.
- Pull a helicopter out of a fight and it keeps shooting on the way out. Told to move while attacking, it used to drop the target at once; now it holds its gun on it for as long as the target is alive and in range, and the move goes exactly where and when it would have. A Comanche backs or slides away with its nose on the target: sent 350 straight back from three Battlemasters it fired 10 more rounds before they fell out of range, and 14 sliding off to the side, where it used to fire one. A plain move never starts a new fight; a helicopter that was not attacking anything just flies.
- Comanches fire their rocket pods sooner. Sent at a spot 800 away, a Comanche used to ease to a stop on the very edge of range before the first rocket left; now it flies in at full speed, fires the moment the spot comes into range and brakes under its own volley, then holds where it stopped. Braking that hard used to carry it past a standstill: it ran 57 past the edge of range and then backed 33 of that up again while it fired. Now it settles within one unit of where it first comes to rest. Any helicopter stopped hard at full speed holds its spot the same way. Four of them fired 6 seconds after the click, where they took 7.6 to 8.4. The rockets steer for the spot by themselves, so the helicopter no longer turns its nose to within 2 degrees of it first: a spot beside a hovering Comanche is hit 3 frames sooner, one behind it 3 frames sooner too. A Comanche whose pods are still reloading fires the moment they are full, as before. Replays recorded before this change, with a helicopter firing at the ground in them, will not play back the same.
- A Helix with the gattling cannon on its back lets the cannon do the aiming. The cannon sits on a turret that turns all the way round, yet the whole Helix used to swing round to point at whatever it was shooting. Now it holds its heading and only the turret tracks. With a Crusader driving circles round it, a Helix that used to turn 336 degrees following the tank does not turn at all, and its cannon fired 458 times where it fired 251. Infantry shooting out of a Helix bunker leave the Helix just as free once they are on its target. The Helix's own nose gun only fires forward, so while the cannon has the target it fires only when the target crosses in front.
- A helicopter leans into the move. It dips its nose to speed up and lifts it to stop, rolls into a slide sideways and comes level again in a hover, never past about 12 degrees and never with a jerk: the lean moves by at most a degree and a half from one frame to the next.
- Helicopters ease in and out of everything they do. Speed builds up over a moment instead of all at once, a stop flares out and settles on the exact spot it was sent to, and a turn winds up to full speed over a third of a second and winds down again before the nose arrives. Sent on a long flight behind itself, a helicopter sets off backwards at once and brings its nose round as it picks up speed; 30 out, the nose is still about 50 degrees off its course, where it used to have finished the whole turn before it got anywhere. Chinooks and Helixes fly the same way as the Comanche, and a gattling Helix keeps its gun on a tank while it slides past. A replay recorded before this change plays back differently.
- Evacuate on any transport vehicle asks where: a Humvee, a Troop Crawler, a Battle Bus, a Technical, a Chinook, a Helix. Click a spot and it drives there, or flies there and lands, and lets everyone out, so a drop behind a ridge is one order where it used to take a move and a second press of the button. A new order on the way calls it off. Hold Alt as you press the button or V and it empties where it stands, as it always did; bunkers and garrisoned buildings still empty on the spot. Combat Drop takes any patch of ground too: with a unit under the cursor the ropes go down on the ground there, where the click used to be refused.

## The frame rate cap is gone

- The picture now runs uncapped; the rules keep their own steady clock.
- A sound's first play no longer freezes the battle. The whole game stopped while the hard disk found the file: up to 187 ms at the worst moment of a two minute fight with eight computer players here, and seconds with anything else busy on the same drive. Files now load beside the game, and the worst frame of that fight fell to 19 ms on Classic from 68 to 140, and to about 42 on the full Reforged look from 111 to 187. The sound starts a little late instead: over a whole match off a cold disk, more than half within 5 ms, 95 in 100 within 100 ms, a third of a second at the very worst. A shot still waiting after half a second is skipped, because by then it is the wrong shot, while replies jump the queue and always play. The rings under a veteran's aura had the same fault, up to 125 ms the first time each kind lit, and now load with the map. The game also kept only 4 MB of sound in memory, the figure from 2003, so sounds pushed each other out and came back off the disk 3,508 times in those two minutes. It keeps 64 MB now, a whole match fits in 39, and the same fight reads about 35 files.
- On a machine with two graphics chips, the game used to draw on the first one it found, which was the slow one. It now uses the dedicated card, and a match holds about 260 frames a second with the trees, the shadows and the filtering left on.
- Display options has a vertical sync box. Off, the picture still runs free. On, it waits for the monitor so the frame does not tear. The box takes effect when you Accept.
- With vertical sync off, the picture really is free again. Ever since the game started drawing through Direct3D 11, fullscreen and windowed games were still held to the monitor's refresh: 164 frames a second on a 164 Hz screen, and a 60 Hz screen sat at 60 and sank into the fifties in a fight, where the old renderer had given players over 450. The same match now takes 2.3ms a frame, over 400 a second, where it was pinned at 6.1ms. Every picture is the same one it was. Vertical sync on still waits for the monitor.
- Menus and lobbies stop at 60 frames a second instead of running the graphics card flat out.
- Options, Display has a Frame Rate Limit box for the match: Off, 240, 144, 120 or 60. It is Off until you pick one, so a match runs as free as it did.
- Your clicks reach the screen sooner with a Frame Rate Limit or vertical sync on. The game looked at the mouse before it sat out the rest of the frame, so a click made during that wait went unread until the next frame was already drawn and showed up one picture late. That cost a click 15 ms on average at a 60 limit, 5 ms at 144, and 4 ms with vertical sync on a 164 Hz screen. It reads the mouse after the wait now. The frame rate did not move: 164.6 a second with vertical sync on that screen before and after, and the same at the 144 limit.
- A slow moment costs you a dropped frame, not a slow game.
- A long match no longer drags every flash it ever lit behind it. The lights a muzzle flash or a blast puts on the ground were kept after they went out, ready for the next one, and the game looked at every one of them, lit or dark, five times a frame. By minute 24 of a four-way Hard match that was close to a quarter of the game's main loop. Spent lights now wait aside until they are needed again, and the game looks only at the ones that are burning. Only drawing a picture ever put a spent light aside, so a replay's fast forward, which draws one picture a game second, and a network match left minimised, which draws none, still piled them up, and a jump forward in a replay landed on a battlefield lit by the muzzle flashes it had skipped. Every step puts them aside now, drawn or not. The hour-long eight-player match we time the game with, played with no picture, finished in 1,723 seconds instead of 2,072, and its steps slower than 16.7ms went from one in ten to about one in two hundred, on the same checksum.
- Explosions no longer catch the picture. The first time each kind of fire, smoke or blast reached the screen, the game stopped for 25 to 60ms to prepare it, and the opening volley of a fight cost 300ms at once. That work is kept on disk and ships with the game, so it happens while the map loads, in about 3ms, and the worst frame of the same battle went from 141ms to 38ms.
- First use of Modern water, GPU particle floods, multisampling and the new shadow casters no longer stalls for a compile: those programs ship ready-made.
- The price, build time and power figures on the command bar buttons stopped costing you frames. All the buttons shared one piece of text, so every figure on the bar was lettered from scratch every frame, about 33 of them. Each now keeps its own: a battle that averaged 14ms a frame averages 11.7ms, frames slower than 60 a second went from one in six to one in a hundred, and the old renderer gets about 0.8ms back too. The money readout was lettered again every frame as well, for a number that had not changed; it is lettered when the number moves. Over a whole battle the game now letters 163 pieces of text where it lettered 68,227.
- The seconds over a building that is producing, or over a superweapon charging, were lettered from one shared line. Every building in view with a different time left had that line made again, every frame. Each building keeps its own, and it is made again only when the second changes. Twelve buildings counting down together, 1,200 frames: 313 letters, where the shared line wrote 6,181. The frame stayed at 8.6ms.
- A screen full of fire and smoke is cheaper to draw. Thirty Inferno Cannons shelling twenty Crusaders used to send the graphics card 459 separate batches of see-through effects a frame, mostly the same texture again and again, and the game looked up the same seven card settings from scratch for every one of them. Matching effects go out together now, and settings that have not changed are not looked up again: 177 batches, and the same battle went from 11.6ms a frame to 8.6ms. It is at 6.7ms now, since the game stopped preparing everything it draws a second time for a copy of the picture nobody sees. Nothing on screen changes, the effects are drawn in exactly the order they were.
- The same battle with the particle limit turned up costs 7.6ms a frame where it cost 9.1ms, and the old renderer went from 9.3ms to 6.3ms. Both were keeping a count of every kind of draw the game makes, and both did it by writing out and reading back a description of each one, on every draw, for a report no player ever opens. They glance at one draw in sixteen now. The new renderer also stopped re-sending the graphics card settings it had just sent.
- The new renderer stopped redoing work between two pieces of ground that look the same. The map's terrain goes out as hundreds of tiles a frame under the same camera and the same settings, and for every tile the game worked the camera's arithmetic out again, rebuilt its description of the surface and of each texture's filtering, and compared the lot with the tile before. It now notices nothing was changed and goes straight to drawing. The fog of war is sent to the card only where it moved since the last frame, instead of all of it every frame. Two Hard computer players on Twilight Flame at 1920x1080 went from 2.46ms a frame to 2.24ms, and every picture is the one it was.
- The command bar and the observer's panel stopped reading their own pages from scratch every frame. The bar's page alone is 38 KB, and the game copied it, lowercased it and hunted through it for the blanks four times a frame before it wrote in a single number. Each page is read once now, and a frame only fills in the numbers. The same two computer players on Twilight Flame went from 2.03ms a frame to 1.84ms watched as an observer, and from 2.75ms to 2.50ms from a player's seat. Every page still comes out letter for letter as it did: two matches filled 270,000 of them both ways and found no difference.
- Ground painted with a third texture, the dirt over grass and the rock over sand, cost a trip to the memory manager for every corner of every such patch on screen, every frame, only to light that corner. Nearly a tenth of the game's time went to taking and releasing the memory manager's lock for it. Lighting a corner asks for nothing now: the same Twilight Flame match went from 1.88ms a frame to 1.71ms as an observer and from 2.56ms to 2.26ms from a player's seat, and eight views over five maps came out the same as before.
- The command bar stopped throwing its own layout away every frame. The few hundred positions and sizes it hands its page were written into a fresh list each frame, copied twice for the frames in front of the buttons, and thrown out, and every price and build time on a button was looked up by copying the text of every figure the bar was already showing. The list is written over in place now, nothing is copied, and the graphics card settings that did not change between two draws are not looked up again. The same Twilight Flame match from a player's seat went from 2.29ms a frame to 1.96ms, and as an observer from 1.64ms to 1.58ms. The picture is the same one.
- Raise the particle limit as far as you like and every puff gets drawn. Past about sixteen thousand smoke and fire sprites on screen the game quietly stopped drawing the rest: a test with 68,000 of them showed barely a fifth. A test with 101,000 now draws all of them at 8.3ms a frame, and in 1,200 frames not one fell below 60 a second. The first version that drew them all took 22.4ms; the rest came from sorting and copying them far less and from sharing the work across every core of the processor.
- Smoke no longer vanishes mid-air when the particle limit is hit, and a million particles cost about four milliseconds. At the limit the game used to delete the oldest puffs to make room, so a plume simply stopped in the sky. On Direct3D 11 the particles past the limit now go to the graphics card, which works out where each one is every frame from its birth alone and keeps it until it fades. Below the limit nothing changes. Alpine Assault with 3,350 snow systems and about 1.05 million flakes in the air took 108.6 milliseconds a frame on the old path, 224 at the slowest one in a hundred, and 83% of its frames ran over 33. The new path takes 4.42 on average, 9.25 at the slowest one in a hundred, 14.0 at the worst, and not one frame in the run fell under 60 a second. Particles that bounce or must not sink into the hill are held on the terrain by the card as well.
- Only the particles past the limit move to the card; everything under it is drawn exactly as before, with its shadows, its place in the smoke map and its sorting. The old path stays on `-d3d9`, on the Classic graphics setting, in headless runs and on macOS and Linux, and `-gpuparticles 0` turns the new one off.
- Big fights no longer drag the picture down into the twenties. Every moving tank and soldier, and every puff of smoke, goes to the graphics card through one shared scratch area, and it was so small that a big fight on Bombardment Beach filled it about fifty times a frame. Each refill made the processor wait for the card, 8 to 12ms of every frame, while the card sat two thirds idle. The area is made full size once now and refills about seven times a frame, in 0.02ms. The same 16,000-frame battle, fast-forwarded, finishes in 226 seconds where it took between 263 and 325, and the seconds that fell under 50 frames a second went from 125 or more to 4.
- Crowded battles run a good deal faster. At 1080p, thirty Inferno Cannons against twenty Crusaders went from 153 to 227 frames a second, and six Brutal computer players on one map from 146 to 240. The slowest one frame in twenty got 22 to 34% shorter, and the slowest one in a hundred 16 to 29%. The game stopped re-sending lights, materials, textures and card settings that had not changed, stopped relighting the terrain when no light had moved, stopped adding up the glow of every fire particle twice, and widened low-colour textures with a lookup instead of arithmetic on each pixel. The new renderer keeps the old one's settings back until something actually reads them, re-sends only the half of each draw's settings that changed, and remembers each patch of ground's colours, its blend coordinates and its tread marks between frames. Units whose shadow cannot reach the screen are no longer drawn into the shadow map, except on maps with reflecting water. The command bar and the console replay what they drew last frame when nothing under them moved, and the HUD checks for changes without rebuilding its text. The rules side runs 4% quicker too: locking, the lists of nearby units, the sleeping-unit schedule and text strings all got cheaper. The picture matches the old build in all eight test views on both renderers, and a recorded match plays back to the same checksum.
- Huge air raids on custom maps no longer drag the battle. On AOD Super V, 400 Raptors and 250 A-10s diving on a base held by 170 Paladins and 50 Avengers put one picture in sixteen past a 60 Hz refresh; now it is one in fifty, and the average step that works out the battle fell from 7.7 to 6.4 ms. Every pair of planes brushing wings in the sky went through the memory manager and a search of an overcrowded list, and every plane's sight checked each aircraft around it for a roof that could block its view. Both are gone, and the battle plays out to the same checksum, replays included.
- A long match costs less late in the game. Four Hard computer players on Twilight Flame, well into the match, went from 111.6 to 136.2 frames a second, and the step that works out the battle from 5.59ms to 4.78ms. The computer left every group it had made and never filled in a list the game went through on every step until the match ended, and that list is cleared now. A unit looking for something to shoot passes over ground that holds nobody it could shoot at, sight is worked out with fewer lookups, and the smoke and fire are gone through once per step instead of once for every picture. Eight views over five maps came out the same as before.
- Every moving unit's skeleton was worked out three times a picture, once for its shadow, once for the scene and once more for the outline drawn when it stands behind a building. It is worked out once now, and late in the same match the animation costs 60% less. With the rules step finding the next unit due for an update a little faster, minutes 24 to 26 went from 119.8 to 123.7 frames a second, and the match still ends on the same checksum.
- Shadows in a big battle cost about a third of what they did. With some 560 tanks, soldiers and buildings throwing a shadow on Twilight Flame, the sun's shadows took 0.90 ms of every picture and now take 0.36, never more than half a millisecond in any second of the fight. Every copy of the same model now goes to the graphics card in one batch, so the shadows that took 916 separate draws take 121, and the card itself spends half as long on them. The shadows land on the same pixels they did.
- Faster drawing in big battles on the Direct3D 11 renderer: each unit and building draw costs about a quarter less CPU, smoke, fire and tracers go out in about half the draw calls with the translucent pass a third cheaper, and shadows and aura rings laid on the ground take less than half the CPU they did. The picture is identical to the bit.
- Late in big matches each frame does less busywork: the mouse-over check and the visibility sweep look only at what is on screen.
- Late in a match the interface costs less: clocks and readouts reuse their text textures instead of making new ones every frame, leader aura rings and guard shields are worked out once a game frame, and health bars, rank insignia and supply readouts over a crowded screen cost about a quarter less to draw.
- The interface spends less time each frame on the fog of war, leaders' aura rings and guard shields, so big late-game battles draw faster.
- Late in a match the picture caught less often. Every ten seconds each computer player looked over its economy, its spending and the enemy army all in one step, 8 to 10ms of work landing on a single picture. Those three now run a fifth of a second apart. With four Hard computer players on Twilight Flame at minutes 24 and 25, pictures slower than 16.7ms went from 29 a minute to 22, and the slowest one in a hundred from 14.7ms to 14.0ms. Two more hitches got smaller in the same match. The map of where units can drive is rebuilt whenever a building goes up or comes down, and that rebuild went from 9.9ms to 7.4ms, with the ones over 8ms halved (90 to 43). A Hard computer steering its Particle Cannon beam now weighs the ground around it in 0.9ms instead of 2.6ms. Neither changes a single move: the match ends on the same checksum.
- Counting a player's units costs less. The computer's scripts and the build menu keep asking how many of some unit or building a player owns, and every answer went through every unit on every one of that player's teams. Each player now keeps its units grouped by type, so an answer looks only at the types it was asked about. Over an hour of eight Hard computer players on Twilight Flame, the step that works out the battle went from 6.15ms to 6.01ms on average and from 13.75ms to 13.25ms at the slowest one in a hundred, and pictures slower than 16.7ms fell from 1,279 to 1,072. The match ends on the same checksum.
- Every armed unit stopped asking its model to show its loaded missiles. Each one asked on every step of the battle, and only the Tomahawk, the Scud Launcher, the Scorpion and the Scud Storm carry missiles you can see on the model; for the hundreds of others the answer was nothing, and it still had to be queued and read back. Those four keep asking, so their racks still empty and refill as they fire and reload. Over an hour of eight Hard computer players on Twilight Flame the battle step went from 7.15ms to 6.81ms on average, pictures slower than 16.7ms fell from 7,065 to 5,826, and minute 50 ran at 8.6ms a picture instead of 10.7. The match ends on the same checksum.
- Computer players' scripts stopped searching the whole map for units that are not on it. The Stealth General's GPS Scrambler script looks for its own Quad Cannon on every step, and with none left the search still walked the map square by square to be sure; it now first asks whether anyone holds one, and a search that reaches past the edge of the map stops at the last square that is on it. Over 114,000 steps of eight Hard computer players on Twilight Flame the battle step went from 5.63ms to 5.37ms on average and from 14.5ms to 14.0ms at the slowest one in a thousand, and the match took 733 seconds instead of 763. The match ends on the same checksum.
- Late in a match the battle stopped doing a whole second's chores on one step. Once a second every ranked leader went through the army to see who stood in its aura, each unit took its self-repair, every neutral building its repair, and each Hard computer player redrew its map of enemy fire in one go.
