Those lumps reached 2 to 6ms on a step already near its limit. Every unit now has its own step of the second and Hard's fire map fills in piece by piece, so an aura or a threat reading can be up to two seconds old where it was one.
- The game no longer freezes for seconds when your hard drive is busy. It writes a log of the match as it plays, and once a second the battle itself stopped to push that log to disk. On a drive already busy with something else, Windows can hold such a write back for seconds, and the whole game stood still behind it: a 2v2 against the computer froze for 7.8 seconds on a single step. The log is written on the side now and the battle never waits for it. Three matches played while another program kept the drive busy froze for 6.2 seconds in two of them before; with the change, the slowest step in all three took 48ms.
- The game's log no longer grows without limit. Players sent us logs of half a gigabyte up to 19 GB, enough to fill a disk, and the launcher could not open them to report a crash. Most of it was the network code writing a line for every order and every frame, which only a developer's build writes now: a 100-second two-player network match went from 10.9 MB of log to 175 KB, and a skirmish from 600 KB to 166 KB. Past 64 MB the log keeps its first 8 MB, which say how the game started and on what machine, and its most recent lines, so it stays under 64 MB however long you play.
- The replay no longer stops the battle either. Every order given in a match went to the replay file on disk the moment it was recorded, and on a busy hard drive Windows held each of those writes back. Two long matches against the computer, played while another program kept the drive busy, stalled 115 times for over a tenth of a second, the worst for 0.63 seconds. The replay is written on the side now, about once a second. The same two matches never stalled past 35ms and finished 40% sooner. The file itself has not changed: a replay recorded by the old game and the new one from the same match is identical byte for byte, the clock times aside. A game that crashes still saves its replay up to the crash; one killed from Task Manager can lose its last second.
- Every animation runs on a clock instead of counting frames.
- Tanks and trucks move the same at any frame rate. Their treads scrolled a fixed step every picture, so at 120 frames a second they ran four times too fast, and a tank turning on the spot rolled both treads forward as if it were driving. Each tread now covers exactly the ground under it. In a tight turn the two run against each other, and backing up runs them backwards. Wheels spin with the distance driven the same way. The hull's springs used to settle four times too fast as well, and every start or stop threw the chassis to its full tilt in a single picture. Now a tank squats as it pulls away and dips its nose when it brakes, easing in over a tenth of a second and settling within half a second. In a corner it leans out, a Crusader up to two and a half degrees. The Humvee, which never moved on its springs at all, rocks too. A run drawing one picture per game tick and one drawing fourteen put every tank in the same pose, to the last digit, for as long as neither skipped a tick.
- A scroll that starts after the camera has stood still no longer lurches. The first frame of the move was timed from the last time the camera moved, so after a few seconds of looking at one spot it was worth three frames of scrolling at once. The clock runs while the camera is still now, and the first frame moves one frame's worth.
- Briefing and cutscene subtitles hold long enough to read again.
- The radar's under-attack pulse throbs instead of strobing, and no longer ends early.
- The main menu surf rolls at its proper pace, not ten times too fast.
- And it is there at all again. The waves breaking on the main menu's beach had been worked out every frame and then drawn nowhere since v1.0.0, so the shore behind the menu was flat water.
- Less work per picture in a big battle. Infantry and other bending models are shaped on every core at once instead of one, the shadow blobs and markers on the ground go to the graphics card in one batch instead of two uploads each, and a material or light identical to the one already set is no longer sent again. What is drawn does not change.
- A network match costs less to work out. Every step, each machine adds up a checksum of the whole game to compare with the others, and late in a four-player match that took 1.26ms; it takes 0.87ms now and comes out with the same number. With 410 units fighting in a two-player network match, the step went from 4.09ms to 3.99ms on average and from 7.9ms to 7.5ms at the slowest one in a hundred. Units in a big battle also spend about a fifth less time marking the ground they are about to cross. Recorded matches play back to the same checksum, and both machines of a network match end on the same one.

## The computer opponent builds a base now

- One wrong value meant the AI built only urgent items and one power plant.
- Rotated AI bases were laid out wrong; buildings now face the right way.
- An AI with no buildings no longer aims everything at the map corner.
- The AI checks ten seconds of supply-line damage, not a third of one.
- One AI decision read leftover memory, so identical matches played out differently.
- Difficulty and AI money change build pace again; every order was pinned at three seconds.
- Computer bases no longer grow buildings inside buildings. When a spot in its plan was taken and it could find no free ground nearby, the computer put the building down on the taken spot anyway, straight through its own. It now looks outwards from the planned spot over ground its trucks could drive, bridges included, so a new building lands next to the base and not across a cliff or a river from it, and when there is truly no room it waits. It still stacked them on sloping ground, which a player caught. The check for what already stands on a spot is taken at a height, and the computer's search took it at the height of the spot it started from, or at zero, so wherever the ground fell away a building standing there was below the check and did not count. A Hard USA put three pairs of supply drop zones exactly on top of each other in one match. Every building is checked at the ground it will stand on now: over the same four four-player matches, the pairs stacked or half inside each other went from five to none.
- An urgent building it could not put up yet no longer stops the whole base. The computer always builds its most urgent request first, and when that request needed something it did not have, it built nothing else either: a Hard China that asked for a bunker before its barracks stood sat on 35,000 until well into the match. It now skips to the first urgent request it can actually build.
- A computer player no longer stands still with money in the bank. When its most urgent building had no room where it wanted it, it looked for room, found none, and looked again, and nothing else in its base went up in the meantime: one Hard GLA sat on 40,000 for most of a match because its Scud Storm did not fit. A request with no room is now dropped and asked for again somewhere else, and the rest of the base carries on. The check for room also no longer passes a spot on a hillside that the builder then refuses. Over eight Hard matches on Winter Wolf, the longest a base waited went from 18,000 frames to 5,400, and the time spent searching fell by six sevenths.
- Its supply trucks go back to work. When a pile ran dry, the trucks parked next to it for the rest of the match and the computer bought new ones instead: a Hard China kept nine trucks, eight of them idle. Idle trucks are now sent to a supply centre with boxes beside it, and a centre whose pile is gone gets no new trucks.
- Its base defences spread out. Every defence the computer asked for at a supply pile went up against the last one, and a Hard China stood seven or eight Gatling cannons shoulder to shoulder at one pile. It now puts at most two beside each pile.
- New buildings go up on the computer's own side of the hill. It used to try spots on circles round its base, measured in a straight line, so a war factory could land across a valley or on a ledge behind a cliff: close on the map, a long drive round, and the dozer was teleported there. It now walks outwards from the base over ground a truck can drive, and the nearest spot by the road wins. Its guns are aimed at the road in. A base defence used to be scored by how much ground in front of it lay nearer the enemy as the crow flies, which pointed guns at cliff faces the enemy can never climb. It now works out how the enemy actually drives to the base and weighs the ground on that route most, and a spot the base cannot drive to is not used at all. On every difficulty.
- Replays recorded before this change play back differently.
- Hard USA opens the way a player does. It used to start on a barracks and hold its first power plant until a second dozer existed, so its first harvest came in at the 74 second mark. It now puts down the power plant and the supply centre straight away and the barracks after them. Over 20 Hard USA against Hard China matches on Tournament Desert, seats swapped both ways, USA won 15 where it won 10. The same opening was tried on China and lost it 17 matches instead of 10, and on GLA it decided too few matches to say anything, so both keep the opening they shipped with.
- The computer no longer shoots at what it cannot see. Its units, and its base defences, used to auto-target through the fog of war - a hard exemption written into the code for computer players only. Stealth works against it now, and so does anything it has not scouted.
- It scouts. There was no such thing as scouting in the computer opponent - it never needed to look, because it could already see everything. One cheap unit now tours the enemy start positions and keeps going round for the rest of the match, replaced out of spare change when it dies. Every difficulty scouts; an opponent that never looks reads as broken, not as easy. And it tours on purpose rather than in a circle: it goes to whichever base it has gone longest without seeing, nearest first, and it does not walk across the map to look again at something it looked at a minute ago - it stays and watches instead. Two scouts never trail each other round the same lap.
- It takes the oil derricks instead of blowing them up. An oil derrick pays whoever owns it and costs one infantryman to walk in - and the computer used to march past the neutral ones and shell yours, which is the one thing you can do with a derrick that earns nobody anything. It now keeps a cheap infantryman doing the rounds of every derrick, refinery and hospital it has found, takes them, and when there is nothing left to take it leaves him standing on the last one instead of walking him home. And it no longer picks a capturable building as a target of its own accord: it can still be ordered to level one, and one that shoots back is still shot back at. That infantryman never took anything before this, though. A Ranger, a Red Guard or a Rebel can only capture once the barracks has taught him how, and the computer never paid for the lesson, so he walked up to a derrick and stood on it for the whole match. It now buys the training the first time it sends him, and keeps him at home until it is done. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- It steals your tanks. A hijacker costs a few hundred and walks off with whatever it touches, and no computer opponent had ever bought one: not one shipped skirmish plan asks for it. A GLA computer now keeps a thief on call as soon as one of your vehicles comes within walking distance, and sends it at the nearest one rather than the richest, because the Humvee it reaches is worth more than the Overlord it dies halfway to. Black Lotus works the same ground on the same terms: she hacks a vehicle that is already in front of her, and does not cross the map to shut one down for a few seconds.
- Nor does it know which start position you took. It used to read that straight off the lobby, for every player, from the first second. Now it works it out: each position it has not looked at is a suspect, and the odds are simply how many opponents are still unaccounted for over how many places they could be - three of you on an eight-position map is 3 in 7 for each. Every empty position its scout crosses off makes the rest likelier, 3 in 6, then 3 in 5. When the numbers meet, it stops looking: three opponents with three places left to be is not a guess, and walking over to confirm it would waste the trip. On a two-player map that is true from the start, so nothing changed there - it never wastes a second hunting for an address it can work out by subtraction. Where it has not worked you out yet, it attacks the position you are most likely to be on, and finds out on arrival.
- Nor does it read your base off the map. Where your base is, what it is worth, which supply dock to expand to and where to aim a superweapon all came off a walk of your object list, in the shroud, from the first second of the match. The computer now only counts what it can see, plus the buildings it has already found - buildings do not walk away. Before it has scouted you, all it knows is where you started, which is on the map preview anyway.
- A map that scripts its own computer player, the way Art of Defense maps script their GLA waves, gets that player back. All of the above ran on top of the map's script and pulled the waves off their routes: on AOD Super V the GLA sent 13 bunches of wave units off hunting on their own in one Easy match of 30,000 frames, and it could start a base of its own beside them. Now it plays the map's script and nothing else, as it did in the original game, on every difficulty. Official and random maps leave their computer players to the game's own scripts and play exactly as before.
- Everything in this section now plays on the official maps and the random ones only, in skirmish and in LAN and online rooms with computer seats. A map you downloaded or made yourself gets Zero Hour's own computer opponent back, the one its maker built and tested the map against: EA's scripts as they shipped, EA's build pace, EA's choice of enemy and its sight of the whole map, no personality whatever the lobby says. Campaign missions and the Generals' Challenge had most of it already, and now get the rest: their computer units see into the fog again as EA's did, shell oil derricks, and leave salvage crates alone, so a mission plays out differently from the last build (the second GLA mission ends its first 6,500 steps on a different world). Missions record no replays, as in EA's game, so none break. Official and random maps keep every computer player as it was, the civilians included. On a copy of Tournament Desert dropped into the Maps folder, two Hard computers now play 24,000 steps without one of the 20 attack waves and 39 economy moves they make on the shipped Tournament Desert with the same seed, and both replays play back to the same world. A replay recorded on a custom map before this change plays back differently.

## Superweapons that go where the damage is

- The computer picked its superweapon target by adding up what your things cost inside the blast, so a supply stash outranked the tank column parked next to it. Anything that can shoot back is now worth several times its price, and base defences and massed armour are what the shot goes looking for.
- It could only aim inside the rectangle your buildings sit in. An attack wave sitting on its doorstep was never a target at all; now your army counts wherever it is standing.
- Under No Superweapons the Nuclear Missile silo is a shop for China's Uranium Shells, Nuclear Tanks and Neutron Shells and nothing else, for you and for the computer alike. It has no missile at all: no launch button, no countdown on anybody's screen, no announcer, and the doors never open. The computer builds one again, but only when one of those upgrades is worth buying for the tanks it owns, and then buys it; it used to rush the silo up as its superweapon. Four China computers on Twilight Flame asked for theirs at about two and a half minutes and had them standing at four and a half to five and a half; now the Hard ones ask at five and a half to six minutes, the silo stands at eight and a half, and Medium puts its own up around nine and a half for Nuclear Tanks. Every other superweapon stays barred for every side, the Kargu Base too, and the USA Superweapon General keeps exactly one.
- Two silos ready on the same second fired at the same spot, because nothing that was already in the air was on the map yet. A spot that has just been aimed at is worth nothing to the next shot and climbs back over ten minutes, so the salvo spreads across your base instead of digging one crater.
- Measured over a half-hour match: a Particle Cannon that fired at the identical spot three times running now spreads six shots over five parts of the map, and comes back to the first one at the end, when what you rebuilt there is worth twice what it killed.
- The spy satellite goes through the same targeting, and it was scanning one cell of one base seventeen times a match. It sweeps now.
- The computer drives its Particle Cannon's beam the way you do. It used to draw the same short S across the aim point and burn empty ground on either side of it; now the beam walks from one cluster to the next, leaving each the moment what stood there is dead. Fired into five groups of six Scorpions, the old sweep killed 4. Medium now kills 8 and Hard, which drives at double speed, 11. Easy keeps the old sweep. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- Medium and Hard aim their strikes at your economy. A supply center, black market, hacker, drop zone, captured derrick, strategy center or palace counts double its price on Medium and triple on Hard, and never less than 1,000 extra, so a cheap derrick still draws fire. The army used to soak up every nuke because it was the only thing that shot back; losing a supply center is felt for the rest of the match.
- Players on v3.1.0 still watched nukes land on their army. The extra weight on anything that shoots back was the same on every difficulty, so it kept winning. Easy keeps it, Medium counts it at half, and Hard drops it and goes for your base: war factories, barracks, airfields and power plants now count like the economy buildings above, and so does a superweapon, though at the 1,000 floor rather than its price, since a strike seldom brings one down. Hard only turns on your army when it knows none of your buildings. Over twelve four-player Hard matches on Twilight Flame, 14 of 33 superweapon shots fell mostly on buildings before and 23 of 36 after; against Easy opponents, 17 of 30 before and 27 of 29 after. The Particle Cannon's beam is driven by the same weights. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- The computer in Generals' Challenge and in missions aims exactly as it did in 2003: price alone, no threat weight, no army hunting and no memory of where it last fired. The earlier note on this said "as before", but the threat weight and the army hunting had reached those opponents too.

## Generals powers the computer actually meant to buy

- It spent every promotion point the moment it had one, on whatever in its list happened to be cheap enough. The strong three-point ability at the end of the list was never reached, because the points were always already gone.
- From Medium up it saves. If the next thing in its own list is only out of reach on points, it waits for them instead of buying filler.
- Which list it draws from now follows its personality, so the powers coming at you tell you which kind of opponent you are facing.

## The computer comes in where you are thin

- The game has kept a value-and-danger map of every square of the battlefield, per player, since 2003. It has a query interface and even a debug view. Nothing in the computer opponent had ever read it - its only users were two map-script actions almost nobody used.
- At the top level the opponent now aims its attacks at where your money is rather than at the middle of your buildings, which is also the middle of your defences.
- It reads that map through the fog like everything else: only ground it has actually seen counts. An opponent that has not scouted you still attacks the old way.

## The computer expands, and defends what it takes

- It never decided to expand. The machinery was all there - place a supply centre beside a pile, pick a pile worth taking, send a team to sit on it - and every piece of it only ran when a map script said so. An opponent that ran its starting piles dry simply stopped earning.
- It now goes and takes the money that is lying around, out of spare cash so the army never pays for it.
- On Hard the expansion comes with a defence structure facing the enemy, placed in the same job. An undefended expansion is a gift.
- Measured: a third more army in the field and a quarter more money spent over the match.
- With Share Income set to All Income it leaves its allies' piles alone. Every payment is already split across the team, so a computer that put a supply centre beside its ally's pile added nothing and emptied that pile twice as fast. It now expands only to piles nobody on its side is working. Over eight 2v2 matches on Twilight Flame, loads taken from an ally's pile went from 396 to 54 and the team's income stayed where it was. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- It leaves a pile alone when someone else is already working it. The computer only checked for its own supply centre beside a pile, so a pile inside an ally's base, or a third player's, looked free, and it walked a supply centre in next to theirs with a Patriot or a Gatling cannon after it. It now skips any pile with another side's building beside it, friend or foe. Over eight 2v2 matches on Twilight Flame, buildings it put down at a pile someone else held went from 116 to 2, and over eight four-way matches from 8 to 4, with spending where it was. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- It keeps its money-makers and its superweapons at home. A Hard computer with a full base looked for room further and further out until the map ended, and a black market or a Scud Storm could go up alone on ground nobody held. Those buildings, and the tech building a superweapon waits on, now go inside the base or at its edge, and when there is no room they are not built: the money goes into another factory. Expansions are held to the same standard: a supply centre only goes to a pile on its own side of the map and within reach of home, never to one with an enemy standing at it, and the next expansion waits until the last one has a gun or a guard beside it. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- A guarded supply pile no longer stops its expansion. One enemy tank parked beside the nearest pile held a Hard computer's expansion for ten minutes while a free pile sat one valley over; it takes the nearest safe pile now, and the unsafe one only when nothing else is left.
- It captures the derricks behind its own base first. Each capture used to send the engineer on to the derrick nearest where he stood, so the round walked out into the middle of the map and the ones at home waited for minutes.
- A building it cannot finish no longer holds its money and its spot all match. The computer could put a supply center down at a far pile in enemy ground, lose every dozer it sent there on the way, and leave the empty scaffold standing: the money stayed spent, and no later expansion or gun went to that pile because the scaffold was already there. Now it cancels the building and takes its money back, as you would, once two dozers have died on the way with nothing built (three on Easy), or once a site away from its base has gone three minutes without any progress (four on Medium, five on Easy). It leaves that spot and its pile alone for three minutes on Hard, four on Medium and five on Easy before it tries there again.
- It puts down a second base when home runs out of room. The moment a computer's base has no spot left for another Command Center inside its edge, on any difficulty and at any minute, it saves up for one and sends a dozer to put it on the nearest start position nobody started on, then a power plant behind it, a gun in front of it, a supply centre at its pile and a second gun. A base with room to spare stays one base. It used to found a war factory out there on the clock alone, room at home or not. Easy claims one empty start, Medium two, and Hard every one it can reach, nearest first. On a full map it builds no second base. Losing the main base no longer ends it in one stroke.
- It reaches further for supplies. A pile beside one of those bases counts as home ground, and the furthest pile it will take on its own grew from 2,000 to 2,500 on Medium and 4,000 on Hard, still only where no enemy stands.
- It stops building money buildings once it has enough. A Hard GLA put up another black market every ten seconds its bank was past its cushion; it now keeps one of each money building on Easy, two on Medium and three on Hard, and expands only until it has three working supply centres on Easy, four on Medium and six on Hard, counting only those beside a pile that still has boxes.
- China trains hackers on every difficulty, not only on Hard, and ahead of the next army unit. It keeps two working outside an Internet Center on Easy, four on Medium and six on Hard, one for every three fighting units past that, and trains them from a barracks with two units in its queue, where one used to be enough to skip it.
- America builds its Supply Drop Zone. The drop zone waits on the Strategy Center, which the computer only put up for its superweapon or late in its script, so Easy and Medium seldom had one. Now any side with no drop zone or black market puts up the building it waits on, at three minutes on Hard, six on Medium and ten on Easy, and then the money building itself, and puts either back when it is lost.
- Idle dozers walk ahead. When the computer knows the next building it wants and is only waiting for the money, a dozer with nothing to do walks over to the spot, so the building starts when the money comes instead of after the walk. It never takes one off a job, off repairs or off a supply run. Medium and Hard do this; Easy waits as before.
- Replays recorded before these two changes play out differently.

## The computer spends its money

- It no longer sits on a pile of cash. Past a level that depends on the difficulty, the more money it has the faster it builds - twice the pile, half the wait, and it stops at four times. It is spending sooner, not building faster: the rate itself is untouched.
- A full bank buys a bigger army. Late in a match the computer's plan allows one of each attack group, so once they were all on the map it only replaced its losses and banked the rest: a Hard USA sat on 117,000 on Twilight Flame. Now every 8,000 in the bank on Hard allows one more copy of each attack group, up to four of them.
- Hard builds past its plan. A war factory, barracks or airfield gets another copy only once every one of its kind has kept units waiting in its queue for 45 seconds, and a factory that was destroyed is put back. The second barracks used to be an opening buy. The Infantry General's plan holds four, and its scripts asked for the second 38 seconds in, before the first had trained anyone, then sat on an empty bank waiting for the third. Now a second factory waits for the queue on every difficulty, the plan's own copies included, and in a Hard Infantry General match on Twilight Flame the second barracks went up at eleven and a half minutes. Supply drop zones and black markets go up one after another as soon as the bank is past a small cushion, whatever else it is buying; they used to wait until production had nothing to ask for, which on a busy map was never, and over twelve four-player matches the count went from 5 to 95. Internet centers follow that same rule. The spot search used to give up two rings outside the opening base, so a full base simply stopped. It now keeps looking further out until the map ends, for factories and power plants; the income buildings stay at home. Strategy centers, propaganda centers and palaces stop at three, so one of them blowing up leaves the tech tree standing. Extra factories still go beside the newest expansion it holds, nearer the fighting. China trains a hacker from every barracks that has room in its queue, not one barracks at a time: 120 hackers across those matches became 375. A hacker left standing still is put to work. It stops at six, an internet center's four plus a couple, because nothing counted them before: a Hard Tank General trained 67 over twenty thousand frames, about two thirds of everything it spent, and every one of them went through the barracks queue its army was waiting in. A player watching it from the other side of the map said China's tank general builds nothing but infantry, and he was right. Seven now, and the teams at the top of its build list are tanks. The limit grows with the match: one hacker for every four fighting units, never more than its Internet Centers have seats for plus four working outside, and never fewer than four. A computer that has not built an army does not buy an economy instead, and one with a full Internet Center and ninety units behind it keeps eight. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- The computer builds more than one barracks, war factory and airfield again, on every difficulty. Since 3.2.0 it stood one of each all match, even where its own plan had two war factories or four barracks: another one waited for units to queue up behind the one being built, and the computer never queues them that way. Every ten seconds it looks at each kind, and once every one it has was busy on four looks in five over the last 90 seconds on Easy, 75 on Medium and 45 on Hard, another goes up; a new one has to fill a whole stretch like that before the next. A factory counts as busy on a look when it has something in its queue or let a unit out since the last look, so one caught between two units no longer starts the wait again; Easy, whose soldiers come out inside ten seconds, was found idle on most looks and never got a second one. An airfield goes by its parking instead, since a full one takes nothing into its queue: it counts as busy while every airfield has its places taken and a plane is waiting for one. There is no limit on how many: an army that keeps all its factories busy gets more of them. The old cap of three, five and eight production buildings and the bank rule that added them are gone. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- Hard saves up for what it needs most. It used to buy whatever the bank covered the moment it covered it, so the drop zone it needed waited while tank after tank rolled off the line. Every purchase is ranked now: income and power come first for the opening six minutes, the army after that, and when the top one cannot be paid for yet its price is set aside and anything that ranks lower waits until the bank holds more than that price. The saving never turns into a hoard. It lapses after forty seconds, and once the bank is past Hard's cash cushion nothing waits at all. The first drop zone and the first black market also go up in those opening minutes without waiting for the cushion. Over twenty matches with Hard computers on Winter Wolf, 27 computer players had a drop zone or black market standing where 19 had, the first one came at five and a half minutes instead of seven and a half, and 104 of them went up against 46. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- The computer researches upgrades on its own, and spends its bank. Upgrades used to come only from a fixed list in its plan, written before anyone knew what it would build. It now looks at the army it actually has and buys the upgrade that army gets the most out of for the price, and an army that beats what it has seen of yours counts for more. Buildings count for little there, so a GLA no longer opens with Fortified Structure. It also keeps a bank of so many seconds of its income and spends anything past that: an upgrade it would otherwise have waited on, extra units from idle factories, and on Hard another war factory or barracks whenever half a minute goes by without the bank coming down. Hard holds half a minute of income, spends what is over it on extra units at up to three times the rate it earns, builds up to eight factories, one every half minute whenever its bank passes twice what it means to keep, and starts upgrading at three minutes. Medium holds a minute, tops its army up at a tenth of Hard's rate, keeps to the factories its plan lays out and starts upgrading at seven. Easy holds two minutes, tops up at a twentieth of Hard's rate, keeps to its plan's factories too and waits twelve minutes and for a much bigger army before it buys an upgrade. Saving up for the most important purchase, which only Hard did, now runs on every difficulty, each below its own bank. Over six matches of Hard against Medium, on a build one small fix short of this one (Medium and Easy now count the factories their plan has yet to build), Hard ended on 1,600 in the bank on average where it had ended on about 12,000, and won all three that finished. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- Hard picks its road into your base. Of the three approaches it takes the one with the fewest guns it has seen along it, and keeps to the one its plan named until it has scouted something. Aiming at your money instead was tried first and walked it straight past your army.
- Hard sends its attack groups out together. A group too small to be a wave on its own waits on the near side of its base until about seven tanks' worth has gathered, or a minute and a half has passed, and then everything waiting leaves on one road at the pace of its slowest unit. A lone artillery piece or a single bomb truck used to drive across the map by itself, and nearly a third of Hard's units died with barely anyone of their own nearby.
- It reads the odds before it attacks. Every attack was sized the same way whoever it was aimed at, so a computer with an army at home went on waiting for a full wave while the enemy across the map had nothing left to fight with. It now weighs its own army against what it has seen of yours, and an army it cannot see it assumes is growing back towards the size of its own. It has to be looking at your buildings before it believes it is ahead. Ahead by about two to one with your base in view, Hard stops waiting and sends each group as it forms. Ahead by about six to one, the computer on any difficulty sends the guards it used to keep at home for the whole match hunting as well, half a minute apart. Outnumbered two to one, Hard and Medium keep their groups at home until twice the usual wave has gathered, and a handful is never sent into an army that size. Two leaks went with it. Units that reached the end of their road into your base used to stop there and wait for something to shoot at them; they now go looking. A group that got reinforcements at home was ordered out again as a whole, which marched the half already fighting in your base back to the middle of the map to start the walk over. Only the ones at home leave now. Over sixteen Hard against Hard matches on Twilight Flame stopped at seventeen minutes, the five that finished took 12 minutes 26 seconds on average where they had taken 13 minutes 55. The other eleven still ran to the stop: the side that is ahead kills units faster than buildings, and a defender with 120,000 in the bank replaces them at its own door. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- Hard stops piling its army up at home. Its plan only sends an attack group while the signal for the next wave is up, and only a group standing in the base at that moment. A group finished a minute later guarded the base until the signal came round again, and one that fell back from a lost fight guarded it for good: one GLA stood 38 of its Angry Mob by its own buildings with 70,000 in the bank. China's Dragon Tank group never left at all, because the attack order its plan names for it is missing from EA's file. Now any attack group standing idle at home joins the next wave. Rich computers also stopped building extra copies of the groups that only ever guard, four sets of tunnel guards where the plan asked for one. Over eight Hard matches on Twilight Flame, the units standing idle at home late in the match went from 43 to 17, the waves sent went from 134 to 319, and kills went up by a tenth. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- Medium and Easy stop piling their army up at home too. A player watched them gather at the edge of their plateau on Twilight Flame and stay there all match, and the fix above had only been made for Hard: one Medium China stood 57 units there with 109,000 in the bank and never attacked once. Now every difficulty calls up the attack groups standing idle at home, Medium every twenty seconds and Easy every minute, and the loose units standing beside them go along. Over two eight-player matches on each, Medium's idle units per player fell from 3.5 to 0.6 and its biggest pile from 57 to 7, while its attacks went from 17 to 80; Easy's attacks went from 2 to 38. Hard came out where it was, 75 attacks against 78. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- The defenders it trains in a hurry go on to fight. Units a Hard computer bought while its base was being hit belonged to no attack group, so once that fight was over they stood wherever it had left them for the rest of the match. They now leave with the next attack, and any of them stuck out on the map goes hunting. An infantryman sent to take an oil derrick or a tech building could also stop halfway and stand frozen at the door for minutes on end; he finishes the job now. Over sixteen Hard matches on Twilight Flame, the computer's fighting units that had not moved or fired for half a minute went from 5.9 a side to 3.6, and it sent 1,155 attack waves where it had sent 1,079. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- It puts more harvesters on a supply centre with more piles around it, instead of the same three numbers everywhere.
- USA's Chinooks stop collecting over the command center. When the pile beside a supply centre ran out, its Chinooks flew home and hovered, and the computer went on buying new ones for its other centres while those sat idle. It only looked for an idle gatherer when a pile stood right next to the centre, a fraction of how far a Chinook looks. An idle gatherer is now sent to any of its supply centres with a pile inside that gatherer's own range, and nothing new is bought while one stands idle beside a pile that has no room for it.
- It keeps its lights on, and keeps them out of reach. Its plan carries a fixed number of power plants and nothing ever adds one, so a raid that took two of them left the base underpowered - radar dark, base defences off, superweapon clock stopped - until a rebuild timer came round and put the new plant back on the spot the raid already knew the way to. It now buys a plant when the margin gets thin rather than when the meter reads zero, and puts it on the far side of the base from whoever it is fighting.
- Spare cash also buys a gun on the side the trouble comes from. Production and income go up around the middle of the base, the power goes behind it, and base defences go out in front, so money that keeps arriving thickens the base in the order a base wants to be thick in. Front means towards the nearest enemy, which is not the same as the one it has decided to attack - that one can be across the map, and a wall built facing it has its back to the neighbour. The walls grow with the army. One gun every minute and a half, never more than ten, used to be the rule; now the computer may stand one gun for every four fighting units it has, so a big army comes home to a fortress and a beaten one rebuilds its tanks before its bunkers. Letting it buy guns on every pass instead was tried first: 241 guns over twelve four-player matches, and they ate the army, down to 60 kills a match from 73. Tied to the army, 71 guns, and the army is the biggest of any version tried, 78 kills a match. A small army no longer means a bare base, though: one gun for every three fighting units, and however small the army, one more every 30 seconds of the match up to 24, so the twelfth is allowed six minutes in. The computer buys them as soon as its bank clears its saving threshold rather than twice that, and a base three or more guns short of its allowance orders two at a time.
- Each gun goes where it sees the most of the way in. The computer used to aim one spot at the enemy's side of the base and, when that was taken, put the gun down wherever it fitted, which on a crowded map meant behind its own factories with nothing to shoot at. Now it looks at nearly a hundred spots around the base and scores each one by the open ground inside the gun's reach that lies between the base and the enemy. Ground hidden behind its own buildings or a cliff counts for nothing, ground at the back of the base counts for very little, and every gun already standing nearby halves the score, so the guns spread along the front instead of piling up on one corner. It only asks the build rules about the best dozen of those spots, and a spot under a building, on unbuildable ground or within reach of the enemy's own base is crossed off first, so the gun usually goes on the first spot it asks about: 296 of 349 did over 72 matches.
- Its guns come as a mix. It used to put up whichever defence came first on the worker's build bar, every time: a Hard USA base put up 22 Patriots for every Fire Base, a GLA one Stinger Sites, and China's own spare-cash guns were bunkers. Now each new gun is the type the base has fewest of, so Patriots and Fire Bases go up in turn, Stinger Sites alternate with Tunnel Networks, and China's Gattling Cannons get bunkers and Speaker Towers beside them. Those two shoot at nothing on their own, so the computer keeps about one of each for every three cannons. A type lost in a raid is the one rebuilt first. Every general's own versions count, and the planned defences its build scripts ask for follow the same rule. Over 48 one-on-one matches between Hard and Normal computers and 24 between two Hards, the same seeds each time, a Hard USA side built 4.9 guns a match where it built 2.4, 1.6 of them Fire Bases where it built 0.1. China went from 4.0 to 9.9 and GLA from 4.9 to 6.9. Hard won 29 of those 48 matches against Normal, where it won 25. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- Hard builds its superweapon as soon as it can pay for one and has the guns to stand it on, and then another. Its scripts held the first one back behind a clock that ran for twelve and a half minutes, seven and a half if you had built your own tech building first, and then allowed exactly one: a player who took on seven Hard computers at once saw a single nuke all match. There is no clock now. The tech building that unlocks it goes up first, and the superweapon follows once the money is in the bank and twelve of its guns stand finished, a rule only the computer plays by (see the lobby section). More follow as the base grows, one for every twelve guns, so a computer holding twenty-four guns can stand two superweapons. The numbers below were measured when four guns were enough. With twelve, a one-on-one between computers rarely lasts long enough: over 96 Hard sides in the same 72 matches, 11 had a superweapon up with four guns and 7 with twelve, the first at 5.4 minutes and most between 8 and 9. Before that rule it put its first particle cannon up at 4.3 minutes on Twilight Flame and its first nuke at 4.9, without a gun to its name. Over 24 matches between two Hard computers on the same map, the first nuke now goes up at 6.2 minutes as a rule, anywhere from 4.4 to 9.8, and the first Particle Cannon at 7.4. The Scud Storm comes last at 7.6 but never later than 8.7, and every GLA side had one inside ten minutes, where 4 of the 32 China and USA sides were still waiting for theirs. The lobby's superweapon limit and Pro Rules still apply to the computer exactly as they do to you.
- Everything in this section is the skirmish computer's, and Generals Challenge and mission opponents play exactly as EA scripted them again. In 2.8.0 they ran the skirmish computer's whole playbook on top of those scripts. A Challenge general on Hard is handed $30,000 with $5,000 more on the way, so General Kwai bought three nuclear silos about a minute into the match, along with power plants, expansions and factories his mission never asked for, all built faster for the money in his bank, and in a fight he pulled hurt units out and repositioned the rest the way a skirmish opponent does. Now Kwai puts up one silo, and only after you build a superweapon of your own, and his tanks come when his script sends them.
- Hard trains more builders when it has work for them. It only ever made a new dozer after losing all of them, so it played every match on the two it had, and every building it bought queued behind those two. On Twilight Flame a third of the China Tank computers never got round to a war factory, never sent an attack, and ended up sitting in a ring of bunkers on a pile of cash. Now, with money in the bank and every dozer busy, it trains another, up to four. Over six four-player matches on that map, every computer built its war factories, the attack waves went from 39 to 82, and each one spent half as much again.
- Hard no longer rebuilds its factories inside your base. A busy computer puts its next war factory beside its newest expansion, and it remembered that expansion forever: after you destroyed the supply centre there, even one it had built right next to your base, it kept putting the factory back up on the same spot. It now only builds beside an expansion it still holds, and only one nearer its own base than yours.
- Hard keeps its lights on. It asked for a new power plant before running out, and the request then sat in a queue behind everything else its plan wanted: one China waited 95 seconds for a plant with 26,000 in the bank, every builder busy, and went dark halfway. A plant now jumps that queue once the margin is thin, a busy builder is taken off whatever it is doing to put it up, and while the base is dark the computer buys nothing else. Over eight four-player matches the time its bases spent without power fell by a third, from 42 minutes to 28 across all of them.
- Its hackers work from home. A hacker set to work wherever it stood, which was the barracks' rally point, so China's income sat at the front of its base. It now goes into an Internet Center with room, or walks to the quiet side of the base first.
- Its helicopters fight. The computer's plan parks every Comanche and Helix on guard, and there they stayed for the whole match. Now when an attack leaves, every helicopter left on guard goes with it and flies over the army at its pace: 97 of them over eight four-player matches, where none had ever left before. A Helix buys its own upgrades, and infantry waiting for the attack climbs into any helicopter it can shoot out of.
- And its helicopters carry people. On Hard, infantry waiting for the attack now boards any helicopter with a seat, not only one it can shoot out of, and a helicopter carrying riders who cannot shoot from it puts them down just short of the fight, on the first ground none of your guns it knows about can reach, from where they go on at you on foot. The boarding never worked before this either: a helicopter the plan had put on guard stayed in the air, so the riders walked up to it and turned away. The same Black Lotus was sent to one Helix three times in two minutes. A helicopter now lands for its riders. The capturer flies too: when the building it is after is a long walk away and a helicopter is waiting at home, it gets in, and the helicopter puts it down beside the building. China's attacks are mostly tanks, so its Helixes still leave with one rider more often than five.
- Its infantry rides in its vehicles. The computer's plan tells a group with a Humvee to climb in and, in the same breath, to stand guard, and the guard order won before anyone took a step: over two Hard four-player matches not one soldier boarded anything, Humvee, Battle Bus or helicopter. Now soldiers standing at home climb into their own group's Humvee or Battle Bus on every difficulty, and the group goes wherever its plan sends it with them shooting from inside. Soldiers waiting for the next attack fill any Humvee, Battle Bus or helicopter at home they can shoot out of, an Overlord or Emperor carrying its battle bunker included, and that vehicle leaves with the attack. A soldier who could not shoot from a vehicle never rides in one, except in a helicopter on Hard, which puts him down short of the fight as before. China's attacks on Hard carry no infantry at all, so its Helixes flew off with the waves empty, 14 times over those two matches, though both had bought the bunker by the middle of the match. Medium and Hard now train soldiers for any helicopter seat they could shoot from that stands empty, an attack ready to leave waits up to twenty seconds for them to climb in, and an empty bunkered Helix whose soldiers are still on their way stays behind for the next attack rather than fly off unarmed. The Air Force General on Medium and Hard also buys up to two Combat Chinooks, where it only ever bought the supply Chinook before. They stay off the supply runs and fill with Rangers. On Hard they fly with the attacks, all eight shooting from inside; Medium mostly keeps them at home, loaded. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- Its buildings have men in them. The computer built Bunkers and Fire Bases, put up its Palace as GLA, and left every one of them empty for the whole match. Now the soldiers guarding its base and the ones standing idle at home climb into its own buildings they can shoot out of, and on Medium and Hard it trains more for the empty seats once it has money to spare. While its base is being hit, the men at home also take any empty civilian building in the base. The soldiers gathered for an attack are never taken off it for this. A Bunker out at an expansion used to stay empty unless somebody happened to be standing next to it; now men walk out from home to fill it, and Medium and Hard train them for it. Out in the field, a Medium or Hard group standing still with your units close by takes the empty civilian buildings around it. Once none of your units is left near a civilian building, the men inside come out and go back to their jobs, where before they sat there for the rest of the match. On Medium and Hard they also get out of any building, a Bunker included, before it falls on them. In one Medium match on Tournament Desert the same Red Guard went into one garage eight times as GLA raids came and went. Over eight Hard matches on Twilight Flame, 173 soldiers went in, each of them once, 88 of them into a Palace and the rest into Fire Bases and Bunkers, with the matches' economy and number of attacks where they were. A first version bought five Red Guards for China's first Bunker a minute into the match, and the computer's own plan, finding the bank empty, sold the whole base in two of eight matches; it now waits for spare money. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- Its Chinooks fly the army. A USA attack walked the whole road, at the pace of its slowest tank. Medium and Hard now buy plain Chinooks for nothing but lift, more of them the bigger the attack and the longer the road: they load tanks and soldiers at home, put them down on the attack's road short of anything the computer has seen that can shoot, and go home for the next load while the attack is under way. The drop is one a straight flight from the base reaches over quiet ground, after the first version flew seven loaded Chinooks in one match straight at a drop beyond an enemy base and lost every one. A Chinook hit hard on the way puts its load down where it is. Neither these nor the Air Force General's Combat Chinooks go on the supply runs unless nothing else is left to gather and nothing else can be bought, and the Combat Chinook is no longer ever bought as a gatherer.
- Its Helixes have jobs. Every Helix the computer owned bought its upgrades in button order, so each one carried a battle bunker whatever it was up against, with napalm on top. A Helix in one of its attack or guard groups now looks at what it knows of your army first and takes the gattling cannon when most of your strength is on foot, the bunker when most of it is in vehicles, and the soldiers trained to sit in that bunker are Tank Hunters rather than Red Guards. Against GLA over four Hard matches that came out 15 bunkers to 6 cannons, each decided on the split at that moment. China on Medium and Hard also buys two Helixes as healers, a third once its army passes thirty units, each under a Propaganda Tower. They hang behind the attack over whichever of its units is most hurt, carry nobody, and pull away when they are hit or when anti-air they know of comes near; over twelve Hard matches they spent 93% of their time out of the base further from the nearest enemy gun than it could shoot. They used to bunch up over the same tank, which got nothing out of it: a unit inside two towers heals no faster than inside one. Each healer now keeps its spot at least a tower's reach, 150, from the others', going to the most hurt unit nobody else's tower already covers, or stepping sideways behind the attack until it is clear of theirs. Two more Helixes take the napalm bomb, or the Nuke General's nuclear one, and raid your base, a factory first and otherwise whatever pays for it or powers it. A raid comes in from the side your known anti-air does not cover, looks for a new way in when a gun turns up ahead, and turns for home when it is hit below half health. Over the same twelve matches 126 raids went out, 23 dropped their bomb, five buildings fell after a drop, and 31 raiders were shot down on a raid. A raider also stops bombing once its run is over. A Helix told to bomb a spot drops another bomb under itself every ten seconds until it gets a different order, and the computer's own orders never counted as one, so a raider that had bombed your base went on dropping napalm all the way home, over your soldiers on the way, and then on its own base for the rest of the match. Over eight Hard matches against America, 104 of 121 bombs fell nowhere near the building they were meant for. On the same matches now, each of the 14 bombs dropped lands on its building, and a raid that turns back before its drop no longer flies out again to finish it once it is home. The Infantry General's Helix has no tower, so it only raids. Replays recorded before this change play out differently. A healer's every move used to sit on top of the guard or attack order underneath it, so once it reached its spot it went back to guarding wherever that order had left it, and the same held for a raider's legs, a hero stepping back from a lost fight and an artillery piece walking up to shell a gun. In one 9000-frame match between two Hard computers, 87 Helix moves landed that way; with real orders instead, 3 did, all from EA's own code.
- The USA computer fields Ambulances. It never built one before. On Medium and Hard it buys one once eight fighting units stand and a second at twenty, and keeps them a little behind the middle of its army, short of every gun of yours it knows about. A soldier of its own under half health who stands near one walks over and climbs in, and gets out again once he is whole. Toxins, anthrax and radiation on its own side of the map get driven to and washed off. Over six Hard matches against GLA on Twilight Flame it ordered 26 Ambulances, called 10 wounded men in and sent them on 19 cleanups of its own ground. They also die a lot: 24 of the 25 that rolled out were lost, and those six matches went no better for the USA than the same six without them (no win either way, 57 kills a match where it had 66). Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- Its Ambulances keep their heads down. A truck with no gun and 240 health used to park a short way behind the army and keep washing the toxins of the fight it stood in. Now one that takes a hit, or finds itself inside the reach of a gun it knows about, drops whatever it was doing, the cleanup too, and backs off towards home to the first ground none of those guns covers. Under half health it drives to the War Factory to be repaired, and the soldiers inside go on healing on the way. It waits twice as far behind the army as before and only cleans a spill well clear of any known gun. A lost Ambulance is replaced after a minute and a half, not the moment the bank allows. Each soldier inside gets out as soon as he is whole rather than waiting for the slowest one, and a soldier walking to the Ambulance leaves his squad until he is out, so the squad's next order no longer marches him away from the door. Over twenty matches with Hard computers on Winter Wolf, 13 of 23 Ambulances were lost where 23 of 26 had been. The share of wounded men who come back out did not move, 18 of the 94 called in against 22 of 108, and why the rest never get out is not known yet. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- The USA computer stops flooding the field with Ambulances. Each lost one used to be bought again every minute and a half, and two USA computers put eight on the road in one sixteen-minute match. Hard now buys six in a whole match at most and Medium three, and Medium keeps only one at a time and waits three minutes to replace it. An Ambulance under fire backs out of reach before it heads for the War Factory to be repaired: sent straight there, it took the shortest road, often through the guns that had hurt it, and 20 of 31 lost Ambulances died on that drive. It no longer drives ahead of the army to wash a toxin pool, which is where three of the four lost in one Hard match died. The wounded men who never came back out are accounted for too. Of 23 called in over six test matches, 17 died within three seconds of the call, still in the fight that hurt them, and the other six all reached an Ambulance and walked out whole. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- The USA computer stops calling its wounded out of a firefight. A soldier still being shot at stays put, and one who has had two seconds' peace walks over from up to twice as far as before, since the hurt men who live through a fight end up well behind the Ambulance's old reach. In six Hard and six Medium matches between two USA computers on Twilight Flame, 14 were called in and none died within three seconds of the call, where 17 of 23 had; six were healed and walked out whole, three died on the walk four to nine seconds later, and four gave up the walk. Two of those four were the computer's own doing: ten seconds into the walk its fight logic saw a hurt soldier and pulled him back towards home, or sent him back to his squad, or its retreat order took him home with the squad he had left. A soldier walking to an Ambulance now gets no other order until he is inside. The same six matches now lose two on the walk where they lost four; those two stood still at the door of an Ambulance they could not reach and gave up, which is still open. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- The computer's Ambulance only cleans the spills it is sent to. Parked behind the army, it used to notice a toxin pool by itself up to 300 ahead and drive into the fight to wash it, past the line the computer keeps it behind. Over twelve Hard against Medium matches between the USA and GLA on Twilight Flame, 7 of 25 lost Ambulances had died within half a minute of a cleanup they started on their own, 650 to 1,350 from home. With the same matches played again, none started one by itself, and 21 were lost. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- Its Ambulances keep a distance from your guns that fits the map. They used to wait just outside the reach of the guns they knew about and back off only once inside one, so a tank rolling forward a second had them in range before they looked again. Now they back off before that: on a big map up to 200 clear on Hard and 160 on Medium, on a small one less, since there the computer's own base can stand that close to your guns. They only ever back off to ground clearer than where they stand; with none to go to they hold still instead of driving back and forth between the army and home. After a hit they stay back 8 seconds on Hard and 6 on Medium, not 4. Not measured yet. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- It comes at you from two sides. An attack big enough to be two sends a third of its strength down the second-quietest road, so you cannot meet the whole thing in one place.
- It holds ground between attacks. Hard gathers its next wave a third of the way along the road to you, not in front of its own base, as long as nothing it has seen can shoot at that spot; otherwise it gathers at home.
- It builds its economy before it comes for you. No attack leaves a computer base in the opening minutes: six on Easy, five on Medium, four on Hard, and on Medium and Hard not before its first supply drop zone or black market stands, when it can build one. Medium and Easy now put that drop zone or black market up in the opening too, where only Hard did before. And it stops sending you two tanks at a time. A group too small to matter waits at home until enough has gathered to be an attack, about two tanks' worth on Easy, two and a half on Medium and five on Hard, even when the computer thinks it is winning. In one Hard against Hard match on Twilight Flame, the USA side's first attack left at six minutes instead of three and a quarter, after its drop zone, and the two sides sent 24 attacks instead of 47, 12 of them one to four units where 43 had been. Medium sent 9 instead of 19. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- Medium spends what it earns. On a map with plenty of supplies its five supply centres bring in 300 a second by the middle of a match, and its plan's three factories spent a sliver of that: six Medium China games against Easy on Twilight Flame ended with 125,000 to 230,000 unspent, and Medium won one of the six inside 25 minutes. Medium now puts a quarter of its spare income into extra units, adds factories up to five once its bank passes three times what it means to keep, and sends a smaller group out on its own. The same six games went to Medium, all six.
- Its artillery stays behind its tanks. Tomahawks, SCUD Launchers, Nuke and Inferno Cannons and Rocket Buggies walked in the same crowd as the rest of an attack, and the one that came round the corner first died to the first tank it met before its long gun was any use. Each one now keeps a little behind the attack's leading unit, farther on Hard than on Easy, and still fires at whatever comes into reach on the way. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- A rich start gets spent. On 50,000 starting money the computer sat on the pile through the opening, because what it spends is a share of what it earns and in the first minutes it earns nothing. What the start handed out over the default now goes out at the difficulty's pace from the first pass, factories included. At the default money nothing changes.

## The computer picks its fights
- Which enemy it goes after was the nearest one and nothing else, plus a rule with its sign the wrong way round: an opponent who had lost his units or his production had his distance treated as half the map, so the computer ignored the one it was about to beat. That is what dragged matches out.
- It now weighs distance, whether the target is crippled - an opportunity, not a distraction - and how much of what it can see that player is worth. Only a genuinely finished enemy is skipped.
- It still refuses to gang up with another computer opponent on one victim, and still gently prefers whoever is already shooting at it.
- An aggressive computer team is supposed to fight its way to where it is sent rather than walk there. It never did. The order to fight was being reissued every frame, and each reissue pushed the moment that unit next looks for a target one step further into the future, so the look never came at all and the team crossed the map through the enemy without firing. Over four and a half minutes of one test match that order was restarted 2,240 times. It is restarted 15 times now.
- And when that switch does happen, the old order stops there. It used to finish its own turn afterwards, steering one last time toward the place the unit was going before the order changed, which is a visible flinch at the head of a column.
- It no longer chases what it cannot see. A stealthed Colonel Burton nobody had detected still counted as seen to the computer, so walking him into its base drew the whole guard after him while not one of their guns was allowed to fire at him. A hidden unit is now hidden from the computer the way it is from you, until a detector or a shot of his own gives him away, and a GLA bomb truck dressed as one of the computer's own units fools it as well. In four staged runs a Burton pacing inside a USA base had the guard sent at him about 70 seconds in every time; now nothing goes for him until the base's first Patriot Battery, which can see him, is up.
- Hard stops feeding you units. Before a group leaves, or a lone reinforcement sets off to join one out on the map, it weighs what it is sending against everything of yours it has seen in the last three minutes, unit type against unit type, and holds back what would only die. A reinforcement waits at home for the next wave instead of crossing the map alone. When you mass one unit it trains the answer between attacks too, Comanches and Helixes included, and stops buying what your biggest group beats. Against waves of Overlords rolling at its base, the share of its groups sent into a fight their units lose fell from 48% to 40%, and units dying alone from 17% to 14% of its losses. Against itself it changed nothing measurable: in 48 matches where only one side had it, that side won 5 and the other 4. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- It stops feeding its idle units to your towers. On a small map your base, or a Patriot at your expansion, stands close enough to its own to count as an attack on it, and it answered by sending whatever stood idle at home at the tower, one or two at a time: one Hard GLA walked eight Quad Cannons and Scorpions into the same Fire Base and Patriot, one after the other. A tower that stays outside its base is now gone after only with a force that outweighs it, double on Hard, half again on Medium, level on Easy, and anything that drives in is still met wherever it stands. In 32 Hard against Medium matches, USA and GLA in both seats, what both sides lost to defences fell from 171,800 to 91,700, everything they lost fell from 1,114,000 to 965,000, and Hard still won 14. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- It stops walking its army into towers and garrisons it has already seen. On Medium and Hard, a group that knows a defence stands in its way waits outside its reach until it is strong enough to take it, and shells it from outside with its longer-range units. It also buys units that beat what it has seen standing there. Before, wave after wave went into the same Gatling cannons. Hard Air Force General against China lost a third fewer units to defences: 1,447 down to 909 over 16 matches. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.

## The computer answers when it is shot

- Computer units used to stand and take it. A group idling in reach of your Tomahawks never looked up, and a tank shooting a power plant went on shooting it with a Gattling Cannon firing into its side. Nothing in the opponent asked who was hitting it. Six Battlemasters shelled by two Tomahawks from past their sight lost three tanks and left both guns standing. On Hard they now have both guns dead nine seconds after the first hit, for one tank; on Medium eleven seconds, for two; on Easy twenty-six seconds, still for three.
- A unit that is hit shoots the gun if it can reach it. If not, and what stands near it is worth more than what covers the gun, they drive over and kill it, whether the computer can see that gun or only its shells. Otherwise it walks to the nearest ground it knows nothing can shoot, holds there and does not walk straight back. Two Battlemasters under four Fire Bases died inside 11 seconds. On Medium and Hard both are now out from under them in five and still alive two minutes later; on Easy one gets out, with 25 health.
- Six Battlemasters taking down power plants beside a Gattling Cannon lost two tanks on every difficulty. Medium now loses none, Easy and Hard one, and all three kill the cannon, which Hard used to leave standing.
- A tunnel or a barracks put up quietly at the edge of a computer's base used to stand there until it fired on something. Nothing had hit the computer yet, so as far as it knew nothing was wrong: on Easy your tunnel outlasted a five minute test and a Patriot battery lived 300 seconds. It now goes after any enemy building or ground unit it has seen inside its base, workers too, and a building raised in the fog counts from the moment it is spotted. With no shot fired, Easy has that tunnel dead in about 100 seconds and the Patriot battery in 70. Hard clears the tunnel in about 120, where it took 160 to 270, and Medium kills a barracks in 40, where it took 100 to 140.
- Hard checks for this every 2 seconds, Medium every 6, Easy every 16, and each sends the nearest idle units it has at home. If those are too few, Easy trains up to what the intruder is worth, Medium half as much again and Hard twice. A computer that cannot see the building does nothing, so a tunnel it never looked at can still stand.
- A computer's helicopters used to hover under your superweapon until it landed. Six Comanches parked in the blast all died to a nuke on Easy and Hard, and Medium kept two. They now leave when they hear the launch warning you hear yourself, spreading out as they go: Hard in a third of a second, Medium in a second and a half, Easy in over three. Hard keeps all six against a nuke, a Scud Storm and a Particle Cannon, Medium loses at most one, Easy loses one to the beam. Easy's Helixes are slower and come out of a nuke alive with next to no health left. The warning never says where the strike is going, so the helicopters fly off from any launch, and those far from it lose a few seconds of the fight.
- Hard looks every third of a second and a tank that is hit takes everything within 300 with it. Medium looks once a second and takes everything within 150. Easy looks every three seconds and answers alone, so it is often too late: past two Tomahawks on the road it answered once in a minute and lost two tanks, the same two as before. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.

## The computer knows when to quit

- Its teams fought to the last man. The word "retreat" appeared nowhere in the opponent's code - the single most visible thing that made it look stupid.
- It now measures the fight, not the health bar: how long its force lasts against how long it needs to finish yours. A unit at a fifth of its health that still out-damages what is shooting it stays; a full-health one being melted leaves. A health percentage gets both of those backwards.
- Two levels of it. On Medium a unit that is personally finished pulls out of a fight its team is still winning. On Hard the whole team breaks off when the exchange is lost. Easy never quits - that is part of what makes it easy.
- It only counts what it can see. An opponent that flinches from something it has not found is reading your unit list again.
- It weighs a fight by what is in it, not by who is nearby: only things that can shoot count, and buildings do not. Its own base is not a reason to feel safe and yours is not a reason to run.
- Its aircraft are left out of it. A retreat order was what took a parked jet off the runway, so while a fight raged near the airfield the whole wing took off, flew at the base, landed, and did it again every few seconds instead of ever reaching you. Aircraft already fly home on their own when the load is spent.
- Matches finish. Two of these opponents used to fail to settle 65% of their games inside sixteen minutes; it is half that now, and they end in under seven minutes on average instead of ten.
- The retreat actually happens now, on Normal as well as Hard. The order home was handed to units that were already fighting, and the game laid it over their attack instead of replacing it, so a team told to break off carried on driving at what it was shooting, and its aggressive mood turned any walk that did start into a fight on the way. A unit that makes it home gets its mood back when it stops walking.
- A beaten team stops running once it is out of range. It used to break off a fight at your front door and walk the whole map back to its base at full health, where nothing repaired it, then stand there until a script or the next wave remembered it. Now it falls back just past the reach of the guns it was losing to, waits, and goes straight back in as soon as that fight turns: your units leave or die, or enough of its own arrive. If the fight still looks lost half a minute later, it goes home and joins the next wave. A team only walks home first when your guns cover the whole road. In 32 Hard against Hard matches on Twilight Flame, 2,748 of 2,756 retreats stopped short of home, and the side doing it lost 92 units a match where it had lost 96, for the same number of kills; that difference is inside the noise of 32 matches. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- It looks after its veterans. A heroic tank cost the computer no more thought than one off the line, and it fought to the last chevron. Now a unit with a rank pulls out on its own health, whatever its team does: under 35% for a veteran, 45% for an elite, 55% for a heroic. It also leaves a fight its team is losing before the team gives up, the higher the rank the sooner, though never one it is even in. It goes to whatever of its side's buildings can mend it, a tank to its repair point or a soldier to his barracks, and home when there is none. The computer also counts a ranked unit for a quarter more per chevron when it weighs one army against another, yours included, since your chevrons are on show. Over eight Hard matches on Twilight Flame it pulled out 422 ranked units, 28 of them heroic, and 358 of those went to a building that mends them. Both sides lost 1,979 units where the same matches had cost them 2,080, and 3% less in value, with the same economy. Replays recorded before this change play out differently. A unit sent off to be mended now leaves its squad on the way, so the squad's next order no longer drags it back into the fight half-repaired; it joins a new squad once it is fixed or home. Before, a Black Lotus at 67% health was sent to her barracks four times in a row and never arrived, and one unit was pulled out twelve times in a match. Over the same two 2v2 Hard matches on Twilight Flame the most any unit was pulled out fell from 12 and 8 to 5 and 2, and the ones still pulled out twice came back mended in between. It still sent some again every thirty seconds from wherever they stood: a GLA Angry Mob member that its mob kept marching off was ordered to the barracks eight times, and a Scorpion on its way to the Arms Dealer was turned back into the fight at a third of its health, because the computer's fight logic saw a hurt tank standing still in the queue and sent it back to its squad. A unit sent off to be mended now gets no other order until it is fixed or home. Over six Hard against Medium matches between GLA and the USA on Twilight Flame, the thirty-second repeats went from 13 to none, every unit pulled out twice had come back at full health in between, and 78 of the 89 that came back did so at full health. It also stops pulling out a unit that is not hurt because its squad is losing: Colonel Burton was walked off at full health. A losing fight now pulls a ranked unit only once it is below 90%; in the same matches, 25 pulled at 90% or more became none.
- It no longer runs from a fight in its own base. Home was where the retreat went, so when you rushed a Normal or Hard computer early, every defender was outnumbered, read the fight as lost, and was ordered back to the middle of the base it was already standing in, walking and not shooting, again every second and a half. Sixteen rebels and four Scorpions sent into a Hard USA base a minute in went a full minute without losing one. A fight at home is now fought where it is. While the base is being hit the computer also keeps its attack groups at home: nothing it has gathered leaves on a wave, nothing waiting to leave gathers out on the road, and the groups guarding the base are no longer called away to join an attack. What was gathered goes once none of your units it knows of stands in its base, or half a minute after the last hit. And it spends on the fight. A minute in, its opening has gone on buildings: a Hard USA had two soldiers and 8,000 in the bank when that rush arrived. Now a base under attack trains fighters from every factory that has room, each one picked against whatever of yours it has the least answer to yet, so sixteen rebels and four Scorpions get Rangers as well as Missile Defenders. It stops buying income buildings and extra factories until the fight is over, puts a gun up between the middle of its base and your units when it finds the room, and sends what it has at home at you once there is enough of it to matter; a handful sent out by twos only feeds you. Over four matches the USA left 36 of those 64 rebels alive where it had left 49. China and GLA already train at the pace their barracks allow, and came out about where they were. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- It also knows when the match is over. A computer player that had lost used to make you hunt down its last harvester in a corner of the map. Now it types "GG" in the chat, under its own name and in its own colour, and two seconds later surrenders the way you would from the menu: anything it still has goes to a living ally, or is destroyed when it has none. It gives up when it has nothing left that builds and nothing that could put a builder back up, while behind, or when everything it owns plus its bank is worth a small fraction of the strongest enemy's: under 20% on Easy, 12% on Medium and 8% on Hard. That has to hold for 30 seconds on Easy, 45 on Medium and a full minute on Hard, so a lost fight or a base being rebuilt does not count, and it never quits before minute 6, 8 or 10 respectively.
