Only skirmish and multiplayer computer players do this; a mission's or a generals' challenge opponent fights on as its map tells it to. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.

## Hard fights each unit from where it is strongest

- Hard keeps a map of what it knows can shoot where. Every gun it has seen, including the bunkers it spotted once, is marked on the ground it reaches, and a gun on a ridge reaches further, the way it does in the game. Its own and its allies' firepower goes on the same map. It picks its road into your base by how much of that road your guns cover, not by how many of them stand near its waypoints. That old count also took in the computer's own tanks as if they were yours.
- It kites. Infantry and anything with a turret step back out of the reach of a slower gun they outrange, from the far edge of their own range, and go on shooting the thing that was closing on them. A base defense it outranges gets the same treatment, so it is shelled from outside its reach instead of driven up to. It does not run from a rifleman its tank could drive over. Cars with fixed rocket racks do not kite, because the turn back to aim cost them more than the step saved.
- It keeps the high ground when the high ground matters. A unit being hit by what it is shooting looks for a rise nearby from where its longer reach lets it keep firing while the other gun no longer reaches it, with a straight road up and no more of your guns covering it.
- Hurt units leave ground they cannot win. One below about a third of its health, standing where your guns outweigh its side's, walks to the first cell on the way home that nothing of yours covers, and rejoins its team when the fight is over.
- A unit walking to a far target stops to shoot what is already in its reach. Four Rocket Buggies sent at the last of four tanks used to drive past the other three with their rockets loaded.
- Over 128 matches on Twilight Flame, one Hard against the same Hard without any of this, the side with it lost 18,048 units where the other lost 18,774, and killed 17,684 where the other killed 16,892. That is a small, steady edge rather than a new opponent. Over 128 matches on small generated maps the two came out even. Two more ideas were tried and taken out again: gathering waves on the nearest high ground, and holding a wave back until it matched the guns on its road. Neither beat not doing it.

## The computer builds against what you field

- Which unit it trained next was a coin flip. It gathered the teams sharing the highest priority number in its data and picked one at random - not one line looked at what it was fighting. An opponent facing nothing but aircraft went on building tanks.
- Now the priority is the start of a score, not the whole of it. What it can *see* you fielding weights the choice, and the weighing is the game's own arithmetic: for every unit it could build and every unit it sees you with, how many shots each needs to kill the other through its armour, how long it waits between them, and what each one costs. A Crusader shell does a tenth of its damage to a rifleman, so your Rebels get Gattlings and your Overlords get Tank Hunters, not whatever the script listed first. Stealth still pushes detectors up.
- How much that weighs depends on the level: nothing on Easy, which is what the game always did, about half on Normal, and the full weight on Hard.
- Anti-air was the computer's oldest hole. It is closed.
- The skirmish no longer catches a hitch the first time the computer picks a team. It works out every unit-against-unit matchup on the loading screen now, in about a millisecond.

## Three difficulty levels, and one open advantage

- Easy, Medium, Hard, the three the game has always had. There were six for a while, with a rung either side of Medium and one above the top; they are gone again, and nothing above the top went with them - Hard now plays what the top of that six-rung ladder played. For a while the top rung was called Brutal on the seat list; it is Hard again, the name the box always printed.
- Every computer player earns half as much again as its trucks, derricks and other income would pay you, on all three levels, and up to triple while it falls behind, and that is the only rule bent for it. No level gets cheaper units, faster building, longer vision or tougher units. What changes between levels is what the computer is allowed to decide: how often it looks at the map, how long it takes to react, whether it counters what you field, whether it masses before attacking, whether it pulls damaged units out.
- Hard used to break that promise without saying so. EA's skirmish scripts handed a Hard computer four free cash drops as the match went on, 10,000 early (5,000 for the GLA), another 10,000, then 15,000 and 20,000 late: up to 55,000 a game that no truck ever hauled. Every general had them. They are switched off, so Hard's bank is what its trucks and oil derricks bring in, doubled like every computer's. The other grants in those scripts, the ones that pay for its first buildings, are untouched.
- A computer that is losing keeps its base. EA's scripts had every general sell off every building it owned the moment its bank fell under 2,000 with no truck, supply building or oil derrick left, or once its last dozer, command centre and factory were gone. Ten seconds later the whole base turned into cash and the match ended on an empty field instead of a fight. That is switched off for all twelve generals at every level, so you finish a beaten opponent by knocking its buildings down.
- Easy looks around and answers late, a little sooner than it used to, and it sends its supply trucks to fit the piles. It never pulls a unit out, never builds against what you field, and stops once the opening base is up. Normal reacts a bit sooner, starts spending once the bank passes 6,000, where it used to wait for 10,000, and answers about half of what you field. A unit that is personally finished still leaves, and it still goes out for a second supply pile. Factories past the opening list stay a Hard behaviour. Hard is the opponent with nothing held back: no reaction delay at all, it builds against what it can see you fielding, it gathers an army before it commits it, and it takes a losing team off the field. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- Measured, not asserted: with both earning double, Hard against Easy over 32 matches on generated maps ends 17 wins for Hard, 5 for Easy and 10 undecided.
- The ladder reads as one ladder wherever a seat is listed. Half of it was named in EA's old words - "Easy Army", "Medium Army" - and half in ours, in the same drop-down, because four separate lists answered "what is this seat called" and no two of them agreed. Every one of them says Easy AI, Medium AI, Hard AI now: the lobby, the seat itself, the game info panel and the online browser.
- All three are in the network and online lobbies as well as skirmish, and the level the host picks is the level every machine at the table plays. A seat also keeps its name, its colour and its start position when the list refreshes, which it did not.
- Making Easy easier means giving it worse decisions, never less money. That is the whole promise.
- The computer also picks a personality each match and keeps it: one plays for the attack, the other for the base. Same resources, spent differently.

## Attack-move actually attacks

- Ctrl on the click advances the group at the slowest unit's pace.
- A plain click lets each unit run at its own speed.
- A unit on attack move looks half as far again as it can shoot, and nothing to do with how far it can see. The two have nothing to do with each other: artillery outranges its own eyes and found nothing this way, while a scout with a long view stopped for things it would spend a minute driving to. One rule, measured against the gun.
- An aircraft only makes that long look forward. It cannot stop and it turns in a wide circle, so a target off to one side or behind is one it has to come all the way round for - which is how a flight of bombers ends up orbiting a corner of the map instead of arriving. Inside sixty degrees of the nose it looks the full distance; outside it, no further than it can already shoot, so it still takes what it is passing.
- Attack-moving through a base shoots the base; buildings were filtered out.
- A new unit heading for its rally point attack-moves there, so it fights what it meets on the way. A dozer, a GLA worker, a supply truck or an empty ambulance has nothing to fight with, and it now just drives there instead of wearing the attack-move order and its colour the whole trip.
- Aircraft make their pass, fly home, rearm and resume your order.
- Nothing walks off the map chasing a target that keeps retreating.
- Being pulled off a chase no longer blinds a unit on the way back. It owes the order a stretch of ground before it is allowed to drive to another fight, and it used to spend that stretch refusing to see anything at all - so a tank rolled past an enemy parked beside it without firing a shot. It still will not go chasing during that stretch. It will shoot whatever is already in front of its gun, which costs the advance nothing.
- A unit turns onto whatever is actually shooting it, then resumes the advance.
- Otherwise it picks the worst thing in range: anything armed before anything that is not, then the more dangerous of the two, and worth fades with distance so it is never the far one it walks the field for. A group ordered through a base no longer stops for the first dozer it passes while the artillery beside it keeps firing.
- Ctrl on the attack-move click no longer shells the ground instead.
- A big selection arrives as a crowd. Two hundred units told to attack-move used to spread along a line and three hundred told to move mostly stood still: the group tried to hold its shape all the way in. Past forty units everyone now heads for the spot you clicked and takes the nearest free ground to it. That ground is handed out from the spot outward, ring by ring, and the edge of a cliff ends it: click on the lip of a ridge and the group fills the top, where it used to send half its tanks down to the foot and back round by the ramp to stand there. Whoever gets there first takes the middle and the slow ones take the edge, and the pile grows back toward the way the group came, so the last tank onto a bridge stops behind the others instead of driving through all of them to the far end. Below forty the group keeps its spacing on the way in, because that is what stops a dozen tanks arriving in single file. A waypoint queued with alt is the exception and now keeps every unit's own spot: only the last point of a queued route gets moved to free ground, so sending a dozen tanks through the same intermediate cell left eleven of them unable to reach it, and the group walked to the first waypoint and stopped there.
- Troop Crawlers wait for their squad to climb back in, up to ten seconds.
- One man who cannot get back aboard no longer parks the Crawler for the rest of the attack move.
- Their squad stays out until the area is clear, instead of piling back in after every kill.
- "Clear" now means as far as the men can shoot, so they finish the enemies in front of them.
- Every man aboard gets out to fight; nobody sits out the battle waiting to be patched up.
- A Crawler that has lost its whole squad carries on with your order instead of idling.
- Attack-move state is saved now, instead of coming back as random memory.

## Selecting and ordering with the mouse

- The key that took every armed thing you own takes infantry only now, and the Hotkeys page calls it Select all infantry.
- A box drawn with Ctrl held takes those units back out of your selection instead of replacing it, so a group is trimmed by dragging over the corner of it rather than picked again from scratch. Held with Alt the box keeps only what can shoot: drag across your base and you get the tanks, not the dozers and supply trucks standing among them. Both are drag-only, and a single click still means exactly what it always did. Hold Ctrl and Shift and drag and you draw a freehand attack line, red like the circle, and on release the enemies near it are shared out as targets. Ctrl alone still draws the fire circle. Shift alone and a drag draws the move line V draws, as long as something you have selected can walk it; with nothing like that selected, Shift and a drag is still the box that adds to your selection, and a Shift click still adds one unit. Pressing Shift used to let go of the Ctrl hold, so the pointer turned back into the ordinary one and the drag grew a selection box instead.
- A box dragged over your army and your economy together takes the army. The dozers, workers, supply trucks and hackers standing among the tanks stay where they are, and ambulances and troop carriers go with the soldiers they look after. A box with nobody military in it takes the workers the way it always did.
- The three buttons are split cleanly now. Left selects, and only selects. A right click gives the order, and a right drag scrolls the map the way it did in 2003: the spot you pressed on stays put, and the further you pull away from it the faster the map runs. The drag only starts once the pointer has really travelled, so a click your hand wobbles a pixel or two is still an order and the camera does not twitch. A pan never throws away the building on your cursor or the power you were about to aim. The middle button turns the view, with no key held, and a middle click without a drag puts the camera back where it started. The wheel zooms toward whatever the cursor is over and the screen edges still scroll. The classic scheme, where left both selected and commanded and right scrolled and deselected, is gone rather than switched off, and the two checkboxes that used to choose between them are out of the options screen.
- How far the pointer travels before a click becomes a drag is yours to set. Drag Threshold on Options > Controls runs from 2 to 50 pixels, and the game's own value was 25. Raise it if selection boxes start by accident, lower it if your drags are read as clicks.
- An isometric camera, on Options > Controls. It looks at the battlefield from far off through a narrow lens, so a tank at the top of the screen is drawn the same size as one at the bottom and a base reads like a city-builder's plan instead of shrinking into the distance. It buys no extra sight. The normal camera's corners, edges and centre are laid over the isometric screen as closely as a flat picture allows, hills and ultrawide screens included: the normal camera still sees a little more at the far corners and the isometric one the same amount more at the near corners, because a perspective view is wider at the back than at the front and an isometric one is not. Pan across a ridge and the picture holds its size and its angle; it does not rise and dip with the ground under it. Campaign cinematics are filmed with the normal camera whatever the box says, and the isometric view comes back when the black bars go. They are shot from ten feet off the ground looking up at a rocket leaving its pad or a skyline, and the isometric camera turned each of those shots into a view from above of somewhere else: the picture lurched sideways every time the shot tilted, and a low shot ran off the edge of the map into a white screen. With the box ticked, USA 1's opening now plays the way it does without it. You still turn and zoom it the way you always did, and the box takes effect the moment you tick it, mid-match included.
- Press V, or the move button, then drag the left button, or just hold Shift and drag, and you draw a line: the selection spreads itself evenly along it, in the order the units already stand, so a column arrives as a firing line instead of a queue. While you drag, it is drawn as a smooth curve through the points the order carries; it used to be a jagged chain of short straight pieces. It is the line you actually drew, curves and all, however far you keep drawing it: a long sweep used to give up partway through and finish as one straight run to the cursor, and now it holds its shape to the end. Letting go over the sidebar finishes the order rather than leaving the line stuck to the cursor. A line pulled up past the horizon into the sky ends where the ground does: the stretch over the sky used to land in one corner of the map, and the units whose stations fell on it walked off there. A soldier riding in a transport or sitting in a bunker gets no station on a move or attack-move line, as a plain click has always left him where he is, so the units that can walk share the whole line instead of leaving gaps where the riders were counted. Draw the line with the left button while attack move is armed and the whole line is an attack move: artillery spread across a front, each gun firing on what walks into it, instead of one clump on one spot. Guard draws the same way. Every line, and the attack circle, is drawn with the button a click on the ground moves your units with. In the default mouse that is the left, and the right button's drag stays the camera. Under the Alternate Mouse Setup it is the right: a right drag with a key armed, Shift or Ctrl held draws the line or the circle, a plain right drag still scrolls the map, and the left drag is the selection box whatever is held. Without an order armed a left drag in the default mouse is the selection box it always was. Armed with attack instead, every unit fires on its own station along the line, which is a barrage laid across a ridge in one drag. `FormationDrag = no` in Options.ini turns the line off if you would rather an armed drag did nothing.
- Selected units draw a line to wherever they are going, and it looks like a building's rally point: EA's blue rally line, with the rally flag in your colour planted on the ground they are headed for. A selected factory shows that one flag at the rally you set; a second disc used to sit at the door as well, so the path around the building read as two destinations. Every order draws one: move, attack move, attack, force fire, ground fire, enter, dock, repair, heal, capture, hack, guard, a waypoint path. An order aimed at something rather than somewhere, a tank to kill, a building to shoot, take or climb into, a unit to guard, ends on the line's joint instead of a flag, a small disc sitting just over the target and riding along with it while it drives, so a flag never stands on a tank. A shift list runs one line through all its stops, a joint on each and the flag on the last bit of ground. With order lines on, that last point gets a joint under its flag as well, so the end of the line reads the same as every stop before it. Units standing together and headed the same way share one thread, from the middle of the knot to the middle of where they are going, so twenty tanks sent across the map draw one line instead of twenty laid on top of each other; a selection spread over the map draws one per knot, and a flank sent on its own still shows. An angry mob draws one thread for the whole mob, not one per rioter. An attack move and a shot at the ground both point at the spot you clicked: the attack move's thread used to wander off to whichever free ground each unit was steering for, and ground fire pointed at the middle of the nearest map cell. An attack move stays pink from start to finish, too. A unit that stopped to fight used to swing its thread onto the enemy it was fighting, and only swung it back to your destination once the enemy was dead. It is not a flash at the moment of the order: the line is asked of the unit every frame, so it lasts until the unit gets there, changes its mind or leaves your selection, and it shows on the formation line while you are still drawing it. A unit that has walked off the edge of the screen still draws its line, which is how you see where the half of your army you cannot see is headed. EA's animated ring still flashes on the ground where you click, with Order Lines on or off. Aircraft draw their thread from the click, not from the moment they leave the runway. A plane parked on its airfield answers an order by starting its takeoff and puts the order itself aside until the wheels are up, so the taxi and the climb, which is exactly the stretch where you are wondering whether the strike went out at all, used to show nothing.
- In a network match an order answers on the click. Every order waits a few steps so that all the machines carry it out on the same one, 50 ms on a LAN and 83 at a 61 ms ping, and for that wait the lines kept pointing where your units were going before, and the enemy you had just right clicked did nothing. Now the target flashes the moment you click it, each unit's line swings to the new spot or the new target on the same frame, a formation line you have just drawn stays on the ground instead of blinking out, and a factory's rally line and flag jump to where you clicked. Once the units take the order, their own lines carry on from there; an order the game turns down falls back to whatever the units are really doing. Only the picture moves early, so replays and network matches play exactly as before.
- A unit standing guard draws its marker on the ground it is guarding. A guard order clears the unit's goal on the way in, so every guard marker used to sit in the bottom left corner of the map with a thread running the whole way across it, whatever the unit was actually watching.
- A selected building wears a white line round its footprint, and a building your selected units are attacking wears a red one, which blinks three times the moment the attack starts and then stays lit. Red wins on a building that is both. The line lies on the terrain point by point, so it climbs a slope with the ground instead of cutting into the hill, and the building hides the stretch behind it. An order aimed at an outlined building now ends on that line, at the point nearest the unit. It used to stop in the air over the roof, where a tall building's line seemed to aim at nothing.
- A is attack and D is attack move, each arming the next order click. A click on the ground with A held down is a shot at that ground, on your own tank a shot at your own tank, and the mode drops again the moment the order goes out, so nothing stays armed behind your back. The click keeps your group, too: an attack click that was not a drag used to run the same deselect an ordinary left click runs, so the order arrived a moment after the units it was meant for had been dropped. Both orders are aimed with the left button, the way a special power is, and a right click puts the key down again without giving any order. Holding ctrl no longer forces fire: A is the one way to shoot the ground, and ctrl on a move is only the shared pace. The two keys turn each other off, and the letters they took were sitting on grid commands that moved. With A armed, pointing at something nothing in your selection can shoot shows the game's can't-do-that pointer: a Sentry Drone before its gun is researched has no weapon at all, and the pointer used to look ready while the click did nothing.
- G is guard, armed the same way and aimed with the same left button. A left click posts the selection on that spot: they hold it, shoot what walks into range and do not chase it off the post you put them on. G looks the way Zero Hour's own guard button always looked: the targeting cross, with the guard range laid on the ground under it. Roll the mouse wheel while G is armed and the circle grows or shrinks before you click, from half the unit's own range out to 500, and the whole group then guards that one circle; leave the wheel alone and the click is the guard Zero Hour always had. Only the ring changes size: the shield in the middle stays as it is, where the old picture stretched it with the ring. The guard button on the command bar arms the same key, so it clicks and drags the same way. Drag the left button with G armed and they post along the line you draw, one unit per station, the way an attack move line spreads them, which is how a hill or a bridge approach gets covered in one gesture instead of a click per tank. A right click puts the key down again. Hold position, which posts every unit on the spot it is already standing on, has moved to H.
- With A armed, or with Ctrl held down, hold the left button and drag a circle instead: the enemies you can see inside it are split across the units that can shoot, as evenly as the numbers allow, in the order both sides stand around the circle. The tank on the left of your group takes the enemy on the left of theirs. Ten of yours against three of theirs put four guns on one and three on each of the others. Three of yours against ten of theirs each take a run of three or four and work down that run. One enemy, and every selected gun takes it. When a unit's target dies the next of its own goes out the same frame, so a strike group clears a circle without you clicking once per tank. It moves on from a target the group has stopped working on, too, rather than only from a dead one: something none of them can reach or hurt used to sit at the head of the list and hold every other target behind it for the rest of the match. That list is the same queue a shift-clicked attack builds, so you can see it: every target still owed has its own thread and marker, in the order they will be taken, instead of one line to whatever is being shot at this second. Hold Alt while you draw the circle and its targets go on the end of what the group is already working through; draw it without Alt and the circle replaces the lot. The circle's rim is red and the ground inside it is washed the same red while you drag it, painted on the map rather than over it, so it runs up the hills inside the circle and your own tanks stand on top of it. The rim sits in the plane of the press, so a hill or a building under the cursor no longer jumps the circle every frame. Any order you give by hand ends the list. Losing a unit does not: the list belongs to the group that was told and carries on with whoever is left, which is worth saying because for a while it did not, and one tank dying threw away every target still owed. Running out of ammo does not cost you the list either. A flight that empties its racks flies home, lands, rearms and comes back to the target it left, and the queue waits for it instead of counting the trip as the group giving up: a circle drawn for four planes used to be empty by the time they were back in the air, one entry lost every two seconds they were away. The threads stay on the ground for the whole trip, too. A plane flying home has no target and no order to read, so the list it was still holding used to vanish off the map the moment it turned for base and reappear only when it was shooting again, which looks exactly like the list being thrown away. What the circle picks up is what you can shoot: a shell or a missile crossing it is on the enemy's side like everything else and used to go on the list as a target, costing the group a two second stall on something that was about to stop existing. A target that has driven into the shroud since you picked it keeps its place in the list but stops drawing its thread, so the line cannot be used to trace it through the fog. An attack-move queued behind other orders keeps the force fire it was given rather than losing it when the attack key drops. A stroke drawn across or near enemies (Ctrl and Shift held, then drag) splits them across the units that can shoot, as evenly as the numbers allow, in the order both sides stand along the stroke. The unit nearest the start takes the enemy nearest the start. Ten guns on three enemies put four on one and three on each of the others. Three guns on ten each work down a run of three or four. The whole group used to walk one list and pour every gun into each enemy in turn. Before that the line poured fire into the ground under it and hit whatever happened to be standing there. A stroke that crosses nobody still fires on the ground along it.
- Shift queues a guard as well, and it is where the line of orders stops. Hold shift with G armed and click, and the group takes up its post once it has finished everything queued in front of it: clear that ridge, then sit on it, in one set of clicks instead of standing over the fight waiting to give the last order. Nothing goes behind a guard, because a posted unit has no next place to be. The thread to the post is drawn in the guard colour like any other guard.
- Shift queues an attack now, not only a move. A or F held down while you shift-click adds a force-attack or an attack-move to the line of orders a group is already holding, and it fires the moment the order in front of it is finished - a target dead, or nobody left chasing an attack-move point. The coloured thread that shows a queued order covers it too, so a queue of "go here, then attack that, then attack-move over there" reads as one continuous line in three colours. The game's own white waypoint markings, which used to draw over the same ground the moment shift went down, are gone - they only ever duplicated what the coloured thread already showed, and doing both left a queued attack sitting under two different pictures of itself.
- The shift queue takes any mix of orders now and stays with the units you gave it to. Move, attack-move, attack a target, draw a formation line, then guard: hold shift, click them in whatever order you like, and the group works down the list by itself. Queue an army's whole route, select something else, go back to your base, and the army keeps going. Before, clicking anything else threw the list away. Each step also starts the moment the one before it is done. It used to wait for the order to travel to the other players and back, which on a 250ms connection was a quarter of a second standing still at every corner. The group keeps together: nobody starts the next order until everyone still alive has finished this one, so a column does not string out behind its fastest tank. Select part of a group and shift-click, and that part takes its own copy of the list with the new order on the end while the others carry on with theirs. Shift-click a group that is already on an ordinary move and the new point goes behind the move instead of replacing it.
- Shift queues whatever a right-click orders, not just moves. Shift-right-click an enemy tank and killing it goes on the list; do it on a building with a Black Lotus selected and taking the building goes on the list. A transport to climb into, a repair bay, a hospital and a supply dock work the same way, and so does an ability armed from the command bar. "Walk here, take that supply center, walk on" is one set of clicks, and the list waits for the capture to finish before anyone sets off for the next point. Upgrades queue as well: shift-click the Overlord's Gatling cannon and it is bought when the Overlord gets there and paid for then. If the money is not in the bank by that time the upgrade is passed over and the list carries on. Each unit with more than one place to go numbers its markers in the order it will reach them, and a step the colour cannot tell apart from a move carries its own cursor next to the number, or the upgrade's picture. A shift-click on one of your own units is still a point on the path. Keep shift down after pressing F, A or G and the key stays armed, so five targets are one key and five clicks instead of five of each; it drops when shift comes up. A guard, a hold or fire on the ground ends a list for good. Nothing queues behind one, whether it was given with shift or without, until an order without shift takes the units off it. Replays recorded before this version that shift-clicked an upgrade, or gave a unit holding a list an ability without shift, play back differently.
- Builders take a shift list too. Hold shift and place a power plant, then a barracks, then a second power plant, and one dozer builds them in the order you put them down: each plan lands on the ground the moment you click, paid for and with its spot held, and the dozer walks to the next one when the last is standing. Before, a dozer on its way somewhere stopped where it was and went to the newest placement. A dozer at work on a site no longer reads as finished to its own list, either: shift-click a move behind a build and it waits for the building, where it used to drive off and leave it half up. Shift-right-click on an unfinished building goes on the list the same way, and if another builder has picked that plan up in the meantime, yours passes it over instead of taking it from him. Transports queue their unloading: move, move, shift and Evacuate, and the passengers get out at the end of the route, and the list goes on only when the last of them is out. One passenger's exit button queues the same way. An order given without shift still replaces the list, an Evacuate included. Replays recorded before this version that shift-placed a building, shift-clicked an unfinished one or shift-unloaded a transport play back differently.
- A capture on the list looks like a capture. Its line ends on the building, and the capture cursor sits beside it even when taking the building is the only order the unit has: one queued capture used to look exactly like a walk to the building's door. The line stays on the building the whole time the capture runs, on the walk over and at the door, where it used to show a plain move and then nothing at all while the building turned. The riflemen who walk in by the door queue a capture the same way Black Lotus does, Rangers and Red Guards included, from the capture button or a shift-right-click.
- Attack move stays armed for as long as shift is down, whether you pressed its key or clicked its button on the bar, so every point you queue is an attack move. Orders given on the minimap are the orders they would be on the battlefield: an armed attack move is an attack move there too, and shift adds to the queue. Passing the pointer over the minimap no longer puts an armed attack move down.
- What the circle picks up is what you can see, and a stealthed unit is not that. Shroud was the only test, so a hidden tank parked in ground you had already cleared went on the list like anything else: drag a circle over open country and the group opened fire on air, one order per hidden unit, which is a stealth detector drawn with the mouse. An undetected unit is not in the circle.
- Ctrl+D takes every unit of the kinds you have selected that is on the screen, and pressed twice inside half a second takes them across the whole map. One tank selected and two keystrokes is your whole armour, wherever it is standing. It was on Shift+Ctrl+E, which is three fingers for something you do in every fight, and it only ever reached across the map when the screen had nothing left to give - so the wide selection happened to you instead of being asked for.
- Next idle unit selects the next combat unit standing with no orders, and the camera stays where you had it, so you can give it an order on the minimap without leaving the fight in front of you. Press again for the one after. It starts without a key; set one on the Hotkeys page. The idle worker key, I, and the idle worker button take you to the worker, unless Jump to Idle Worker is off in Options > Interface.
- That key comes in one per arm as well, so finding the jet that landed and sat down no longer means paging past every idle tank first. Select all idle units takes every combat unit standing with no orders on the screen without moving the view, or across the whole map when the screen has none, and pressed twice inside half a second it takes the whole map anyway. An aircraft-only and a vehicles-only version sit beside it. All of them start without a key.
- Garrison nearby buildings fills a town with one key. The infantry you have selected walk into the buildings around them, and when one fills the rest move on to the next, until the area has no free seat. You used to split the squad and click each building yourself.
- Go get repaired or healed clears a mixed selection after a fight. Each unit goes to its own nearest building that can fix it, a tank to a repair bay and a wounded soldier to where he heals, so nobody has to sort them first. Both keys start unassigned; set them on the Hotkeys tab in Options or on the launcher's Hotkeys page.
- Soldiers no longer stand beside a building they were sent into. On Alpine Assault a man walking to one of the rail yard huts stopped at its wall and never went in, whether you clicked or pressed the key.
- Replays recorded before this change no longer match.
- Shift and a number puts what you have selected into that control group and keeps everyone already in it, the way StarCraft does it. Fresh tanks off the line join group 1 with one key, where you used to select group 1, shift-click the new tanks in and press Ctrl+1 again. The selection stays as it is. Retail used Shift and a number to pull a group into your selection instead; that is gone, and Alt and the number still centres the view on the group.
- Ordering a very large army works. A selection of more than 254 units reaches the game whole, and Ctrl+number groups keep all their units.
- Your number-key groups are listed down the left edge of the screen, one to a cell of the same steel tray the production queue sits in: a picture of its most numerous unit with the group's size on it, the group's hotkey on a small key in the picture's corner and a health bar under it. The key of the group you picked sits pressed in. A group whose units are shooting or being shot at blinks red until three seconds after the last shot, so you see which group is in a fight without hunting for it. Pick a group by its number and a tray of build buttons waits between the superweapon countdowns and the general's powers, and everything built from it goes straight into that group. It starts tucked away: only a small green-tipped notch sticks out of the right edge of the screen, so the battlefield stays clear until you want it. Click the notch and the tray slides out under a pointed ledge carrying the group's key and size; click it again and it slides back. A group with a building in it gets no tray at all. While that group is still what you have selected, every new unit from the tray joins your selection the moment it rolls out of the factory, so your next order already takes it along; pick something else in the meantime and your selection is left alone. Every side gets the panels in its own command bar's metal. The factory with the shortest queue takes the order, and the new unit walks to its group on its own, shooting at whatever it meets on the way. White dashes with a dark edge mark its way on the minimap, with a square where it is headed, and the group carries a "+1" until it gets there. Reinforcing the tanks at the front used to mean building, finding the fresh tank at the factory, sending it and adding it to the group by hand.
- After a move order each unit's own stopping place lights up as a thin ring on the ground, the size of that unit's body, and fades in a second and a half. Twenty tanks sent to one click spread out when they arrive, and the rings show where each of them will actually stand. Attack moves and guard orders draw them too, in their own colours.
- Hold Alt and drag with the middle mouse button, or hold Alt and turn the wheel, to tilt the camera between 20 and 60 degrees. Home resets heading, tilt and zoom, the way Numpad 5 does.
- The side buttons on your mouse tilt the camera five degrees a press, forward flatter and back steeper, on Windows, Mac and Linux. The game used to ignore them.
- The screen edges scroll the map again in a borderless or ordinary window. Since 3.0.0 every player runs the Classic mouse, and the Classic mouse kept the 2003 rule of no edge scrolling in a window, whatever the "Edge Scroll In A Window" option said. Only fullscreen still scrolled. The option decides it now, and borderless always scrolls, since there is no desktop around it to move the pointer onto.

## Aircraft, guards, and orders that used to be ignored

- From the game's angle a Comanche over a ridge and a Comanche over your base can sit on the same spot of the screen. Aircraft in the air now hang a thin line straight down to the ground or water under them, so the foot tells you where the plane really is and the length how high. The line hangs from the plane's belly instead of cutting across its fuselage, is drawn as a thin even thread in the owner's colour over a faint dark edge so it holds on sand and snow without crowding the picture, and ends in a small diamond of the same colour where the filled ring and disc used to sit, so you can tell whose plane is over that spot from the ground alone. An enemy stealth plane's line goes the moment it starts to cloak, so it cannot give away where the plane went. China's Artillery Barrage no longer fills the sky with a dozen lines: its shells come from invisible guns that counted as aircraft, and those are left out now, along with anything else that only pretends to fly. A parked plane has none, and cutscenes draw none. A high plane at the very bottom edge of the screen can lose its line there, and so can one whose line would be taller than the screen. If the lines are clutter to you, Aircraft Altitude Lines under Options, Interface turns them off; they start on.
- Two jets on one airfield could deadlock waiting for each other; now they go.
- Losing the airfield no longer leaves its aircraft circling rubble forever.
- A jet looking for a new airfield no longer locks parking spaces it never uses. The search booked a space at every airfield it looked at on the way to the nearest, and each of those stayed booked for that jet until it died: an empty spot on the tarmac no other plane could land on and the airfield could not build into.
- A jet whose airfield is gone no longer haunts your base. One that still had a bomb or a missile on board was let off the fuel clock EA gives every homeless jet, so with every other airfield full it hung over the ruin for the rest of the match, half dead and never repaired: a damaged Aurora orbiting a base of ten full airfields. It now circles the ruin with the empty ones, checks every second for a free spot, lands on the first that opens and goes down when its fuel runs out. A jet a map places in the air without an airfield still waits instead, and so does a helicopter, which has no fuel clock to run out.
- Repaired aircraft fly to the rally point instead of hovering over the pad.
- Infantry leaving a captured building follow its rally point too.
- The Spectre gunship's crosshair answers your right click. Its gun only walked its fire toward a new spot while it was already shooting, so moving the crosshair onto ground the gun could not reach that moment froze the fire on the old spot for the rest of the orbit. Now the cannon rakes across to every click inside the target circle and the howitzer follows it there; a click outside the circle stops at its edge, as before, and the plane keeps circling where you called it. It also opens up on enemies anywhere in the circle when the crosshair sits on empty ground, which EA had only let the computer's gunships do. Yours and the computer's now follow the same rules. Measured on Alpine Assault: moved three times in one orbit, the first move had shells on the new spot under two seconds after the click, and four Battlemasters parked in the circle were all dead before the plane left.
- Right-click a selected factory or barracks and its rally point is gone. Before, a rally point could be moved and that was all.
- A Chinook unloads its passengers one at a time, not stacked in one frame.
- Campaign reinforcements flown in by Chinook land again. That one-at-a-time unloading sent a mission's scripted Chinooks home with their cargo still aboard, so on the second American mission the dozers announced at the docks never got off, and neither did the next one.
- A guarding unit no longer fights itself between returning to post and shooting back.
- Every unit of yours on guard carries a small steel shield over its head, selected or not, in place of the blocky "G" it used to wear. The shield has smooth edges and a lit and a shaded half, and it shrinks as you zoom out the way the health bars do: at 1080p it was 24 pixels tall over every unit at every zoom, and it is now 18 up close and 11 from the opening camera, about the height of an infantryman's head.
- An Ambulance cleans up the toxins around it without being told. Its hose reaches 100, and that was all it ever looked at, so one parked a truck's length from a toxin pool sat and watched it. Standing idle or on guard, it now notices a pool, an anthrax cloud or a radiation field up to 300 away, drives over, washes off every one in that circle, and goes back to where it stood; one that was on guard is back on guard. A unit you are moving is never pulled off its order, and any order you give while it is cleaning ends the cleanup. Put down 150 to 250 from two Ambulances, one idle and one guarding, three poison fields were gone inside 16 seconds, both trucks were back on their spots, and a third Ambulance driving past a fourth field went straight on to where it was sent. The Cleanup Area button works better for it too: an Ambulance sent to clean an area used to shoot only at what was already in reach once it got there and stood still in front of the rest, and once the area was clean it never counted as idle again, so it ignored the next spill. An Ambulance guarding a tank goes back to guarding the tank after a cleanup, not the patch of ground it left from, so it follows the tank again: with the tank driven 600 away after the cleanup, the Ambulance reached it 17 seconds later. One that gives up on a spill it cannot drive up to no longer goes back for the same spill every time it stands idle; telling it to clean the area yourself still sends it. Giving up never actually happened, though: it counted only the looks that found it standing still, and it ordered the drive again every time it stopped, so a look nearly always caught it moving. It now gives up after eight looks in a row that find it parked no nearer the spill, and leaves the whole patch round it alone, since a toxin field is many spills and the next one in the same field drew it straight back. One still driving, round a river say, is left to get there, but not for ever: 20 seconds on one patch with nothing washed off and no nearer and it gives up too. Sent at two fields on a cliff top, an Ambulance stayed under the cliff for the fields' whole lifetime without once giving up, and never went for a third field put down on open ground 225 away. In the same test now it gives up on the cliff top 22 seconds after it set off, never looks at that patch again, not even at a fresh field put down there, and washes the open-ground field away. The computer's Ambulances keep to that too, and one the computer pulls off a cleanup under fire leaves that patch alone afterwards instead of being sent straight back to it. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- Jets on guard attack what is inside the circle you drew. A plane on guard flies to its post and circles it, and since guards stopped shooting at enemies hidden in fog it only went after what that loop brought into its own sight: a Raptor guarding a circle of 700 hung over the post for the whole 80 seconds of the test with a power plant 550 out, and an Aurora circled for ten seconds before it found the same one. Aircraft are back on the original rule and take anything in the circle, fog or not. The Raptor's first missiles now land 11 seconds after the order and the Aurora's bomb after 9, and neither flies over the post first. Ground units still leave alone what they cannot see. A replay recorded before this change plays back differently.
- H now sets a stance for the group. Defensive is how your units have always behaved: they fire on what comes into range and stay put. Aggressive lets them go after anything they can see, the way the computer's own units do, so a group left on aggressive clears the ground around it without being told. The button shows the stance the selection holds.
- A queued attack move finishes its fights before the next order on the list goes out. The first enemy it met used to count as arriving, so a list of attack moves round a town skipped ahead a step at every skirmish and the group was off to the last point while the first was still contested. Replays recorded before this version play back differently.
- A unit sent out to answer a shot, whose target then died, is supposed to walk home. When that walk cannot start, because the unit cannot move or the pathfinder has no way back, the failure was taken to mean someone was still in range, and the unit went back into the attack on a target that was already gone. Both ends of that attack find nobody and hand it back to the walk, which fails again, so the loop runs out inside the same step and starts over on the next one. One match wrote 67,416 lines about it, and every line is pushed out to disk as it is written. The failed walk now counts as the walk being over. The unit looks once more, and with nobody there it goes back to what it was doing. A save that caught the chase dropped it on load; it picks the target back up. A soldier whose tunnel is gone did the same thing, and a computer match wrote 80 of those lines. With no tunnel he waits and looks. A replay recorded before this change plays back differently.
- Engineers can clear mines and booby traps they cannot see.
- A helicopter no longer boards a transport from the air.
- A building in the fog takes orders. Send infantry into a fogged garrison, a Ranger at a fogged oil derrick or a hacker at a fogged supply center and they go, where the click used to turn into a plain move to the spot. The cursor and the walk over go by what you last saw there, so if the building was taken, filled or emptied while you were not looking, nothing on your screen says so until your men get close enough to see it, and then they stop. Ground you have never seen stays out of reach.
- A computer player's reinforcement catches up with the team it joined. A unit sent to a team already walking a waypoint path took the team's orders without the path itself, which crashed the match; the crash was stopped by leaving the newcomer standing where it spawned, and now it picks up the route from wherever the team has got to. Found and fixed by T0T0W.
- Select a big army, right click once, and all of it goes. In a crowd, units step aside to let a neighbour past, and a unit that stepped aside at the moment it was working out its route forgot the order and stood where it was. Out of 120 units sent across a small map, 7 were left behind, and the bigger the selection the more of them stayed. Now 200 out of 200 get there. Clicking on a building did the same thing to the whole group: there was no open ground right under the cursor, so nobody was given a place to stand. The group now stands around the building.
- The whole unit limit moves on one click. The lobby allows 840 units in a match, and the game could only keep 512 of them waiting for a route at once: sent across the map together, 329 of 841 never took a step, then or ever. All 840 go now, whether one player owns them or two armies of 420 are crossing through each other, and the game never falls behind: the click itself costs 13 milliseconds, and no moment of the march took longer than 33, the time the game has for each step of the battle. With all 840 on screen the picture averages 30 frames a second on the new renderer and 37 on the old one, 2.7 milliseconds quicker than before because a crowd of infantry now redraws its shadows' poses in turns instead of every soldier every frame.
- A tank in a column no longer parks behind the one in front while that one drives away. Touching the tank ahead cut its speed a little more every moment and never let it come back, so once the leader had paused, the follower sat at a dead stop until their hulls came apart and then crawled back up to speed. Every pause at the head of a column rippled down it as a line of tanks standing still. The follower now picks its speed up again as soon as the one in front moves off. Across eight maps, stops of a second or more behind the unit ahead fell from 27 to 19 in a 30-unit squad and from 1169 to 781 in a 200-unit army, the longest single stop in that army went from 14.6 seconds to 9, and the last tank of the squad arrives 6.6 seconds sooner. In computer-against-computer matches, the time units spent jammed so hard that the game counted them stuck fell from about 1.3 seconds a match to half a second.
- Tanks and infantry sent together no longer trip over each other. A tank that caught up with a soldier of its own side marching the same way told him to step aside, and a soldier who steps aside forgets his route and stands for a full second before he may ask for another. In a mixed squad of 20 Crusaders and 10 Rangers every one of the 28 second-long stops across eight maps was exactly that. The tank now rolls through a soldier walking its way, the way soldiers already walk through each other; one standing still or crossing its path is still asked to move. Stops of a second or more fell from 48 to 12 in that squad and from 977 to 546 in a 200-unit army, and both arrive sooner: the last Crusader 2.5 seconds earlier, the whole army 1.9 seconds earlier on average. In computer-against-computer matches, time spent wedged fell 11%.
- Infantry no longer clogs a road your tanks are driving down. A soldier who walked into the side of a tank stood there until it left, and a tank queueing in a town street does not leave: on Alpine Assault one Ranger waited four and a half seconds against the flank of a Crusader that was itself waiting for the one in front. A soldier who meets a vehicle now walks round it and steps a little away from the hull, and a tank coming at a marching soldier slows to a third of its speed instead of ordering him aside, which used to cost him his route and another second on the spot. With 36 soldiers walking one way down that street and 12 vehicles driving the other, the soldiers' stops of a second or more fell from 35 to 6 over three matches, and on the slowest of them the last Ranger arrives 41 seconds after the order where he used to take 55. The vehicles get through sooner too. A replay recorded before this change plays back differently.
- Two columns that meet head-on get past each other. The game has a rule for it, written by the original team: two tanks nose to nose for a second drive through each other. A counter that reset itself every frame meant it never once fired, so the front pair stood there, sometimes for more than seven seconds, and everything behind them queued. It fires now, after a quarter of a second. Twenty tanks meeting twenty in the open used to stop 104 times and bring the last one in after 72 seconds; now they stop once, and the last one arrives after 23. Two armies of 420 crossing the map through each other get there in half the time: the Crusaders' average trip went from 167 seconds to 91, the Battlemasters' from 149 to 75.
- A group you send round a corner goes round it side by side. Every tank used to work out its own route, every one of those routes ran over the tip of the corner, and the whole group squeezed onto that one point with the outside tanks cutting across the inside ones to reach it. Now the group takes one route and each vehicle drives its own lane of it: the outside lane swings wide, the inside one stays clear of the wall, and where the street narrows the lanes close up over a few corners rather than zigzagging. A tank whose place is short of the click stops at it, instead of driving its lane to the far end and coming back. Twenty-four tanks sent through the streets of Alpine Assault came to a dead stop 7 times a crossing instead of 10 and spent a third less time pressed against each other, and the column in the Forgotten Forest trailer scene gets its last tank home 20 seconds sooner. Infantry, and any group whose route crosses a bridge, still find their own way. A replay recorded before this change plays back differently.
- A group takes a bridge down the middle of the road, and that is the quick way over. For a while the deck kept its full width and the lanes only closed up to it at the ramp, because the Kandahar bridge on Golden Oasis is wide enough for three Crusaders abreast. At today's tank speed it was slower than the single file. With it and the gap a tank left behind a stopped one (see Tanks and cars move as they did in Zero Hour), the last of twenty Crusaders reached the far bank 44.1 seconds after the click where the single file took 28.3, and the wide deck alone cost 7.5 of those seconds. Over the long bridge the two tanks on the outside lane rolled down the bank beside the ramp and stood there until the match ended. Every tank drives the middle of the road over a bridge and up to its ramp again, and with the gap gone as well twenty Crusaders over the Kandahar bridge have their last tank across in 29.3, 30.2 and 28.4 seconds on the three test runs, against 28.3, 31.6 and 32.5 for the old single file at the same speed; over 21 runs it is sooner in 18 and 31.0 seconds on average against 33.2. Eight Overlords over the same bridge are all across in 41.9 seconds instead of 50 to 61.
- No tank is left under a bridge any more. A tank that came up beside a ramp instead of onto it could drive on underneath the deck and sit there at full throttle for the rest of the match, shaking against the side of the ramp while it tried to reach the deck over its head; it was never counted as stuck, because shaking looks like moving. One tank in ten sent over the long bridge on Golden Oasis never got across that way. Now twenty out of twenty get across on each of the twelve runs we made, the last one after 35 to 42 seconds. A tank that keeps to the middle of the road never reaches the bank beside the ramp in the first place, and one that ends up shaking on the spot next to a bridge on its route still asks for a new way round to the ramp.
- Overlords stop getting stuck on bridges. An Overlord is wide enough that its route often met a ramp at the corner, and the bank at the corners of the long bridge on Golden Oasis sits lower than the deck. The Overlord was taken up onto the bridge, then a moment later judged too low for it as the bank fell away, put back on the ground, and it drove on underneath the deck and rocked there for the rest of the match. One Overlord in eight sent over that bridge never crossed. The ramp mouth now accepts a tank coming up from a low bank: eight out of eight get across on every test, the last one 22 seconds sooner, and twenty Crusaders over the same bridge arrive about three seconds sooner on average. A replay recorded before this change plays back differently.
- A jet shot down in the air flies on before it falls. Its wings stopped working on the frame it was hit, so it dropped almost vertically and hit the ground under the spot it was killed at, which is the one thing a plane doing three hundred knots cannot do. It keeps its lift now and gives it up over the next second or so, carrying forward and nosing over as it goes.
- And the bombers come down at all. A B-52, a Spectre gunship, a cargo plane and an A-10 all left the falling speed out of their data, and nought means the lift exactly cancels gravity: shot down, they flew on at cruising height, burning, and blew up in the air still level. Every one of them now falls at half gravity or better, and the fireball waits for the ground instead of going off on a timer somewhere over the map. Measured on the way in: a B-52 falls for 2.8 seconds and lands, where it used to detonate at a hundred feet. On the way home it still did not: after the drop a bomber flies off the map on a precise course that is allowed three times its normal lift, which held a dead one up with lift to spare. A bomber shot down after its run now comes down like one shot down before it.
- Jets that end up on top of their target swing wide and come back on a straight run. A Raptor that came over a tank too close to fire used to bank toward it and keep banking, with the tank sitting inside its turn: one ordered onto an Overlord driving along beside it circled the tank for two and a half seconds without a shot and needed 7.3 seconds to get its four missiles off. It now holds its heading until the tank is far enough behind to turn round on, and comes back lined up: 4 seconds. A target behind the wing or just past it gets the same treatment, where the jet used to turn in, find itself over the target again and fly out anyway. Over 42 staged passes with the Raptor, the MiG, the Aurora and the Stealth Fighter, aimed at targets beside, under and behind them, parked and driving, the slowest Raptor run went from 7.3 seconds to 6.4 and the slowest MiG run from 5.6 to 4.7; on average the Raptor empties its racks 0.3 seconds sooner and the MiG 0.26. The Aurora drops its bomb on the same frame as before, a jet lined up on its target flies the same run as before, and jets fighting aircraft are untouched. A replay recorded before this change, with jets attacking the ground, will not play back the same.
- A supply truck told to go somewhere as it pulls off the dock goes there. It used to finish the docking it had just left and drive back to the supplies, throwing your order away.
- Jets fire as they come in and break away before the target instead of flying over it. An earlier release already said so, and it was not true: the frame a jet's last round left the rack its attack ended, and the flight home carried it on over the target or turned it across. A Raptor sent onto an Overlord driving away beside it passed 11 units from the tank's centre, right over the turret, and needed a second pass for its fourth missile. A jet now opens fire the moment the target comes into reach, where it used to close to halfway between its reach and its minimum range first, and turns away as soon as its last round is gone, to whichever side its turn clears the target by more, counting the bank it is already in. That Raptor now puts all four missiles into the Overlord in one pass, the last 6.7 seconds after the order where it used to land at 11.9, and clears the tank by 137. Sent head-on at parked tanks, the Raptor, the MiG, the Aurora and the Stealth Fighter pass them at 123, 166, 108 and 99 where they passed at 67, 113, 47 and 67. Every jet fires as many rounds as before for the same damage. The Stealth Fighter has the shortest reach and lets its second missile go about 115 from a tank it is chasing, so it still passes that one at 50. A jet carrying out a standing order, guarding an area or on an attack-move, still heads straight home when its racks run dry, as it did. A jet still turning onto its target no longer abandons the run. A replay recorded before this change, with jets attacking the ground, will not play back the same.
- The Aurora keeps its speed through its bombing run instead of pulling the handbrake. It braked on the straight in to the target, from 390 to 250 before the bomb went, and right after the drop it stalled to under 160 inside a second and crawled over the target's air defences at 120, which is where Auroras kept dying. It now drops at full supersonic speed, 477 in a staged run, is still doing 430 three seconds later and only settles to its return speed on the way home, slowing as gently as the original game let it. At that speed it cannot turn away in time, so a parked target sees it pass overhead the way the original Aurora always did, too fast for the defences there to track. On an attack-move it spots its target late and has less run-up, so it drops at 354 where it dropped at 205 and takes 2.8 seconds to slow to 160 where it took one. Coming round onto a target beside its wing it flies a wider turn and drops later, two seconds later in one staged pass. Raptors, MiGs and Stealth Fighters no longer ease off on the way in either and fire a few frames sooner, for the same damage. A replay recorded before this change, with jets attacking, will not play back the same.
- Aircraft guarding an area attack buildings first, then vehicles, then infantry, so an Aurora no longer drops its bomb on a lone soldier.
- Auto garrison also puts infantry into a friendly transport with free seats when no building nearby has room. A Chinook sitting on a supply dock is at work, though, and your infantry no longer board it there and stop the haul; they take another transport. An idle Chinook hovering nearby now counts: it was passed over as an aircraft in the air, so a Ranger with one 80 away walked to a Humvee 210 away, and now the Chinook comes down and takes him.

## The same game on both screens, and after loading

- A unit with nowhere to stand appears where asked, not at a random point.
- Loading a save remembers what your guards were guarding.
- A turret loaded from a save is still tracking what it was tracking, and a worker loaded mid-job carries on with it, instead of both snapping back to their default state.
- A unit that was driving somewhere when you saved is still driving there when you load. One flag was written to the save twice and another not at all, so every loaded unit came back claiming to stand still, and everything that asks - a bike waiting for its rider, a mob following its leader, an ability that breaks if you move - believed it.
- A game saved after losing a supply center loads again. When a truck looked for somewhere to drop its cash and found a center that had been destroyed, it took the center off one list and counted it off the other, so the save recorded the wrong number of supply docks and could not be read back.
- Your units decide the same way on both machines whether to chase what they spotted on their own. That answer was read from uninitialised memory, so the same order could send one player's tank after a target and leave the other's standing.
- A game saved with Gattling Cannons or Patriot batteries built past your power plants loads again. The load gives each building its power back one at a time, so the base ran short for a moment halfway through, and switching the defences off in that moment closed the game with "sleepy update module illegal index". Defences come back from a save in exactly the state you left them.
- A shell already in the air finishes its flight after a load instead of going off in the launcher's face. It keeps the launcher's veterancy bonus too, and a smart bomb keeps homing.
- Supply trucks queued at a dock carry on after a load. Their place in the queue was written to the save and never read back, so every dock stopped letting anyone in until a thirty-second timeout sent the trucks round again.
- A cargo plane or bomber on its way off the map at save time flies on after a load. Its heading was not saved, so the first turn read as a sharp one and the plane was destroyed where it was.
- An EMP pulse, a bike being scuttled, a building's evacuation side and a horde's bonus all come back from a save as they went in.
- A computer whose base was under attack when you saved still knows it after a load, and keeps its army at home as it would have.
- Where a supply dock's waiting spots are is the same on every machine. A dock with fewer spots in its model than in its data filled the rest from leftover memory, a different place on each computer.
- A building's toppling bursts are timed the same on every machine. They were timed off the picture's random numbers and created game objects, so two players could see different debris.
- An aircraft carrier remembers the order it was given, and each runway its own ramp.
- A barracks that has already put its mob on the street does not put a second one out after a load.
- Effects tied together - a smoke column and its embers - stay tied together across a save.
- A loaded save puts the world back in the order it was saved in, so the match plays on from where it was instead of resolving everything backwards.
- And it shows you your own memory of the fog, not everyone else's: a loaded game used to draw what every player remembered on top of the world.
- Saved units come back with the map's weapons, not the stock ones.
- Restarting a skirmish restarts the same skirmish, with a replay that plays back.
- Replays sound and look the way they did when you played them.
- Restart keeps the same random colours, starting corners and armies.
- Somebody quitting no longer reports a desync to everyone still playing.
- A power sabotage no longer follows a player into the next match.
- Muting sound effects or speech no longer desyncs the game.
- A replay of a match you played yourself plays back. Every recording with a human seat whose units moved went out of step at the first check, three seconds in: the playback shared those units' sight with the person watching the replay, which the match itself never did. Taking over a computer side with Shift-Ctrl-T is written into the replay as well, so a recording plays back past it.
- A Particle Cannon beam hurts the same on every machine. How far its damage reached was read off the picture of the beam, and a machine catching up after a stutter damaged with a beam a few frames old. A cannon an enemy happened to spot while it stood idle could also go dead on that enemy's machine alone.
- A map with its own rules no longer follows you into the next match. A custom map can change armour, upgrades, what a building leaves behind and a side's starting setup; a machine that had played one kept those values until the game was restarted, and fought the next match with them while everyone else used the stock ones. And a map sent to you over the network is played with its rules file, where the receiving machine used to skip it.
- A building full of stealthed Jarmen Kells or Hijackers no longer shuffles them between windows on one screen only when a detector sweeps over it.
- A unit whose firing animation has its own set of barrels fires from the same barrel on every machine, whatever each player's camera happens to be looking at.
- A unit queued in a factory by a map script is numbered the same on every machine, so cancelling it works everywhere and not just for its owner.
- A map script that waits on a sound, a music track or a camera move now decides on the same frame on every machine.
- A match starts from the number the lobby agreed on, whatever the battle behind the menu was doing when the host pressed start.
- Graphics detail no longer decides whether a piece of debris exists or how long a death takes.
- The first building of a computer player is no longer held back a frame on a machine that already played a match that session.
- Two allied vehicles blocking each other in a narrow pass no longer read freed memory while they make way, which could crash the game or split it.
- A cheat every machine refused during a network game is refused in the replay of it too.
- An install that differs where it matters can no longer join and split the match later. The game's check at the door now also covers the command buttons the computer player builds from and every unit model, whose shape decides where shots leave the barrel. And a map's own rules file counts as part of the map, so two players with the same map and different rules get it sent across instead of fighting with different armour.
- The computer player's sense of which unit beats which comes out the same on every processor. It used the runtime's logarithm, which takes a different path on processors with newer instructions.
- The price of all of the above: a replay recorded on an earlier version can go out of step on this one where it has a Particle Cannon, an EMP, a stealthed garrison or two allies making way for each other in it.
- Pausing no longer leaks a little memory for every sound that was about to start.
- A sound cancelled before it started really is cancelled. The check compared a pointer against a handle - two different things sharing one slot - so it never matched and the sound played anyway.
- Angles come from the game's own table, identical on every machine.
- Defeat, second maps and the sync fingerprint each had a drift bug; fixed.
- The mismatch check now covers whole units and all sixty-eight special powers.
- Order numbering no longer scrambles your commands after about fifteen hundred orders.
- A network game runs at the speed it says it does.
- A frame of orders now travels in one datagram instead of four or five: the packet was still the 476 bytes a 2003 modem could carry, and every extra datagram was another chance to arrive late.
- Input delay is measured from simulation speed now, not your graphics card.
- One player's slow graphics card no longer slows the whole match. A network game runs at the pace of its slowest machine, and a machine that could only draw 16 pictures a second also only advanced the game 16 times a second, so everybody played in slow motion. It now skips pictures to keep up with the game, the way single player already did. Two machines on one desk: with one of them held to 16 pictures a second the match used to run at half speed, and with it held to 10 the match now runs at 28 of its 30 frames a second, the two machines agreeing on every frame.
- One lost packet costs a round trip instead of a flat two seconds.
- An online match no longer settles at 20 frames a second. Every time a machine sat waiting for the other player's orders, the wait was counted as that machine being slow, the whole room was slowed down to match, and the slower room waited just as often. A two-player match on 2026-09-29 played its whole six minutes at 21. Waiting now counts as waiting: two machines at a 260 ms ping with 3% loss were told to run at 27 before and at 30 now, and play at 27.6 instead of 25.7.
- A link that drops the odd packet no longer drags the whole room into slow motion. The game held its outgoing packets back for up to half its input delay, replies included, so it measured every connection as far slower than it was and waited longer and longer for anything lost. Three players on a 50 ms link losing one packet in fifty used to sink from 30 frames a second to 13; they hold 21 now, and two players losing one in a hundred hold 27.
- A bad connection no longer turns the match into a slideshow. The orders each player sends now go out three times, 30 ms apart, so a lost packet is covered by the next one instead of by a resend that came most of a second later while everyone waited. Three players on 120 ms links losing one packet in twenty went from 6 frames a second to 19; two on 200 ms links losing one in ten went from 6 to 23, and the 50 ms room above from 21 to 26. The copies cost a few bytes and nothing on a clean line.
- Your clicks are answered sooner online. The game worked out how far ahead to schedule orders from the two slowest connections in the room and counted the host as one of them, so a two-player game waited out a whole round trip where half of one is the wire. At a 200 ms ping the delay between a click and the units moving drops from about 310 ms to 215; three players at 250 ms go from 500 to 370. Pings up to 300 ms and more are measured as they are now instead of being cut off at half a second, which left those links a window too short for them.
- The readout in the top right corner now carries the frame number, and in a network game how many frames the room can still play before it has to wait on somebody, out of the input delay it is running with, plus the frame rate the slowest machine has set for everyone. "ready 4/7   room 29fps" is a healthy match; ready sitting at 0 is the stall you are about to feel.
- Two players who each lost the other's last packet no longer freeze until the disconnect screen. Each asked the other to send it again, and each only resent what it had already played, which was nothing, so on a link with a tenth of a second of delay and one packet in twenty lost the match stopped for good one second in. Now the packet goes again and the match carries on.
- A match of three or more players no longer clogs up after a lost packet. When one player asked another, not the host, for a frame he had missed, the answer was acknowledged to the host instead of to the player who sent it, so that player never heard back and resent the same frame every two seconds for the rest of the match. A copy of someone else's frame could also carry the number of an order that player still had on the way, and the acknowledgement for the copy cancelled the order's own resend. Answers are acknowledged to whoever sent them now, under the number their author gave them, and a player who misses a frame asks for it on the host's measured timing instead of waiting two seconds first. Two-player games are unchanged.
- A three-player match starts sooner on a bad connection. When a frame did not arrive in time the game asked the players who had it one at a time, and the link between two non-host players timed its first guess off how long the other machine took to load the map, which is not a delay on the wire. Everyone missing is asked at once now, and loading no longer counts as a sample of the connection. At 125 ms of ping with 75 ms of jitter and 3% packet loss, the longest wait at the start of a match went from 2.7 seconds to 0.8, and from 4.1 to 1.1 with one slow-loading machine. Two-player games are unchanged.
- A player whose game crashes or whose line dies no longer holds the rest of the room for over a minute. The disconnect screen came up after 12 seconds of silence and then started a fresh 60-second countdown, so everyone else sat for 72 seconds before the game let the player go. The countdown now runs from the last thing that player sent and lasts 30 seconds, so the match carries on about half a minute after they went quiet. A vote to drop them still works as before, and anyone still talking is never on the clock.
- A desynced match stops at once instead of playing on as two games.
- Two players on different factions can play a LAN or VPN match again. 3.0.0 and 3.0.1 put every USA against GLA, China against USA and China against GLA game out of sync in its first second, while two players of the same side played on: the mismatch check had started counting the map scripts' timers and flags, and some of those scripts follow each player's own faction, so the two machines never agreed on them. The check leaves them out again, as Zero Hour always did.
- A single lost packet no longer freezes the match for twenty seconds. The game now asks for the
  missing frame back after a fifth of a second instead of waiting out the disconnect timer, so
  nobody sits in front of a vote screen for a player who never went anywhere.
- A freeze no longer costs everyone two seconds of input delay for the rest of the match: time
  spent stalled is not mistaken for how slow the connection is.
- A player leaving is reported as a player leaving, not a desync.
- A desync now writes a per-object report on both machines for comparison.
- LAN refuses to start between two machines whose game files differ.
- A player whose name holds a comma, a colon or a control character is turned away at the door instead of scrambling the lobby's idea of who is in the room.
- Opening the online login screen no longer crashes the game when it remembers a password.
