Each line sits on a black band that thins out over the battlefield. A line about a player opens on his general's flag with his name in his colour; the rest open on a gold mark. A smoke signal or a beacon goes in, and so does a player beaten or gone, for a player and a watcher alike. Six lines at most, ten seconds each, the newest at the bottom, and the feed steps up over the production queue's row whenever that is out. Missed something? Press Enter: while the chat is open the last twelve lines come back, however old they are, and the chat moves up to stand clear of them. A line with no player opens on a steel plate the size of a flag with a gold exclamation mark lying across it, so every line's words start in the same column.
- A superweapon's wait is written in plain seconds - 200, not 3:20 - so it compares with every other countdown on the screen at a glance. Once it is charged the number goes away entirely and the picture itself breathes in your colour, which is the one thing you want to catch out of the corner of your eye.
- The countdown inside a strip picture moved down into its bottom left corner and carries the unit with it - 45s, 200s - on a translucent plate. In the middle of the picture it sat on the one thing the picture is there to show, and the plate it lost when it was in the middle earns its place down in the corner, where a pale cameo was swallowing the digits and their shadow together. This applies to the superweapon countdowns in the top right as well.
- Every picture in the row stands in a tray - the same tray your general's powers stand in down in the corner, your own side's copy of it, so the American, Chinese and GLA strips each carry their own metal. The tray is turned back to front, because that bar grows out of the right hand corner and the strip grows out of the left, so its heavy rail leads the row instead of standing between every pair of pictures. It is never stretched to fit, and side by side the trays close up behind each other by exactly what that bar closes its own up by, so a row of them reads as one run of metal rather than a line of loose boxes. Stacked they stand clear of each other instead: a picture in a column carries its whole tray, with none of the one above it cutting across its top edge. The strip is flush against the left edge, and a black rectangle laid over the battlefield is gone.
- The queue stands up out of the corner instead of lying across the bottom of the screen. It is a column now, five pictures high, growing upward from just above the command bar with the next thing to arrive at the bottom of it - so the one picture you actually read is always in the same place, a thumb's width above the buttons, and it does not move when six more tanks are ordered. What is left over closes the column as a sixth cell wearing a "+N". A busy base used to lay its whole queue across the battlefield; now it costs one picture's width of screen, whatever it has coming. Playing under the new steel command bar it lies down again, as a row: a steel tray on the radar's side standing just over the under-attack light, the twin of the general's powers on the other side, the next thing to arrive against the screen's left edge and the rest running right. Each picture sits in a framed cell the size of a power's, so the two trays read as a pair.
- A slot in it is a slot of that bar to the pixel, at every resolution - the size is measured off the bar itself rather than guessed - so the queue is read at a glance instead of squinted at: these were postage stamps a third of that size. Ten tanks ordered back to back are one picture with an x10 in its corner rather than ten copies of the same tank eating the row, so what is left of the row still says what else is coming.
- The buildings your workers are raising stand in that same column, not in one of their own: a war factory going up is a picture in the queue at the point its time puts it, between the tank that lands before it and the one that lands after. One column is the whole answer to what your base has coming, read bottom to top in the order it arrives, and it no longer takes a second strip of screen to say the slower half of it. Each site carries its own sweep and the seconds it still needs. Click one and the camera goes there - a half-finished building under fire on the far side of the map is one click away instead of a hunt across the minimap - and none of them can be cancelled by mistake: a building already standing is sold or lost, never cancelled, so Ctrl over it does nothing.
- The superweapon strip in the top right stands in the same metal, the right way round this time: it is anchored to the right hand edge and grows leftwards, which is the way that bar in the corner grows, so its rail closes the row against the edge of the screen. The black rectangle behind those pictures is gone with it, and the countdowns are the size of the ones down in the corner rather than half of it.
- Nothing in a row of trays lies over the picture in the tray beside it any more. A slot used to slide an eighth of a tray back under its neighbour so a row would read as one run of metal, and what it actually did was drop that neighbour's rail across the left edge of every cameo but the last - visible on the general's powers along the bottom right and on the superweapon countdowns along the top. They step a whole tray now, sideways as well as upward, which is what the queue column down the left has always done.
- A game opens with nothing selected, so your first click is not a rally point.
- Your general's powers no longer climb the right hand edge of the screen. They sit three abreast, filling from the bottom corner where the first one has always been and wrapping upward, so a general holding eleven of them still reads as a block instead of a ladder from the radar to the sky. Each row stands in steel only as wide as the powers in it, the way the superweapon countdowns do: seven powers are two rows of three with a single one on top against the screen's edge, where the tray used to be a full three by three with an empty dark corner. The keys follow the same shape: the first press picks a row, the second picks the power in it, so every power is two keys away - F1 F1 for the one in the corner, F2 F1 for the row above it. Only the keys you can press next are written on the pictures, so you are never reading eleven labels to find one, and Escape drops a row you thought better of - so does clicking a power with the mouse, and so does four seconds' pause, so a key hit by mistake in a fight never turns your next one into a superweapon. Rows with nothing in them yet cannot be picked at all: early on, when you hold three powers, only the row you have answers a key.
- The second key of that pair works now. Anything that touched the interface at all - a promotion, a unit rolling out, a building captured somewhere across the map - was quietly forgetting the row you had just picked, and in a real fight that happens several times a second, so the pair almost never completed and the powers looked as though they answered no key at all.
- The key written on a power is drawn over its cooldown sweep instead of under it. A power still charging had its label buried by the black wedge sweeping across the picture, which is exactly when you want to know which key it is.
- The tilde key opens the general's promotions, and Escape closes them - Escape used to bring up the pause menu on top of the open screen, leaving the small exit button in its corner as the only way out. The screen is five columns wide and 1 to 5 now name them: each number sits in the corner of the science that column would sell you next, and pressing it twice buys that one - once to mark, once to spend, so a point is never gone to a key hit in a hurry. Buy the top of a chain and the number drops onto the next rung down, so a whole column goes in with one finger while the fight carries on behind you.
- `S` stops your units again; the key was simply never bound.
- Every button carries its build, research or cooldown time in the corner.
- A single selected unit wears a gold bar filling toward its next rank.
- Timings everywhere: buildings, queues, superweapon charge, upgrades being researched.
- A charge bar now says how many seconds are left.
- Aircraft always show how many attack runs they have left.
- The corner readout separates game time from real time, and sim rate from fps. It also says DX11 or DX9 after the frame rate, which is what your machine is actually drawing with: a graphics card that cannot start Direct3D 11 falls back to 9 without a word, and a frame rate means nothing until you know which of the two it belongs to. The 64-bit game writes x64 after it, so a screenshot says which build took it.
- Your computer's own clock leads that readout, so you can see the time without leaving the match.
- Pausing stops both clocks.
- Every row and every countdown stands in real metal, cut from the same tray the general's powers sit in down in the corner - the side your command bar is showing. Watching a match there is no bar of your own, so the superweapon countdowns used to fall back to a flat black box for the whole match; now they wear the metal of the player you are watching, and follow it when you switch seats.
- Watching, the command bar is down to the radar. Pick a player to follow in the camera panel and you are looking at him and his money, the way his button in the list did; pick nobody for everybody. The bar stays ControlBar Pro's observer bar the whole match, in a replay as well: following a player or clicking his tank no longer turns it into his side's bar. Picking drops whatever you had selected, so the promotions on screen are that player's and not the owner of the tank you last clicked. The portrait panel in the right corner comes up when you select something and goes when you click empty ground, so an empty match leaves the bottom of the screen to the battle.
- Watching, the bars over the buildings are everyone's too - what each factory is turning out, and how long the superweapons have left. An observer used to see none of it.
- Watching, the camera can drive itself. Two drop-downs in the camera panel on the right, above the board, say who has it and which player you follow, and you can follow nobody. The Director goes to the fight with the most on the line over the last five seconds, where a dead Overlord counts for more than six riflemen being shot at and anything happening to a superweapon counts three times over. It stays with that fight eight seconds, leaves after four for one two and a half times the size, and after twenty seconds on the same fight, or as soon as the fight has burnt down to half of what it was, a third bigger is enough. So a 4v4 is watched like a broadcast rather than hunted for, and it does not hop between spots every few seconds. Any general's power used on the map outranks every fight. For a nuke the camera goes straight to the target and waits there for it to come down and stays through the blast. The particle cannon's beam is followed along its whole sweep, and a Scud Storm or a carpet bomb is watched until the last explosion has died down. Then it goes back to the fighting. The camera glides between places and slows into each one, and only cuts when the next one is across most of the map. When nobody is shooting it no longer parks on empty ground: it goes round what is worth seeing, an army on the march, a superweapon, a base going up, the rest of a base, the dearest first and nine seconds each, and does not come back to one of the last three while there is anything else to show. With a player picked it keeps to his fights and his own armies and buildings. Player camera shows his screen: a human player's camera comes over the network five times a second, smoothed in between, and a computer player, who has no camera, gets the Director narrowed to his own fights. Scroll with the keys or a drag, turn the view or click the radar and the camera is yours again, still following the same player. The edge of the screen does not scroll while it drives: the panel on the right stands on that edge, and reaching for it used to hand the camera back to you, so the Director stopped following the fighting the first time you went to change a setting. In a replay with the recorded camera switched on in the options, the player you follow still drives the camera the way his button in the old list did.
- Watching, the Director climbs over a wide battle until the whole of it is on the screen, and comes back down to your own height when it moves on or you take the camera. The mouse wheel still zooms while it drives, and it keeps what you chose. It stops short of the map's border too, where a fight on the edge used to come with a black corner of nothing beside it. A nuke or a Scud Storm is shown leaving its silo even when the Director has only just arrived at another fight; before, the launch was over by the time it was allowed to move. Rewinding a replay leaves your camera settings as they were, where a rewind used to hand you back a free camera with nobody followed. And following one player while a superweapon wiped out everything he had at the spot could close the game. It no longer does.
- The Director stands further back. It used to frame the unit the shots came from and miss the tanks fighting just beside it; now it watches every place from 200 paces over your own height, so the whole fight and what is around it are on the screen. Its climbs and descents take a couple of seconds and ease in and out, and gliding over hills no longer pumps the picture in and out over every ridge. A superweapon or a general's power is one shot now: when the screen split to show the silo and the target, the camera used to drop low when the split closed and then spend ten seconds climbing back up, and it comes out of the split at the height it was heading for.
- Watching can be filmed. Start the game with `-directorrecord` and the Director has the camera from the first second, with nothing over the picture but the radar, and the whole match goes into one video; the game closes itself when the match is decided or the replay runs out. Beside `-replay` it turns an old match into footage, and beside four computer players it films a match nobody played. It plays the match twice. The first time there is no picture and the game runs as fast as the machine goes, 8,000 frames of a four-player match in 17 seconds, writing down where each fight starts and when each superweapon fires; the second time it films, and the camera is already at a fight four seconds before the first shot instead of arriving halfway through it. When two fights are about to start far apart the screen splits three seconds before the second begins, and only when the first run saw the Director's own fight go on for the whole time the split will be up, so the second picture never sweeps in and straight back out. A skirmish the first run saw come to nothing is not cut to, and neither is a special power that hurts nobody: an Air Force general's spy satellite every minute used to pull the camera to empty ground, where a carpet bomb or an artillery strike still gets it from the launch. Each half keeps its own fight. The main camera used to leave for the second half's fight as it began, and the two halves glided past each other over empty ground and swapped places; now it takes that fight over only once its own is finished, and the second half closes as it does. The two runs compare the whole state of the game every 30 seconds, and if they ever disagree the rest is filmed the old way, finding fights as they happen. A skirmish without `-seed` is handed one, the same for both runs. The film opens on every player at once: the screen cut into one picture per player along lines that meet round the radar, two players on a diagonal and four on an X, each picture on that player's base. Every picture gets the same share of the screen, whatever its shape: the lines used to stand at a fixed 45 degrees, and on a 16:9 screen three players got a sliver of 14% at the top and two big halves below, and at 21:9 the sliver was 10%. Now each has a third. Seven seconds in they sweep away to the Director's single view, which stays on the first player's base until something happens instead of gliding across empty ground to another one. When two real fights far apart are both worth watching, the radar slides out of its corner, then the second fight sweeps in from the corner along the screen's diagonal, carrying the radar in a frame of the same line to the middle, one fight on each side with its own camera gliding to it. Going back is the same film run backwards: the second fight sweeps out with the radar, and the radar slides back into its corner. The lines are the Reforged gold on a dark edge, so they read on snow and at night, and they run straight into the radar's frame. In its corner the radar sits flush against the bottom and left of the picture with a thin gold edge on its top and right only, where it used to stand in a heavy frame a few pixels in from the corner. Under each line and round the radar lies a soft band of the Reforged blue. The pictures slide into place first, and only then does the gold draw out from where the lines meet, over most of a second, with the band fading in behind it and the radar's frame tracing its gold round the map once the radar has arrived; going out, the gold pulls back in before the pictures leave. The opening plays it the same way from the first player's full view. While the screen stays cut a bright white-gold light runs out along every line every five seconds, the opening included. At first all of this ran inside the half second the pictures take to slide, and on film the lines were already whole by the third frame. While the screen is cut, each picture frames its own fight: the camera puts it in the biggest round space its slice has clear of the lines and the radar, and rises until the whole fight fits there with room to spare, never lower than the Director flies and never more than three times as high. A fight that spreads is let out smoothly; one that shrinks does not make the picture pump in and out. The single view rises and settles over a second and a half when it reaches a fight, where it used to glide in for seconds and then step back up in a third of one, and the hand-over between the cut screen and the single view is one camera: the opening's last picture used to jump sideways about fifty paces the moment it became the Director's. When the Director moves onto the second half's fight, that half is the one that stays: it widens to fill the screen and carries straight on as the single view, where the other half used to fill the screen and the camera then cut across the map. The opening frames each player's base the same way. A split holds at least six seconds after its second picture is all the way in and ends once the second fight has burnt down to a quarter of the first, and the picture then stays whole four seconds even for a fight the first run saw coming, so it does not flicker between one and two. Inside a split no picture ever jumps. A split ends the usual way after eighteen seconds, or the moment either half's fight is over or moves on to somewhere else, and only then does the camera go where the next fight is; in an eight-player film one split stayed up for three minutes while the main half was thrown across the map to six new fights, once by 2,900 paces as it was still sweeping in. The two fights have to be further apart than either half's picture is wide once it has risen to fit its fight, so no piece of ground shows in both: at a fixed 660 the two halves of a 1v1 showed the same bridge from neighbouring angles. A crowd beside the Director's fight that the first run saw as part of it does not split the screen either; that was the Director's own fight spreading, and the second half swept in for two seconds before the camera followed it there. Only the video shows the other pictures; the window keeps the Director's own fight under the lines. Two bases going up are not a fight, and the split ends the moment the camera's own fight and the second one turn out to be the same. The pictures go straight into ffmpeg as they are drawn, so an hour of 1080p does not need tens of gigabytes of disk first; put ffmpeg beside the game or on your PATH, because without it nothing is recorded and the game says so and closes. While the screen is split the score bar slides up off the top with the radar's slide, so the pictures have the whole screen, and it comes back down when they go; it hangs in the radar's own frame, a thin gold edge on a soft blue halo down its sides and along its foot. The film carries a score bar across the top in the Reforged colours, the match clock in a tab over it and every side in one row, "Team A vs Team B vs" a player alone: a card a player, his colour along its top, his name in that colour, his general (a computer player goes by his general with his difficulty under it, where every one of them used to read "Hard AI"), then on one line his cash and what his army cost, the army's figure labelled so the two never get mixed up; the bar is 77 rows of a 720p picture for a 1v1 where its first cut took 126: the general or difficulty stands at the right end of the name's line instead of on a line of its own, and the clock, the armies' bar and the colour strip along each card are thinner. A player's name past about fourteen letters ends in an ellipsis, so one player called thirty letters long no longer widens every card on the bar or runs into the general beside his own. The plates over the opening's and a split's pictures and the Defeated and Victory banners cut a long name the same way, each to the room it has; a computer player's general is always written out whole. A team's cards sit together under its name and its army's total. Under the whole row is one bar the armies pull on, each player's share in his colour and a gold mark at the middle when two sides play, so whoever is past it is ahead. From five players on the cards stand in two rows, a team never broken across them, and each card keeps to one line, the name and the army's value, so the type stays at its full size: eight players in one row had shrunk it to letters six pixels tall that nobody could read in motion. Eight alone take 94 rows of a 720p picture, a 4v4 with its two team names 130. A dark colour like purple is lightened where it is text, so it reads on the bar's ground, and the gold player's colour gets a dark edge two pixels wide even at 720p so it does not melt into the gold lines. A skirmish can be staged in any shape now, 4v1 or three players alone beside a pair: `-team 4 0` puts slot 4 on team 0. The opening seats teammates next to each other and names their team on their plates, and a split names a team as "Team A" where a player alone keeps his own name. Each picture of the opening names its player on a plate hanging just over his command centre, and the plate stays on the building as the camera rises and the pictures sweep away. The name sits over his general and team in smaller type, and the plate stays wholly inside its picture: in an eight-player opening the lines used to cut it down to "ank General Team A", and in a 4v1 the top one hid under the score bar. Each half of a split names the players in its fight, in a plate inside its own slice clear of the lines and the radar, and while the halves sweep in it rides above its fight, where it used to slide down over it. It is sized from the screen's height and reads the same at 720p and 1080p, and the pictures under it are framed below it, so no base or fight sits behind the bar. Any recorded clip also plays its animations at their real speed now. The animation clock used to move by however long each picture took to save, and a slow disk made every explosion in the footage run fast. In a two-player film each half of the split belongs to one player for the whole match, the first player in the upper left and his opponent in the lower right from the opening's two bases on, each half on wherever that player's own guns are firing or, when they are quiet, on his base and his army; the screen used to show whichever two fights were hottest, often both in one player's half, and a 1v1 now splits about every twenty seconds where an earlier rule had cut it to a few times a match. The radar draws a view box for each half while the screen is cut, where it used to mark only the upper left one.
- The film shows who fired what. When a player uses a general's power, a small flag drops out from under his card in the score bar carrying the power's icon, hangs there four seconds and pulls back up; a superweapon's flag is edged in gold. Every power a player fires gets its flag the moment he fires it, the command centre's spy satellite included, so a power with nothing to film still shows on the bar, and a player who fires two in quick succession has them wait their turn under his card. An upgrade he finishes buying drops its own flag the same way, behind any power waiting there. A power that lands takes the camera straight away: the Director used to finish the four seconds it gives any shot first, and in the first cup film a spy satellite was on screen three seconds late. With the first run's notes the camera is already waiting where the power will land before it is fired. A superweapon is filmed where it hits, not in its silo. Two powers landing far apart at once split the screen, one half each, however recently the last split went: fights still split only rarely. A power holds the camera thirty seconds at most; a particle cannon fired into the middle of the map kept it there for eight minutes in the first cup film while every other power went by unfilmed, because the battle round its target never stopped. Riflemen shooting at riflemen count for a quarter of what they did, so a small infantry skirmish rarely takes the camera from tanks, buildings or a power. The single view no longer carries an "X vs Y" plate under the score bar; the halves of a split and the opening keep theirs. A player knocked out no longer blinks out of the bar. His card flashes red with a line drawn through his name, and a second later it closes while the cards beside it slide into the room it leaves, where the whole row used to jump on the frame he lost. At the same moment a banner opens across the lower part of the picture with his name and general under a red Defeated. The match no longer cuts off on the frame the last card falls, either: the film runs three and a half seconds past the decision, so the last defeat plays out and the winner's banner comes up in gold beneath it.
- Watching, tick Fog of war under the camera and you see what the player you follow sees and nothing more: black where he has never been, grey where he has been, none of the enemy he cannot see, and an enemy base as he last saw it. Stealth goes by his eyes too: a Jarmen Kell he has not found is gone from the screen and the radar, and his own stealthed units show the way they show him. It stays on whoever drives the camera, until you switch it off or follow nobody. Switch to another player and his fog comes in whole, shadows included: a building he has never seen casts nothing on his grey ground. An observer used to have no fog at all: the whole map, all match, with no way to see the game the way one of its players was seeing it.
- An ally, and anyone watching, now sees a stealthed unit's muzzle flash, its promotion and the cash it earns - if they can see the unit at all. Those three asked 'is it mine' instead of 'can I see it', so allies and observers got nothing.
- A match started from the command line with `-observer` and `-takeover` is watched as an observer again. The game sat the watcher in the first driverless seat instead, so he saw that player's fog, and an enemy Colonel Burton, Black Lotus or Jarmen Kell walking under his camouflage was not drawn at all until he fired. Now every stealthed unit shows translucent, the way its owner sees it. The match itself plays exactly as before.
- Watching, the match opens on the middle of the map. An observer has no start position, so the game looked for the camera waypoint of "player zero", did not find it, and fell back to the corner of the map: every match watched from the stands began pointed at empty ground in the south west.
- Watching, you can click a stealth building. The rule that stops you selecting an enemy you cannot see never asked who was asking, so an observer, and a player already knocked out, could see a stealthed structure on the map and not pick it up to read it. A spectator commands nothing and sees everything already, so there is nothing there to give away.
- Watching, the promotions every general has bought are on screen the whole match: a strip of them in the bottom right corner, one row per player in his own colour. There was nowhere else to find this out - the promotion screen filled itself in with the watcher's own player, who has no general and no command sets at all, so a spectator got a blank screen.
- Watching, clicking one player's unit watches him, and clicking empty ground puts the whole match back. The screen wears his side's metal and the promotions on the right are his alone. The promotion key then opens his promotion screen, on his side's artwork, with his skill points and his rank - greyed out, because they are not yours to spend. It is the same size a player's is; picking his unit rebuilt the bar under a watcher and the screen came up a quarter narrower, its pictures squeezed thin. With nothing selected the key does nothing; there is no one general to show.
- A general who has taken Artillery Barrage to level 3 shows one Artillery Barrage on the promotions strip, not three copies of the same picture in a row.
- The strips close up again: across a row the trays slide an eighth of a tray under each other, so a row reads as one run of metal. The cameos never overlap each other, because every tray goes down before any picture does.
- Watching, the top left corner is clear. The promotions and superweapon shelves that stood there are gone.
- Watching, an observer's board sits on the right of the screen, built from the command bar's own steel, and the steel is the watched side's: grey for America, red for China, sand for GLA, changing when you select a unit of another side: every player's general, his name in his colour, the number in gold, and under it a bar in the same colour as his name. In a two-sided match the bars used to go green for one side and red for the other, so a blue name could stand over a red bar. It opens on net worth, the cash in hand plus what everything the player has standing would cost to build again, counted twice a second, richest first. Its drop-downs close when you click anywhere else, on the battlefield, the radar or another drop-down, instead of staying open until you picked something in them.
- The number the board ranks by is yours to pick from the drop-down at its top: net worth, cash, income per minute, army value, kills and losses, the general's rank and power. The list re-sorts the moment you choose. The command bar's keys pick them too while you watch, Q W E R T Y and A, and the drop-down writes each stat's key beside it.
- A button under the list opens the armies: every player's six most expensive kinds of unit in cameo trays, with how many of each he has on the field. The generals' emblems on the board stand bare, with no tray round them.
- The drop-downs on the right open over the board instead of pushing it down the screen.
- The superweapon countdowns and the promotions each general has bought moved into a panel on the left, one row per player with his general at the head of it, where they used to be two strips down the right-hand edge.
- A superweapon coming ready or being fired is a line of that feed: whose it is, its picture and its name, then "ready to fire" in green or "launched" in red. Only a watcher used to be told, and only when one came ready.
- The feed also says when a general's power is used, when a promotion is bought, and when a superweapon, a Strategy Center, a Propaganda Center or a Palace goes up and when it is finished, each with its picture. A player is told that about himself and his allies, a watcher about everybody; a finished superweapon is told to everybody, as the announcer already did. A Spectre Gunship called from three command centers on the same frame is one line, not three. A player whose last dozer dies, or last worker for the GLA, gets a line too, since he can build nothing more until he makes another.
- Watching, the selected unit's health shows beside its portrait again, and the right-hand column (the camera and follow drop-downs, the board, the armies) and the replay strip are drawn at the command bar's scale, about 30% smaller than they were, so one HUD Size setting sizes all of it. Clicking or dragging the radar while the camera is on Director or Player used to be undone a moment later by the automatic camera; the click takes the camera now and it stays where you put it.
- Chat sits in the bottom left corner over the event feed, with room left for the whole feed so neither covers the other, the way Dota writes it: each line opens on the speaker's general's flag and his name in his colour. A conversation stays up for ten seconds after its last line and then fades out as one. Enter talks to your team and Shift+Enter to everybody, in a dark typing bar under the lines that says whom it goes to, with the last eight lines kept up while you type. The next Enter after sending opens the chat again straight away. Watchers can chat now as well, and so can a player who has been beaten; what they write reaches the other watchers and never the players still fighting.
- Both are an ordinary web page with a stylesheet, in the game's Window folder. Change the colours, the sizes or the order there and the next match you watch draws it that way, and the page opens in a browser too.
- A minimised command bar stays minimised. Changing seats, or clicking another player's unit while watching, put the whole bar back up over the battlefield you had just cleared. A new match still opens with the bar up.
- The command bar's frame is drawn new, in the same steel as the boards. Each panel holds one thing and is exactly its size, the radar, the command grid, the portrait with the experience bar, and wears a steel border outside it. Grey for America, red for China, sand for GLA. It slides and minimises with the bar, and like the boards it is a page in the Window folder; take the page away and the old painted bar comes back.
- The command bar is laid out anew, all of it running rightwards from the bottom left corner, and it is smaller: at 1920x1080 it stands 248 pixels tall where the old bar took 312, and it ends a third of the way across, so the rest of the screen's bottom edge is battlefield but for the general's powers in the corner. The radar sits in the corner, taller than before so its top lines up with the power bar's, with your general's experience bar standing beside it, and on its top edge the under-attack light, the skills key with your rank's stars on that, and over the stars the idle worker button whenever a worker stands idle. Next to it is one grid of eighteen buttons, six across and three down, and every button is its own key: Q W E R T Y over A S D F G H over Z X C V B N. No more two-key building shortcuts and no second bars: a dozer's buildings, a factory's units, a unit's abilities and upgrades and its orders all share the grid, each a single press. The orders stay put whatever you select. For a unit, A attacks, S stops, D attack-moves, V moves, Z ejects the passengers, X guards and C holds position; for a building, N sells it, B sets its rally point and Z empties its garrison. Workers keep three of their own: N clears mines on every side's worker and dozer, H swaps a GLA worker between real and fake buildings, and B is the Demolition worker's suicide charge. Everything else goes in rows by what it is for. A dozer or worker puts what makes your army along the top row, barracks, factories, airfield and command center; its defenses along the middle row; power, supply, tech and the superweapon along the bottom. Every side's builder files the same kind of building on the same row, so the war factory is up top whether you play USA, China or GLA, with nothing selected as well. The GLA fakes take the top row too, and H swaps between real and fake from the same place on both. A unit's abilities and upgrades share the top row, a building's upgrades sit on the row under the units it trains, and a transport's or a bunker's passengers gather in the bottom right corner, one button each. A row that runs out of room carries on in the row below it, so a command center's general's powers read in order from A across to Z and never end up beside the dozer. Only the buttons your selection has are drawn, and with nothing selected the grid stays as a plate of bare steel. Its buttons are a fifth bigger than the rest of the bar's, so what you build stands out. Attack, hold position and move are buttons now, where no unit ever had one, with pictures painted to sit among the game's own: a crosshair on a red plate over a burning sky, a raised palm on a blue one, an arrow on a green diamond. V, or a click on the arrow, is a move for the left button: the next click on the ground sends the selection there, and a left drag lays them out along the line you draw. Beside the grid, on the bottom edge of the screen, runs a portrait bar only as long as what it holds. Select one unit and its upgrades follow its portrait; select a group and the bar holds every kind of unit in it once, each with how many you have, the one Tab has picked lit and the rest dimmed. Point at an upgrade and its card tells you what it is and what it does; point at a group's picture and it names the unit and how many you have. The power bar lies along the top of the grid, and your money sits on its left end, so both are one glance from the buttons you spend them on. The Legacy mouse and keyboard and the W A S D camera are gone from the Options screen: there is one way to play, and an Options.ini that still names them loads as it always did.
- HUD Size on the Interface page of Options draws the command bar and everything along the bottom of the screen at 115, 130 or 150 percent of the size your resolution gives it. On a big monitor at a high resolution the bar can be read from the sofa again. It changes the moment you Accept.
- Every panel of the bar is only as big as what it holds now, and stands on the bottom of the screen. The radar's border runs out to the screen's left edge. The power bar lies in a steel groove of its own along the top of the command grid, twenty cells that light up from the left with your production and fill the groove when full, the consumption marked by a white needle across it. The money stands on the power bar's left end in a steel plate of its own, the figure in a dark well that is only as wide as the figure. It widens the moment your money gains a digit and waits three seconds before it narrows again, so it keeps still while the figure bobs around 10000 as you build. The figure and your income stay on one line at every resolution; at 1280x720 the income used to drop under the money and hang out of the plate. Everything the old painting filled round them is battlefield again, and a click there lands on the battlefield.
- The bar's own buttons are drawn to match, steel caps lit gold under the pointer and pressed in when pushed. The menu is a small square with three bars in the screen's top left corner. The idle worker button is a key like the smoke signals', a hard hat on it, in a steel tab over your rank's stars, where it no longer hides the end of the power bar. While a worker stands idle it flashes amber a little faster than once a second, and goes dark the moment every worker has a job. The bar's steel is 40 percent darker than it was, so the pictures on it stand out and it sits quieter against the battlefield. Each button stands in its own dark cell with steel running between them, and the steel is laid over the edge of every picture the way a frame holds a card, the whole picture showing inside it. The production queue and the general's powers are framed the same way. The power bar is sunk into the same steel as the build grid, lying along its top, and is as long as the grid on every side, where it used to change length from one faction to the next. The build grid's panel no longer carries an empty strip down its left side. There is no chat button any more: Enter opens the chat as it always did. The beacon button is gone from the bar too; the smoke signals over the radar are how you point your team at a spot. The portrait sits in the radar's lit steel too. The experience bar beside it is ten gold rungs in a sunk groove, climbing from the bottom as you earn your way to the next rank, and your rank stands in a steel tab on the portrait's top right corner, a key sunk in it like the idle worker's with one star for every rank there is, gold up to the one you hold. A watcher has nothing to promote and no longer gets the tab, which used to hang half into the screen's corner. Its button goes with it: a watcher who clicked a unit used to find an empty patch of screen there that still showed the promotions tooltip and opened the promotion screen. The portrait's grid is steel between dark cells on every side, where America's was drawn in blue lines that matched nothing else on the bar. That key is the promotions button: point at it and it comes up with a gold rim, it blinks bright in your side's own steel while you have a promotion to spend, and a click opens the promotion screen. That screen is rebuilt in the same steel and half its old size: each rank's promotions stand in a grid of build-button cells five wide, like the command grid, an empty place a dark hole, each rank in a steel well of its own with its heading, the wells a plate's thickness apart, the grid's steel laid over the edge of every picture so the picture sits in its cell like a card in a frame, your rank and the points to spend on one line over the experience bar, and Done in the last row's spare place. A gold rim marks what you have bought and a light one what you can buy now. It comes up the way the Esc menu does, the battlefield behind it dimmed to 65% black and the screen fading in over an eighth of a second; the side's old painted screen no longer fades in over it for the first nine frames. The bar has no minimise arrow any more: it is only as big as what it holds. The radar sits sunk in a bezel of lit steel, bright along the top and shadowed down the right, and the build grid and the money wear the same steel, the figure in a dark window of its own, and the under-attack light is a long red lamp set in a steel tab on its top left corner, dark until you are hit and then blinking. No words on it, so it reads the same in any language.
- The general's powers you have bought and can fire, the column that climbed the right edge of the screen, stand in the bottom right corner now in a tray of the bar's own steel. The first sits in the corner against the right edge of the screen, and each one you gain takes the place to the left of the last, three to a row before a new row starts above, so the tray is only ever as big as what you hold and an empty one takes no room at all. Each power sits on a dark cell three quarters the size of a build button, where the side's old tray art used to frame it. It is always out; there is no button to fold it away.
- Three buttons sit side by side in a step of the radar's own steel, on its top edge: the smoke signals Alt+Z, X and C send. Press one and the pointer turns to a cross; your next click puts the signal there, on the ground or on the radar, and a right click or Escape takes it back; until now a button dropped its smoke in the middle of your view. Every signal now leaves a mark on the ground in your colour for ten seconds, and the radar ping lasts as long: crossed swords to attack, a shield to defend, an eye to look, each in a ring a few tanks across, fading out over its last two seconds. Each is a key sunk into the steel with a sharp white picture on it instead of a word: a crosshair to attack, a shield to defend, an eye to look. Point at one and it comes up out of its well as lit steel with a gold rim, and it sinks in darker while you hold the button down. They rise into place one after another from the bottom of the screen when the match starts. A game with nobody on your side to see the smoke, a skirmish against the computer or a replay, has no signal buttons at all.
- Tooltips wear the bar's steel. Point at a build button and a card opens right above it rather than in a fixed box at the side: the name on a steel header in your side's colour with the price in gold at its end, every "Power Supplied: 5" or "Strong: infantry" line of the description laid out as a label and a bold figure, then the unit's health, damage, attacks a second, damage a second, range and build time in gold, counted with the upgrades you own. Under them every upgrade that touches the unit and what it does to it: a Gattling Tank's card says Chain Guns takes its damage from 15 to 18 and its damage a second from 37 to 46, a Humvee's that TOW adds a 50 damage missile with a range of 317, and an upgrade you already bought turns gold. Point at the upgrade itself and the card lists the units it changes, Composite Armor putting a Crusader from 480 health to 680. An upgrade you already own still says what it does: its card keeps the description and puts the already-purchased note under it. At the bottom, "not enough money" or what you still need in a sunk red note at the bottom. Point at something on the battlefield and a small dark box beside the pointer names it, its owner's colour in a stripe down the left edge.
- The readout in the top right corner is a box of its own: the time of day, the match time and the real time beside it, the logic rate and the frame rate, the renderer and the frame number. In a network game it adds how many frames are ready out of the input delay, the room's frame rate and the traffic in and out, and under a unit limit your count against it. It is on unless you switch it off: untick Info Box on Options > Interface and the superweapon timers move up into the corner it left.
- The steel between the build buttons, the portrait's grid and the promotion screen's cells is half as wide as it was, so the pictures take the room. The queue's tray has a thinner rim. The portrait and its upgrade icons sit under the portrait's grid, framed the same way as every other picture on the bar.
- Point at Camo Netting's icon beside a GLA unit's portrait and its card used to say MISSING where the description belongs. EA left a second Camo Netting button in the data that no building offers, its text name mistyped, and the card read that one first. It reads the button you buy it from now.
- The arrow between a figure and its upgraded value on a card came out as three stray characters. It is an arrow again.
- Every figure on a build card says in brackets what it counts. Damage is one shot of the main weapon before the target's armour, attack speed has the reload counted in, damage a second is the two multiplied, a range of 10 is one square of the placement grid, and the build time is what your power and factories give you right now. The upgrade list says which side of the arrow is without the upgrade and which is with it, and an armour upgrade such as Composite Armor says that less of each hit gets through instead of a bare "stronger". English and Turkish.
- The command bar slides up from the bottom of the screen again when a match starts. The new steel frame had been drawn at its final place from the first frame, so the buttons rose into a frame that was already standing.
- A building that is still going up shows Cancel on S, and the seconds it has left across the top of the grid. A map building that hands out units shows that countdown there too, with the bar under it. Sell stands on N. One that sets a rally point puts that on B instead. Both used to stay where the old command panel had drawn them, off the new grid.
- The Escape menu is Zero Hour's own again, the window, the logo, the buttons and the way it opens, along with the box that asks whether you really want to leave. The steel plate that replaced it for a while, and ControlBar Pro's version after that, are gone. Options on it opens the whole options screen. The promotion screen opens across the middle of the screen.
- Watching, click a player's button on the observer bar and you see through his eyes: his fog and his camera. The same button again, the cancel button or Esc gives you the whole map and the camera you had before.

## Placing buildings

- The placement grid is drawn on the ground and follows the slope, and reaches twice as far as it used to.
- Unbuildable ground is a soft red wash, crossed out square by square.
- The grid tells you why a square is closed. Red is something standing on it. Yellow hazard stripes on a dark wash are the ground itself: water, a cliff, rock no vehicle crosses, and the strip along the map's edge where nothing may be built, which used to look like open dirt until the ghost turned red over it. A building too big for the slope it is on stripes the ground under it as well, so a red ghost on a hillside no longer leaves you hunting for the rock that is not there. The stripes and the red tell apart by pattern as well as by colour.
- Running out of money no longer strands the ghost on the map.
- Holding shift and clicking out a row of buildings no longer stops halfway and selects one.
- Hold shift and drag, and the row is one stroke. Press where the first building goes, drag the way the row runs, and a ghost appears for every building that fits end to end along the line, all facing the way the first one was turned. The row runs exactly the way you drag it, at 20 degrees as happily as along the map's edge, and packs the buildings as close as their shape allows: one turned onto the line of the row stands wall to wall with the next, and a factory keeps its door lane clear. A row of Power Plants turned square to the map packs 44 apart; it used to go down on whole grid squares, 50 apart, with a strip of dirt at every joint. It stops at the last building your bank can pay for. A ghost that lands on a rock or someone's tank turns red and is left out when you let go; the rest go up. With two or three workers selected the buildings are shared out to the nearest free one, and the ones nobody is free for wait as plans until a worker comes off its job. A plain drag still turns the building, and walls still tile the way they always did.
- While that row is on the cursor, the wheel opens and closes the space between the buildings, one grid square a notch. The one where you pressed and the one under the cursor stay put; what changes is how many stand between them and how far apart those are. It will not pack them any tighter than they already sit against each other, and it will not take either end away to make the gap. Letting go places the row and takes the building off the cursor, so the next click is not another one. Holding shift and clicking them out one at a time still keeps the ghost up.
- Hold Alt and drag while placing a building, and you lay out a block of them instead of a row. Ghosts stand for as many as your money covers, a blocked spot is skipped, and your builders work through the block in order.
- With nothing selected the command bar shows your builders' buildings again, and only those: clearing mines and the Demolition worker's suicide charge stay on a worker you actually select. Put one down and the idle worker nearest the spot walks over and builds it; when every worker is busy, the nearest one takes it on after the job in hand. A shift-dragged row placed this way is shared out among your idle workers. The bar keeps showing the same worker while you place, so a GLA worker switched to fake buildings stays on that page, and a fake is only ever handed to a worker who is on it. That last part holds with workers selected too: select a real-page and a fake-page worker together and a building goes to the one that can build it, where it used to go to the nearest and be refused. A replay with such a mixed selection in it plays back differently. The worker lending the bar its buildings no longer shows up beside them: its portrait, name and health filled the selection box, and players took the empty bar for a selected worker. The box stays empty until you select something. The one interface took all of this away for everyone; it is back as Build Without A Worker on the launcher's Options page, on unless you untick it, and off the bar stays empty until you select a worker, as in 2003.
- Turning a building no longer turns everything you build afterwards. A wheeled heading still carries from one wall to the next, but the next supply centre comes out facing the way it was designed to.
- A building you point at blocked ground slides to the nearest spot it fits, and lands there.
- The pointer keeps its build cursor while you place, even passing over your own buildings.
- GLA defences get a range ring while you site them.
- The ground a defence on your cursor can shoot into is painted red. It used to be the thin white guard circle, which read as the edge of a building's footprint more than as a field of fire; now it is a thin line in the owner's colour, and the line sits exactly where the game stops allowing the shot: the weapon's range measured from the edge of the building, not from its middle. While any building is on your cursor, or when you click a turret, every armed building of yours and your allies' shows its reach as well, and one player's overlapping circles join into one outline, so the gap between two Patriot batteries is something you can see before you pay for the third. The enemy's defences draw nothing, not while you place a building and not when you click one of them: how far a Gattling Cannon reaches and which corner behind it is blind are things you learn by losing a tank there. An observer still sees every side's.
- Inside that red area, the ground the defence cannot see is shaded. A Patriot battery, a Gattling Cannon or a Fire Base does not shoot through a building - the game refuses the shot when a solid structure stands between the gun and its target - so from where your cursor is, each building in range throws a shadow that starts at its near wall and runs out to the edge of the reach, a wedge that swings as you move the defence round the corner of your War Factory. Hills count as well. The game will not pick a target when the ground rises between the top of the gun and the top of a tank, so the far side of a ridge goes dark too, and a valley beyond it lights up again where the gun can see down into it. The shade lies on the ground as one piece and follows its slopes. A corner one of your turrets, or an ally's, already sees into is not a hole, so it stays bright: the shade is only what nothing of yours can shoot. A Stinger Site or a bunker gets no shade, because a building in the way does not stop them. Click one of your defences, or an ally's, that is already standing and it shows the same shade from where it stands, its own and nobody else's, so the corner behind your War Factory is there to see after the turret is built too.
- A defence's ring is now the ground it actually fires on. A Patriot battery's ring sat at the reach of the missile it only fires when another Patriot calls for help, twice as far as it shoots on its own, and a Gattling Cannon's at the reach of its anti-air gun, so a tank could park well inside either ring and never take a shot. Both rings now end where the ground gun ends, about half their old size. A Fire Base cannot drop a shell right under its own walls, and that patch round it is shaded now. The shade behind a hill is worked out for the lowest raider in the game, a Rocket Buggy or a Combat Cycle, so ground left bright is ground the gun sees whatever drives over it.
- Clicking a turret in a base full of them no longer drags the game down. Every circle's outline was worked out again against every other circle on every frame, so with 120 Patriot batteries on the map one selected battery took the game from 94 frames a second to 53. The outlines are worked out once and kept until a building goes up, comes down or comes out of the fog: the same base now holds 83 with the battery selected against 84 with nothing selected.
- Selecting a GLA supply stash no longer puts reach circles round every defence on the map. The stash spawns workers, a worker carries a weapon for clearing mines, and that was enough to count the stash as armed.
- Two buildings can no longer be put down on the same spot online. A build order travels to the other players before anything appears on the ground, and every click made while it was in flight was answered by a map that still showed the square as empty - so a shift-held row on a bad connection came out as buildings standing inside each other. The ghost now knows about the orders you have already spent, and turns red over them or slides to the square beside; and the order itself is checked again where it lands, on every machine, after the first building is standing. A second one aimed at the same ground is refused there and costs you nothing. What the ghost remembered of each order was the square around the building rather than the building, and a building standing at an angle, which is how most of them come out, fills barely half its square: a shift-clicked row of them found its neighbour in the way, slid off, and left a gap. It remembers the building's own outline now, and five Power Plants clicked side by side stand wall to wall.
- A building you put down next to another snaps against it. Click a little short of the neighbour, or a little into it, and the ghost slides along the way you stepped until the two touch, lined up with it. Clicking out a row by eye used to leave a strip of dirt at every other joint, or zigzag when the buildings stood at an angle to the row: the grid only has room for a building every 10, a diagonal building touches its neighbour somewhere in between, and a ghost pushed back out of a neighbour was thrown a whole square too far. Leave more than a square and a half between them and the gap stays where you put it.
- A right click drops the building on your cursor even when the click wobbled on the way. Pull far enough to scroll the map and the building stays, so you can go and find the spot first. Sending a dozer off somewhere in the middle of a shift-held row moved it and left the ghost riding the cursor, because the cancel only counted a press that had not moved a pixel and a hand on the way to a destination always moves a few.
- The command bar is driven by its own grid of keys - the buttons in the shape they are in, under your left hand - and there is no longer a switch for it. It shipped off by default, which meant nobody ever saw it.
- Escape cancels what you were doing before it opens the menu.

## Where the money is, and where it is coming from

- Supply piles and docks say what is left in them, in cash, over the pile. No more guessing which expansion is worth taking from the art on the model. Point at a pile and the tooltip puts a percentage beside the cash: what is left of what the pile started with.
- Every build button carries its price in the top right corner, opposite the build time already in the other one. It was only ever in the tooltip, which means hovering one button at a time to compare two of them.
- A structure's button says what it does to the power grid, in the fourth corner: what it draws, or what a plant puts back. Money and time were already on the button and power is the third thing a base spends; it was the one figure you had to hover for, which is the wrong way round for the building you are putting up because the lights went out.
- A worker leaves a supply pile the instant its load is done. After taking its last box it used to stand at the pile for one more full loading cycle, taking nothing. Every worker you own now brings in a little more money per trip.
- A worker loads in one go instead of a box at a time. It used to take one, wait a loading cycle, take the next, wait again; now the whole load changes hands once and the wait is that load's worth of time - four boxes cost what four boxes always cost, in one stretch rather than four. Money in the bank is unchanged, which is the point: three headless matches on the same seeds came back within a few percent of what they earned before.
- A GLA worker can no longer mint money standing still. Build a stash as close to a supply pile as the game allows and a worker could end up in the gap between them, touching both. It loaded at the pile and unloaded at the stash without taking a step, a $75 box every second, and the popups stacked over its head. Every hand-over now waits until a worker could have walked the gap, so that worker earns what a worker walking the shortest trip earns: with a stash hugging a pile, two workers brought in 101 boxes in a minute before and 50 now. Workers that do walk are untouched; a stash placed so they have to earned exactly the same, box for box, before and after.
- A supply trip pays what it paid in the original game. A GLA worker brings back one box, $75, a Chinese truck four, $300, and a Chinook eight, $600; the Chinook was never touched. Workers and trucks load at their old speed again, and Worker Shoes adds its 8 dollars a box on top of the speed. From v3.0.0 to v3.5.1 a worker carried three boxes and a truck six, each loading slower to match, which held all three sides between 49 and 60 dollars a second off one pile at any distance. That evening out is gone with the bigger loads: when these numbers were last measured, in October, five workers made 90 a second with the stash beside the pile and 27 with it 250 feet away, while three trucks stayed near 50 and three Chinooks at 55. Turkiye's truck is built on the Chinese one and carries four boxes too. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- Supply points refill themselves, slowly, and faster the more of a base has grown around them. A warehouse used to be a fixed lump of money that ran out and left the map with nothing to fight over: whoever mined out the middle first had the game, and the second half of every match was played on income neither side could earn any more. Six hundred dollars comes back every forty seconds standing on its own, every twenty with one supply centre built near it, every thirteen with two - up to what the point started with, never past it. A single box was too little to be worth the trip: a hundred dollars every forty seconds is less than the harvester earns going to fetch it, so a mined-out point stayed mined out as far as anybody playing was concerned. Both sides expanding onto the same patch make it richer and then have to decide which of them keeps it.
- Your workers tell you a supply point has run dry once a match. With piles refilling, they ran dry again and again, and every time the same worker said so.
- Workers stop hesitating on their way in and out. A dock has a queue outside it and a worker treated its place in that queue as a destination: it drove to the spot, stopped dead, waited a frame, drove to the door, stopped again, and only then went in - twice a load, and nearly every load with nothing else queued. With the dock empty it drives straight in. The first version of that also skipped the walk to a supply pile or a GLA stash, which have no door of their own, so a worker a long way off played its loading animation where it stood and was paid anyway. In a four-player test match 72 loads were picked up or dropped off away from the dock, one of them 613 feet from it; now there are none.
- Workers leave other players' supply piles alone. A truck whose pile ran dry went to the nearest pile it could reach, and that was often the one next to a neighbour's supply centre, where it either stood in his queue or stood idle beside the pile with nowhere of its own to carry the boxes. A pile now belongs to whoever has the closest supply centre beside it, and your trucks, Chinooks and workers only pick their own or a free one. The computer counts those piles out too, so it no longer buys trucks for a neighbour's supplies. Across two 4v4 matches on Twilight Flame, trucks were sent to someone else's pile 109 times; now none are, and the money mined stayed within about one percent. A truck you send to a pile yourself still goes where you sent it.
- The white bar over a building's health bar means one of two things: a factory working through its queue, or a superweapon charging. Oil derricks, the black market, supply drop zones, hackers and workers carried one too, each on a money clock nobody can hurry, and a base full of them buried the two bars worth reading. They wear only their health bar now.
- A hacker already at work stays at work when you tell a group of hackers to hack. It used to fold its laptop away and set it up again, and the payout it was halfway to started over from nothing. One that is packing up takes the order and unpacks again. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- A hacker you leave standing goes to work by itself. After ten seconds with no order it walks into your nearest Internet Center with a free seat, if one is close by, or else opens its laptop where it stands. Any order you give starts the ten seconds over, and one you stop, or call out of a building, stays put until you give it another. The computer's hackers already did this.
- A hacker earns six times the experience per payout it used to. On the long rank ladder EA's rate never got a hacker to Heroic in a whole match; now it gets there in about the 17 minutes it took in the original game. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- A hacker working from inside an Internet Center shows what it earns. The green figure floats over the building on every payout, the way it does over one sitting in the field. It never appeared, because the game asked the hacker whether it could be seen and a garrisoned unit is not drawn at all - which is the one place a hacker is meant to work.
- Factories take a hundred units in the queue, not nine. The build queue only ever had nine buttons and that had become the limit.
- A match can pay everyone a wage. `MoneyPerMinute` in `GameData.ini` drops the same sum into every
  living player's account on the minute, on top of whatever they are mining, which is the knob a
  map needs to run a game that is not about holding the supply piles. Zero, and therefore
  absent, unless somebody asks for it: on a stock install nothing changes. Measured on one seed with
  four Hard computers at 7,777 a minute, three of the four spent between 3,400 and 6,200 more in
  the first three minutes and put the difference on the map.

- The minimap says where the money and the capturable buildings are, with the dollar and the star from the lobby map preview. Oil derricks, hospitals and repair pads never showed on it at all, and supply piles vanished with the rest of the map under the fog, so the two things worth walking a rifleman across the map for were the two things the minimap would not tell you about. They are marked on ground you have walked over, one mark per place rather than one per pile, and the mark stays through the fog once you have been there, because a supply pile does not move. A pile that runs dry drops off it. Country you have never scouted keeps its marks to itself: for a while the minimap gave you every dollar sign on the map from the first second, which is a scouting report nobody paid for.

## Health bars

- You pick who wears one. `HealthBars` in `Options.ini` takes 0 for everyone, 1 for smart, 2 for the selection only and 3 for nobody. Smart is the one worth trying: a bar over a unit at full health tells you what its absence would have told you, so healthy units go bare and anything that has been hit stays marked, with whatever you have selected or are pointing at readable either way. 2 is what the original game did. The default is 0, so nothing changes until you change it.
- A health bar keeps its size against the unit at any resolution. It was a fixed number of pixels wide and three tall, so the bigger the screen the thinner the thread over a tank.
- Health bars are green to red again, the way Zero Hour drew them: green at full health, yellow at half, red near the end. For a while they wore the owner's colour, and a red player's healthy tank looked like one about to die. A disabled building keeps the blue. If you liked knowing whose a bar was at a glance, the launcher's Options page has it back as a choice: Health Bar Color set to Player Color paints every bar in its owner's colour, and the length alone says how hurt it is. Green to red stays the default.
- A building's bar sits above its roof rather than inside its art.
- A unit that is inside a transport and also disabled wears the blue bar. Being carried and being knocked out were asked as one question, so the two together answered no: a squad EMP'd inside a bunker, or hacked while riding a Battle Bus, looked perfectly healthy from outside.
- A building being captured wears a capture clock under its health bar, filling in the colour of whoever is taking it. The building flashes while a rifleman works on it, which says somebody is at the door and nothing about whether that is nearly over: the choice between driving across to shoot him and carrying on with your fight was made blind. The bar runs from the moment he reaches the door to the moment the building changes hands, and Black Lotus hacking one gets the same bar.
- The progress bar stacked over the health bar is white, on a factory turning out a tank and on a silo charging. It was yellow, which is a colour the game already spends on your own units and on damage, and a strip of it sitting directly above a coloured health bar read as part of the same bar.
- A slow gun shows when it can fire again. A Nuke Cannon sat still for ten seconds after every shell with nothing on screen to say when the next would come. Now an amber bar over the health bar fills through the reload, on your own unit while it is selected or under the pointer. Only a gun that fires slower than one shot in three seconds gets one: every tank gun in the game reloads in about two, and a bar that empties before you can read it is noise. The Nuke Cannon, the Inferno Cannon, the artillery platform, SCUD and Tomahawk launchers, the Scorpion's missile and the Comanche's anti-tank missiles wear it.
- The reload bar stays off the quick shooters. It used to go up whenever a wait ran past three seconds, and a reload after a fast clip does that too: a Paladin that zapped one infantryman with its point defence laser wore the bar for the next four seconds, and so did a Rocket Buggy after every volley and a Comanche after its rocket pods. Those fire about as often as a tank does, so the bar now goes by how many shots a gun gets off in a minute, reload included.
- A Dozer clearing mines no longer wears the reload bar. Its scoop takes four seconds between mines, which counted as a slow gun, so the bar came up over every Dozer sweeping a minefield as if it were waiting to fire. Clearing mines is not firing, and the Worker's clearing goes without the bar too.
- Every garrisonable building shows how full it is, whoever holds it, with a green chip for each soldier inside and a hollow one for each free window. A city block nobody holds wears nothing over it, where a map full of houses used to carry a row of grey boxes on every roof. A Barracks wears its row only while a soldier is inside healing, where it used to carry ten empty boxes for the whole match. A Tunnel Network still shows its free slots when nobody is in it; untick Empty Building Slots on Options > Interface and it wears its row only while somebody is inside.
- A vehicle's load stays private.
- What you have selected wears a white frame just outside its bar, so a selection is still readable in a crowd where every unit carries a bar - and the bar itself keeps its owner colour all the way round.
- Lamps, barrels, rocks and bushes no longer wear health bars.
- Nor does a booby trap. It cannot be shot and has one hit point, so its bar was a full green line that never moved, hanging over something that is meant to be hidden.
- A soldier killed by toxin or fire no longer melts or runs burning under a full health bar. The game swaps the dead man for a stand-in that plays the death for three seconds, and with bars on for everyone that stand-in wore one, full to the end. Anything you cannot click, which the townsfolk walking about a map also are, goes without a bar now, as it did in the original.
- The planes a general's power calls in wear their health bars again. A-10s, B-52s, B-3s, the MiG napalm strike, the carrier's Raptors, the carpet bomber and every side's cargo plane with its paratroopers or supply crates cannot be clicked either, and the change above took their bars along with the dead soldiers'. Your anti-air is shooting at them, and now you can see it working.
- A plane that only delivers, the Supply Drop Zone's cargo plane or a paradrop, no longer trails a row of empty passenger boxes. It is a hundred-seat transport nobody can order to unload, and with some game data it drew all hundred boxes in a line across the screen beside its health bar. A transport you cannot select shows no boxes now; your Chinook and your Battle Bus keep theirs.
- The Spy Drone shows its health to its owner. It never had a bar: it is marked as something nothing can interact with, so enemies leave it alone, and the rule that keeps poison clouds bare took the drone's bar along with theirs. EA's own note on the drone's other marking says you can point at it to see its health, and now you can.
- Bridges no longer float a health bar over the middle of the river. There was never anything under it: the span is part of the terrain, and the bar belonged to an invisible marker standing in the water.
- The bar is part of the unit now: click it and you select whoever it belongs to. Zoomed out, an infantryman is a few pixels of helmet under a bar that is far easier to hit, and a unit half behind a building still has its bar in the clear. It only answers clicks that would have missed everything anyway, so it never takes a click away from the unit you were actually pointing at, and right-clicking bare ground under a bar still orders a move. And it stands down the moment you have something selected: with a force in hand your clicks are aimed at the ground, and a bar hanging over that ground used to cost you the whole selection and hand you back a single passer-by.
- The city itself stops wearing them too. A building nobody owns shows a bar only if there is something to do about it - troops can go inside, or it can be taken. A row of houses does not, and neither does the concrete apron each of them stands on, which is a separate two-thousand-point object that was drawing a second bar down at street level.

## Twenty-two-year-old bugs, found by testing

- A Supply Drop Zone's cargo plane shot down on its way off the map no longer says "unit lost". Nor does a paradrop plane, an A-10, a B-52 or any other plane a general's power sends over, nor a single member of an angry mob. None of them is a unit you command, and the score never counted them as lost; only the announcer did, so with six drop zones up a "unit lost" could come every twenty seconds for planes that had already delivered.
- A match no longer freezes when a unit attacking or hunting with its team changes its orders at the wrong moment. Switching targets could throw away the unit's order logic while it was still being used; the log then filled with "no state 0, in state 10" and the game stopped on one frame until Windows closed it. The order logic now lives until the switch is done.
- A Nuke Cannon on guard stays deployed between targets. After every kill it packed up to drive back to the spot it was already standing on, then set up again, so a guarding cannon spent most of a fight folding and unfolding: four Technicals driven into its range one after another cost it four pack-ups and four set-ups, and now cost it none. It still packs up for a move order or a target out of reach. The Sentry Drone guards the same way. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- A Nuke Cannon no longer sets up for something that is about to leave. It took 3.3 seconds to unpack for any target in reach that instant, so a Humvee driving through was gone when it finished, and it packed again without a shot: 6.7 seconds with the barrel in the air for nothing. It now looks at where a moving target is headed, at the speed it has that moment, and unpacks only if that target will still be in reach. A target that stands still in reach always gets the unpack. The look used to come one moment too late: on the instant you gave the order the cannon had not yet taken the target as its own, so a Humvee that had set off a sixth of a second earlier still got the full unpack and drove out of reach before the barrel was up. It looks from the instant of the order now; in the test the cannon stays packed, follows the Humvee and sets up once it parks. The Sentry Drone takes the same look over its one second of unpacking. Replays recorded before this change play out differently.
- Pressing Continue after a campaign mission goes straight to the next one. The main menu used to wake up behind the score screen on the way out, show its buttons and start loading its own background battle, so the menu sat on screen over the next mission's load.
- The main menu no longer opens with a man screaming. The battle behind it is staged the way EA laid it out: Jarmen Kell sits on the cliff over the GLA infantry as scenery, and the extra reach high ground gives in a match let his rifle hit them from nearly twice its range a quarter of a second after the menu came up. High ground adds nothing behind the menu now, so the first soldier falls about six seconds in, under the battleship's shells, as he always did. Soldiers' death cries on the battlefield also sit back at their own volume; the boost that lifts your units' replies over the guns had been catching them too.
- A civilian car no longer drives into your base in the first minute of every game. A map's civilians are owned by a computer player like any other, and the scouting pass looks for anything of that player's that can drive - so it was picking a parked car out of the scenery and sending it to a start position. A side with no faction and no build list has nothing to learn from the map and does not scout.
- A rifleman pulled off an oil derrick mid-capture left it flashing and chiming for the rest of the match, and the derrick changed hands anyway with nobody standing on it. Walking away now stops the capture, whether you or the computer gave the order.
- Every countdown on screen was a second too long. Rounding up a whole number of seconds gave a whole number plus one, so a ten second build said eleven - production queues, buildings going up, superweapons, all of it.
- A Chinese silo researching an upgrade while its missile charged drew both bars and both countdowns in the same row of pixels. They stack now.
- Soldiers moving diagonally ran up to 40% faster than their own stat sheet. Tanks and cars still do, as they always did in Zero Hour.
