Middle-mouse panning left the screen too, and edge scrolling in a window is still yours by name in `Options.ini` if the default is wrong for your setup.
- Grid placement, 45 degree building rotation, snapping to nearby buildings, nudging a blocked building and 45 degree camera steps are checkboxes on the Controls page in both Classic and Reforged, and every one starts unticked, the way 1.04 played. A setting you saved while they were on does not carry over: the boxes start empty once and remember what you pick after that. Snap to Nearby Buildings pulls a building put down a cell or so short of another one flush against its edge. Nudge Blocked Placement slides a building whose spot is taken by a rock or another building's footprint to the nearest place it fits, instead of turning it red under the cursor. With grid placement off a building goes down exactly where the cursor puts it, and the white grid lines under the ghost go with it. The red squares where nothing can be built still show, so you can see the rock before you click on it.
- The mouse wheel has its own Zoom Speed slider on the Controls page, in both interfaces, and at 100% a notch moves the camera as far as it always did. The slider above it is now called Camera Scroll Speed and says what it covers: the screen edge, the arrow keys and the right-button drag. That drag never followed it. Only a small minimum under the drag changed with the slider, so moving it from 50 to 100 made a 40 pixel right drag about two percent faster; the whole drag follows it now, and at the default it drags exactly as before.
- A page no longer says its own name twice. Every tab used to open onto a heading repeating the word already written on the button you just pressed, with a rule under it dividing nothing from nothing.
- An open dropdown covers what is under it instead of the other way round. The list of resolutions grew downwards behind the labels below it, so half the entries were readable and half were words on top of words.
- Every button, slider and checkbox is the artwork the game already had, down to the fonts and the hover colours.
- The Graphics page says what you are choosing. A grey line under the detail preset tells you what that preset turns on, and that picking it only fills in the boxes until you press Accept. Labels say what you will see: Cast Shadows and Flat Shadows instead of 3D and 2D, Ground Pattern, Soft Shorelines, Trees And Bushes, Units Behind Buildings. Every tooltip, in English and Turkish, ends with when the setting takes effect: on Accept, from the next map, or the next time the game starts. Antialiasing and texture filtering used to promise a change "when the display device resets" that never came during play; they say next start now, which is when they apply, and antialiasing says plainly that only the old renderer uses it.
- Writing a line into `Options.ini` by hand still works, and the screen shows you what is in there when it opens. Window mode takes effect the moment you accept it; antialiasing applies the next time the game starts.
- The Defaults button still resets what it always reset, which is the original settings. The new rows keep their values.
- The main menu's buttons no longer show through the options screen. Solo Play to Exit Game used to sit as faint ghosts behind the right of every page; they step aside while the screen is open and come back when it closes. The main menu's logo and frame stay.
- The options screen matches the other menus. Refresh NAT and the Hotkeys page's Change, No key and Game's key buttons are lettered in capitals like Accept and Cancel, and the Hotkeys lists use the menus' colours: a heading green, a key you changed gold, an empty one grey-blue, and only a clash red. The notes under the resolution, the detail preset and the Hotkeys lists take the same grey-blue.

## The whole game in Turkish

- Options, Gameplay, Language: English or Türkçe. Pick Türkçe and the next launch has Turkish menus, command bar buttons and their tooltips, unit and building names, general's powers, mission briefings, objectives, hints, loading screens, score screens, the lobby, the strategy advice after a match and the credits. That is 3,853 lines, every one the game shows except the ones that read the same in both languages: multiplayer map names, people's names, and unit codenames like Crusader and Overlord, which Turkish players call them anyway.
- It reads like a game, not a dictionary. One glossary of more than 1,400 terms fixed every name before a line was written, so the building your tooltip calls Savaş Fabrikası is a Savaş Fabrikası on the button, in the briefing and in the hint. GLA briefings keep their zeal, Chinese ones their drill and American ones their clipped radio voice.
- Percentages are written the Turkish way, "yüzde 25", and every number the game fills into a sentence lands where it should. A check runs over the whole file on every build and refuses a line whose blanks do not match the English, the mistake that turns a translated tooltip into a crash.
- The one-key shortcuts work in Turkish. Kışla and Komuta Merkezi both wanted K on the dozer, and the game hands a letter to the first button that asks and leaves the others with none, so 297 places on the command bars had a button that answered no key. Each now has its own letter inside its own name, and the ones that sat on İ or Ş, which the shortcut never caught, moved to a plain letter: the Dozer is D, the Worker I. One clash is left, on the Tank general's command center, where Tank İndirme and Toplanma Noktası both want T and Tank İndirme has no other letter free.
- Voices and videos stay as your install has them. Your language is your own screen's business: two players in one match can read it in two languages.
- A line the translation does not carry falls back to English instead of showing a key name, so a string added later never leaves a hole.

## Now in German too

- Options, Gameplay, Language has a third entry, Deutsch. The next launch speaks German everywhere the Turkish version does, from the main menu to the credits: 3,848 lines. Map names, people's names and the unit codenames stay as English players know them, Crusader, Overlord and Scud Storm among them.
- One name per thing. A Tech-Gebäude is a Tech-Gebäude in the tooltip, the hint and the academy advice, every radio message from headquarters opens with EINGEHENDE FUNKMELDUNG, and the fog over unexplored ground is Kriegsnebel wherever the game mentions it.
- You are a General and the game says du to you. Percentages read "25 Prozent", and the same check that guards the Turkish file refuses any German line whose blanks would not match the English.
- The one-key shortcuts work in German. No two buttons on a command bar share a letter, so Bewachen, Stopp and Sammelpunkt each answer their own key on every unit and building that carries them. One exception is left, on the Boss general's upgraded barracks, where Colonel Burton and Neutronenminen both want N.

## It fits your monitor

- The writing on screen grows with your monitor now. Every panel is stretched to your resolution and always was, but the text inside it stayed the size it was drawn at in 2003, and what growth there was stopped dead at twice - so on a 2560 wide screen a command bar three times its original size still wore eight point lettering. The keys on the build buttons, the prices and the build times were the worst of it: at 2K they were drawn, and unreadable.
- The strip of everything your base is building follows the screen too, instead of staying a row of postage stamps under a command bar three times its size.
- On a widescreen monitor the command bar is three pieces instead of one stretched strip. It was drawn for a 4:3 screen and every measurement in it is multiplied by your resolution separately across and down, so at 16:9 the whole thing came out a third wider than it is tall: square build pictures as rectangles, and one slab of metal across the entire bottom edge. The radar now sits hard in the left corner, the build grid in the middle, the selected unit's panel hard in the right corner, each at the size it was drawn at, and the battlefield shows through the two gaps that opens. At 4:3 the three pieces meet and it is the bar it has always been. The three pieces reach the screen: the paintings stop a pixel or two inside their own edges, which left a hairline of ground down both sides and along the bottom, and anything that close to an edge is now that edge. The American middle piece stands on the bottom edge like the other two sides' do, instead of hanging ten units high with a band of battlefield under the build grid, your money now sits in the middle of its readout instead of riding the top rim of it, and the build buttons are centred in the panel they are drawn on instead of pushing against its left edge with a strip of empty metal on the right. The stray pixels along the right-hand edges of the pieces are gone: a one-pixel light line down the side of the middle piece, and a lit speck sitting in the battlefield next to the bottom corner of the Chinese radar. Both were the same thing. The bar's artwork was being rescaled as it went to the graphics card, which left the last column of each picture holding a mirrored copy of it, and the last column of pixels on screen drew from there.
- The rest of the interface is drawn at the command bar's size, not the screen's width. The queue strip, the superweapon countdowns, the generals' powers bar down the right edge and the rank screen were each measured against how wide your monitor is, and the bar they sit beside is measured against the smaller of the two dimensions - so on a 16:9 screen a queue picture came out a third bigger than the build button it is a picture of, and the power slots were oblong where they were drawn square. One size for all of it now, and it is the bar's own.
- The generals' powers bar stands on the right edge of the screen instead of hanging off it. It slides in from the right when a power is ready, and the slide stopped one step short of where it was going and left the window there - twenty-one pixels out at 1024x768 - so the rightmost column of powers was drawn half off the monitor and could not be clicked. Every panel in the game that slides in sideways had the same fault; the ones that slide up and down never did.
- The writing on a build button keeps its size against the button. The hotkey letter, the price, the build time and the queue count were sized off how wide your monitor is while the bar they sit on is sized off the smaller of its width and its height, so the wider the screen the further the lettering grew away from the cameo underneath it. One size for both now, and it is the bar's.
- Text keeps pace with the panel it sits in. The original grew its lettering at seven tenths of the rate it grew the panels, so the bigger your screen the more empty metal surrounded every label: at 1920x1080 a tooltip's text was two sizes smaller than the box drawn for it. It grows at the full rate now, which puts it at exactly the proportions the artists laid out at 800x600.
- Text is heavier. Every letter's soft edge was two thirds see-through, so light writing on the dark panels thinned to hairlines at the sizes tooltips and buttons use. The edges keep more of their weight now, while the solid middle of each stroke is unchanged.
- Build tooltips no longer paint one letter of the unit's name yellow. That letter was the old one-key shortcut, and the grid keys on the buttons replaced it; the yellow copy was drawn on top of a gap left in the name, so any letter the yellow pass could not draw, the ş in a Turkish name for one, simply went missing from the word.
- An ultrawide monitor gets the same interface as a 16:9 one. Everything still sized off how wide the screen is came apart at 32:9: on a 5120x1440 screen the lettering was drawn at two and a half times what the panel under it had grown to, the clock and speed readout crept into the top corner because its margins were flat pixels, and a health bar reached across the whole base of the building it belonged to. All of it now measures off the same number the command bar does. Scale a 32:9 screenshot down to 16:9 and the two lie on top of each other.
- The camera shows the same ground whatever shape your monitor is. The game holds the angle it sees across the screen fixed and lets the up-and-down angle shrink as the screen widens, which at 32:9 left fifteen degrees of world against twenty-nine at 16:9 - the same barracks filled twice the height of the screen, and it read as a zoom nobody asked for. Above 16:9 the view opens sideways instead, so a wider monitor buys more battlefield rather than a closer look at less of it. Nothing at 16:9 or below moves.
- The camera reaches the corners of the map. It stopped short of every edge by an amount that changed with the zoom and the angle, so a base in a corner never came to the middle of the screen. It now goes 200 units past any edge of the map, whatever the zoom. `CameraBoundaryMargin` in `Options.ini` sets how far, and 0 puts the old limit back.
- The medals on the player info card are round on any screen. They were stretched across and down separately, so a wide monitor turned each one into an oval.
- Minimising the command bar sends all three panels down, and they slide back up when you bring them back. The old minimise dropped the bar a tenth of the screen and left a strip of metal, a readable money box and the top of the radar dish lying along the bottom edge, which is neither the bar nor out of the way. The radar and the middle go off the screen entirely; the selection panel stops with the row its minimise tab is in standing on the bottom corner, so what you click to bring the bar back is that tab with its own artwork behind it, not a button floating over the battlefield. 
- Everything on the command bar that each faction places for itself lands where that faction's artwork paints it. The bar's own arithmetic was overwriting those positions with the ones it had used a moment earlier, so every panel wore the generic layout's vertical placement instead of its own: the minimise button drew a second tab below the painted one, arrow and all, and the GLA money sat high enough in its box to touch the frame. One arrow now, one tab, and the number in the middle of its readout - and the same correction reaches the worker, beacon, chat and options buttons down the side of the grid. The American power bar sits in its rail as well: it was drawing on the ledge above the rail, which put the left half of the bar on the battlefield rather than on the bar, and left the rail it reads in standing empty.
- Two stray letters, an "S" and an "M", no longer appear over the battlefield beside the selection panel the first time you minimise the bar and bring it back. They are the labels on the two unused minimise buttons the 2003 layout ships hidden; minimising hid them a second time and un-hid them on the way back.
- The markings on a build button - the shortcut letters, the price, the build time, the queue count - are set bold. At seven points against a busy cameo the light weight read as part of the picture.
- Menu panels slide in at the same speed whatever your monitor is. They travel the width of the
  screen but moved at a fixed forty pixels a step, so the wider the screen the longer every
  transition took: twenty steps at 800 wide, sixty-four at 2560.
- A screenshot no longer takes the game down when the window is bigger than the desktop. Asking for
  a 1600x1200 window on a 1080-tall monitor puts part of it off the screen, and the capture read
  the whole client area out of a buffer that stops at the desktop's edge.
- A screenshot is a picture of the game. With anti-aliasing switched on, the capture could not read
  the frame the game had just drawn, so it photographed the desktop instead and said nothing about
  it. In a window with something in front of the game, that something is what you got: a browser, a
  chat window, whatever was on top. It reads the frame itself now, anti-aliasing or not, and what is
  in front of the window makes no difference to what comes out.
- The arrow on a dropdown is square at every resolution. It was drawn into a slot of a fixed 21 pixels wide however tall the box around it was stretched, so the bigger the screen the more the arrow was squeezed.
- The promotion screen closes when you press its key again, however fast you press it. The screen fades in, and the fade drives the window itself for several frames either way - so a second press during the fade read the screen as still shut and opened it again, and a press just after it was closed was undone by the fade's next frame.
- The command bar stops changing under you while you are using it. With nothing selected the bar shows one of your builders so you can place a structure without picking a dozer first, and it showed whichever one happened to be idle - so a dozer finishing a building on the far side of the base took the bar over, dropping a half-typed build hotkey and taking the structure off your cursor. The builder you are working with keeps the bar.
- The command bar's artwork moves with the command bar. Minimising it slid the buttons off the bottom of the screen and left the metal they sit on painted over the battlefield; the same painting stood still through the slide the bar makes when a match opens. It travels with the bar and goes with it.
- The lines from your selection to where it is headed can be switched off. Options > Interface has an Order Lines box, on by default. Off, a unit sent to one place shows no line to it, and only the line goes: the marker on the spot or on the tank or building it was sent at stays, and so does the ring flashing where you clicked. For a few versions the box took those away too, which left a click with no sign it had landed. A shift queue and a waypoint path keep their lines, stop to stop, and a building's rally line stays too: those are plans you are still reading, and with the box off v3.0.0 took their lines away as well. The line you draw while dragging a formation still shows, because that one is the order being given. It changes the moment you press Accept.
- Zoom to cursor is a box on Options > Controls again, in Classic and Reforged, and starts unticked: the wheel zooms on the middle of the screen, as it did in 1.04, until you ask for the cursor. A tick saved while it defaulted on does not carry over. It also stopped fighting you. The camera corrected itself a frame after each step of the zoom, so the ground slid off the cursor and was pulled back the whole way in, and the last pull landed after the zoom had finished, as a small jump towards the cursor. And a wheel spun over a spot with no ground under it, out past the edge of the map, threw the camera to the corner of the map. The ground under the cursor stays under it on every frame now, and a spot with no ground zooms on the middle of the screen.
- Scrolling keeps up with the zoom. The camera moved the same distance over the ground at every height, so right down on the ground the map flew past and from the farthest zoom it crawled, ten times slower across the screen, and turning the scroll speed up hardly showed. The pace now follows the zoom: where a map opens it is exactly what it was, zoomed out it covers ground as fast as the picture shows it, and the scroll speed slider sets that pace at every height. Arrow keys, the screen's edges and a right drag all go by it, in Classic and Reforged alike.
- Orders land where you clicked when the camera is right down on the ground. Zoomed all the way in, a right click sent the units to the corner of the map instead of to the spot under the pointer, and the marker and the line went there with them. The game works out what you clicked on by firing a line from the camera at the ground, and that line was thrown away whenever the camera itself had dropped below the height of the tallest hill on the map - so it went wrong on hilly maps first and stayed fine on flat ones, which is why it looked random.
- Click through the command bar wherever its metal is not. The bar is three shaped plates with sloped tops and cut corners, but it caught clicks over the whole rectangle each plate sits in, so a unit standing in the sky above the radar's slope, or in the notch beside the command grid, could not be clicked or ordered to. Between 3 and 22 percent of each plate's rectangle is empty, depending on the side and the panel. Those parts belong to the battlefield now, and the buttons and metal still take every click they did.
- Drag the camera across the radar. Press on the radar and keep the button down, and the camera follows the cursor over the map until you let go; before, it jumped once per click, so crossing the map meant clicking your way over it. The left button that moves the camera with a click is the one that drags it, and with nothing selected the right one does too. Run the left button off the side of the radar and the camera waits at the edge of the map. It keeps following while the arrow keys are scrolling too, which used to leave the drag dead until the key came up. A selection box dragged onto the radar from the battlefield leaves the camera where it is.
- Widescreen resolutions are back in the options menu, and the list works during a match. It was greyed out the moment a game started, because changing it rebuilt the menus and then pushed the main menu over whatever you were playing. It rebuilds the menus for later and leaves you on the battlefield with the command bar back up.
- Changing the resolution during a match no longer takes the game down. Two things were behind it. The old command bar's windows were handed back while the menu system still had them on its list, so the next thing that painted a button read whatever had since been written over it. And the bar itself was thrown away and built from scratch, which handed out fresh copies of every build button while your factories, your repair crews and the promotion screen went on pointing at the old ones. The bar's windows are rebuilt now and the bar keeps everything that is not a window.
- One command bar, not three. Changing the resolution during a match rebuilt the bar and left the old one behind, still drawn and still taking clicks at the size of the screen it was built for - and the confirmation box you answer afterwards rebuilds it a second time, so two mode changes in a row put three command bars on top of each other across the bottom of the battlefield. The code that was meant to throw the old one away asked the window system for a window called "ControlBar.wnd", and the bar's window is called "ControlBar.wnd:ControlBarParent", so it never found anything to throw away and never had.
- Your money is still your money after a resolution change. The command bar is rebuilt at the new size and its readout comes back holding the placeholder its layout ships with, three dollar signs, and the game only writes a number into it when the amount changes - so until you next sold, spent or collected something, that is what the box said.
- The menus you already had open are rebuilt at the new size too. A panel is stretched to the screen once, when it is built, so everything on screen when the mode changed - the in-game menu, the diplomacy panel, the chat line, the replay controls - carried on wearing the shape of the screen that had gone: drawn a proportion of a screen away from where it belongs, and on a smaller screen partly off the edge. The in-game menu is the one that mattered. It pauses the match and takes input off you until you press Return, and pressing Return is impossible when the button is no longer on the monitor.
- The command bar stays on the bottom edge of the screen. Minimising it and bringing it back lifted a few pieces that had never gone down in the first place, and every rebuild of the layout lifted them a little further, so over a long match the bar climbed off its own strip and the build tooltip, which is placed against it, ended up above the top of the screen. Each piece is now put back by exactly the amount it was moved by.
- The other half of that had the money readout, the general's tabs and the column of small buttons stranded a couple of hundred pixels above the bar, floating over the battlefield with the bar itself still sitting where it belongs. The bar takes a fifth of a second to slide back up when you un-minimise it, and anything that redrew the panel artwork during that fifth of a second measured every one of those pieces against a bar that had not arrived yet, then wrote the wrong answer down as if it were the right one. Switching general, changing faction colours and a resolution change all redraw it, so in a long match it happened sooner or later. The bar is put where it belongs before any of that is measured. Over six thousand frames of a match that minimises and rebuilds the bar every second, the top edge of everything it owns now reads the same number every single time.
- Tooltips stay on the screen. A tooltip is drawn to the right of the pointer, and near the right or bottom edge it jumps to the other side to make room, which was all the original code did about edges - the man who wrote it left a note saying so. Nothing then checked where it had jumped to. A wide one, and the game will wrap a tooltip to the full width of the screen when the text asks for it, jumped clean off the left edge with the first half of the sentence outside the monitor; a long narrow one hovered near the top went off the top. Both are put back on the screen now, and the pointer sits over the corner of the box rather than the words going where nobody can read them.
- The rank screen is one painting instead of a stretched one. It is sized from that painting at the same scale as everything else and centred on the screen, rather than multiplied out separately across and down from the corner it was authored in - which on a widescreen monitor made it a third too wide and pushed it off centre.
- Borderless fullscreen: start with `-borderless` and the game fills the screen at your desktop resolution with no frame and no display mode change, so alt-tab is instant, nothing on the desktop gets shuffled around behind it, and a second monitor stays usable. Screen-edge scrolling works there, the way it does in fullscreen. The loading picture still opens as its own small window with your desktop around it, and the game only takes the screen once it has something to draw.
- Borderless and fullscreen keep the mouse on the game's own screen while you are playing. With a second monitor beside it the pointer slid straight over the edge onto the other screen, so edge-scrolling toward that side did nothing and the next click landed on your desktop. The game has asked for the pointer to be held since 2003, but only a mouse driver the game never uses ever did it. Alt-tab still lets go, and coming back takes the pointer only once you move it over the game again. A plain window leaves it free, as before.
- Fullscreen, borderless and windowed are one saved setting now, so borderless no longer means adding a switch to your shortcut every time. `WindowMode` in `Options.ini` takes 0, 1 or 2 in that order; a switch on the command line still wins for that one run. Picking a different one applies when you press Accept instead of the next time you start the game: the window loses or gains its frame and the display device is rebuilt on the spot. Borderless takes your desktop resolution and nothing else, so while it is selected the resolution list greys out and the other two modes hand it straight back.
- Play on whichever monitor you like. Options > Display has a Monitor box that lists every screen on your desktop by its number and its name, and the resolution list under it holds the sizes that screen can show rather than the ones the main screen happens to have. Fullscreen changes that monitor's resolution and leaves the others alone, borderless covers it at its own resolution, and a window opens in the middle of it. The game used to go on the main monitor and nowhere else. It moves when you press Accept, and the next launch opens on the same screen.
- Antialiasing is a saved setting as well: `MSAA` in `Options.ini`, 0 for off through 4 for sixteen samples. `-msaa 4` still works and still wins for that run. Whatever your card will not give is stepped down instead of refused, so asking for six samples gets you four rather than nothing.
- Texture filtering is yours to set. `TextureFilter` in `Options.ini` takes 0 for bilinear, 1 for
  trilinear and 2 for anisotropic, and `Anisotropy` takes the sample count, 0 meaning whatever your
  card offers. The default is anisotropic at the card's maximum: retail shipped bilinear with point
  mip selection, which was a 2003 fill-rate budget and is why distant ground shimmered.
- Picking High detail gives you high resolution textures. The setting was ignored: the resolution came from a machine benchmark that answers 'low' on anything modern, so there was no way to ask for better.
- The main menu plays its battle again instead of showing one still picture. The game asks Windows how much memory the machine has and compares the answer against a 256MB minimum, and on a machine with more than 4GB installed that answer arrived as minus one - so the better the machine, the more certain the game was that it did not meet the 2003 minimum. It switched off the animated menu, forced textures down and, at the preset detail levels, took the trees out. It reads the real figure now.
- A setting you typed into `Options.ini` by hand survives opening the options screen. A value the
  matching slider could not reach was thrown away rather than clamped, and the slider then sat on
  its minimum - which is what got written back when you pressed Accept. Whatever the slider cannot
  show now reads as the nearest end of its track instead of the bottom of it.
- The Default button in the options menu no longer throws away your resolution. It reset the display along with everything else, dropping you to 800x600 with no undo.
- Text does not vanish at large sizes. Any font over 100 points simply failed to load, which on a 4K screen is a missing line of interface.
- Zoom further out, with the whole map drawn instead of black corners. The ceiling is twice what it was again, which is the difference between watching your own half of the map and watching both.
- The zoom-out ceiling is the same for everyone; no setting buys you a wider view.
- A nuke or a Scud Storm launched from the bottom of a fully zoomed-out screen climbs out of the top of it before it turns. EA flew the nuke at 500 and topped the Scud out at 634, low enough that from that height you watched the whole flight and knew where it was going before it got there. Both now climb to about 900, out of the picture on every screen shape from 16:9 to 5:4. The nuke flies faster to keep its time, so a far shot lands when it always did; the Scud missiles are a third faster at cruise and land a far shot within a twentieth of a second of the old time. A near target waits about half a second longer, since the missile still has the extra height to climb and come down.
- The wheel covers that whole range in about fourteen notches instead of thirty-eight.
- Hold Ctrl and the wheel zooms five times as fast. With a building on the cursor, Ctrl and the wheel still turn the building.
- The wheel brings the camera a quarter nearer the ground than the game's own limit, the same for every player, so the Closer Zoom slider is gone from Options > Controls. Zoomed all the way out, the camera now stops about a tenth lower than it did.
- Zoom toward the cursor works; the spot under your pointer stays there.
- Zoomed in over uneven ground, the camera holds still. Keeping the spot under the pointer moved the camera over different ground, the camera then settled to a new height, which moved it again, and on hilly ground that went on forever as a slow rocking forward and back.
- The camera stays above the ground. Zoomed in on a slope it used to end up inside the hill it was looking over, and the world opened up along the near plane.
- The far edge of the view opens with the height, instead of stopping at a distance fixed for the stock zoom - which is what put black beyond the terrain when you zoom out past it.
- The box on the radar follows the camera when you pan. It only ever redrew itself when the zoom or the angle changed, so scrolling left it behind.
- The camera turns in whole 45-degree steps, instantly, while you hold the key.
- Edge scrolling works windowed, and scroll speed no longer follows your frame rate. It also stops when you take the pointer off the window. Windows says nothing about a cursor that has walked out onto the desktop, so the game kept reading the last edge it crossed and the map slid on its own until you brought the mouse back. A game that has only just opened asks Windows where the pointer actually is instead of assuming the top left corner, which is an edge like any other and used to drag the camera there before you had touched anything.
- Edge scrolling starts as the pointer nears the edge of the screen and speeds up the closer it gets, reaching the old speed at the edge itself. Over the command bar and the minimap nothing moves until the last three pixels.
- Taking over another base no longer squeezes the picture into the top four fifths of the screen.
- A match opens with the camera 300 over the ground, close enough to read your base, in Classic and Reforged alike. Start Zoomed Out on Options > Controls opens it as far out as the wheel goes instead; it starts unticked.
- Hold Ctrl and roll the wheel to turn a building before placing it.
- Buildings can snap to the grid the game itself plans movement on. Tick grid placement on the Controls page; it starts unticked.
- The grid under a structure is drawn, with blocked squares crossed out.
- Snapping now uses the true cell offset and the building's concrete apron.
- A building faces the way you drag it, read at the moment you release.
- The mouse pointer stays visible for the whole placement.
- How see-through the structure on your cursor is, and whether it drops a shadow, are yours to set:
  `BuildPlacementOpacity` and `BuildPlacementShadows` in `GameData.ini`. The defaults are what the
  game always did.
- The menus move at whatever speed you want them to. `MenuTransitionSpeed` in `Options.ini` is a
  percentage: 100 is the pace the slides and fades were drawn at, 400 gets you from the main menu to
  a skirmish setup in a quarter of the time, 25 is for looking at them.
- The right mouse button can stop dragging the camera. With the alternate mouse layout it is the
  selection button, so every selection drag was also a camera drag; `RightMouseScroll = no` in
  `Options.ini` hands it back and leaves the middle button and the screen edge to scroll with.
- Alt+F4 and the window's close button quit the game. Both have always sent the message that means
  "leave now", and nothing was listening for it: the handler was switched off in 2003 and never
  switched back on, so the X in the corner did nothing and the only way out was the menus. A match
  in progress stops recording its replay first.
- The menus fill the screen again, in both interfaces and at every resolution. For a while they stood in a 4:3 frame in the middle, and in Classic the screen past it was black: at 2560x1080 that was 560 pixels of nothing down each side of the main menu, and players read it as a game that had not found their monitor. The main menu, skirmish, LAN, options, the load screens and the score screen are stretched edge to edge the way Zero Hour always drew them. The dialogs a match opens over the battlefield, the Esc menu and the options and save screens among them, keep their drawn shape in the middle. The dark plate behind Exit, Restart and the options screen covers the whole picture.

## Soldiers cast real shadows

- A shadow now softens as the thing casting it leaves the ground. Tracks, feet and crates keep the
  hard edge they always had, because the shadow starts where the object does; a helicopter's slides
  out from under it and spreads as it climbs, and pales with the same height, the way the sky fills
  a shadow back in. The game drew every shadow as one hard silhouette before this, whether it came
  off a tank's hull or off something twenty metres up, and edges that sharp are the tell that a
  picture was computed rather than photographed. This is what the game draws with now; a machine
  that cannot run the newer picture keeps the old shadows on its own, and Classic Graphics puts them
  back on any machine.
- A hovering helicopter has its shadow back, rotor blades and all. The softening spread a
  Comanche's thin body so wide that nothing of it was left on the ground, and the spinning blades
  never reached the shadow at all. Now the blades turn in the shadow as a star under the fuselage,
  still softer than a tank's.
- Headlights light the ground instead of shading it. At night a Humvee, an Avenger or a Sentry
  Drone with its lights on laid its own beam on the ground as a dark wedge in front of it, as if
  the light were a solid thing standing in the moonlight, and civilian cars, trucks and the lamps
  on night buildings did the same. A beam or a glow casts nothing now. Rotor blades, leaves,
  fences and flags keep their shadows. With nine vehicles parked on Dark Night's village square,
  44 beams and glows around them came out of the shadow.
- Zoomed all the way out, the top of the screen has its shadows. The sun's view of the battlefield
  was a fixed square around the middle of the screen, and from full height the far ground at the top
  lies well outside it, so buildings, trees and tanks up there stood on bright ground with nothing
  under them. The square now opens to whatever the camera sees, up to two and a half times as wide.
  At a map's normal playing height nothing changes.
- Shadow edges hold still while you scroll. The sun's view was meant to move across the map a whole
  shadow pixel at a time, and the rounding that did it measured the camera from itself, so it always
  came out at zero and every scroll slid the shadows' grain under the world: edges crawled and
  sparkled. And on a map with a low sun, the far end of a zoomed-out view lay past the depth the
  sun's view covers, so the ground up there lost its shadows and buildings nearest the sun dropped
  out of the map. The depth now grows with the view.
- A shadow stays on the ground when the thing casting it is just off the edge of the screen. A tree
  standing past the edge was dropped along with its shadow, so scrolling made shadows on the ground
  in view go out all at once; on Tournament Desert about eleven trees at a time were missing that
  way. Buildings and units on the older renderer did the same when they stood just past the edge.
  Now anything whose shadow can land in view keeps casting it.
- A building stands on the ground instead of sitting on top of it. There is a soft patch under every
  structure's footprint, the darkening a corner traps in daylight, and the shadow it casts starts at
  its own wall rather than a step away from it. The frame's corners and creases get the same
  treatment through the finishing passes. The patch goes with the building's shadow in the fog: an
  enemy base you have never scouted used to leave its dark footprints on grey ground, a map of
  where every building stood.
- A bridge stops the sun. A tank crossing one used to throw its shadow twice, on the deck where it
  belongs and again on the ground under the bridge, because the light went straight through the
  stone. The bridge now casts its own shadow across the bank and the water below it, a unit on the
  deck shadows the deck alone, and the side of the bridge that faces away from the sun is in shade.
- Infantry shadows are built from the pose: arms, head, weapon, moving with him.
- `UseShadowVolumesForSkins = No` puts the old flat blobs back.
- Scuds, rockets and falling bombs cast a shadow running along the ground. A missile climbing
  straight up throws a thin streak away from the sun now. It used to lay a short blob on the ground
  that spun every frame, as if the missile were tumbling. A missile that has climbed out of the top
  of the picture keeps its streak on the ground you can see; it used to vanish with the missile.
- An aircraft's shadow lands where the sun puts it, not underneath the aircraft. Every plane and helicopter in the game's own data asks for a sun "no lower than 89 degrees", so each one cast its shadow straight down and towed it along directly below itself at any height, while the tank beside it was lit by the map's real sun and threw its shadow off to the side. Aircraft now take the same sun as everything else: a helicopter's shadow slides out from under it as it climbs, and a plane's runs ahead of or behind it depending on the hour the map is set at. On a map lit by a very low sun the shadow is held to what a 30 degree sun would cast, so it does not stretch across half the screen. The flat blob shadows under missiles and bombs follow the same ray.
- A big smoke cloud darkens the ground under it and fades as it does.
- Smoke and dust stand in the sunlight. A column off a burning building throws a soft shadow as thick as the smoke is: a puff of dust barely tints the sand, a black plume darkens the ground, the tanks and the houses under it and the smoke behind it. The column itself is bright on the side facing the sun and goes dark on the far side, and a cloud drifting through a building's shadow greys over with everything else in there. A cloud used to cast a round patch straight down whichever way the sun stood, and took no shade from anything. Fire casts nothing, it is light. A machine that cannot run the newer picture keeps the round patch.
- Fire lights its own smoke. The bottom of a column over a burning tank glows orange from the flames under it and flickers with them, then goes grey as it climbs out of their reach; an explosion's flash warms the smoke drifting past it. Smoke used to keep the same flat grey right down into the fire. Both renderers draw it. On the newer picture the glow stays lit where the column's own shadow falls, so a fire burning on the far side of a plume still shows orange through it instead of going dark with the smoke around it.
- Rockets leave smoke. A Tank Hunter's or a Missile Defender's rocket, a Comanche's pods, a Raptor's missiles and a Patriot's used to fly on a thin bright line of fire and nothing else. Now one unbroken white vapour line hangs behind each one for just over a second, sitting on the fire line rather than floating above it, the width of the rocket where it leaves and about a sixth of a tank at its tail. A Patriot's line stays whole at full speed instead of breaking into a string of dots, a rocket that curves leaves a curve, and a volley of six stays six lines instead of one white bar. The fire line and the flash at the nose are still there. Scuds, Tomahawks and TOW missiles get the same treatment: EA let their exhaust swell into an orange-grey column 40 to 55 across, wider than the launcher that fired it, and now it opens on a short warm flash at the nozzle and runs out as a white line 6 to 12 across that follows the missile's climb without gaps. A Scud or a Tomahawk no longer drags a white ball of light behind it bigger than the launcher that fired it: the flash sits on the nozzle, about the width of the missile, and you see the missile climb and come down. The flash at the nose of the smaller rockets is half as bright, so a volley reads as rockets rather than a smear of light. On a low particle setting, or when the frame rate falls under 25, the rockets' white line is the first effect to go: with the slider at 300, a rocket fight that keeps the slider full draws no line at all and gives all 300 to the explosions and the rockets' own fire.
- The soft blob shadow for trees and scenery had never been drawn at all.
- Every one of the 128 tree types casts now, plus the bushes and palms.
- A tree's shadow is the tree. Trunk, crown, and the gaps between the leaves, lying along the
  ground in the direction the map's own sun points, and stretching the way a low evening sun
  stretches one. It sways when the tree sways, leans away from the tank pushing past it, and falls
  over with the tree when the tree comes down.
- The palms too, and every other tree the map placed as a real object rather than scenery. There
  are 278 of them on Golden Oasis and they had nothing under them at all; their shadow runs up and
  over the dunes instead of lying flat, because it asks the ground how high it is at every point it
  covers.
- Fences, walls and props cast a real shaped shadow, worked out once.
- Each of these switches off in `GameData.ini`.
- Shadow Quality on the launcher's Options page sets how sharp the shadows are. Medium is what the
  game always drew. High doubles the detail for about 64 MB of video memory, and Low halves it to
  free memory on a weak card, with the soft edges staying as wide as before at every level.

## Bright things can glow

- Explosions open on a white-hot flash. A tank shell, a rocket, a bomb truck or a dying tank now starts with a white core that cools through yellow and orange in a third of a second before EA's fireball takes over, and the core is as big as the blast: about a tank's width for a shell, much wider for a Scud Storm missile, a MOAB or a Daisy Cutter. On the default renderer the core spills into the screen's glow.
- A tank that blows up flashes once, short and warm, and its fire tears into five or six burning scraps that spin apart instead of swelling as one ball. Fourteen sparks fly up out of it, each dragging a short glowing streak that shrinks as the spark slows and falls; Explosion Debris Trails turned off takes them away. The fire, sparks, shrapnel, thrown dirt and the smaller blasts that follow spread over the tank's own hull and line up with the way it faced, so a long vehicle burns along its length and a small one goes up small; all of it used to burst from a round patch in the middle. The Overlord and the Emperor blow up the same way along their long hulls, torn fire and sparks included. A building that falls throws its fireballs, dust and shards over the ground it stood on: a firebase still goes up in one tight burst, while an airfield burns from end to end. Classic Graphics keeps EA's blast, and the Spectre's and the Firebase's howitzer shells keep the flash they had.
- Big blasts light the ground further and for longer. Every explosion's light is warmer and holds a little longer, and a bomb truck, a Scud, a bunker buster, a carpet bomb or a nuke throws a wide orange glow that fades over one to two seconds. Falling buildings, the Daisy Cutter, the MOAB, nukes, exploding cars and suicide bombers used to light nothing at all.
- The heaviest blasts leave bigger craters and send a ring of heat haze out across the ground for a second and a half to two seconds, if Heat Effects is on. Heat haze bends what is behind it by a few pixels now. On a blast that size it used to lay a second copy of the ground over the first, shifted by as much as twenty pixels, so the trees and ridges inside a nuke's ring came out doubled.
- A nuke pulls the picture into itself. For a quarter of a second the ground around the blast bends inward toward it, then a dome of shock rises out of it, running flat across the ground in front and standing up behind, rolling well past the fireball and shoving the battlefield aside as it passes, weaker the further it gets. Each Scud Storm missile does a smaller version of the same, and Nuke Cannon shells, Scud Launcher missiles, Tomahawks and bomb trucks give a short kick that is gone in half a second, so a battery firing all match never turns the screen to jelly. This is the default renderer; Classic and the old renderer keep only the heat ring.
- Up to a thousand craters stay on the ground in a long match, where the game kept five hundred and quietly dropped the oldest.
- A nuke flattens a town from the middle out. EA's missile did all its damage on one frame a second after it landed, so every building under the cloud blew up together. The blast now rolls out from the point of impact with the orange heat ring and reaches the edge six tenths of a second later, levelling each building and toppling each tree as it gets there, and burning the ground in the same ring. What each thing takes is unchanged. A replay recorded before this, with a nuke in it, will not play back the same.
- An explosion lights everything around it, smoothly. On the default renderer the light of a blast reaches every tank, soldier, building and patch of ground it can see, fading out with distance, where the ground used to brighten in blocky squares and a model took only four lights at once, so in a big fight half the tanks next to a burning wreck stayed dark. The 32 blasts nearest the camera light at the same time, and a wall with its back to the fire stays in shadow. The light brightens what it falls on by three quarters at most: a nuke's took the ground to white within a few frames until it was held there.
- A bright cloud no longer shows what is behind it as a line drawing. Inside a nuke's white cloud, or a falling War Factory's fireball, every tree and wreck under it used to come out as a thin grey outline, and the picture's sharpening ringed each dark piece in white. Both stop where the frame is bright. A yellow or orange fireball still drew them, because the shading that darkens corners was laid over the finished picture and read the fire as dark: an Aurora's bomb on a War Factory showed its chimneys, its lattice and the trees beside it as dark outlines through the flames. Corners are now shaded before any fire or smoke is drawn, so a blast of any colour covers what is behind it.
- Smoke and fire no longer end on a straight line where they meet the ground or a building. A puff that sinks into a hillside or drifts against a wall thins out over its last few metres, softly enough that a nuke's haze and a Scud's grey smoke no longer come out as stacked, stair-stepped terraces, and a toxin cloud lying low over the ground keeps its body instead of breaking into hard-edged green islands. No effect fades over more than its own size now, so a small spark close to the ground keeps its light. This is the default renderer; Classic and the old renderer keep the hard edge they had in 2003.
- Fire burns instead of fading. Every flame and fireball in the game, 182 kinds from a burning soldier to a nuke's mushroom, starts white-hot and cools through yellow, orange and red to a sooty dark as it dies, eats away from its thin edges in rather than going see-through all at once, and licks and flickers, so a fire that used to be a still picture getting dimmer now moves. Green toxin and anthrax fires keep their colour. Default renderer only; Classic and the old renderer draw fire as they did.
- A tank dying and a mid-sized building going down leave a column of dark smoke climbing out of the wreck after the fireball, and a building no longer goes down behind a white flare. From 3.3.0 to 3.4.1 those two and a tank shell landing went off as a smooth orange ball with grey smoke puffs stacked over it like cotton wool, which looked like a toy; they explode in the game's own fire again, ragged and streaked with soot.
- That smoke no longer outstays the fight. The black column over a dead tank hung for almost seven seconds and a building's for ten, in a game where the next tank is usually dead by then, and it was the darkest thing on the field. A burning tanker truck's soot ran for seventeen. All of it now thins out and is gone about three seconds after the blast, along with the brown cloud of EA's own tank explosion and the ribbons behind thrown wreckage. The fire on the hull is untouched.
- Gunfire shows at the zoom you play at. A rifle's tracer was a third of a unit wide, about one pixel from the default camera, and a bullet hit nothing you could see. Tracers from rifles, Gattlings, Humvees, Technicals and Quad Cannons are now twice as wide and half again as long, the muzzle flash is half as big again, and every hit kicks up sparks and a puff of dirt where it lands. A tank shell burns a short hot streak behind it all the way to the target, where it used to be a grey sliver you could not pick out between the flash and the blast. A Crusader's, Battlemaster's, Scorpion's, Paladin's or Overlord's shot used to be a soft white glow drifting out in front of the gun, wider than the tank; it is now a short orange blast at the barrel tip, with a bigger flame and smoke puff behind it. A shell landing throws dirt and sparks around its blast. The colours are the ones the game always used, and no weapon does anything different.
- Blasts throw fragments that smoke. The bigger explosions fling hot sparks into the air, each drawing a thin dark line of smoke that climbs, fans around the blast and curves down. A Stinger, a rocket pod, a tank shell or a rocket used to throw them too, and a fight filled with them; they now show on a bomb, a heavy shell, a Scud or a building, five that climb several times a tank's length, and on a nuke, a MOAB, a Daisy Cutter or a large building, eight that arc over its own fireball and hang for a couple of seconds. A vehicle that blows up throws burning pieces that drag near-black smoke and bounce where they land, and the turret, wheels and plates it throws off trail smoke and flame too, then smoulder a moment on the ground. The fragments and their smoke are the first effects the particle limit and a lower detail setting drop, so a bigger fight keeps its explosions and loses some lines. What a weapon does is unchanged. Rather have the explosions as they always were? Explosion Debris Trails in the launcher's Options turns all of it off, for you alone: the other players in your match keep whatever they picked, and nobody's game falls out of step over it.
- A China mine going off under a tank now throws a column of dark earth twice the tank's height, scatters clods round it and leaves a low black smoke and a scorch, with a short jolt of the screen; it used to puff a pale spray of specks that looked like dust kicked up. An EMP mine throws no earth, so you can tell which kind went off: it lights a blue ring across the ground, a crackle of blue sparks and a short blue flash at the spot; EA's flash grew until it washed the whole screen white for a fifth of a second. What a mine does is unchanged.
- A base out of power looks out of power. A building that switches off when your power runs short, or one a hacker shut down, drains to a cold grey and sags darker, and its windows and lamps go out. Every few seconds it blinks dark for an instant or its lights catch again for a moment, and blue sparks jump on its walls where something shorts. A tank or building hit by an EMP crawls with thin blue arcs for as long as it stays dead, where it used to just turn dark grey.
- Your own stealthed units look like glass, not like ice. In 3.0 a camouflaged Rebel, a Pathfinder or Colonel Burton came out under a blue skin with bands running up it, which players rightly called ugly. The blue is gone: the ground behind him shows through his body in its own colours and bends, a slow lens that ripples along him and pulls harder at his outline, with a muted share of his own paint left in it. The bend is what you find him by: each face of him tips the ground behind it its own way, so his shape shows even on plain sand, and the bend never drops below a few pixels, and a cool haze that thickens at his outline makes a cloaked squad or a camouflaged base read at a glance at the zoom you play at, still as glass and without turning white. Up close a building's flat wall bends across its face. At the default camera that bend was only a few pixels on a soldier, and your cloaked infantry showed nothing but their health bars, so your own cloaked troops and vehicles now also carry a cool see-through ghost of themselves, about a third of their paint, with a pale outline that finds them on sand and on a dark road alike; a cloaked building, big enough for its bend to read, stays plain glass. It moves slowly and never fizzes. He breathes solid at the top of the 2003 pulse and back to glass at the bottom. Going invisible, the paint eases into that lens, then the pulse takes over. Coming out, the bend eases off until the paint is whole. An enemy a detector finds fades into heat the same way. His shadow fades with him, to between a quarter and a half of its strength as he breathes, where it used to lie on the ground at full strength and give him away before his body did; on Classic and the old renderer the shadow stays whole. When an enemy detector has found him, his whole body beats amber along with his edge, so a spotted building reads as spotted and does not just turn tan. On every renderer, a stealthed unit of yours no longer comes out solid whenever no building is on the screen: the game drew it a second time without its see-through. An enemy stealth unit your detector finds used to turn into a flat orange shape with no paint; now it shows as heat, its own shading run from dark red through orange to a warm yellow that stops short of white, so you can still tell a tank from a soldier and bright GLA paint keeps its detail, with a burning outline and a slow glow climbing it that flares on every sweep of the detector. A found building keeps two thirds of its own colours under an orange wash and a softer outline, where it used to turn into a solid orange block that drowned out every unit on the screen. The fine scan lines of 3.0 are gone, since zoomed out they broke into stripes. Under the black and white view a mission script turns on, or the motion blur, a found enemy and a spotted unit of yours used to come out in plain paint, as if nobody had found them, and a base out of power showed no sign of it; they keep the 2003 heat and tint for those moments now. The see-through parts of a model take the same look as the rest of it, where they used to stay plain. This is the default renderer; Classic and the old renderer keep the 2003 look for all of these.
- An enemy that cloaks in front of you no longer pops out of sight. Its paint leaves along a shimmering line that crosses it in about 0.4 seconds, and nothing is left behind: it used to pass through the glass look your own cloaked units wear, which told you exactly where it went. One that fires from cloak grows back in from nothing the same way, and a unit that comes out already cloaked no longer flashes into view for a frame first. When an enemy detector finds a building of yours, its amber eases in over half a second and fades out in 0.3 seconds, where it used to switch on and off. Your own detector's reveal builds as heat from the feet up instead of the whole body snapping in at once. Shadows change with the body now, where they used to go a moment before it, and a cloaked unit that leaves the screen halfway through its fade leaves no shadow or reflection behind. All of this was timed on film at 60 pictures a second. It is Direct3D 11 without Classic Graphics; Classic and Direct3D 9 still hide and show a unit at once.
- The first outage, EMP, cloak or detection of a match no longer catches the picture. Each of those looks is a small drawing program of its own on every model it dresses, and until now the game built each one the first time it came on screen, 25 to 60ms of a single frame, so a whole base browning out at once could stack several into one. They come with the game now: a match, both look scenes and the main menu that compiled 61 programs while playing compile none.
- A hidden base no longer burns in plain view. The fire and smoke on a stealthed building or unit, damage flames and chimney smoke alike, kept drawing for the enemy while the building itself was invisible, so a burning Stealth General base under Camo Netting stood out as a column of black smoke on an empty patch of ground. The enemy now sees none of it until a detector finds the building, and then all of it. On your own side the flames and smoke go faint with the building and breathe with it, the fire a little stronger than the smoke, so they no longer sit at full strength beside the glass. A China mine field is the one exception. It has no body, only EA's soft glint swelling and fading on each of its eight mines, and fading those with the field faded them to nothing, so from 3.1.0 your own mines showed you nothing at all. The glints are EA's again, white on standard and cluster mines and purple on EMP mines, and they show at full strength to you and your allies; the enemy sees them only once a detector finds the field. The Reforged picture's soft smoke edges no longer swallow them either: a glint sits on the ground, and the fade that keeps a smoke puff from ending on a hard line used to thin it to nothing, so a mine field's glints now meet the ground the way they do on the old renderer. This holds on every renderer, and the smoke's shadow and the light its fire throws on nearby smoke go with it. A hit on a hidden unit gives it away no more either: a laser landing on a parked Listening Outpost you had not found threw sparks, a lens flare and a flash of yellow light on the ground round what looked like an empty spot. Now nothing shows until you find it.
- Effects fade out instead of blinking off. The rings a nuke sends across the ground, and any spark, flash or puff whose own colours never reached nothing, used to vanish at full strength on their last frame. Each one now dims away over its last quarter of a second, or over a quarter of its life when it lives shorter than that. One that was already fading looks the way it always did.
- Toxin, anthrax and radiation pools lie on the ground. A pool is a carpet of puddle pictures spread up to 140 paces from where the shell or the spray came down, and every one of them was drawn dead flat at the height of that one spot: on a hillside the uphill half of the pool disappeared into the slope and the downhill half hung in the air above it. Each puddle now bends over the ground underneath it, on both renderers, and a pool on a bridge stays on the deck. The pool also holds still. It used to throb twice a second, because every half second the pool's poison fired a fresh batch of puddles that swelled out of black to full green and back to black in two seconds, each batch somewhere new. Now it comes up in half a second, stays one pool at full colour for as long as it does damage, and fades over its last three seconds, or over three seconds from the moment the fog of war closes over it. It is not frozen, though: each puddle fades down and back up on its own beat, so the surface shimmers like something liquid while the pool as a whole never pulses. Four Scud warheads landing on one spot used to stack into a white-hot blotch in the middle; overlapping pools now share their light and the middle stays toxin green. The ground under it takes on its colour, green for toxin and the anthrax colours for anthrax, so it looks spilled rather than shone onto the grass. China's radiation keeps its orange but glows instead of browning the grass, which made it look like a scorch mark, and small bubbles swell out of it and pop. A nuke's radiation lies on the hillside as a pool from three seconds after the blast, where its first ten seconds used to be flat squares cutting into the slope.
- A Scud Storm or a carpet bomb shakes the screen as hard as it should. The game cut a pile of heavy shakes back to a mild one, so a run of missiles or bombs landing together shook less than one of them alone. Each now shakes a step lighter and the run builds up. Demo traps and Aurora bombs shake now, and a falling building shakes harder the bigger it was.
- The shake knows how close you are. A shell landing in the middle of the screen kicks the camera half as hard again as it used to, one at the edge of the range barely moves it, and a heavy hit settles over about a second instead of stopping dead after half of one. The cut that put a pile of shakes back to a mild one is gone too: past the limit the camera holds at full shake.
- A nuke, a Scud warhead or a bomb truck going up near the camera kicks it once, hard, and lets go. The worst of it is over in a quarter of a second, where a heavy hit used to rumble on for a whole one. One of these more than 150 paces away shook nothing at all, less than half the screen at the normal zoom; it reaches three times that now. A big building coming down close by adds a jolt of its own, a step under a nuke. Classic Graphics and the Direct3D 9 picture keep the old shake.
- Camera Shake, under Options, Controls, turns all of it off for anyone who hates it. It is on by default.
- A damaged building's fires burn bigger, and its smoke runs darker and longer, the closer it gets to falling.
- Only the picture changed: damage, timing and what dies are what they were, and a recorded match plays back to the same checksum. In a test fight with a nuke and a Scud Storm the game carried 1631 effect particles where it carried 1610.
- Tanks and buildings come apart in more pieces, and the pieces stay. A Crusader throws 19 plates and scraps where it threw 12, an Overlord 9 where it threw 3, and a Scorpion, a Marauder or a Paladin five more bits of scrap each. A falling building adds the biggest slabs of its rubble, heavy enough to hop low and land close: a large base building throws 55 pieces where it threw 39, a War Factory 45 and a Power Plant 45. Wreckage lies on the ground for three seconds before it starts to sink, where EA gave it one, so a battlefield still shows what died on it after the smoke has gone. All of it is EA's own wreckage, thrown more often. The pieces are part of the match, so a replay recorded before this change plays back differently. In a test of rocket waves against tanks the busiest moment went from 791 things on the map to 898, and the game's rules took 3% longer a frame.

- Water reflects what stands over it. The pools on Golden Oasis hold their palms upside down and the
  stone bridge's arches under the bridge, and the lakes on Fortress Avalanche carry the pines on
  their banks. Helicopters hovering by the river show dark and upside down in the water under them;
  they were left out at first, because the mirror skipped every unit the game had set aside that
  frame for its behind-building markers. The game has had a mirror in it since 2003, wired to a test sea no shipped map turns
  on; the water you actually play beside gets it now. The reflection only ever darkens: open water
  keeps the exact colour the map painted it, and a black shroud stays black. The water shows only
  what the land does: an enemy hidden under the fog of war, or a stealthed unit, used to give itself
  away in the reflection. A palm shows the same in sunlight as under the fog: whatever stands over
  the water darkens it by one amount, where a sunlit palm used to be nearly as bright as open water
  and vanished the moment the fog lifted off it. It is not free, since the world is drawn a second
  time for the mirror, but the mirror leaves the ground out, draws only the part of the screen the
  water covers, and only every other frame while the camera holds still. On one 1280x720 view of
  Golden Oasis, where the river fills the screen, a frame takes 6.7ms against 5.8ms with no
  reflection; before that work it took 8.3ms.
- Bright things can bleed light into the air. The glow setting works on the new renderer now: it used to glow at one fixed strength there whatever the box said, and Off did not turn it off. On top of that, picking any level stacked the old renderer's glow over the new one, so the battlefield got two hazes at once. Now there is one, it follows the box the moment you change it, and a fresh install starts on Medium, which is the look the new renderer always had.
- Two dropdowns on the display page, not two percentages. Glow is off, subtle, normal or strong; what glows is only the brightest, bright things, or most of the picture. The numbers underneath were a strength you had to find by experiment and a brightness that ran backwards, where turning it down put more of the screen in the haze, and nothing on screen told you that.
- Scorch marks follow the texture quality setting like everything else. The terrain and the trees
  dropped to the resolution you asked for and the burn marks did not, so on Low the ground went soft
  underneath craters that stayed sharp.
- Texture quality reaches the ground on the new renderer. Turned down, it softened the units and
  buildings and left the terrain, the trees and the scorch marks at full size, because the new
  renderer kept its own full copy of those and ignored what the setting had asked for. They drop
  with everything else now, and the change shows during a match without a restart.
- The craters a map ships with stay on the ground. Scorch marks live in a list of 500 and the list
  makes room by throwing away its oldest entry - which is always one the level designer placed, so a
  long battle rubbed out the map's own burn marks one at a time. Only marks the fighting made are
  thrown away now.
- Units stop going see-through for no reason. The game marks a unit that is standing behind a
  building so you can still make it out, and the flag that says "yes, something is in front of this
  one" was set once and never cleared - so the first unit genuinely behind a wall made every unit
  checked after it see-through too, wall or no wall. On a busy screen that was most of them.
- The outlines of your units behind a building stay switched on. If the screen was lost for a
  moment, an alt-tab or a resolution change, the game turned the setting itself off, so the
  outlines were gone until you found the box and ticked it again.
  A lost screen now hides them only while it lasts.
- Bloom and antialiasing work together. Turning bloom on with antialiasing on gave you a black battlefield under a live interface: the glow pass draws the world into its own picture first, and that picture came with a depth buffer nobody had cleared, so every triangle in the scene was rejected as being behind something that was not there.
- Lakes stop showing jagged bands of shore while you scroll. The glow and smoothing effects draw the world into a picture of their own, and that picture was never wiped between frames, so the water kept reading last frame's shoreline from wherever the camera had just been.
- A switch you write in `Options.ini` by hand takes `yes`, `true`, `on` or `1` for on. Only the
  exact word `yes` used to count, so a line spelled any other way read as off and looked like a
  setting that did not work.
- Explosions light what is around them: 89 of them, from a tank shell to the Scud Storm,
  throw a warm flash that fades over a third of a second. A night fight used to be muzzle
  smoke over unlit ground.
- Heat haze bends the picture as far up and down as it does side to side. The vertical pull was
  half the horizontal one, which nobody could see while the haze was reading its sideways figure
  for both directions, and became a visible lean the moment that was fixed.
- Cutscenes and briefings play at the colour depth your card actually offers. Every video but the
  EA logo was dropped to sixteen bit on the way in, on any machine - the test that was meant to
  limit that to a 2003 low-memory PC is commented out in the same line - and it was dropped there
  even on a device that had just reported it could not do sixteen bit at all.
- Snow falls as snow again. On the new renderer every flake near the camera was drawn as big as a
  power plant, because each winter map sized its flakes in screen pixels, capped at 10 or 16, and the
  new renderer read a different figure from the same file that has no cap at all. Flakes on Bitter
  Winter are the same size as they are on the old renderer now.

## It does not crash

- A GLA tunnel that belongs to no player no longer crashes the game when a unit near it looks for a target. With no owner there is no tunnel network behind it, and the check for hidden men inside asked that missing network for its first passenger. Three crash reports from 3.5.1 came from it, two of them the same network match seen from both machines.
- Loading a save could crash on the Generals' Challenge loading screen, the one with two generals facing each other, when the mission named a general the screen could not find. Its right half now stays empty and the mission loads.
- A sound cut off in the middle no longer takes the game down a moment later. The game stopped the sound and freed it, but Windows' audio mixer only stops reading on its next pass, a hundredth of a second on, and two players' games died with the mixer reading what had just been freed. Every sound now plays from a copy the mixer gives back itself when it is done. A load screen movie skipped to its last frame threw its sound away the same way, and now leaves it to the mixer too.
- That copy did not end the mixer crash: two 3.3.0 players still met it. Each sound channel was reused for the next sound by stopping it, emptying it and handing it new audio, and now and then Windows' mixer carried its place in the old sound over as one step before the start of the new one, then read eight gigabytes past it. Every sound now gets a fresh channel that nothing has played before, which is how Windows' mixer is normally used.
- The game no longer crashes now and then as a match starts or a new unit comes on the field. Since 3.2.0 the battle runs beside the picture, and both sides ask the game's files whether a model or a texture is there. The answers go into one shared list, and two answers written at once tore it, which took the game down later in some unrelated place. Two reads from the same game archive at once could also hand one of them the other's bytes. Each now waits its turn.
- Text on the screen, a message line or a unit's label, no longer crashes the game with the Direct3D 11 picture on. Three players met it on 3.2.0 in the same spot. The picture keeps a note of every texture it has copied, and a texture thrown away on the battle's side struck its note off while the picture was writing a new one in. The battle's side now leaves the striking off to the picture, which does it before its next look.
- A tank or helicopter carrying an add-on on its back, an Overlord's Gattling Cannon or a Helix's bunker, no longer crashes the game now and then. Since 3.2.0 the battle runs beside the picture, and the picture, seating the add-on on its carrier, finished the carrier's waiting model changes while the battle was still adding to that same list. The picture now takes the carrier as the last step between pictures left it.
- Giving an order no longer crashes an install whose model archive lacks the small marker drawn at the end of an order line, as one repack's does. The marker used to show only on a rally point, so such an install got away with it; now every order draws one. The line is drawn without the marker there.
- A graphics setup that cannot make a single texture now gets the message that Direct3D could not start, instead of "Uncaught Exception during initialization". One player met the crash three times in a row on the Direct3D 11 picture with a dxgi.dll in the game folder: even the plain stand-in the game shows for a missing texture could not be made, and the first texture loaded fell on it.
- The rings the battle lays on the ground, a nuke's target circle or a Spectre gunship's, no longer crash the game now and then. Since 3.2.0 the battle runs beside the picture, and those rings were laid and lifted from the battle's side while the picture was walking the list of them, so the picture could read a ring that had just been thrown away. They are laid and lifted between pictures now.
- A save that will not load now says so in a box instead of crashing the game. The load had already put half the units in when it stopped, and clearing them away again went through a list of every unit's timers that the half-done load had left out of step, so the game wrote into memory it did not own.
- A dozer whose driver was sniped no longer crashes the game. A dozer left standing looks for a damaged building of its owner's to repair, and first asks whether its owner's tunnels get it there quicker. A vehicle with no driver belongs to nobody, and nobody has no tunnels, so the question took the game down. One player met it on 3.2.0 ten minutes into a match against GLA.
- Loading a save from the in-game menu no longer crashes when a paratrooper is still hanging under his chute. Clearing the old match away took the chute first, the soldier "landed" off the map, died, and his death blast tried to build its debris for players that were already gone. A paratrooper cleared away with the match now just goes.
- Rewinding a replay no longer stops the game with "sleepy update module illegal index". A Cold Fusion plant with Control Rods puts its bonus power back as the rewind finishes loading, and that switched the player's buildings off or on again at a moment when the game was not ready to wake them. A rewind now finishes exactly the way loading a save does, with every building's power as it was saved.
- A skirmish on a custom map whose maker left out the script list for one side no longer crashes as the match starts. The win and defeat checks go on that side, and there was no list to add them to; it gets an empty one now.
- A replay that shows the followed player's own pointer no longer swaps that pointer from the battle's side while the picture is drawing it. The swap rebuilds the pointer's picture and its text, and on 3.2.0 it could happen halfway through a frame; it waits for the frame's end now, like everything else the battle hands the screen.
- A graphics driver that stops responding no longer takes the game down through the radar. The battle carries on while the picture is lost, and the radar kept redrawing its unit dots into a texture that had nothing behind it. It skips the redraw until there is something to draw into.
- Your aircraft's ammo pips no longer crash the game. They have shown all the time since the jets learned to fly, and they are lined up with the health bar, so a plane drawn without a health bar took the game down. Such a plane shows no pips.
- Starting a match with the Direct3D 11 picture on took the game down. Both devices were presenting into the same window, the old one lost itself, and the fog texture then locked a surface that was never made.
- Selling with more than one building selected no longer takes the game down. Each building that goes up for sale is taken out of the selection, and that rebuilt the group the sell order was still working through, so the second building was read from memory that had already been handed back. A player lost a match an hour in this way.
- A machine whose graphics stack faults while the Direct3D 11 picture is being set up starts the game anyway, on the Direct3D 9 picture. A player's report showed the fault happening inside Windows' own graphics library, before the game got an answer back, and it ended in "Uncaught Exception during initialization". An overlay hooking the graphics calls or a stray dxgi.dll in the game folder is the usual cause. Until now the only way past it was typing -d3d9.
- A campaign mission could crash on its very first frame with the Direct3D 11 picture on, if the screen had been reset before it by an alt-tab or a change on the display options page.
